h: paediatric history & examination growth, development & nutrition paediatric history and examination differ from adult practice because the history is often given by a parent or carer, the child is examined according to age and cooperation, and growth, development and social context are part of every assessment. a structured, opportunistic and child-friendly approach yields most of the diagnosis. observation before touch gives the most reliable findings in a young child normal values for heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure change with age; always use age-specific charts a perinatal, feeding, developmental, immunisation and social history is part of every paediatric assessment plot every measurement on the correct growth chart; a single point is less useful than the trajectory do not examine the throat of a child with suspected epiglottitis or severe upper airway obstruction include and examine the child, not just the parent; interview adolescents alone for part of the consultation inconsistent history and injuries incompatible with developmental stage suggest non-accidental injury innocent murmurs are asymptomatic, soft, systolic, and vary with position altered consciousness, lethargy or poor response to stimulation grunting, severe recession, apnoea or cyanosis prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia out of proportion to fever, or hypotension (late sign) non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with fever bruising or fractures in a non-mobile infant, or an injury pattern inconsistent with the history bile-stained vomiting in an infant headss adolescent psychosocial screen: home, education/employment, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide/depression/safety abcde airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure - structured assessment of the acutely unwell child principles of the paediatric consultation structure of the history presenting complaint and its history in the words of the parent and child, with duration, severity, associated features and what has been tried past medical history: admissions, operations, chronic illness, allergies, medicines perinatal history: antenatal problems, gestation, mode of delivery, birth weight, neonatal unit admission, jaundice, feeding problems feeding and diet: breast or formula, weaning, current diet, appetite, vitamin supplements growth and development: parental concerns, milestones, school progress, previous measurements in the personal child health record (red book) immunisation status and travel history family history: consanguinity, inherited conditions, early deaths, atopy, tuberculosis contacts, three-generation pedigree where relevant social history: who lives at home, siblings, housing, smoking, school or nursery, finances, social worker involvement, child protection history systems review and, in adolescents, a headss screen (home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide/depression) general examination and vital signs systems examination cardiovascular: precordial activity, heart sounds, murmurs (innocent murmurs are soft, systolic, variable with posture, with no thrills), femoral pulses, liver edge, capillary refill respiratory: rate, recession, grunting, nasal flaring, stridor, wheeze, crackles, chest shape; count the rate over a full minute abdomen: inspection, gentle palpation, liver and spleen, masses, hernial orifices, genitalia, anus; distraction and bent knees help neurological: tone, posture, reflexes, primitive reflexes in infants, cranial nerves, gait, coordination, fundi when feasible ent: examine the ears last; look for tonsillar exudate, cervical lymph nodes hips: barlow and ortolani in neonates; examine the spine and skin for dimples and tufts skin: bruising (note location, pattern and age consistency), rashes, birthmarks, signs of neglect safeguarding and communication

growth & growth charts growth, development & nutrition growth is the most sensitive indicator of a child overall health. accurate measurement and plotting on population reference charts allow detection of faltering growth, short or tall stature, obesity and abnormal head size, and the trajectory over time is more informative than a single value. measure accurately and plot on sex-specific charts; use gestation-corrected age in preterm infants babies regain birth weight by 2 weeks and double it by about 5 months crossing two major centile lines suggests a growth problem mid-parental height gives a genetic target range of about 8-10 cm either side bone age is delayed in constitutional delay and hypothyroidism/gh deficiency but normal in familial short stature weight-for-height below -3 sd defines severe acute malnutrition girls have the pubertal growth spurt earlier and at a lower peak than boys head circumference up to 2 years reflects brain growth weight falling across centiles with ill appearance or dehydration height velocity below the 25th centile for age short stature with disproportion, dysmorphic features or learning difficulty rapid head growth with bulging fontanelle, vomiting or sunsetting eyes obesity with short stature (consider cushing syndrome, hypothyroidism, prader-willi) weight milestones birth weight doubles at about 5 months, triples at 1 year, quadruples at 2 years normal growth measurement and charts use a calibrated infantometer for length up to 2 years (lying) and a stadiometer for standing height; weigh infants naked and children in underwear head circumference is the maximal occipitofrontal circumference, taking the largest of three readings uk practice uses uk-who growth charts from birth to 4 years and uk 1990 charts thereafter; who standards are used internationally (breastfed infants as the norm) correct for gestation: until 1 year for babies born at 32-36 weeks and until 2 years for those born before 32 weeks sex-specific charts; 9 centile lines are 0.4, 2, 9, 25, 50, 75, 91, 98 and 99.6; the 0.4th and 99.6th centiles correspond approximately to -2.67 and +2.67 sd z-scores (standard deviation scores): weight-for-height below -2 is moderate and below -3 severe wasting; height-for-age below -2 is stunting; weight-for-age below -2 is underweight bmi is plotted from age 2 years; overweight is at or above the 91st centile and obese at or above the 98th in uk clinical practice interpreting growth short stature familial short stature: short parents, normal growth velocity, normal bone age constitutional delay of growth and puberty: delayed bone age, late puberty, family history of late developers, eventual normal adult height pathological: growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, turner syndrome, cushing syndrome or glucocorticoid excess, prader-willi, skeletal dysplasia (achondroplasia), chronic disease (coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease, cystic fibrosis), malnutrition and psychosocial deprivation first-line tests: coeliac serology, thyroid function, full blood count, esr/crp, urea and electrolytes, bone age x-ray, karyotype in girls; second-line growth hormone stimulation tests abnormal head size

developmental milestones & surveillance growth, development & nutrition developmental milestones in four domains - gross motor, fine motor and vision, hearing speech and language, and social, emotional and behavioural - mark the expected skills of children at each age. knowing the normal range allows early identification of delay, regression and conditions such as cerebral palsy, autism and hearing impairment. four domains: gross motor, fine motor and vision, hearing speech and language, social/behavioural limit age: independent sitting 9 months, walking 18 months, pincer grip 12 months, single words 18 months regression is always abnormal and needs urgent investigation correct for prematurity until 2 years social smile appears at about 6 weeks and is a key early marker primitive reflexes should disappear by 4-6 months; asymmetry or persistence is abnormal hand preference before 12 months suggests a contralateral hemiplegia any speech and language delay requires a hearing test loss of previously acquired skills no social smile by 8 weeks or poor visual fixation not sitting by 9 months or walking by 18 months no babble by 12 months, no words by 18 months, or no pointing hand preference before 12 months or asymmetry of tone walking delay in a boy with calf pseudohypertrophy or gowers sign (check creatine kinase) limit ages sit by 9 months, walk by 18 months, words by 18 months, sentences by 3 years principles of development milestones by domain gross motor: head control at 3-4 months; sits unsupported 6-8 months (limit 9 months); crawls or bottom-shuffles 9-10 months; pulls to stand 9 months; walks independently about 12-13 months (limit 18 months); runs 18 months-2 years; climbs stairs, jumps and kicks a ball at 2-3 years; hops and rides a tricycle by 3-4 years fine motor and vision: fixes and follows 6 weeks; reaches and grasps 4-5 months; transfers objects 6 months; pincer grip 9-12 months; tower of 2-3 bricks 15 months, 6 bricks 2 years, 9 bricks 3 years; scribbles 15-18 months; copies a circle 3 years, cross 4 years, triangle 5 years; draws a person with 6 parts by 5 years hearing, speech and language: social smile 6 weeks; laughs 3-4 months; babbles 6-9 months; says mama/dada non-specifically 9 months and specifically by 12 months; 2-3 words by 12-15 months; 50 words and two-word phrases by 2 years; three-word sentences by 3 years; understandable speech to strangers by 3-4 years; tells stories by 5 years social and emotional: smiles at 6 weeks; stranger awareness 6-9 months; waves bye-bye, plays peek-a-boo 9-12 months; drinks from cup 12 months; spoon use 18 months; dry by day 2-3 years; parallel play 2 years, cooperative play 3-4 years; dresses self by 4-5 years primitive reflexes and neurological development surveillance and screening developmental surveillance relies on parental concerns, observation, and structured checks at routine contacts (newborn exam, 6-8 week check, 1 year, 2-2.5 year review, school entry) tools: denver ii, ages and stages questionnaire (asq), schedule of growing skills, griffiths and bayley scales (formal assessment); in resource-limited settings, who motor milestones and the road to health card universal newborn hearing screening using otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response vision screening: red reflex at birth and at 6-8 weeks; squint and amblyopia screening by age 4-5 years refer to a child development team or neurodevelopmental paediatrician when milestone limits are not reached, when there is regression, or when parents are worried red flags in development

global developmental delay & learning disability growth, development & nutrition global developmental delay (gdd) is significant delay in two or more developmental domains in a child under 5 years, while intellectual disability (learning disability) is the diagnosis applied when intellectual and adaptive functioning are persistently impaired. causes are varied, and a systematic search for a cause helps with prognosis, recurrence risk and management. gdd means significant delay in 2 or more domains in a child under 5 years intellectual disability is iq below 70 with impaired adaptive function chromosomal microarray is the first-line genetic test; test fragile x in boys always check hearing and vision first regression suggests metabolic, neurodegenerative or epileptic encephalopathy fetal alcohol spectrum disorder and down syndrome are leading preventable and common causes respectively hypothyroidism and phenylketonuria are treatable causes found on newborn screening management is multidisciplinary and involves education plans and family support loss of acquired skills seizures with developmental plateau hepatosplenomegaly or coarse facies (storage disease) acquired microcephaly or rapid head growth suspicion of abuse or neglect hearing or visual impairment not previously identified treatable causes think: thyroid, phenylketonuria, lead, sensory loss, epilepsy, iodine/iron deficiency definitions and epidemiology causes prenatal genetic: chromosomal (down syndrome, microdeletions, copy number variants), single gene (fragile x, rett syndrome, tuberous sclerosis), inherited metabolic disease prenatal environmental: congenital infection (cmv, toxoplasmosis, rubella, zika), fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, maternal drugs (valproate), maternal diabetes, iodine deficiency perinatal: prematurity, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, neonatal hypoglycaemia, kernicterus, intraventricular haemorrhage postnatal: meningitis and encephalitis, head injury including non-accidental, epilepsy and epileptic encephalopathy, hypothyroidism, lead poisoning, severe malnutrition and deprivation unknown in a large proportion, especially in mild cases; neurodevelopmental conditions often coexist (autism, adhd, cerebral palsy) assessment investigations first tier: hearing and vision assessment, thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin, lead where exposure possible, creatine kinase in boys with motor delay genetic: chromosomal microarray (first-line genetic test, replacing routine karyotype), fragile x testing in boys and in girls with a suggestive picture, and increasingly whole exome or genome sequencing metabolic: urea and electrolytes, amino acids, urine organic acids, lactate, ammonia, biotinidase, creatine metabolites when features suggest inborn errors neuroimaging (mri brain) when there is microcephaly, macrocephaly, focal signs, seizures, regression or dysmorphism eeg if epilepsy is suspected; rett syndrome (mecp2) in girls with regression and hand wringing management

immunisation & vaccine schedules growth, development & nutrition immunisation is one of the most effective public health interventions, preventing millions of childhood deaths a year. paediatricians must know the national schedule, the types of vaccine, contraindications and how to respond to adverse events and catch-up needs. live vaccines (bcg, mmr, varicella, rotavirus) are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression and pregnancy preterm infants are immunised according to chronological age minor illness is not a contraindication to vaccination mmr does not cause autism rotavirus vaccine first dose must be given before 15 weeks because of intussusception risk do not restart a vaccine course; just continue from where the child left off hepatitis b vaccine plus immunoglobulin for babies of hepatitis b surface-antigen positive mothers measles vaccine is given at 9 months in high-burden regions and at 12 months in low-burden countries anaphylaxis after vaccination - give im adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (1:1000) and call for help persistent inconsolable crying or hypotonic hyporesponsive episode (report and review) fever above 39 c or signs of sepsis after vaccination - do not attribute to the vaccine without assessment child on high-dose steroids or chemotherapy offered a live vaccine severe local reaction extending beyond joint or lasting more than a few days live vaccines remember the list: bcg, mmr, varicella, rotavirus, yellow fever, oral polio and nasal influenza are live principles and vaccine types live attenuated: bcg, mmr, rotavirus, varicella, oral polio, yellow fever, nasal influenza inactivated whole: injectable polio, hepatitis a toxoid: diphtheria and tetanus subunit/conjugate/recombinant: pertussis (acellular), haemophilus influenzae b, pneumococcal conjugate, meningococcal acwy and b, hepatitis b, human papillomavirus live vaccines are contraindicated in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy; two live vaccines not given together should be separated by 4 weeks uk routine schedule (summary; schedules change, check current national guidance) 8 weeks: 6-in-1 (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, hib, hepatitis b), rotavirus, menb 12 weeks: 6-in-1 (second), pneumococcal conjugate, rotavirus (second) 16 weeks: 6-in-1 (third), menb (second) 1 year: hib/menc booster in some schedules, pneumococcal booster, mmr, menb booster 2-3 years onwards: annual influenza (nasal) vaccine for eligible children around 3 years 4 months: 4-in-1 pre-school booster (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio) and second mmr early adolescence (school year 8-9): hpv and 3-in-1 teenage booster (tetanus, diphtheria, polio); menacwy bcg is offered selectively to infants at increased risk of tuberculosis; hepatitis b vaccine to infants of infected mothers at birth who expanded programme on immunization contraindications, precautions and adverse events true contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component; live vaccines in severe immunodeficiency or pregnancy not contraindications: mild illness without fever, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), family history of adverse reaction, allergy to egg in most cases (mmr is safe), breastfeeding, history of jaundice, stable neurological conditions common reactions: fever, local redness and swelling, irritability; mmr can cause a mild measles-like illness 6-10 days later; bcg causes a local papule and scar rare: anaphylaxis (about 1 per million), febrile convulsions after mmr, intussusception with the first rotavirus dose (very small risk); rotavirus first dose should be given before 15 weeks there is no link between mmr and autism: this claim has been conclusively refuted report suspected reactions via the yellow card scheme; anaphylaxis treated with intramuscular adrenaline special groups and catch-up

breastfeeding & infant feeding growth, development & nutrition breast milk is the ideal food for infants, providing nutrition, immune protection and bonding. who recommends exclusive breastfeeding for about 6 months followed by complementary foods with continued breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond. paediatricians need to support lactation, recognise problems and advise on safe alternatives. exclusive breastfeeding for about 6 months, then complementary foods plus breastfeeding to 2 years colostrum is rich in iga and is the first immunisation good attachment prevents most nipple pain and low supply breastfed infants need vitamin d supplements; babies receiving under 500 ml formula daily too contraindicated in infant galactosaemia in low-resource settings hiv-positive mothers on art should exclusively breastfeed for 6 months cows milk is not a main drink before 12 months; honey is avoided because of botulism early introduction of peanut and egg reduces allergy risk in infants weight loss over 10 percent of birth weight, or no regain by 2 weeks fewer than expected wet nappies, dark urine or persistent pale stools with jaundice hypernatraemic dehydration with lethargy in a breastfed neonate mastitis with systemic upset or abscess maternal drugs incompatible with breastfeeding attachment signs wide gape, chin to breast, more areola above than below, deep rhythmic sucks with swallows composition and physiology benefits infant: fewer gastrointestinal, respiratory and ear infections, lower risk of necrotising enterocolitis in preterm infants, sudden infant death syndrome, atopic disease, type 1 diabetes and later obesity; improved neurodevelopment mother: faster uterine involution, lactational amenorrhoea (only reliable if exclusively breastfeeding, baby under 6 months and amenorrhoeic), lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer and type 2 diabetes society: lower cost, no contamination risk, environmental benefit in low-resource settings, exclusive breastfeeding in the first six months reduces infant mortality substantially from diarrhoea and pneumonia establishing breastfeeding problems and contraindications sore or cracked nipples: usually poor attachment; correct position, treat candida if present engorgement and mastitis: continue feeding, express, simple analgesia, antibiotics (flucloxacillin) if mastitis not resolving; breast abscess needs drainage perceived low supply: assess feeds, weight and output; increase frequency and skin contact tongue-tie (ankyloglossia): consider frenotomy only if feeding is affected breastmilk jaundice and breastfeeding jaundice: see neonatal jaundice contraindications: infant galactosaemia; maternal hiv in settings with safe replacement feeding (in resource-limited settings who supports exclusive breastfeeding with maternal antiretroviral therapy), untreated active tuberculosis (until treated), htlv-1, maternal chemotherapy or radioactive iodine; illicit drug use most maternal drugs are compatible; check the bnf or lactmed; avoid amiodarone, lithium, cytotoxic agents and chloramphenicol formula feeding and weaning

severe acute malnutrition (kwashiorkor & marasmus) growth, development & nutrition severe acute malnutrition (sam) is defined by severe wasting, nutritional oedema or very low mid-upper arm circumference in children 6-59 months. it remains a major cause of child death worldwide. kwashiorkor and marasmus are the two classic forms, and modern management is community-based for uncomplicated cases and inpatient stabilisation for complicated cases. sam: weight-for-height below -3 sd, muac below 11.5 cm, or bilateral pitting oedema kwashiorkor has oedema; marasmus has severe wasting without oedema use resomal rather than standard ors for rehydration; avoid iv fluids unless in shock always check for hypoglycaemia and hypothermia on admission give antibiotics to all admitted children even when there is no clear infection do not give iron in the initial stabilisation phase f-75 for stabilisation then f-100 or rutf for catch-up growth uncomplicated sam with good appetite is managed in the community with rutf hypoglycaemia or lethargy, unconsciousness hypothermia below 35 c severe pallor, signs of shock or sepsis heart failure with fluid overload (rapid pulse and respiratory rate, hepatomegaly) corneal clouding or ulceration from vitamin a deficiency refusal of feeds, persistent vomiting or severe diarrhoea who key priorities hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, hydration, electrolytes, infection, micronutrients, feed: treat these in order of urgency definition and classification clinical features marasmus: wizened old man face, severe muscle and fat wasting, baggy skin folds, alert and irritable, ravenous appetite kwashiorkor: pitting oedema (feet, legs, face), apathy and misery, flaky-paint dermatosis, sparse depigmented hair (flag sign), hepatomegaly from fatty liver, anorexia hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, dehydration (hard to assess), bradycardia and low blood pressure, signs of infection may be absent micronutrient deficiencies: vitamin a (xerophthalmia), iron, zinc, folate, potassium, magnesium; features of cardiac impairment with fluid overload pathophysiology assessment and management treat or prevent hypoglycaemia: feed 10 percent glucose or sugar water; give iv 10 percent dextrose 5 ml/kg if unconscious treat or prevent hypothermia: keep warm with kangaroo care; avoid bathing treat or prevent dehydration: use resomal (low sodium, high potassium) orally or by nasogastric tube; iv fluids only in shock, and cautiously (10 ml/kg/h over 2 hours with half-strength darrow solution or ringer lactate with 5 percent dextrose) correct electrolyte imbalance: potassium and magnesium supplementation; do not give iron in the initial phase treat infection: broad-spectrum antibiotics (amoxicillin routinely, gentamicin or ceftriaxone if complicated); measles vaccination; test for hiv and tb correct micronutrient deficiencies: vitamin a, folic acid, zinc; iron only after appetite returns start cautious feeding: f-75 (75 kcal/100 ml) 130 ml/kg/day divided into 8-12 feeds achieve catch-up growth: transition to f-100 or rutf at about 150-220 kcal/kg/day and protein 4-6 g/kg/day; weight gain over 10 g/kg/day is good provide sensory stimulation and emotional support prepare for follow-up: immunisation, nutrition education, home visits complications and outcome amoxicillin vitamin a zinc

t: Vitamin & micronutrient deficiencies (rickets, vitamin A, iron)
h: vitamin & micronutrient deficiencies (rickets, vitamin a, iron) growth, development & nutrition micronutrient deficiencies cause a large burden of disease worldwide. vitamin d deficiency produces rickets, vitamin a deficiency causes blindness and increases infectious mortality, and iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia in children. prevention through diet, supplementation and fortification is highly effective. rickets: low phosphate, raised alp, wide cupped metaphyses; treat with vitamin d and calcium hypophosphataemic rickets is vitamin d resistant and treated with phosphate plus active vitamin d vitamin a deficiency causes night blindness, bitot spots and keratomalacia give vitamin a to children with measles iron deficiency anaemia: microcytic, low ferritin; oral iron for 3 months after hb normalises excess cows milk (over 500 ml daily) in toddlers is a common cause of iron deficiency scurvy presents with painful limbs and bleeding gums vitamin k at birth prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany in an infant corneal clouding or ulceration in a malnourished or measles child severe anaemia with heart failure (hb below 5 g/dl) bone deformity, fractures or severe short stature in rickets failure to respond to adequate oral iron rickets signs rosary (rachitic), wide wrists, bowed legs, harrison sulcus, craniotabes, delayed teeth rickets and vitamin d rickets treatment nutritional rickets: oral cholecalciferol (vitamin d3) 3,000-6,000 iu daily (or 150,000-300,000 iu single stat/stoss doses in some protocols) for 8-12 weeks followed by maintenance 400-600 iu daily; ensure calcium intake treat hypocalcaemia first if symptomatic: iv calcium gluconate 10 percent 0.3 ml/kg slowly with ecg monitoring hypophosphataemic rickets: oral phosphate and alfacalcidol, or burosumab (anti-fgf23); vitamin d alone is ineffective prevention: daily vitamin d supplement for infants and at-risk children; maternal supplementation in pregnancy; sun exposure and fortification vitamin a deficiency iron deficiency anaemia other deficiencies zinc: acrodermatitis enteropathica, growth failure, diarrhoea; zinc 20 mg daily for 10-14 days reduces diarrhoea duration and recurrence iodine: congenital hypothyroidism, goitre, cretinism; prevented by salt iodisation vitamin b12 and folate: megaloblastic anaemia; b12 deficiency from vegan diet, pernicious anaemia, ileal disease; folic acid before pregnancy prevents neural tube defects vitamin k: haemorrhagic disease of the newborn; prevented by intramuscular vitamin k at birth vitamin c (scurvy): irritable child, gum bleeding, subperiosteal haemorrhages and pseudoparalysis; seen in restrictive diets and autism thiamine (beriberi), niacin (pellagra), vitamin e and others seen in specific settings ferrous sulphate (elemental iron) cholecalciferol vitamin a

obesity & faltering growth (failure to thrive) growth, development & nutrition obesity and faltering growth lie at opposite ends of the weight spectrum. childhood obesity is rising worldwide and causes metabolic, orthopaedic, psychosocial and cardiovascular complications. faltering growth (failure to thrive) describes inadequate weight gain in early life, most often from insufficient calories, and requires a structured search for organic and social causes. uk obesity definition: bmi at or above the 98th centile simple obesity is usually accompanied by tall stature; short stature suggests an endocrine or genetic cause slipped upper femoral epiphysis presents with hip or knee pain in obese adolescents faltering growth is usually due to insufficient calories; organic causes are in the minority observe a feed; many cases are diagnosed by watching mealtime interaction coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis and cows milk protein allergy are leading organic causes catch-up growth after an adequate diet confirms non-organic faltering growth acanthosis nigricans signals insulin resistance obesity with short stature or poor growth velocity hip or knee pain with limp in an obese adolescent (sufe) headache with visual blurring (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) faltering growth with vomiting, diarrhoea or respiratory symptoms suggesting organic disease suspected neglect or signs of non-accidental injury weight loss in an adolescent suggesting an eating disorder or serious illness causes of faltering growth intake, absorption, utilisation, losses/requirements - think "not enough in, not absorbed, lost, or used up" obesity: definition and causes complications and assessment metabolic: insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes (acanthosis nigricans), dyslipidaemia, metabolic-associated fatty liver disease cardiovascular: hypertension; later coronary disease respiratory: obstructive sleep apnoea, asthma orthopaedic: slipped upper femoral epiphysis, blount disease, knee pain endocrine: early puberty in girls, polycystic ovary syndrome; boys may appear to have a small penis because of a suprapubic fat pad neurological: idiopathic intracranial hypertension psychosocial: bullying, low self-esteem, depression, eating disorders assess: bmi centile, blood pressure, waist circumference; fasting glucose or hba1c, lipids and alt in higher-risk children; sleep history obesity management faltering growth: definition and causes assessment and management of faltering growth history: pregnancy and birth, feeding (volume, type, mealtime behaviour), vomiting, stools, respiratory symptoms, developmental progress, family growth patterns, social and psychological situation examination: plot weight, length, head circumference and weight-for-length; look for dysmorphism, pallor, clubbing, heart murmur, hepatosplenomegaly, signs of neglect observe a feed and the parent-child interaction; a food diary is helpful first-line tests only if indicated by findings: urinalysis and culture, full blood count, ferritin, urea and electrolytes, coeliac serology, thyroid function; sweat test, hiv, stool studies by history management: treat the underlying cause; dietitian-led energy fortification (e.g. 120-150 kcal/kg/day target); feeding advice and behavioural support; multidisciplinary involvement (health visitor, social work); admission for observation and supervised feeding if needed or if neglect suspected monitor weight regularly; most children respond to adequate calories (catch-up growth)

adolescent health & normal puberty growth, development & nutrition puberty is the period of sexual maturation and growth acceleration that transforms child to adult, driven by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. paediatricians must know the normal sequence and timing, recognise early and delayed puberty, and provide confidential adolescent healthcare covering mental health, risk-taking and sexual health. girls: breast bud is the first sign (tanner 2), menarche about 2 years later boys: testicular volume of 4 ml or more is the first sign of puberty precocious puberty: before 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys peak height velocity is early in girls and mid-late in boys constitutional delay is the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys delayed puberty with anosmia suggests kallmann syndrome central precocious puberty is treated with gnrh analogues gynaecomastia in pubertal boys is common and usually self-limiting precocious puberty in a boy (high chance of cns or testicular pathology) headache, visual field defects or growth failure with pubertal delay primary amenorrhoea with short stature (turner syndrome) or absent breast development at 13 years hard unilateral testicular mass with early virilisation disclosure of self-harm, abuse, sexual exploitation or suicidal ideation weight loss and amenorrhoea suggesting anorexia nervosa headss home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide - screening tool for adolescent psychosocial history physiology and tanner staging precocious puberty delayed puberty definition: no breast development by 13 years in girls or no testicular enlargement by 14 years in boys, or more than 5 years between first signs and menarche/complete genital development constitutional delay of growth and puberty (commonest, mainly boys): family history, delayed bone age, normal prepubertal growth then late catch-up; treat with reassurance or a short course of low-dose testosterone if distressed hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: functional (chronic disease, coeliac, inflammatory bowel disease, anorexia nervosa, excessive exercise), hypopituitarism, craniopharyngioma, kallmann syndrome (anosmia), prader-willi hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: turner syndrome (girls), klinefelter syndrome (boys), gonadal damage from chemotherapy or radiation, autoimmune oophoritis investigations: bone age, lh, fsh, oestradiol or testosterone, thyroid function, prolactin, coeliac screen, karyotype in girls, mri as indicated adolescent health triptorelin or leuprorelin (gnrh analogue) testosterone (low dose)

newborn examination & routine care neonatology the newborn examination is a head-to-toe check performed within 72 hours of birth and again at 6-8 weeks, aiming to detect congenital abnormalities such as heart disease, hip dysplasia, cataracts and undescended testes. it is paired with routine care: vitamin k, feeding support, screening tests and immunisation. early detection changes outcomes, so a systematic approach is a core clinical skill. nipe focuses on heart, hips, eyes and testes and is done within 72 hours and again at 6-8 weeks an absent or abnormal red reflex needs urgent ophthalmology review (cataract, retinoblastoma) absent or weak femoral pulses suggest coarctation or critical left-sided obstruction barlow is provocative and ortolani is reductive - a clunk, not a click, is significant caput crosses sutures; cephalhaemotoma does not jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological until proven otherwise vitamin k prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn normal newborn respiratory rate is 40-60 breaths per minute and heart rate 110-160 per minute cyanosis, grunting or pulse oximetry failure - possible critical congenital heart disease absent femoral pulses or a significant murmur with signs of poor perfusion absent red reflex or leukocoria bilious vomiting, abdominal distension or failure to pass meconium within 48 hours jaundice within 24 hours, or a sick, hypotonic or poorly feeding baby ambiguous genitalia - do not assign sex; urgent specialist review for congenital adrenal hyperplasia 4 organs of nipe heart, hips, eyes, testes - the four screening targets of the newborn examination definition & purpose general inspection and head-to-toe examination general: colour (pink, pale, plethoric, jaundiced, cyanosed), tone, posture, cry, alertness, respiratory effort, dysmorphic features. measure weight, length and head circumference and plot on centile charts. head: fontanelles (anterior open and flat, 2-3 cm; posterior small), sutures, caput succedaneum, cephalhaemotoma, moulding. palpate for cranial defects. face and eyes: symmetry, palpebral slope, epicanthic folds. red reflex must be present and symmetrical in both eyes; absent or white reflex (leukocoria) suggests cataract or retinoblastoma. mouth: inspect and palpate the hard and soft palate for cleft; look for tongue-tie, natal teeth, epstein pearls. neck and clavicles: palpate clavicles for fracture; check for webbing, torticollis. chest and heart: respiratory rate (normal 40-60/min), recession, grunting. cardiac: apex, heart sounds, murmurs, femoral pulses (absent or delayed suggests coarctation), colour and perfusion. abdomen: soft, no masses; liver edge may be palpable 1-2 cm; umbilical stump with two arteries and one vein; check for hernia or gastroschisis scar. palpate kidneys gently. genitalia and anus: male - testes descended, meatus position (hypospadias), phimosis normal; female - labia, clitoris, vaginal skin tags and white discharge normal; patent anus. spine and sacrum: inspect for sacral dimple, hair tuft, naevus or swelling suggesting spina bifida occulta or tethered cord. hips: barlow and ortolani tests. limbs and skin: count digits, polydactyly, syndactyly, talipes (fixed vs positional), palmar creases, birthmarks. neurology: tone, spontaneous movement, moro reflex, grasp, rooting, suck, stepping. hip examination routine care and screening vitamin k: given intramuscularly (1 mg) or orally to prevent vitamin k deficiency bleeding (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn); newborns have low stores, sterile guts and low breast milk vitamin k. feeding: encourage skin-to-skin and breastfeeding within the first hour; expect up to 10% weight loss in the first week with regain by day 10-14. blood spot (heel prick) screening on day 5: includes phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and mcadd, with further conditions in many countries. newborn hearing screening (otoacoustic emissions and/or automated auditory brainstem response) before discharge or within the first month. pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease (pre-ductal right hand and post-ductal foot): saturations below 95 percent or a difference over 2-3 percent need review and echocardiography. immunisation: bcg (in tb-endemic areas or high-risk groups), hepatitis b birth dose where recommended, oral polio in some settings. safe sleeping advice, car seat use, cord care and jaundice vigilance are standard discharge counselling points. normal variants and benign findings erythema toxicum (red blotches with central pustules, day 2-3), milia, mongolian blue spots, salmon patches (stork bites, naevus simplex), sebaceous hyperplasia. caput succedaneum (crosses suture lines, resolves in days) versus cephalhaemotoma (does not cross sutures, appears at 12-24 hours, can cause jaundice). breast engorgement and pseudomenstruation due to maternal hormones; transient tachypnoea settles over hours. positional talipes can be corrected passively; fixed talipes equinovarus needs orthopaedic referral. phytomenadione (vitamin k)

neonatal resuscitation & apgar score neonatology most babies make the transition to air breathing without help, but about 10 percent need some assistance and 1 percent need advanced resuscitation. the approach is the newborn life support algorithm, which prioritises lung inflation and ventilation because bradycardia at birth is almost always due to hypoxia. the apgar score describes the condition of the baby at 1 and 5 minutes but must never delay resuscitation. neonatal collapse is usually respiratory - open the airway and give 5 inflation breaths first dry, wrap and keep warm; hypothermia worsens acidosis and hypoxia compressions are 3:1 for newborns, started only after effective ventilation fails to correct heart rate under 60 heart rate is the best indicator of response to resuscitation adrenaline dose is 10 mcg/kg iv (0.1 ml/kg of 1:10,000) apgar score should not guide the timing of resuscitation use air for term infants and 21-30 percent oxygen for preterm infants, guided by oximetry take cord arterial gases when asphyxia is suspected heart rate under 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation no chest movement despite repeated inflation breaths pallor and shock suggesting blood loss persistent poor tone or seizures after resuscitation pneumothorax or diaphragmatic hernia suspected from poor response apgar appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration - each scored 0, 1 or 2 abc-d airway, breathing, circulation, drugs - in that order, with drying and warmth first transition at birth preparation and risk factors anticipate need: prematurity, meconium-stained liquor, breech, shoulder dystocia, instrumental or emergency caesarean delivery, fetal distress, multiple pregnancy, maternal sedation or infection. prepare a warm resuscitation area (radiant heater), warm towels, a clock, suction, mask, neopuff or self-inflating bag, oxygen blender and pulse oximeter. preterm babies under 32 weeks need a plastic bag or wrap without drying to prevent heat loss. newborn life support algorithm start the clock. dry the baby, remove wet towels, cover (head covered) and keep warm. delay cord clamping by at least 1 minute if the baby is stable. assess tone, breathing and heart rate. if breathing is adequate and heart rate over 100/min, keep with mother. if gasping or not breathing: open the airway (head in neutral position, jaw thrust if floppy) and give 5 inflation breaths of 2-3 seconds each. look for chest movement. reassess heart rate. if it rises, the chest wall moves and breathing begins, continue to support; if the heart rate does not improve, re-check airway position, jaw thrust, two-person technique and consider suction under direct vision. if no response and heart rate is slow (under 60/min) despite chest movement, start chest compressions at 3 compressions to 1 breath (rate 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute) using the two-thumb encircling technique over the lower third of the sternum, depth one third of chest diameter. reassess every 30 seconds. if heart rate remains under 60/min, give adrenaline and consider volume. use air for term babies, 21-30 percent oxygen for preterm babies, titrated to pulse oximetry targets (about 60 percent at 2 minutes, 80 percent at 5 minutes, 90 percent at 10 minutes). apgar score drugs and special situations adrenaline 10 mcg/kg (0.1 ml/kg of 1:10,000) iv via umbilical venous catheter; may repeat 30 mcg/kg if no response. intraosseous route is an alternative. volume: 10 ml/kg of 0.9 percent saline or o-negative blood if hypovolaemia suspected (pallor, poor response, known blood loss). meconium-stained liquor: if the baby is vigorous, no suction needed. if floppy and not breathing, inspect the oropharynx and remove thick obstructing meconium under direct vision, then begin inflation breaths. routine intubation and suction is no longer recommended. glucose 2.5 ml/kg of 10 percent dextrose for documented hypoglycaemia post-resuscitation. post-resuscitation: check glucose, temperature, maintain oxygen saturations, consider therapeutic hypothermia for babies 36 weeks or more with moderate to severe encephalopathy (see hie). stopping resuscitation and counselling adrenaline (1:10,000) 0.9% sodium chloride 10% dextrose

neonatal jaundice neonatology jaundice affects about 60 percent of term and 80 percent of preterm babies in the first week. most is physiological and harmless, but it can also signal haemolysis, sepsis, metabolic or liver disease, and severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cause kernicterus. recognising pathological patterns and treating according to gestation- and age-specific thresholds is key. jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise prolonged jaundice is over 14 days in term and over 21 days in preterm babies conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia always needs investigation - think biliary atresia pale stools and dark urine with jaundice mean obstruction until proven otherwise rhesus disease, abo incompatibility and g6pd deficiency are the major haemolytic causes phototherapy thresholds are gestation- and age-dependent - use charts kernicterus causes athetoid cp, deafness and upward gaze palsy do not diagnose breast milk jaundice until other causes are excluded jaundice within 24 hours of birth pale stools, dark urine or conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia hypotonia, lethargy, high-pitched cry or arching - possible bilirubin encephalopathy rapid rate of rise of bilirubin (over 8.5 micromol/l/hour) jaundice with signs of sepsis or hypothyroidism causes by day day 1 haemolysis or infection; day 2-14 physiological; after 2 weeks prolonged - think thyroid, infection, biliary atresia, breast milk physiology and epidemiology causes by timing within 24 hours (always pathological): haemolytic disease - rhesus, abo incompatibility, g6pd deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis; congenital infection (torch); sepsis. day 2-14: physiological jaundice, breastfeeding jaundice (poor intake), sepsis, polycythaemia, bruising/cephalhaemotoma, g6pd deficiency, crigler-najjar syndrome, galactosaemia. after 14 days (21 in preterm): breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, urinary tract infection, biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, cystic fibrosis, hypopituitarism, tpn cholestasis. conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (conjugated bilirubin over 25 micromol/l or over 20 percent of total) is never physiological - consider biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, infection. assessment history: timing of onset, gestation, family history of haemolysis, maternal blood group and antibodies, feeding, urine and stool colour, previous sibling jaundice. examination: visible jaundice from head to toe (kramer progression - face to toes as bilirubin rises), hydration, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, bruising, neurological signs. visual assessment is unreliable especially in dark skin: measure with a transcutaneous bilirubinometer (if over 24 hours and over 35 weeks) and confirm with serum bilirubin when high. investigations: total and conjugated bilirubin, full blood count and film, reticulocytes, blood group and direct antiglobulin (coombs) test of mother and baby, g6pd, culture and crp if unwell. for prolonged jaundice: split bilirubin, tfts, urine culture, galactosaemia screen, liver function, stool colour chart, ultrasound. management complications acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia then hypertonia, arching (opisthotonos), high-pitched cry, seizures. kernicterus (chronic encephalopathy): athetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural deafness, upward gaze palsy, dental enamel hypoplasia. risk is increased by prematurity, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia and haemolysis. biliary atresia: pale stools and dark urine; kasai portoenterostomy before 8 weeks of age gives the best outcome. intravenous immunoglobulin

prematurity & respiratory distress syndrome neonatology preterm birth (before 37 weeks) is the leading cause of neonatal death and long-term morbidity. respiratory distress syndrome is caused by surfactant deficiency and presents within hours of birth with grunting, tachypnoea and recession. antenatal corticosteroids, early cpap and surfactant have transformed outcomes. surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse and rds in preterm infants antenatal steroids are the most important single intervention for preterm lung maturity chest x-ray shows ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms early cpap and surfactant reduce need for ventilation and bpd transient tachypnoea of the newborn mimics rds but improves within 48-72 hours always give antibiotics until sepsis is excluded in a preterm baby with respiratory distress keep oxygen saturation targets at 90-95 percent to reduce rop and bpd caffeine reduces apnoea and bpd in very preterm babies increasing oxygen requirement or apnoeas on cpap sudden deterioration - think pneumothorax, ivh or pulmonary haemorrhage persistent hypotension and acidosis suggesting sepsis or pda bilious aspirates or abdominal distension suggesting nec absent breath sounds on one side or scaphoid abdomen suggesting diaphragmatic hernia rds features grunting, recession, tachypnoea - the triad of neonatal respiratory distress definitions and epidemiology pathophysiology of rds clinical features onset within minutes to 4 hours of birth. tachypnoea (over 60/min), grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession, cyanosis. worsens over the first 48-72 hours, then improves as endogenous surfactant production rises. chest x-ray: ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms and low lung volumes; severe cases show white-out. blood gas: hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, mixed acidosis. prevention and treatment antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) for women at risk of delivery before 34-35 weeks, ideally 24 hours to 7 days before birth, reduce rds, ivh, nec and mortality. delayed cord clamping, thermal care (bag/wrap), delivery in a unit with nicu. early nasal cpap (5-8 cm h2o) for spontaneously breathing infants; less invasive surfactant administration (lisa) or insure (intubate, surfactant, extubate) for those needing more than 30-40 percent oxygen. surfactant (poractant alfa 100-200 mg/kg) instilled into the trachea; reduces mortality and pneumothorax. mechanical ventilation with low tidal volume targets, volume guarantee, caffeine for apnoea, permissive hypercapnia, oxygen saturation target 90-95 percent. supportive care: temperature 36.5-37.5 c, fluids, parenteral and early enteral feeding, antibiotics until sepsis excluded, treatment of pda if haemodynamically significant. differential diagnosis and complications transient tachypnoea of the newborn (term, caesarean, settles in 24-72 hours), pneumonia/sepsis (especially gbs), meconium aspiration, pneumothorax, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, persistent pulmonary hypertension, cyanotic heart disease. complications: pneumothorax, pulmonary haemorrhage, pda, ivh, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, rop, nec. poractant alfa (surfactant) caffeine citrate betamethasone (maternal)

t: Complications of prematurity (BPD, ROP, IVH, apnoea)
h: complications of prematurity (bpd, rop, ivh, apnoea) neonatology survivors of preterm birth are at risk of a spectrum of short- and long-term complications affecting the lungs, eyes, brain, gut and development. the main conditions are bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, intraventricular haemorrhage and apnoea of prematurity. anticipation, screening and follow-up reduce disability. bpd is oxygen dependence at 36 weeks postmenstrual age rop screening is for babies under 32 weeks or under 1.5 kg ivh is most common in the first 72 hours and is diagnosed by cranial ultrasound grade iii-iv ivh and pvl predict cerebral palsy caffeine reduces apnoea, bpd and cerebral palsy risk apnoea in a preterm infant needs a search for an underlying cause correct for prematurity when assessing development until 2 years long-term follow-up should include hearing, vision, growth and neurodevelopment new apnoea or bradycardia episodes in a previously stable infant - infection, ivh, nec bulging fontanelle or rapidly increasing head circumference abdominal distension or bile-stained aspirates rising oxygen requirement after 2 weeks suggesting pda or evolving bpd plus disease on rop screening needs urgent treatment complications of prematurity bpd, rop, ivh, nec, pda, apnoea - the 'big six' to recite in the exam bronchopulmonary dysplasia (bpd) bpd management prevention: antenatal steroids, gentle ventilation or cpap, caffeine, avoiding excess oxygen and fluids, good nutrition, treating pda and infection. treatment: oxygen to saturations 90-95 percent, fluid restriction, diuretics, short courses of postnatal steroids in ventilator-dependent infants (balanced against neurodevelopmental risk), nutritional support. palivizumab for rsv prophylaxis in selected infants; vaccinations including influenza and pneumococcus. long-term: recurrent wheeze, readmissions, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale, poor growth. retinopathy of prematurity (rop) intraventricular haemorrhage (ivh) apnoea of prematurity and other complications apnoea of prematurity: cessation of breathing over 20 seconds or with bradycardia/desaturation due to immature respiratory control; peaks at day 2-7. exclude sepsis, hypoglycaemia, ivh, nec, seizures, pda and anaemia. treat with caffeine, cpap and sometimes ventilation. patent ductus arteriosus: murmur, bounding pulses, widened pulse pressure, heart failure; treat with fluid restriction, ibuprofen or paracetamol, or ligation. necrotising enterocolitis (see nec), feeding intolerance, late-onset sepsis, osteopenia of prematurity, anaemia and hearing impairment (ototoxic drugs). neurodevelopment: cerebral palsy, cognitive and behavioural difficulties, learning problems; follow-up with developmental assessment at 2 years corrected age. caffeine citrate ibuprofen

neonatal sepsis & meningitis neonatology neonatal sepsis is a serious bloodstream infection in the first month of life and a leading cause of neonatal death worldwide. it is classified as early onset (under 72 hours, vertical transmission) or late onset (after 72 hours, hospital or community acquired). presentation is non-specific, so a low threshold for investigation and prompt antibiotics saves lives. gbs and e coli are the main causes of early-onset neonatal sepsis signs are non-specific - treat early if in doubt always take blood cultures before antibiotics and consider lumbar puncture first-line empirical regimen is benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (uk) add amoxicillin to cefotaxime for meningitis to cover listeria csf in neonates: white cells over 20/mm3 suggests meningitis neonatal meningitis often has few specific signs - a bulging fontanelle is late aciclovir should be added in suspected hsv infection temperature instability, apnoea, or poor perfusion in a newborn seizures or a bulging fontanelle sudden hypoglycaemia or unexplained metabolic acidosis neutropenia, thrombocytopenia or dic maternal fever with prolonged rupture of membranes organisms of early-onset sepsis gbs, e coli, listeria - the gel of early-onset infection epidemiology and aetiology risk factors maternal gbs colonisation or previous gbs-affected baby, maternal fever over 38 c, chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes over 18 hours, preterm labour. prematurity, low birth weight, invasive procedures, central lines, parenteral nutrition, prolonged hospital stay. male sex, congenital abnormalities, poor hygiene and unclean cord care in resource-limited areas. clinical features non-specific: poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, temperature instability (fever or hypothermia), hypotonia, apnoea or bradycardia. respiratory distress, tachypnoea, grunting, cyanosis; tachycardia, poor perfusion, hypotension. jaundice (especially within 24 hours), hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia, vomiting, abdominal distension. seizures, bulging fontanelle and neck stiffness are late signs of meningitis; meningitis often has no specific signs. investigations blood culture before antibiotics (essential); fbc with differential (neutropenia, raised immature:total ratio), crp (serial values; initial may be normal), glucose and blood gas. lumbar puncture in any baby with suspected sepsis who is stable, with positive blood cultures, or with clinical signs of meningitis. urine culture in late-onset sepsis; chest x-ray if respiratory signs; swabs. csf in meningitis: raised white cells (over 20 per mm3 in neonates), high protein, low glucose, positive gram stain and culture, pcr for hsv and enterovirus. management supportive care and complications oxygen or ventilation, fluid resuscitation 10 ml/kg boluses, inotropes, correct glucose, treat seizures. complications: septic shock, dic, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, cerebral abscess, seizures, hearing loss, neurodevelopmental impairment. prevention: intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for gbs risk (benzylpenicillin), clean cord care, hand hygiene, line care and breast milk feeding. benzylpenicillin gentamicin cefotaxime

birth asphyxia & hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy neonatology birth asphyxia is impaired gas exchange around birth leading to hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis. when it causes a neonatal encephalopathy with multi-organ effects it is called hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (hie). it affects 1-3 per 1000 live births in high-income countries and many more in low-resource settings, and therapeutic hypothermia has improved outcomes. hie needs evidence of an acute perinatal event plus an encephalopathic baby therapeutic hypothermia must be started within 6 hours of birth cooling is 33-34 c for 72 hours then slow rewarming over at least 6 hours sarnat staging guides severity and prognosis seizures may be subtle - use aeeg or eeg avoid hyperthermia, hypoglycaemia and hypocapnia in encephalopathic infants multi-organ dysfunction is common (kidney, liver, heart, gut, lung) mri at the end of the first week is the best prognostic tool seizures or abnormal tone in the first 24 hours after a sentinel event persistent metabolic acidosis, rising lactate or anuria apnoea or inability to establish spontaneous breathing hypotension unresponsive to fluid rising temperature or infection during cooling cooling criteria 36 weeks or more, under 6 hours old, ph under 7.0 or be 16 or worse (or need for resuscitation), with moderate/severe encephalopathy definition and causes pathophysiology clinical features and staging mild (sarnat stage 1): hyperalert, jittery, normal or increased tone, sympathetic overactivity, no seizures, resolves within 24 hours. moderate (stage 2): lethargic, hypotonic, weak suck and moro, bradycardia, seizures common, may last days to 2 weeks. severe (stage 3): stuporous or comatose, flaccid, absent reflexes, apnoea, seizures, burst suppression on eeg. multi-organ dysfunction: renal (acute kidney injury, oliguria), cardiac (myocardial ischaemia, hypotension), hepatic (raised transaminases, coagulopathy), lung (persistent pulmonary hypertension, meconium aspiration), gut (nec), haematological (thrombocytopenia) and metabolic (hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia from siadh). investigations cord or first blood gas (ph, base deficit, lactate), glucose, electrolytes, calcium, urea and creatinine, lfts, coagulation, full blood count, cultures. continuous amplitude-integrated eeg (aeeg) or conventional eeg to detect seizures and background activity. cranial ultrasound early to exclude haemorrhage; mri at 5-14 days is the best predictor of outcome (basal ganglia and thalamic injury, posterior limb of the internal capsule). management resuscitate following nls; avoid hyperoxia and hyperthermia. therapeutic hypothermia (whole body cooling to 33-34 c) for 72 hours then slow rewarming, started within 6 hours of birth, for infants 36 weeks or more with moderate to severe encephalopathy and evidence of acidosis or need for resuscitation. reduces death and disability (nnt about 7). supportive care: ventilation if needed, maintain normoglycaemia, correct electrolytes and calcium, restrict fluids to avoid cerebral oedema, treat hypotension with inotropes, avoid hypocapnia. seizure control: phenobarbital first line; levetiracetam, phenytoin, midazolam as second-line. transfer to a cooling centre early; passive cooling (turn off heater, avoid overheating) while arranging transfer. prognosis phenobarbital glucose 10%

necrotising enterocolitis neonatology necrotising enterocolitis (nec) is an inflammatory bowel necrosis affecting mainly preterm infants, usually in the first 2 weeks after feeding starts. it presents with abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and bloody stools, and can progress to perforation, sepsis and death. early recognition, bowel rest, antibiotics and timely surgery are the pillars of management. nec mostly affects preterm babies in the first 2 weeks after feeds start pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal x-ray is characteristic bell staging i, ii and iii guides management breast milk is protective and slow, standardised feed advancement reduces risk treat with bowel rest, ng decompression, antibiotics and parenteral nutrition surgery is indicated for perforation or clinical deterioration despite medical therapy strictures can present weeks after recovery short bowel syndrome is the major long-term complication of extensive resection bilious vomiting or aspirates in a preterm infant abdominal distension with erythema or tenderness blood in stool with deterioration free air on abdominal x-ray falling platelets, rising crp and metabolic acidosis nec x-ray signs pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, pneumoperitoneum - the radiological triad epidemiology and pathogenesis clinical features feeding intolerance, increased gastric aspirates, bilious vomiting or aspirates. abdominal distension and tenderness, visible bowel loops, erythema of the abdominal wall. bloody stools (fresh or occult), diarrhoea or absent stools. systemic: apnoea, lethargy, temperature instability, hypotension, metabolic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia. late: perforation causing peritonitis, shock, dic. investigations abdominal x-ray: dilated bowel loops, thickened bowel wall, pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas, pathognomonic), portal venous gas, pneumoperitoneum (football sign; free air on lateral decubitus film) and fixed dilated loop. bloods: fbc (low platelets, neutropenia), crp, blood gas (acidosis), lactate, coagulation, cultures, electrolytes and glucose. serial abdominal x-rays every 6-12 hours and ultrasound for bowel wall perfusion and gas. bell staging stage i (suspected): temperature instability, apnoea, mild distension, occult blood in stool; non-specific x-ray. stage ii (definite): pneumatosis intestinalis, absent bowel sounds, tenderness; iia mildly ill, iib moderately ill with metabolic acidosis and thrombocytopenia. stage iii (advanced): severe sepsis, shock, dic; iiia bowel intact, iiib perforation with pneumoperitoneum. management complications and prevention acute: perforation, sepsis, shock, dic, death (mortality 20-30 percent, higher in surgical nec). late: intestinal strictures (colonic, weeks later), short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure, cholestasis, poor growth, neurodevelopmental impairment. prevention: antenatal steroids, breast milk (maternal or donor), standardised feeding protocols with slow advances, probiotics (where used per local policy), avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and treating pda. metronidazole gentamicin

t: Neonatal hypoglycaemia & infant of a diabetic mother
h: neonatal hypoglycaemia & infant of a diabetic mother neonatology neonatal hypoglycaemia is a common metabolic problem in the first days of life, most often transitional and mild but sometimes causing seizures and brain injury. infants of diabetic mothers are particularly at risk because fetal hyperinsulinism persists after birth. prompt detection and treatment prevent long-term neurological sequelae. operational threshold in at-risk babies is below 2.6 mmol/l idm have hyperinsulinism causing hypoglycaemia in the first hours early frequent feeding prevents most transitional hypoglycaemia symptomatic hypoglycaemia needs iv 10 percent dextrose 2 ml/kg persistent hypoglycaemia needs a critical sample and endocrine work-up idm are at risk of rds, polycythaemia, cardiomyopathy and birth trauma hypoglycaemia in a term baby after day 3 is not physiological - investigate beckwith-wiedemann syndrome causes hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia with macroglossia and exomphalos seizures, apnoea or reduced consciousness with low glucose glucose below 1.0 mmol/l hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48-72 hours or needing high glucose infusion rates associated hepatomegaly, hypotonia or poor growth suggesting metabolic disease midline defects or micropenis suggesting hypopituitarism hypoglycaemia risk groups sga, lga, idm, premature, sick - the babies who need glucose monitoring definition and causes persistent and pathological hypoglycaemia hyperinsulinism: congenital hyperinsulinism (genetic), beckwith-wiedemann syndrome, idm. hormone deficiency: hypopituitarism, growth hormone or cortisol deficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia. inborn errors: glycogen storage disease, fatty acid oxidation defects (mcadd), galactosaemia, hereditary fructose intolerance. suspect when glucose requirement exceeds 8-10 mg/kg/min (glucose infusion rate), hypoglycaemia lasts beyond 7 days, or severe/recurrent episodes. infant of a diabetic mother complications of maternal diabetes in the baby macrosomia and birth injury (shoulder dystocia, erb palsy, clavicle fracture, birth asphyxia). respiratory distress syndrome (insulin delays surfactant), transient tachypnoea. hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, polycythaemia and neonatal jaundice. hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (septal hypertrophy), congenital heart disease, neural tube defects. caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis), small left colon syndrome, renal vein thrombosis. preconception glycaemic control and folic acid 5 mg reduce malformation risk. clinical features and management often asymptomatic. symptoms: jitteriness, tremor, irritability, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, apnoea, cyanosis, seizures and hypothermia. screen at-risk babies by pre-feed blood glucose at 2-4 hours of age, early and frequent feeding (within the first hour), skin-to-skin contact and monitoring until two consecutive values above 2.6 mmol/l. asymptomatic with glucose 1.0-2.5 mmol/l: feed immediately with breast milk or formula, consider buccal 40 percent glucose gel (200 mg/kg, 0.5 ml/kg), recheck in 30-60 minutes. symptomatic or glucose below 1.0 mmol/l, or failing to respond: iv 10 percent dextrose 2 ml/kg bolus, then infusion 5-8 mg/kg/min; increase rate as needed; central line for concentrations over 12.5 percent. glucagon 200 mcg/kg im/sc if no iv access; hydrocortisone or diazoxide for persistent hyperinsulinism after endocrine review. take a critical sample (blood glucose, insulin, ketones, lactate, cortisol, gh, free fatty acids) before treating if hypoglycaemia is persistent or unexplained. 10% dextrose bolus glucagon diazoxide

congenital infections (torch) neonatology congenital infections are acquired in utero or at delivery and cause a recognisable pattern of growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, eye and brain abnormalities. the classic group is torch: toxoplasmosis, other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus, zika, hiv), rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex. cytomegalovirus is the commonest congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural deafness. cmv is the commonest congenital infection and a leading cause of non-genetic snhl toxoplasmosis causes the triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification rubella causes cataracts, deafness and pda early congenital syphilis presents with snuffles, rash on palms and soles and bone changes neonatal hsv presents at day 5-14 and needs iv aciclovir immediately test urine for cmv within the first 3 weeks of life periventricular calcification suggests cmv; diffuse suggests toxoplasma live vaccines (mmr, varicella) are contraindicated in pregnancy blueberry muffin rash, petechiae or low platelets in a newborn conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with hepatosplenomegaly seizures with vesicular rash in the first 2 weeks - hsv failed hearing screen or abnormal red reflex microcephaly with intracranial calcification torch toxoplasmosis, other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus, zika, hiv), rubella, cmv, herpes simplex toxoplasma triad hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification general principles cytomegalovirus (cmv) most common congenital infection (about 0.5-1 percent of births); transmitted transplacentally, at delivery, or via breast milk. symptomatic at birth: microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, petechial rash, chorioretinitis, small for gestational age. long-term: sensorineural deafness (progressive, may appear later), cerebral palsy, learning disability, visual loss. diagnosis: urine or saliva pcr or culture within the first 3 weeks; dried blood spot pcr retrospectively. treatment with valganciclovir (16 mg/kg orally twice daily for 6 months) for symptomatic cns disease or deafness; monitor neutropenia. toxoplasmosis toxoplasma gondii from undercooked meat or cat faeces; maternal primary infection in pregnancy. classic triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse intracranial calcifications; also seizures, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly. diagnosis: maternal and neonatal serology (igm, igg, iga), pcr of amniotic fluid. treatment: pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with folinic acid for 12 months; spiramycin in pregnancy. rubella congenital rubella syndrome: sensorineural deafness, cataracts (leukocoria), congenital heart disease (pda, pulmonary artery stenosis), microcephaly, blueberry muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly. prevented by mmr vaccination before pregnancy; live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy. diagnosis: rubella igm and pcr; infants shed virus for months and are infectious. syphilis early congenital syphilis (under 2 years): snuffles (rhinitis), maculopapular rash on palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, osteochondritis and pseudoparalysis, anaemia, condylomata lata. late: hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, saber shins, mulberry molars, interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness. treatment: benzylpenicillin for 10 days. antenatal screening and treatment with penicillin prevents transmission. herpes simplex and other infections hsv: acquired mainly at delivery from genital infection (primary maternal infection highest risk). presents days 5-14 with skin, eye, mouth lesions (sem), encephalitis (seizures, lethargy) or disseminated disease with hepatitis. treat with iv aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 14-21 days. give aciclovir early if suspected. varicella: fetal varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia, scarring, microcephaly) in first 20 weeks; perinatal varicella if maternal rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery - give vzig. parvovirus b19: hydrops fetalis and severe anaemia. zika virus: microcephaly with brain calcification and arthrogryposis. hiv: antiretroviral prophylaxis for mother and baby; avoid breastfeeding in high-income settings. investigations and prevention urine cmv pcr, serology, fbc and film, lfts, cranial ultrasound/mri, ophthalmology and audiology assessment. prevention: handwashing and avoiding children's saliva (cmv), avoiding undercooked meat and cat litter (toxoplasma), rubella immunity check and mmr before pregnancy, syphilis and hiv antenatal screening, caesarean section for active genital herpes, and vzig for susceptible exposed pregnant women. aciclovir valganciclovir benzylpenicillin

birth injuries & transient neonatal conditions neonatology birth injuries result from mechanical forces during labour and delivery, and range from trivial bruising to life-threatening haemorrhage or nerve injury. many neonatal findings are transient and benign. recognising which are harmless and which need action is an important newborn skill. cephalhaemotoma does not cross sutures; caput does subgaleal haemorrhage can be life-threatening - monitor for shock erb palsy affects c5-c6 and gives the waiter's tip posture no recovery of brachial plexus palsy by 3 months needs surgical referral clavicle fracture is the commonest birth fracture facial nerve palsy from forceps usually recovers spontaneously shoulder dystocia is associated with brachial plexus injury unexplained fractures need consideration of abuse or bone disease expanding boggy scalp swelling with pallor or shock bulging fontanelle, seizures or apnoea after instrumental delivery persistent brachial plexus palsy beyond 3 months or associated horner syndrome respiratory distress with an elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic nerve injury) multiple fractures of different ages waiter's tip erb palsy: adducted, internally rotated, extended elbow, pronated forearm, wrist flexed risk factors scalp injuries caput succedaneum: oedematous swelling of the presenting part, crosses suture lines, present at birth, resolves in days. cephalhaemotoma: subperiosteal haemorrhage, does not cross sutures, appears hours after birth, may take weeks to resolve and cause jaundice; underlying skull fracture is uncommon. subgaleal (subaponeurotic) haemorrhage: bleeding in the potential space beneath the aponeurosis, associated with ventouse; boggy swelling crossing sutures and expanding, can hold up to 250 ml of blood and cause shock, anaemia and coagulopathy. medical emergency. chignon: mark from ventouse cup; benign. skull fractures: linear (usually asymptomatic) or depressed (may need neurosurgery). intracranial and ocular injury subdural, subarachnoid and intraventricular haemorrhage can occur with instrumental delivery; presentation with apnoea, seizures or a bulging fontanelle. subconjunctival and retinal haemorrhages are common and benign unless extensive. nerve injuries erb palsy (c5-c6, upper brachial plexus): arm hangs by the side, adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended and forearm pronated (waiter's tip), absent moro on the affected side, grasp preserved. usually resolves within 3 months; if no recovery by 3 months refer for microsurgery. klumpke palsy (c8-t1): claw hand with weak grasp, sometimes horner syndrome; worse prognosis. phrenic nerve palsy (c3-c5) causes diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory distress, often with erb palsy. facial nerve palsy: asymmetric crying face with inability to close the eye on the affected side, due to forceps pressure; usually resolves in weeks. differentiate from central causes (forehead spared in upper motor neurone lesion) and congenital absence of depressor anguli oris. fractures and soft tissue injury clavicle fracture: commonest fracture, often shoulder dystocia; crepitus, reduced arm movement, usually heals in weeks with no treatment. humeral or femoral fractures: more likely after breech delivery; immobilise. bruising, petechiae (facial after cord around neck), abrasions, lacerations and sternomastoid tumour (haematoma, torticollis) occur and usually resolve. consider non-accidental injury and bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta) if multiple fractures without explanation. transient neonatal conditions erythema toxicum, milia, miliaria, mongolian blue spots, salmon patches and harlequin colour change. physiological weight loss, breast engorgement and pseudomenstruation due to maternal hormones. transient tachypnoea of the newborn, physiological jaundice, transient hypoglycaemia. epstein pearls (palate cysts), natal teeth (assess), sucking blisters. phytomenadione

croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) respiratory paediatrics croup is a viral infection of the upper airway causing a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor. it mainly affects children aged 6 months to 3 years, peaks in autumn, and is usually mild, but a minority develop severe airway obstruction. parainfluenza virus is the commonest cause of croup barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor in a child 6 months to 3 years steroids benefit all severities; single dose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally nebulised adrenaline is for moderate to severe croup and acts within minutes but lasts about 2 hours do not agitate the child or examine the throat if epiglottitis is possible the steeple sign on x-ray is not required to make the diagnosis cyanosis and drowsiness are late signs of impending respiratory failure recurrent croup should prompt consideration of an underlying structural airway abnormality stridor at rest with marked recession drowsiness, agitation or exhaustion cyanosis or low oxygen saturation drooling, toxic appearance, or inability to swallow (think epiglottitis or tracheitis) poor response to steroid and adrenaline, or recurrent episodes croup triad barking cough + hoarse voice + inspiratory stridor definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features prodrome of 1 to 3 days of coryza and low-grade fever, then onset of barking cough and hoarse voice, typically worse at night inspiratory stridor, initially only on crying or agitation, then at rest in more severe disease respiratory distress signs: tracheal tug, intercostal and subcostal recession, nasal flaring, tachypnoea child is usually alert, wants to be held, and is able to drink; drooling and toxic appearance are not features of croup symptoms usually last 48 hours but cough can persist for up to a week severity assessment mild: occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest, no or mild recession moderate: stridor at rest, moderate recession, but the child is not agitated or lethargic severe: stridor at rest with marked recession, agitation or lethargy/drowsiness, tachycardia, pallor or cyanosis (a late sign); impending respiratory failure investigations croup is a clinical diagnosis; do not distress the child with unnecessary examination (avoid throat examination with a spatula if epiglottitis is suspected) pulse oximetry is the key monitoring tool; hypoxia is a late and ominous sign neck x-ray (steeple sign on ap view) is not needed routinely and should not delay treatment consider viral pcr only for infection-control or atypical presentations management all severities: single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (0.6 mg/kg is also used in some guidelines); alternatives are oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg or nebulised budesonide 2 mg moderate or severe: nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) 1:1000, 0.5 ml/kg up to 5 ml, with oxygen if hypoxic; effect starts in 10 to 30 minutes but lasts only 2 hours, so observe for rebound for at least 2 to 4 hours severe or not responding: call senior help and anaesthetist/ent early; heliox may help; intubation with a smaller-than-expected tube is the last resort discharge criteria: no stridor at rest, comfortable work of breathing, reliable carers and able to return antibiotics are not indicated unless bacterial tracheitis is suspected complications & prognosis respiratory failure and need for intubation (under 2 percent of admissions) bacterial superinfection (bacterial tracheitis), pneumonia, otitis media pulmonary oedema (rare, after relief of severe obstruction) recurrent or spasmodic croup, or croup beginning under 6 months, should prompt assessment for subglottic stenosis, laryngomalacia or reflux overall prognosis is excellent with full recovery dexamethasone prednisolone budesonide nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 nebulised

stridor, epiglottitis & bacterial tracheitis respiratory paediatrics stridor is a harsh, high-pitched noisy breathing sign of upper airway obstruction. epiglottitis and bacterial tracheitis are rare but life-threatening causes that require immediate airway expertise, while the commonest causes are croup and laryngomalacia. inspiratory stridor = supraglottic; biphasic = glottic/subglottic; expiratory = tracheobronchial epiglottitis: toxic child, drooling, no cough, tripod position, rapid onset hib vaccination has made epiglottitis rare, but think of it in unvaccinated children never examine the throat or distress a child with suspected epiglottitis bacterial tracheitis mimics severe croup but fails to respond to adrenaline and steroids laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of chronic stridor in infancy and usually self-resolves first-line antibiotic in epiglottitis is iv ceftriaxone after securing the airway a silent or quieter child with stridor may be exhausted drooling, inability to swallow and tripod posture toxic appearance with high fever and stridor stridor at rest with cyanosis, exhaustion or reduced conscious level stridor in infant with feeding difficulty, failure to thrive or apnoea sudden onset stridor and choking (foreign body) the 4 ds of epiglottitis drooling, dysphagia, dysphonia (muffled voice), distress, with no cough stridor: definition and localisation causes of stridor acute: croup, epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, inhaled foreign body, anaphylaxis and angioedema, retropharyngeal abscess, burns or inhalation injury chronic or since birth: laryngomalacia (commonest in infants), vocal cord palsy, subglottic stenosis, tracheomalacia, laryngeal web, haemangioma, vascular ring laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor worse on feeding, crying and lying supine, onset in first weeks and resolving by 12 to 18 months epiglottitis management of suspected epiglottitis do not examine the throat, lay the child flat, take blood or cannulate before the airway is secure;
