distress may precipitate complete obstruction keep the child calm on the parent lap, give humidified oxygen only if tolerated call the most senior anaesthetist, ent surgeon and paediatrician immediately (airway team) intubation under general anaesthesia in theatre with a surgeon ready for tracheostomy after the airway is secured: blood cultures, then iv ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) for 5 to 7 days; extubation is usually possible in 24 to 48 hours once an air leak and a reduced swelling are confirmed offer prophylaxis (rifampicin) to household contacts for hib and ensure vaccination of the index case bacterial tracheitis investigations and approach acute severe stridor is a clinical emergency: investigations must not delay airway management chronic stridor: refer for flexible laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy to identify structural lesions chest and neck x-ray may show thumb sign (epiglottitis), steeple sign (croup), or tracheal narrowing, but are secondary to airway safety barium swallow or ct/mri if a vascular ring is suspected (biphasic stridor with feeding difficulty) ceftriaxone iv rifampicin

bronchiolitis respiratory paediatrics bronchiolitis is an acute viral lower respiratory tract infection of infants causing inflammation and obstruction of the small airways, most often due to rsv. it is the commonest reason for infant hospital admission in winter, and management is mainly supportive. rsv causes most bronchiolitis typical age is under 12 months with peak at 3 to 6 months in winter fine crackles and wheeze with poor feeding after coryzal prodrome management is supportive: oxygen, fluids/feeds, minimal handling bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated apnoea is a risk in young and premature infants palivizumab and newer rsv immunisation reduce severe disease in high-risk infants indications for admission include saturations below 92 percent, poor feeding and apnoea apnoea or irregular breathing oxygen saturations persistently below 92 percent respiratory rate over 70 or grunting with severe recession feeding less than half of normal or signs of dehydration age under 6 weeks or high-risk comorbidity exhaustion, drowsiness or rising pco2 safe admission triggers saturations low, apnoea, feeding poor, exhaustion or distress definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features preceding 1 to 3 days of coryza, then dry cough, tachypnoea, nasal flaring, grunting and recession fine inspiratory crackles with or without expiratory wheeze; hyperinflated chest poor feeding (often the reason for admission), irritability, mild fever apnoea may be the presenting feature in young infants, especially premature infants and those under 6 weeks symptoms peak at day 3 to 5 and cough may last 2 to 3 weeks risk factors for severe disease prematurity (especially under 32 weeks), age under 3 months chronic lung disease of prematurity, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease, down syndrome exposure to tobacco smoke, overcrowding, no breastfeeding investigations diagnosis is clinical; routine chest x-ray, bloods and viral testing are not required pulse oximetry guides oxygen therapy consider x-ray if severe, atypical or suspicion of another diagnosis (collapse, pneumothorax) blood gas if in severe respiratory distress nasopharyngeal aspirate or pcr mainly for cohorting and infection control management oxygen to maintain saturations at 92 percent or above (nice; some guidelines use 90 percent or 94 percent) fluid and nutritional support: small frequent feeds, nasogastric feeding or iv fluids at about 2/3 maintenance if unable to feed safely nasal suction for blocked nose high-flow nasal cannula or cpap for increasing work of breathing; picu for apnoea or failure not recommended: salbutamol, ipratropium, nebulised adrenaline (except trial in some centres), systemic or inhaled steroids, antibiotics, nebulised hypertonic saline (limited evidence), chest physiotherapy antibiotics only if bacterial coinfection is suspected (e.g. otitis, consolidation) prevention, complications & prognosis hand hygiene, reduced smoke exposure, breastfeeding, cohorting in hospital palivizumab monthly in winter for selected high-risk infants (chronic lung disease, haemodynamically significant chd); maternal rsv vaccine and nirsevimab are now available in many countries complications: apnoea, respiratory failure, secondary bacterial infection, dehydration post-bronchiolitic wheeze is common; association with later asthma in some most infants recover fully within 2 to 3 weeks oxygen palivizumab

childhood asthma respiratory paediatrics asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable airflow obstruction causing recurrent wheeze, cough, breathlessness and chest tightness. it is the commonest chronic disease of childhood, and good control relies on preventer therapy, trigger avoidance and a personal action plan. asthma is variable airflow obstruction with airway inflammation viral infection is the commonest trigger in children diagnose with spirometry and reversibility in over-5s; clinical trial of treatment in under-5s check technique, adherence and triggers before stepping up therapy use a spacer with pmdi in all children a silent chest is life-threatening, not reassuring oral steroids early in acute attacks provide a written personal asthma action plan and annual review silent chest, cyanosis or exhaustion in an acute attack spo2 below 92 percent in air unable to speak or feed in sentences poor response to initial bronchodilator previous near-fatal or picu admission frequent hospital admissions or poor growth on high-dose ics abcde of asthma review adherence, beta-agonist technique (inhaler), control level, day-night symptoms, exacerbation history definition & epidemiology pathophysiology & triggers viral infections (commonest trigger in children) allergens: house dust mite, pollen, pet dander, moulds exercise, cold air, emotion or laughter passive and active smoke, air pollution, strong odours drugs: nsaids and beta-blockers in susceptible individuals clinical features and diagnosis episodic wheeze, cough (often nocturnal or early morning), breathlessness, chest tightness; symptoms worse with triggers examination may be normal between attacks; look for hyperinflation, harrison sulcus, eczema, nasal polyps/allergic rhinitis diagnosis in children over 5 years: spirometry showing obstructive pattern (fev1/fvc below lower limit of normal) with bronchodilator reversibility of 12 percent or more, raised feno, peak flow variability children under 5 years: diagnosis is clinical; a trial of treatment with review is used and a label of asthma is often deferred chest x-ray not needed unless diagnostic uncertainty or complications atopy tests (skin prick, specific ige) support but do not confirm diagnosis chronic management step 1: as-needed short-acting beta-agonist (saba) or low-dose ics-formoterol reliever step 2: add regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ics) or leukotriene receptor antagonist (ltra) in under 5s step 3: add long-acting beta-agonist (laba) to ics, or maintenance and reliever therapy (mart) in older children; or ltra step 4: increase ics dose, add ltra/theophylline; refer to specialist step 5: specialist care including biologics (e.g. omalizumab, mepolizumab) and oral steroids spacer with face mask or mouthpiece for all children using pmdi; a written personal asthma action plan; annual influenza vaccination and yearly review acute asthma moderate: spo2 92 percent or above, able to talk, no features of severe attack severe: spo2 below 92 percent, too breathless to talk or feed, heart rate over 125 (over 5y) or 140 (2 to 5y), rr over 30 (over 5y) or 40 (2 to 5y), use of accessory muscles life-threatening: spo2 below 92 percent with silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion, altered consciousness, arrhythmia or hypotension oxygen to spo2 94 to 98 percent; salbutamol 4 to 10 puffs via spacer (10 puffs if severe), repeated every 20 minutes or nebulised 2.5 to 5 mg oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg (max 40 mg) for 3 to 5 days, started early add nebulised ipratropium 250 micrograms every 20 to 30 minutes if poor response iv magnesium sulfate 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes for severe attack; iv salbutamol or aminophylline in picu for life-threatening disease chest x-ray only if suspected pneumothorax or consolidation complications & prognosis poorly controlled asthma: school absence, exercise limitation, growth faltering with high-dose steroid pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, lobar collapse many children improve in adolescence but some relapse as adults side effects of ics: oral candida, growth velocity reduction (small, about 1 cm), adrenal suppression at high dose salbutamol (pmdi + spacer) prednisolone ipratropium nebulised magnesium sulfate iv

pre-school wheeze respiratory paediatrics wheeze is very common in children under 5, and most episodes are triggered by viral infection in children who do not have asthma. distinguishing episodic viral wheeze from multiple-trigger wheeze guides treatment and prognosis, and most children outgrow it by school age. most pre-school wheeze is virally triggered and resolves by school age episodic viral wheeze differs from multiple-trigger wheeze, which is more asthma-like atopy and family history increase the chance of persistent asthma trial of ics or ltra with review is used instead of a firm early diagnosis of asthma always consider alternative diagnoses if wheeze is persistent, unresponsive or starts at birth avoid tobacco smoke exposure short oral steroid courses are used only in severe attacks spirometry is not feasible in most pre-schoolers wheeze present since birth or from first weeks failure to thrive or chronic wet cough focal or persistent chest signs, clubbing sudden onset of wheeze with choking (foreign body) poor response to bronchodilator and steroid stridor with wheeze or feeding problems wheeze check watch growth, history of onset/atopy, exclude alternatives, examine chest/clubbing, zero smoke, evaluate treatment response definition & epidemiology classification episodic (viral) wheeze: wheeze only during discrete colds, with the child symptom-free between episodes multiple-trigger wheeze: wheeze during colds and also with other triggers such as exercise, laughter, cold air, allergens or smoke; symptoms may occur between colds features raising likelihood of persistent asthma: atopy (eczema, food allergy), family history of asthma or atopy, wheeze apart from colds, nocturnal symptoms, eosinophilia, positive response to treatment clinical assessment features suggesting an alternative diagnosis: wheeze from birth, failure to thrive, chronic wet cough, persistent focal signs, recurrent infections, onset with feeding or choking, stridor, clubbing, cardiac murmur differentials: bronchiolitis, cystic fibrosis, inhaled foreign body, aspiration or gord, tracheobronchomalacia, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiency, vascular ring, bronchiolitis obliterans investigations usually clinical; chest x-ray if atypical or persistent focal signs allergy tests (skin prick, specific ige) can support atopic phenotype sweat test, immunoglobulins, bronchoscopy, high-resolution ct, ciliary studies for suspected alternative diagnoses spirometry and feno are generally not possible below age 5 management acute episode: salbutamol via pmdi and spacer (2 to 10 puffs as needed), oxygen if hypoxic. oral steroid (prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg for up to 3 days) is considered in moderate-severe attacks, particularly in hospital avoid triggers including tobacco smoke; encourage smoking cessation in carers episodic viral wheeze with frequent or severe attacks: trial of intermittent or daily ltra (montelukast) or intermittent ics multiple-trigger wheeze: trial of daily low-dose ics for 6 to 8 weeks; stop and review: if symptoms recur on stopping, restart as asthma review diagnosis if there is no response: re-examine, reconsider alternatives annual influenza vaccination and personal action plan prognosis salbutamol pmdi + spacer montelukast prednisolone

pneumonia in children respiratory paediatrics pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma and remains the leading infectious cause of death in children under five worldwide. in high-income settings it is usually mild and treated at home with oral amoxicillin, while in resource-limited settings who fast-breathing criteria drive community case management. pneumonia is the leading infectious cause of death in under-fives worldwide streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest bacterial cause beyond the newborn period viruses cause most pneumonia in children under 5 years who fast-breathing thresholds: 50 per minute (2 to 11 months), 40 per minute (1 to 5 years) oral amoxicillin is first-line even for most severe cases in resource-limited settings chest x-ray is not routinely needed for uncomplicated pneumonia think empyema if fever persists beyond 48 hours of treatment add a macrolide for mycoplasma in school-age children hypoxia, cyanosis or severe respiratory distress inability to drink or feed, lethargy, convulsions persistent fever after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy age under 3 months, severe malnutrition, hiv, or immunodeficiency unilateral dullness suggesting effusion who danger signs (pneumonia) cannot drink, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic/unconscious, stridor at rest, severe malnutrition definition & epidemiology aetiology neonates: group b streptococcus, escherichia coli and other gram-negative organisms, listeria infants and under 5 years: viruses (rsv, rhinovirus, influenza) predominate; bacterial causes include streptococcus pneumoniae (commonest), haemophilus influenzae, staphylococcus aureus over 5 years: streptococcus pneumoniae, mycoplasma pneumoniae, chlamydia pneumoniae special: staph aureus (post-influenza, cavitation, pneumatoceles), pneumocystis jirovecii in hiv, mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical organisms clinical features fever, cough, tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, chest indrawing, difficulty feeding examination: bronchial breathing, reduced air entry, dullness to percussion, localised coarse crackles abdominal pain (lower lobe pneumonia) or neck stiffness (upper lobe) can mislead atypical pneumonia (mycoplasma) has insidious onset, dry cough, headache, extra-pulmonary features severe: hypoxia (spo2 below 92 percent), cyanosis, inability to feed or drink, convulsions, lethargy who classification fast breathing: 50 or more breaths/min at 2 to 11 months, 40 or more at 1 to 5 years -> pneumonia: oral amoxicillin at home for 3 to 5 days lower chest wall indrawing -> in the updated who guideline also treated with oral amoxicillin at home if no danger signs any general danger sign (unable to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy, stridor in calm child, severe malnutrition, spo2 below 90 percent) -> severe pneumonia: admit, oxygen, injectable antibiotics investigations diagnosis is clinical; pulse oximetry in every child with respiratory distress chest x-ray is not required routinely for mild cap; indicated if severe, complications, or atypical course bloods (crp, fbc, cultures) in children admitted with severe illness; blood culture before antibiotics in severe cases pleural fluid aspiration if effusion, urine antigen/pcr as available hiv testing and tb investigation in high-prevalence areas management oxygen if spo2 below 92 percent (94 percent in high-income picu context) or below 90 percent in who guidance mild-moderate cap: oral amoxicillin 40 to 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses for 3 to 5 days (check local guideline); duration 5 days in uk severe or not able to take oral: iv benzylpenicillin, ampicillin or co-amoxiclav/ceftriaxone, plus flucloxacillin or clindamycin if staph suspected add a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin) if mycoplasma suspected or no response to first-line therapy in hiv-exposed infants with severe pneumonia consider pneumocystis (high-dose co-trimoxazole + steroid) supportive: fluids, antipyretics, nutrition, nursing at the 30 degree position review at 48 hours if no improvement; consider empyema complications & prevention parapneumonic effusion and empyema: persistent fever, pleuritic pain, dullness; treat with drainage and prolonged antibiotics, fibrinolytics or vats lung abscess, necrotising pneumonia, pneumatocele, pneumothorax, sepsis prevention: pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, hib vaccine, measles vaccine, breastfeeding, reducing indoor smoke, zinc and vitamin a supplementation, hiv prevention amoxicillin azithromycin co-amoxiclav iv

cystic fibrosis respiratory paediatrics cystic fibrosis (cf) is an autosomal recessive multisystem disease caused by mutations in the cftr gene, leading to thick secretions, chronic lung infection and pancreatic insufficiency. newborn screening and cftr modulator therapy have transformed survival, with median predicted survival now beyond 40 years. autosomal recessive, cftr gene on chromosome 7, f508del commonest sweat chloride over 60 mmol/l is diagnostic newborn screening uses immunoreactive trypsinogen then genetics meconium ileus is almost pathognomonic in newborns pseudomonas aeruginosa causes chronic infection and decline in lung function pancreatic enzymes with all fat-containing food and fat-soluble vitamins cftr modulators (e.g. elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor) have changed prognosis males are almost always infertile due to absent vas deferens meconium ileus or bilious vomiting in the newborn haemoptysis, pneumothorax or acute respiratory failure distal intestinal obstruction syndrome with vomiting and abdominal mass drop in lung function or weight despite therapy acquisition of burkholderia cepacia polyuria, polydipsia or weight loss (cf-related diabetes) cf features pancreatic insufficiency, chest infections, salty sweat, meconium ileus, infertile males ("pcsmi") genetics & epidemiology clinical presentation newborn: meconium ileus (about 15 to 20 percent), prolonged jaundice, positive newborn screening (raised immunoreactive trypsinogen) infancy: failure to thrive despite good appetite, steatorrhoea (bulky, pale, offensive stools), recurrent chest infections, rectal prolapse, salty-tasting skin, hypoelectrolytaemic metabolic alkalosis (pseudo-bartter) in hot weather childhood: chronic productive cough, wheeze, nasal polyps, sinusitis, finger clubbing, bronchiectasis, distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (dios) adolescence: cf-related diabetes, liver disease, delayed puberty, male infertility (absent vas deferens) organisms: staphylococcus aureus and haemophilus influenzae early, then pseudomonas aeruginosa (chronic infection), burkholderia cepacia complex (poor prognosis), mrsa, aspergillus, non-tuberculous mycobacteria diagnosis newborn screening: immunoreactive trypsinogen on heel-prick blood spot, followed by cftr mutation analysis sweat test (pilocarpine iontophoresis): sweat chloride over 60 mmol/l is diagnostic, 30 to 59 is intermediate and under 30 is unlikely genetic testing of cftr for confirmation and modulator eligibility faecal elastase (low in pancreatic insufficiency) culture of sputum or cough swab, chest x-ray (hyperinflation, bronchial wall thickening), ct chest, lung function management respiratory: airway clearance physiotherapy daily, exercise, mucolytics (dornase alfa, hypertonic saline), inhaled antibiotics for pseudomonas (tobramycin, colistin), regular azithromycin as anti-inflammatory in some patients, prompt iv antibiotics for exacerbations nutrition: high-energy, high-fat diet (120 to 150 percent of normal energy), pancreatic enzyme replacement (creon) with meals and snacks, fat-soluble vitamins a, d, e, k, salt supplements cftr modulators: ivacaftor for gating mutations; elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor for people with at least one f508del; improve lung function, weight and exacerbation rates gastro/hepatic: dios management, ursodeoxycholic acid in liver disease, screening for cf-related diabetes from age 10 with annual ogtt infection control: segregate patients to avoid cross-infection with pseudomonas and burkholderia; vaccinations incl. annual influenza end-stage: non-invasive ventilation, lung transplantation complications bronchiectasis, haemoptysis, pneumothorax, respiratory failure and cor pulmonale pancreatic insufficiency, dios, gord, cirrhosis and portal hypertension cf-related diabetes, osteoporosis, delayed growth and puberty allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis infertility in males (congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens); reduced fertility in females resource-limited settings pancreatic enzymes (pancrelipase) dornase alfa tobramycin inhaled

inhaled foreign body & choking respiratory paediatrics inhaled foreign bodies and choking are major causes of accidental death in young children, mostly aged 6 months to 3 years who put objects in their mouths. prompt recognition and correct first-aid are lifesaving, and unrecognised foreign bodies cause chronic cough, wheeze or recurrent pneumonia. peak age 1 to 3 years; commonest object is nuts or food foreign body is always a differential for sudden unexplained wheeze, cough or stridor a normal chest x-ray does not exclude foreign body rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive treatment infants: 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; older children: 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts never perform blind finger sweeps button batteries in the oesophagus are an emergency prevention advice: do not give whole nuts under 5 years sudden choking with cyanosis or silent breathing unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry after choking history persistent stridor or inability to speak recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe suspected button battery ingestion choking steps back blows x5, then thrusts x5 (chest in infants, abdominal in children), reassess, repeat; cpr if unconscious definition & epidemiology clinical presentation acute choking: sudden onset coughing, gagging, cyanosis, stridor or inability to cry or speak, often witnessed while eating or playing complete airway obstruction: silent, unable to breathe, cough, or cry; rapidly loses consciousness after the choking episode: asymptomatic period then cough, localised wheeze, reduced air entry on one side, or stridor chronic or missed fb: persistent cough, recurrent or non-resolving pneumonia, unilateral wheeze, haemoptysis, lung collapse examination can be normal; unilateral hyperinflation (ball-valve), reduced breath sounds or wheeze are suggestive immediate management of choking effective cough (crying, able to speak, breathing): encourage coughing, monitor, call for help ineffective cough but conscious: call for help; infant under 1 year: 5 back blows (head down) then 5 chest thrusts; child over 1 year: 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts (heimlich); repeat cycles unconscious and not breathing: call emergency services, open airway, 5 rescue breaths, then start cpr (15 compressions to 2 breaths); check mouth for visible object before each breath hospital: oxygen, direct laryngoscopy with magill forceps for visible laryngeal object; senior anaesthetic and ent help; surgical airway if unable to remove or ventilate investigations chest x-ray inspiratory and expiratory (or lateral decubitus) films: radio-opaque objects visible; for radiolucent objects look for air trapping, hyperinflation, mediastinal shift or atelectasis normal x-ray does not exclude aspiration (up to 30 percent are normal) bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic: rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is the gold standard for removal in children ct chest or flexible bronchoscopy may be used in selected stable cases suspicion on history alone justifies bronchoscopy even if x-ray normal special hazards button batteries: oesophageal impaction can cause mucosal burns within 2 hours; urgent endoscopic removal; give honey or sucralfate while awaiting if recommended by local guidance magnets (multiple) risk perforation and fistula organic items such as peanuts cause intense inflammatory reaction grapes and sausage pieces are particularly dangerous because they conform to the airway complications & prevention hypoxic brain injury, death, pneumonia, atelectasis, bronchiectasis, pneumothorax airway oedema or perforation after removal prevention: avoid whole nuts under 5 years, cut grapes lengthways, supervise meals, avoid small toys and loose parts for under-3s, keep batteries and magnets out of reach teach parents and carers basic paediatric first aid

tuberculosis in children respiratory paediatrics tuberculosis (tb) in children is a paucibacillary disease caused by mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually acquired from an infectious adult. it is a major global killer with difficult diagnosis, and most childhood cases are curable with a standard multidrug regimen. children get tb from infectious adults; find the source case childhood tb is paucibacillary so smear microscopy is rarely positive standard regimen is 2hrze followed by 4hr always test for hiv in children with tb tb meningitis is the most severe form with high mortality; use steroids mantoux positive: 10 mm or more; 5 mm or more in hiv/malnutrition bcg protects against severe disseminated forms in young children preventive therapy for young contacts after excluding active disease fever, headache, vomiting and altered consciousness (tb meningitis) miliary pattern on chest x-ray respiratory distress with lobar collapse hiv infection or severe malnutrition poor adherence or relapse (consider drug resistance) ripe rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol - intensive phase drugs drug side effects rifampicin: orange fluids, hepatitis; isoniazid: neuropathy, hepatitis; pyrazinamide: hepatitis, hyperuricaemia; ethambutol: optic neuritis epidemiology & transmission stages of infection tb exposure: contact with an infectious case, negative tests, no symptoms tb infection (latent): positive tuberculin skin test or igra, no symptoms, normal chest x-ray tb disease: symptoms and/or abnormal imaging; pulmonary (primary complex), pleural, lymph node, miliary, cns, bone and joint, abdominal primary tb: ghon focus plus hilar lymphadenopathy; may progress to complications (lobar collapse from nodal obstruction, effusion, miliary spread) clinical features persistent cough over 2 weeks, fever, weight loss or failure to thrive, night sweats, lethargy tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula): painless matted cervical nodes miliary tb: fever, hepatosplenomegaly, respiratory distress, choroid tubercles tb meningitis: subacute headache, vomiting, irritability, cranial nerve palsies (esp. vi), hydrocephalus, reduced consciousness spinal tb (pott disease): back pain, gibbus; abdominal tb: ascites, abdominal masses adolescents may present with adult-type cavitating pulmonary disease and are infectious diagnosis history of tb contact is key; clinical scoring systems are used in resource-limited settings chest x-ray: hilar or paratracheal lymphadenopathy, consolidation, collapse, miliary pattern, cavitation tuberculin skin test (mantoux): positive if induration 10 mm or more (5 mm in hiv or malnourished); igra (interferon-gamma release assay) is more specific and unaffected by bcg microbiological confirmation: gastric aspirates, induced sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate, stool; xpert mtb/rif (ultra) preferred first test; culture for sensitivity other tests: lymph node fna, csf (high protein, low glucose, lymphocytes), ct/mri head, hiv test in every child with tb treatment dosing is weight-banded using fixed-dose combination tablets in resource-limited settings give pyridoxine (vitamin b6) with isoniazid in at-risk children (malnourished, hiv, breastfed) directly observed therapy to improve adherence monitor lfts if symptoms of hepatitis; drug-resistant tb requires specialist regimens hiv co-infection: start art within 2 to 8 weeks of tb treatment and watch for iris latent tb or preventive therapy: isoniazid 6 months, or isoniazid + rifampicin 3 months, for children under 5 years who are contacts (after excluding active disease) prevention & contact tracing bcg vaccine at birth in high-burden countries protects against severe disease (meningitis, miliary), with limited effect on pulmonary tb contact tracing: screen all household contacts; treat infectious source adult infection control: children are rarely infectious unless adolescent or cavitary; isolation of infectious adults notify tb cases to public health authorities isoniazid rifampicin pyrazinamide ethambutol

pertussis (whooping cough) respiratory paediatrics pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by bordetella pertussis, characterised by paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop. it is most dangerous in young infants, in whom apnoea and pneumonia can be fatal, and is prevented by vaccination including maternal immunisation in pregnancy. bordetella pertussis, gram-negative coccobacillus catarrhal phase is most infectious; paroxysmal phase gives whoop and post-tussive vomiting young infants present with apnoea rather than whoop lymphocytosis on blood film; pcr on nasopharyngeal swab macrolide early limits spread; supportive care is main treatment maternal vaccination in pregnancy protects newborns pneumonia is the leading cause of death notifiable disease; treat contacts and vaccinate apnoea, cyanosis or bradycardia in an infant age under 3 months or incompletely vaccinated marked leucocytosis (wbc over 50) pneumonia, hypoxia or exhaustion seizures or reduced consciousness phases catarrhal (1-2 wk) -> paroxysmal (2-8 wk) -> convalescent (weeks to months) definition & epidemiology clinical course incubation 7 to 10 days (up to 21) catarrhal phase (1 to 2 weeks): coryza, mild cough, low-grade fever - most infectious paroxysmal phase (2 to 8 weeks): bouts of repeated forceful coughs followed by an inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, cyanosis, subconjunctival haemorrhages, facial petechiae; child is well between bouts convalescent phase (weeks to months): decreasing cough, "100-day cough" infants under 6 months may lack a whoop and instead have apnoea, cyanosis, gagging and bradycardia; adults have prolonged cough investigations full blood count: marked lymphocytosis (white cell count often over 20, sometimes over 100, a poor prognostic sign in infants) pcr of nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate (best in first 3 weeks); culture on bordet-gengou or charcoal agar (low sensitivity) serology (anti-pertussis toxin igg) in older children and adults presenting late (over 2 weeks) chest x-ray: perihilar infiltrate ("shaggy heart"), may show pneumonia or collapse notify to public health management admit infants under 6 months (particularly under 3 months) and any with apnoea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty, hypoxia or pneumonia macrolide antibiotic within 3 weeks of cough onset reduces infectivity but not symptoms unless given early: azithromycin (10 mg/kg once daily for 3 days in infants over 1 month; 5 days under 1 month), or clarithromycin; erythromycin avoided in neonates (pyloric stenosis); co-trimoxazole if macrolide intolerance and over 2 months supportive: oxygen, gentle suction, small frequent feeds or ng feeding, minimal stimulation, cardiorespiratory monitoring for apnoea cough suppressants, steroids and salbutamol have no proven benefit severe: picu, ventilation; exchange transfusion considered for extreme leucocytosis with pulmonary hypertension isolate for 5 days after starting macrolide (or 3 weeks of cough if untreated) offer chemoprophylaxis (macrolide) and vaccination to household contacts, particularly if there are infants or pregnant women in the third trimester complications apnoea, hypoxia and sudden death in young infants pneumonia (commonest cause of death), atelectasis, bronchiectasis seizures and encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage pulmonary hypertension in severe infant disease subconjunctival haemorrhage, hernias, rib fractures, weight loss prevention azithromycin clarithromycin co-trimoxazole

heart murmurs & the cardiac examination cardiology up to half of all children have an innocent (functional) murmur at some point, and these are far more common than pathological murmurs. the skill is a systematic cardiac examination that separates innocent flow murmurs from the murmur of structural heart disease and decides who needs an echocardiogram. innocent murmurs are soft, systolic, short, vary with posture and are asymptomatic all diastolic murmurs are pathological a thrill implies a pathological murmur always palpate femoral pulses in every infant with a murmur venous hum is the only common innocent continuous murmur and disappears on lying flat still murmur is a vibratory musical murmur at the lower left sternal edge fixed splitting of s2 is the hallmark of asd pulse oximetry screening picks up duct-dependent and cyanotic lesions before symptoms cyanosis or saturation below 95 percent absent or weak femoral pulses poor feeding, sweating and tachypnoea in an infant murmur with a thrill or a diastolic component murmur in a neonate in the first days with shock or collapse murmur with dysmorphic features or a family history of sudden death or cardiomyopathy pathological murmur - 8 ss systolic loud (3/6+), thrill, spreads, second sound abnormal, sound added (click), symptoms, syndrome, sick neonate definition & epidemiology cardiac examination in children general: colour (pink, pale, blue), respiratory rate and effort, sweating on feeding, growth and weight centile, dysmorphic features (down, turner, noonan, williams) hands: clubbing (late sign of cyanotic disease), capillary refill, temperature of extremities pulses: rate, rhythm and volume; always palpate brachial and femoral pulses together - radio-femoral delay suggests coarctation; collapsing pulse suggests pda or aortic regurgitation; weak or absent femorals in a neonate is a red flag blood pressure: use an appropriately sized cuff; measure the right arm and a leg if coarctation is suspected precordium: visible pulsation, hyperactive precordium (volume overload), thrills (palpable murmur, always pathological), apex position, parasternal heave (right ventricular hypertrophy) auscultation: s1, s2 (splitting, loudness of p2), added sounds (clicks, s3), then murmur - timing, loudness, site, radiation, quality, effect of position finish with the liver edge (hepatomegaly suggests heart failure), lung bases and the sacrum for oedema common innocent murmurs still murmur: age 2-7 years; vibratory, musical, low-pitched systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge; louder supine and quieter on sitting up; no radiation pulmonary flow murmur: school-age and teenagers; soft ejection systolic at the upper left sternal edge; normal s2 with normal splitting; louder in high-output states venous hum: age 3-8 years; continuous soft hum below the clavicles, loud when upright, abolished by lying down, turning the head or compressing the jugular vein peripheral pulmonary flow murmur of infancy: soft systolic murmur radiating to the axillae and back in a well infant under 6 months, usually disappears by 6 months carotid bruit: short systolic murmur heard over the neck, usually in older children features of a pathological murmur diastolic or continuous murmur (other than a venous hum) pansystolic murmur (vsd, mitral regurgitation) grade 3/6 or louder, or any palpable thrill abnormal second heart sound: fixed splitting (asd), single or loud p2 (pulmonary hypertension) ejection click (aortic or pulmonary stenosis, bicuspid valve) abnormal pulses, hepatomegaly, cyanosis, failure to thrive, tachypnoea or poor feeding investigations & management ecg and chest x-ray add little for an isolated asymptomatic murmur but help in suspected heart failure or arrhythmia four-limb blood pressures if coarctation is suspected hyperoxia test historically used to differentiate cardiac from respiratory cyanosis; echocardiography has largely replaced it discharge with reassurance once innocent features are confirmed; no follow-up or activity restriction needed

t: Acyanotic congenital heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, AVSD)
h: acyanotic congenital heart disease (vsd, asd, pda, avsd) cardiology acyanotic congenital heart disease is dominated by left-to-right shunts (vsd, asd, pda, avsd) that increase pulmonary blood flow, plus obstructive lesions. small defects are asymptomatic murmurs; large shunts cause heart failure in infancy and, if untreated, eisenmenger syndrome. vsd is the commonest congenital heart lesion; small vsds are loud and benign heart failure from large vsd or pda appears at 4-8 weeks as pulmonary resistance falls fixed split s2 with ejection murmur at the upper left sternal edge indicates asd pda gives a continuous machinery murmur and collapsing pulse; treat in preterm infants with prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors avsd is common in down syndrome and shows a superior axis on ecg eisenmenger syndrome is shunt reversal with cyanosis and contraindicates repair a smaller vsd is louder because of higher velocity through the defect pulmonary vascular disease is the reason to repair large shunts early poor feeding, sweating and tachypnoea with failure to thrive in an infant hepatomegaly and gallop rhythm indicating decompensated failure recurrent chest infections requiring admission new cyanosis in a child with a known shunt (eisenmenger) fever with a murmur and no source (endocarditis) left-to-right shunts vsd, asd, pda, avsd - the "ds" that do not turn blue until late (eisenmenger). definition & epidemiology pathophysiology ventricular septal defect (vsd) small restrictive vsd: loud harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, often with a thrill; asymptomatic; 70 percent or more close spontaneously by school age large vsd: heart failure at 4-8 weeks with poor feeding, sweating, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly and failure to thrive; softer murmur, loud p2 and a mid-diastolic flow murmur at the apex management of large vsd: diuretics, ace inhibitor, caloric supplementation (nasogastric feeding), then surgical patch closure at around 3-6 months if failure persists complications: infective endocarditis, pulmonary hypertension, aortic regurgitation (subarterial vsd), right ventricular outflow obstruction atrial septal defect (asd) ostium secundum is commonest; ostium primum is part of an avsd often asymptomatic in childhood; diagnosed on a murmur or at school age signs: soft ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge from increased flow across the pulmonary valve, fixed widely split s2, mid-diastolic tricuspid flow murmur ecg: incomplete right bundle branch block and right axis deviation (secundum); superior axis (primum) treatment: device closure in the cath lab or surgery at 3-5 years if there is right heart volume overload; small defects may close spontaneously untreated, adults develop atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension and paradoxical embolism patent ductus arteriosus (pda) the duct normally closes functionally within 24-72 hours; pda is common in preterm infants continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle, bounding or collapsing pulses, wide pulse pressure preterm infants: increased respiratory support, apnoea, poor weight gain and failure to wean ventilation; treated with indometacin, ibuprofen or paracetamol, or ligation term infants and older children: percutaneous device occlusion; small silent ducts are often left alone eisenmenger syndrome causes differential cyanosis (toes more blue than fingers) when ductal flow reverses atrioventricular septal defect (avsd) investigations & general management chest x-ray: cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings in large shunts ecg: ventricular hypertrophy patterns and axis help to define the lesion echocardiography confirms the anatomy, size of shunt and pulmonary pressure heart failure therapy: furosemide, spironolactone, ace inhibitor, high-calorie feeds endocarditis prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended but good dental hygiene is advised furosemide captopril ibuprofen (pda in preterm)

tetralogy of fallot & tet spells cardiology tetralogy of fallot is the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond infancy. it combines a large vsd with right ventricular outflow obstruction, giving a right-to-left shunt and variable cyanosis, and hypercyanotic (tet) spells are a paediatric emergency. tof = vsd, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy pulmonary stenosis severity, not the vsd, determines cyanosis boot-shaped heart with oligaemic lung fields on x-ray a tet spell is treated with knee-chest position, oxygen, fluids, morphine, then propranolol or phenylephrine the murmur gets softer during a spell as flow across the outflow stops squatting raises systemic vascular resistance and improves saturations associated with 22q11 deletion; check calcium and immune function corrective surgery at 3-6 months is standard sudden worsening cyanosis with hyperpnoea and irritability loss of consciousness, seizure or focal neurology in a cyanotic child (stroke, abscess) child with tof who is dehydrated or iron-deficient fever with headache in cyanotic chd (brain abscess) prolonged spell not responding to first-line measures tof components prove: pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, vsd. definition & epidemiology anatomy & pathophysiology large non-restrictive vsd (malalignment type) right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (infundibular, valvar, or both) overriding aorta that receives blood from both ventricles right ventricular hypertrophy (a consequence, not a primary lesion) clinical features presentation: cyanosis of increasing severity at 1-6 months as the infundibulum narrows; or an asymptomatic murmur in a pink child loud ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge from pulmonary stenosis, single s2, right ventricular heave clubbing and polycythaemia develop in older infants and children squatting in toddlers increases systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting hypercyanotic (tet) spells: sudden onset of deep cyanosis, hyperpnoea, irritability, loss of the murmur, and sometimes loss of consciousness, seizures or stroke; typically on waking, after feeding or crying complications: cerebral abscess, stroke (especially with iron-deficiency anaemia), infective endocarditis, sudden death investigations pulse oximetry: low saturations that do not rise normally in 100 percent oxygen chest x-ray: boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) with upturned apex and concave pulmonary bay; oligaemic lung fields; right-sided aortic arch in 25 percent ecg: right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy echocardiography is diagnostic and defines coronary anatomy (an anomalous left anterior descending can cross the outflow tract and alters surgery) full blood count: polycythaemia and iron status - treat iron deficiency which raises stroke risk management long-term outcome surgical survival for repaired tof exceeds 90 percent at 30 years pulmonary regurgitation after transannular patch causes right ventricular dilation and arrhythmia, needing pulmonary valve replacement in adolescence or adulthood residual vsd, ventricular tachycardia and sudden death are late risks lifelong cardiology follow-up with periodic mri assessment morphine propranolol sodium bicarbonate

t: Transposition of the great arteries & other cyanotic lesions
h: transposition of the great arteries & other cyanotic lesions cardiology in transposition of the great arteries the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left, creating two parallel circulations that are incompatible with life unless blood mixes. it is the commonest cyanotic lesion presenting in the first days of life and needs prostaglandin and early surgery. tga is the commonest cause of cyanosis presenting in the first week of life aorta from the right ventricle, pulmonary artery from the left ventricle - parallel circuits survival needs mixing via asd, vsd or pda hyperoxia test: pao2 does not rise above 15 kpa (about 100 mmhg) on 100 percent oxygen in cyanotic chd chest x-ray: egg on a string/side with narrow mediastinum start prostaglandin e1 early and arrange balloon atrial septostomy arterial switch operation is performed within the first 2-3 weeks infants of diabetic mothers are at higher risk for tga central cyanosis in the first 24-48 hours of life not responding to oxygen metabolic acidosis and collapse in the first week (duct closing) persistent oxygen saturations below 95 percent on newborn screening apnoea after starting prostaglandin infusion pulmonary oedema with cyanosis in a neonate (obstructed tapvd) five ts of cyanotic chd tetralogy of fallot, transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous return. definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features cyanosis within the first hours to days of life in an otherwise well-looking, well-grown term infant often no murmur; a single loud s2 is heard because the aorta lies anterior tachypnoea without respiratory distress (comfortable tachypnoea) rapid deterioration, metabolic acidosis and collapse when the duct closes chest x-ray: egg-on-side cardiac silhouette with narrow mediastinum and increased pulmonary vascularity ecg: right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy (normal for neonates but persistent) management resuscitate: airway and breathing support, correct acidosis and hypoglycaemia start prostaglandin e1 (alprostadil) infusion immediately to maintain ductal patency while awaiting echocardiography; watch for apnoea at higher doses echocardiography to confirm diagnosis and coronary artery pattern balloon atrial septostomy (rashkind procedure) to enlarge the atrial communication if mixing is inadequate definitive treatment: arterial switch operation (jatene) within the first 2-3 weeks of life, moving the great arteries and re-implanting the coronary arteries late complications: supravalvar pulmonary stenosis, coronary ostial stenosis, neo-aortic regurgitation other cyanotic lesions tricuspid atresia: absent tricuspid valve with hypoplastic right ventricle; cyanosis, left axis deviation on ecg; treated with staged palliation (fontan pathway) total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (tapvd): pulmonary veins drain to the right atrium; infracardiac obstructed type causes severe cyanosis and pulmonary oedema; snowman sign on x-ray in the supracardiac type truncus arteriosus: single arterial trunk gives rise to aorta and pulmonary arteries; heart failure plus mild cyanosis; associated with 22q11 deletion ebstein anomaly: apical displacement of the tricuspid valve; massive right atrium, box-shaped heart on x-ray; association with maternal lithium and wpw syndrome pulmonary atresia with intact septum: duct-dependent pulmonary circulation hypoplastic left heart is cyanotic and duct-dependent; see duct-dependent lesions alprostadil (prostaglandin e1)

coarctation, aortic stenosis & duct-dependent lesions cardiology duct-dependent lesions are those where systemic or pulmonary blood flow relies on a patent ductus arteriosus. they present as neonatal shock or cyanosis when the duct closes in the first days, and early recognition and prostaglandin e1 save lives. duct closure in the first 1-2 weeks precipitates collapse in duct-dependent lesions think of duct-dependent chd in every collapsed neonate with shock (sepsis mimics) absent or weak femoral pulses suggest coarctation prostaglandin e1 maintains ductal patency; avoid excessive oxygen coarctation is associated with turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve hlhs requires staged palliation: norwood, glenn, fontan rib notching occurs in older children but not neonates williams syndrome causes supravalvar aortic stenosis collapsed neonate with poor perfusion and absent femoral pulses grey, shocked baby at 3-10 days with acidosis, oliguria and tachypnoea cyanosis not responding to oxygen exertional syncope or chest pain in a child with aortic stenosis severe hypertension in a child with weak femoral pulses duct-dependent systemic chia: critical coarctation, hypoplastic left heart, interrupted aortic arch, aortic stenosis (critical). definition & epidemiology coarctation of the aorta narrowing at the aortic isthmus opposite the duct; associated with bicuspid aortic valve, turner syndrome and vsd neonatal (critical) coarctation: collapse at 3-14 days as the duct closes with poor feeding, grey colour, tachypnoea, absent femoral pulses, cold lower limbs, metabolic acidosis and renal failure older child: hypertension, radio-femoral delay, systolic murmur between the scapulae, headaches, leg claudication chest x-ray: rib notching in older children (collateral intercostal vessels) and figure-of-three sign treatment: prostaglandin e1, inotropic support, then surgical repair (end-to-end anastomosis); balloon dilation for recoarctation late complications: persistent hypertension, recoarctation, aneurysm, intracranial berry aneurysm aortic stenosis valvar stenosis (commonly bicuspid valve) is the commonest; subvalvar and supravalvar types occur (williams syndrome) critical neonatal aortic stenosis: duct-dependent systemic circulation with heart failure and shock children: ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, ejection click, thrill in the suprasternal notch, narrow pulse pressure symptoms: exertional chest pain, syncope, dizziness; risk of sudden death with severe stenosis during exercise treatment: balloon valvuloplasty (valvar) or surgery; restrict competitive sport in moderate to severe stenosis hypoplastic left heart syndrome (hlhs) recognition & emergency management suspect duct-dependent chd in any neonate with shock, cyanosis or heart failure, particularly in the first 2 weeks four-limb blood pressure and pulses; pre and post-ductal saturations hyperoxia test and ecg; echocardiography is definitive start prostaglandin e1 early, even before confirmation, in a collapsed neonate; avoid high-flow oxygen which constricts the duct and lowers pulmonary resistance correct acidosis, give inotropes carefully and ventilate if apnoeic after prostaglandin transfer to a specialist cardiac centre alprostadil (pge1) dopamine / adrenaline

heart failure & cardiomyopathy in children cardiology heart failure in children is most often caused by congenital heart disease with large shunts in infancy, whereas cardiomyopathy, myocarditis and rheumatic heart disease dominate later childhood. infants present with feeding difficulty, sweating and tachypnoea rather than the classic adult picture. hepatomegaly is the most reliable sign of heart failure in infants infants with heart failure present with feeding difficulty, sweating and tachypnoea large vsd, pda and avsd cause failure at 4-8 weeks as pulmonary resistance falls neonatal failure suggests duct-dependent left heart obstruction, svt or asphyxia dilated cardiomyopathy is the commonest childhood cardiomyopathy hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes sudden death in athletes treatment: diuretics, ace inhibitor, beta-blocker, nutrition, and treat the cause bnp helps differentiate cardiac from pulmonary causes of breathlessness shock with poor perfusion, oliguria and acidosis (cardiogenic shock) syncope or arrhythmia in a child with cardiomyopathy sudden-onset heart failure after a viral illness (fulminant myocarditis) infant with feeding intolerance, hepatomegaly and pallor on feeds (alcapa) family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy dynamic hocm murmur louder with standing and valsalva (less preload), softer with squatting and lying (more preload). definition & causes fetus: severe anaemia (haemolytic disease, parvovirus), tachyarrhythmia, structural lesions causing hydrops first week of life: duct-dependent left-sided obstruction (hlhs, critical coarctation, critical as), neonatal asphyxia, severe anaemia, svt, sepsis 1 week to 3 months: large left-to-right shunts (vsd, pda, avsd) as pulmonary resistance falls, anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (alcapa) older children: cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, rheumatic heart disease, kawasaki disease, anthracycline toxicity, thalassaemia iron overload, arrhythmia, hypertension, severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, post-surgical failure of the fontan circulation resource-limited settings: rheumatic heart disease, severe anaemia, malnutrition, chagas disease and endomyocardial fibrosis clinical features infants: poor feeding with breathlessness during feeds, sweating (especially forehead), tachypnoea, recurrent chest infections, faltering growth, irritability signs: tachycardia, gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly (the most reliable sign), cool peripheries, weak pulses, cardiomegaly; peripheral oedema is unusual in infants older children: exercise intolerance, fatigue, orthopnoea, abdominal pain or vomiting from gut congestion, peripheral oedema, raised jugular venous pressure wheeze can mimic bronchiolitis or asthma (cardiac asthma); always examine for hepatomegaly severe low-output state: cold shock, poor perfusion, oliguria, acidosis and hypotension investigations chest x-ray: cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio above 0.6 in infants), pulmonary venous congestion, pleural effusions ecg: ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmia, ischaemic pattern (alcapa shows anterolateral q waves) echocardiography is essential to define structure, ventricular function and ejection fraction bnp/nt-probnp raised in heart failure and helpful to separate cardiac from respiratory causes blood tests: fbc, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, troponin, thyroid function, glucose, calcium, carnitine; metabolic screen in cardiomyopathy cardiac mri and endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases of myocarditis or infiltrative disease management diuretics: furosemide (loop) and spironolactone to relieve congestion; monitor potassium ace inhibitors (captopril, enalapril) reduce afterload and preload; check renal function and potassium beta-blockers (carvedilol, bisoprolol) started cautiously once stable in chronic failure from dilated cardiomyopathy digoxin is now used less often but has a role in svt with failure and in some infants with large shunts nutritional support: high-energy feeds (130-150 kcal/kg/day), nasogastric feeding, treat reflux and anaemia inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone, adrenaline) for acute low-output states; mechanical support (ecmo, ventricular assist devices) and transplantation as bridge or destination avoid fluid overload; restrict fluids to 2/3 maintenance in acute decompensation cardiomyopathy & myocarditis dilated cardiomyopathy (commonest): idiopathic, post-viral, familial, metabolic, duchenne muscular dystrophy; poor systolic function with dilated ventricles hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: autosomal dominant sarcomere mutations; asymmetric septal hypertrophy; risk of sudden death in adolescents during exertion; infants of diabetic mothers have transient septal hypertrophy restrictive cardiomyopathy: rare; atrial enlargement and restrictive filling myocarditis: viral (coxsackie b, adenovirus, parvovirus, sars-cov-2); presents with heart failure, arrhythmia or chest pain after an illness, with raised troponin alcapa: infantile heart failure and ischaemia on feeding; treated by surgical reimplantation furosemide spironolactone enalapril carvedilol

t: Acute rheumatic fever & rheumatic heart disease
h: acute rheumatic fever & rheumatic heart disease cardiology acute rheumatic fever is an autoimmune inflammatory reaction to group a streptococcal pharyngitis in genetically susceptible children aged 5-15. it remains a major cause of acquired heart disease worldwide and is diagnosed with the revised jones criteria. arf follows group a streptococcal pharyngitis 2-4 weeks earlier diagnosis uses revised jones criteria with evidence of recent streptococcal infection carditis is the most serious manifestation and the only one that causes lasting damage migratory polyarthritis responds dramatically to aspirin chorea can occur as the only manifestation and may be delayed mitral valve is most commonly affected; mitral stenosis is the classic chronic lesion secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin prevents recurrence esr/crp are normal in pure sydenham chorea new murmur or heart failure after sore throat or fever pericarditis or pericardial effusion severe carditis with shock or complete heart block missed secondary prophylaxis in a child with known rhd fever and new murmur in rheumatic valve disease (endocarditis) jones (major criteria) joints (polyarthritis), o = heart (carditis), nodules (subcutaneous), erythema marginatum, sydenham chorea. definition & epidemiology pathogenesis diagnosis - revised jones criteria major criteria: carditis (clinical or subclinical on echo), polyarthritis (migratory in low-risk; polyarthralgia or monoarthritis acceptable in high-risk), chorea (sydenham), erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules minor criteria: fever (38.5 c or more in low-risk, 38 c in high-risk), arthralgia, raised esr/crp, prolonged pr interval on ecg carditis: new murmur (mitral regurgitation, carey coombs mid-diastolic murmur, aortic regurgitation), cardiomegaly, pericardial rub or effusion, heart failure sydenham chorea: involuntary purposeless movements, emotional lability, hypotonia, milkmaid grip; may appear months after infection with normal inflammatory markers erythema marginatum: pink non-itchy rings on trunk and proximal limbs; subcutaneous nodules over bony prominences and extensor tendons investigations aso titre (peaks at 3-6 weeks), anti-dnase b, throat swab; esr and crp raised ecg: prolonged pr interval (first-degree heart block) echocardiography to detect carditis and baseline valve damage, including subclinical carditis blood cultures if endocarditis is suspected; exclude juvenile arthritis, sle, septic arthritis, reactive arthritis management benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units im single dose (or oral penicillin v for 10 days) to eradicate streptococci anti-inflammatory: aspirin or naproxen for arthritis and mild carditis; steroids (prednisolone) for severe carditis with heart failure heart failure management with diuretics and ace inhibitors; surgery for severe valve disease chorea: valproate or carbamazepine in severe cases, rest and a calm environment bed rest during active carditis; return to activity guided by markers and echo secondary prophylaxis is essential: benzathine benzylpenicillin every 3-4 weeks (or oral penicillin v twice daily); duration at least 5 years after the last attack or until age 21, whichever is longer, and for 10 years or until age 40 (sometimes lifelong) in patients with carditis or established valve disease complications & prognosis rheumatic heart disease: chronic mitral stenosis (commonest long-term lesion), mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation complications include atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension and infective endocarditis recurrences are likely without prophylaxis, with worsening valve damage each time prevention: prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis, improved housing and community-level screening programmes benzathine benzylpenicillin (treatment) benzathine benzylpenicillin (prophylaxis) aspirin prednisolone

kawasaki disease cardiology kawasaki disease is an acute medium-vessel vasculitis of young children and the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. prompt treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin within the first 10 days reduces coronary artery aneurysms from about 25 percent to under 5 percent. fever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 principal features (crash: conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue, hands/feet) treat with ivig 2 g/kg within 10 days to reduce coronary aneurysms coronary artery aneurysms are the major complication thrombocytosis occurs in the second to third week incomplete kd is more common under 1 year and has the highest aneurysm risk ivig resistance (fever persisting 36 hours) needs second-line therapy live vaccines are delayed 11 months after ivig echocardiography at diagnosis and 1-2 and 4-6 weeks fever 5 days or more in an infant with irritability and rash (incomplete kd) signs of shock, hypotension or heart failure (kd shock syndrome or mis-c) coronary aneurysms, particularly giant (8 mm or more) ongoing fever 36 hours after ivig chest pain, ecg changes or raised troponin suggesting infarction crash and burn conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue (oral changes), hands and feet changes - all with fever for 5 days or more. definition & epidemiology clinical features and diagnosis bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection with limbal sparing oral changes: red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, erythematous oropharynx polymorphous rash (maculopapular, erythema multiforme-like, scarlatiniform; not vesicular) extremity changes: erythema and oedema of hands and feet in the acute phase, periungual desquamation in weeks 2-3 cervical lymphadenopathy (at least 1.5 cm, usually unilateral, single node) other: marked irritability, sterile pyuria, abdominal pain, hydrops of the gallbladder, aseptic meningitis, arthritis, bcg scar erythema in young infants incomplete kawasaki disease investigations inflammatory markers: raised crp and esr, neutrophilia, anaemia, thrombocytosis in the second week (platelets often exceed 500) low albumin, raised alt, sterile pyuria, raised troponin or nt-probnp in some echocardiography at diagnosis, at 1-2 weeks and at 4-6 weeks; additional imaging if aneurysms are present ecg for arrhythmia and ischaemia coronary artery z-scores classify involvement: dilatation, small (z 2.5-5), medium (z 5-10), giant aneurysm (z 10 or above or 8 mm or more) management intravenous immunoglobulin (ivig) 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10-12 hours, ideally within 10 days of fever onset (also if later with ongoing inflammation or aneurysm) aspirin: moderate to high dose in the acute phase (30-50 mg/kg/day divided in some protocols, or 3-5 mg/kg/day in others), then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg once daily antiplatelet until 6-8 weeks if no coronary changes ivig-resistant disease (persistent fever 36 hours after infusion): second dose of ivig, corticosteroids (prednisolone or methylprednisolone), or infliximab/anakinra steroids as primary adjunct for high-risk patients (e.g. japanese risk score) large aneurysms: anticoagulation with warfarin or low molecular weight heparin plus aspirin; lifelong follow-up and cardiology input avoid live vaccines (mmr, varicella) for 11 months after ivig; give annual influenza vaccine in children on aspirin to avoid reye syndrome complications & prognosis coronary aneurysms (typically weeks 2-4), thrombosis, myocardial infarction, sudden death myocarditis, pericardial effusion, valve regurgitation, arrhythmia kawasaki shock syndrome and macrophage activation syndrome in a minority most children without coronary involvement recover fully; those with giant aneurysms need lifelong surveillance intravenous immunoglobulin aspirin (low dose) prednisolone

arrhythmias (svt, long qt, heart block) cardiology paediatric arrhythmias range from benign sinus arrhythmia to life-threatening conditions. supraventricular tachycardia is the commonest symptomatic tachyarrhythmia in children, whereas long qt syndrome and complete heart block are less common but important causes of syncope and sudden death. svt in infants has a rate above 220 per minute and a narrow qrs with no rate variability vagal manoeuvres first, adenosine second, synchronised cardioversion if shocked adenosine is given as a fast bolus with a saline flush and warns of transient asystole wpw shows a short pr interval and delta wave on sinus rhythm lqt1 is triggered by exercise (swimming), lqt2 by noise, lqt3 by sleep jervell and lange-nielsen: long qt with congenital deafness congenital complete heart block is caused by maternal anti-ro/la antibodies avoid verapamil for svt in infants collapse or syncope during exercise or swimming family history of sudden death under 40 or unexplained drowning tachycardia with shock or heart failure wide-complex tachycardia in a child heart rate persistently below 50 per minute with symptoms svt management ladder vagal manoeuvres -> adenosine 100/200/300 micrograms/kg -> synchronised dc shock 1 then 2 j/kg if unstable. normal rhythm and paediatric ecg supraventricular tachycardia (svt) most often atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia through an accessory pathway, including wolff-parkinson-white syndrome (delta wave and short pr on sinus rhythm), or av nodal re-entry in older children infants: poor feeding, pallor, irritability, sweating, tachypnoea, heart failure if prolonged (over 24 hours); older children: palpitations, chest discomfort, dizziness rate typically 220-300 per minute in infants (above 220) and 150-250 in older children, narrow complex, regular, with no beat-to-beat variability and abrupt onset and termination differentiate from sinus tachycardia (rate under 220 in infants, variable with activity, p waves present, identifiable cause) atrial flutter, ectopic atrial tachycardia and junctional ectopic tachycardia are other forms management of svt stable child: vagal manoeuvres - ice-cold water to the face (diving reflex) for infants, valsalva or blowing against resistance in older children; never apply carotid massage or eyeball pressure in infants adenosine rapid iv bolus via large proximal vein followed by saline flush: 100 micrograms/kg, then 200 micrograms/kg, then 300 micrograms/kg (maximum single dose 12 mg) unstable (shock, severely reduced consciousness, heart failure): synchronised dc cardioversion 1 j/kg, then 2 j/kg; give adenosine first if iv access is immediately available and it does not delay cardioversion chronic prophylaxis for recurrent episodes: propranolol, flecainide or amiodarone; infants often outgrow svt by 1 year older children with recurrent svt or wpw: radiofrequency catheter ablation avoid verapamil in infants under 1 year because of the risk of cardiovascular collapse long qt syndrome (lqts) diagnosis: ecg with qtc, exercise testing, genetic testing and family screening treatment: beta-blockers (nadolol, propranolol) for all symptomatic and most asymptomatic patients, avoid qt-prolonging drugs and trigger activities, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for survivors of cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope on therapy, left cardiac sympathetic denervation treat torsades acutely with iv magnesium sulphate sudden unexplained syncope during exercise or from loud noise needs an ecg for qtc heart block first degree: prolonged pr interval; seen in rheumatic fever, lyme disease, myocarditis and in normal children; no treatment second degree mobitz i (wenckebach): progressive pr lengthening then dropped beat; often benign in children at rest second degree mobitz ii: fixed pr with intermittent dropped beats; risk of progression, needs pacing third degree (complete) heart block: av dissociation; congenital form is caused by transplacental maternal anti-ro/ssa and anti-la/ssb antibodies (sle, sjogren syndrome) damaging the fetal conduction system; may also occur in structural heart disease or after cardiac surgery congenital complete heart block: fetal bradycardia (60-80 per minute), hydrops fetalis; pacemaker needed for symptomatic infants, heart rate below 50-55, wide qrs or low cardiac output other rhythm problems premature atrial and ventricular ectopics: common in healthy children, disappear on exercise, need no treatment; investigate if frequent, multiform, couplets or associated with syncope or cardiomyopathy ventricular tachycardia in children is usually pathological - consider channelopathy, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, post-surgical scar, electrolyte disturbance or drug effect brugada syndrome and catecholaminergic polymorphic vt cause arrhythmic syncope and sudden death in adolescents adenosine propranolol magnesium sulphate

infective endocarditis cardiology infective endocarditis in children is an infection of the endocardium or heart valves, mainly in those with congenital heart disease, prosthetic material or, in resource-limited settings, rheumatic valve disease. it is uncommon but serious, with prolonged fever, new murmurs and embolic phenomena, and requires blood cultures before antibiotics. fever with a murmur and cardiac risk factors is endocarditis until proven otherwise viridans streptococci are the commonest cause in native valve disease; s. aureus is more virulent take 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics modified duke criteria guide diagnosis echocardiography detects vegetations; a negative echo does not exclude disease treat for 4-6 weeks with iv antibiotics surgery is needed for heart failure, abscess or resistant infection routine antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer recommended in the uk; dental hygiene is crucial fever for more than a week in a child with congenital heart disease new regurgitant murmur or signs of heart failure with fever focal neurological signs (septic emboli, stroke) persistent bacteraemia despite treatment prolonged pr interval on ecg (aortic root abscess) signs of endocarditis - from jane fever, roth spots, osler nodes, murmur, janeway lesions, anaemia, nail-bed haemorrhages (splinters), emboli. definition & epidemiology aetiology viridans streptococci (oral flora): commonest cause in native valve disease and after dental procedures staphylococcus aureus: acute, aggressive, common in healthy valves, lines and post-operative infection; includes mrsa coagulase-negative staphylococci: prosthetic material and lines enterococcus, hacek organisms (haemophilus, aggregatibacter, cardiobacterium, eikenella, kingella), candida and other fungi in immunosuppressed or neonatal patients culture-negative endocarditis: prior antibiotics, fastidious organisms such as bartonella and coxiella clinical features subacute onset: prolonged low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss, night sweats, anaemia, arthralgia acute (s. aureus): high fever, rapid valve destruction and heart failure new or changing murmur (regurgitant lesion) in a child with fever embolic and immunological phenomena: splinter haemorrhages, osler nodes (painful pulp nodules), janeway lesions (painless palm and sole macules), roth spots (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres), petechiae, clubbing, splenomegaly, haematuria complications: heart failure, stroke or mycotic aneurysm, abscess, renal infarct or glomerulonephritis, osteomyelitis, pericarditis investigations and diagnosis fbc (anaemia, leucocytosis), esr and crp raised, urinalysis for haematuria, complement and rheumatoid factor in prolonged cases ecg for prolonged pr interval suggesting aortic root abscess ct/mri brain if neurological signs management prolonged iv antibiotics through a central line, guided by cultures and sensitivities: 4-6 weeks for native valve, 6 weeks or longer for prosthetic valve empirical regimen for native valve while awaiting cultures (stable child): benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus gentamicin; add flucloxacillin or vancomycin if staphylococcal infection is likely; seek microbiology advice streptococcus viridans: benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (with gentamicin in some regimens) s. aureus: high-dose flucloxacillin (vancomycin for mrsa) with rifampicin and gentamicin for prosthetic material surgery: heart failure not responding to medicine, uncontrolled infection, large or mobile vegetations with embolism, abscess, prosthetic valve dysfunction, fungal infection anticoagulants are generally avoided because of haemorrhagic stroke risk prevention benzylpenicillin gentamicin flucloxacillin

gastroenteritis & dehydration gastroenterology & hepatology acute gastroenteritis is sudden-onset diarrhoea with or without vomiting, usually viral, and is a leading cause of childhood admission and death worldwide. the key task is to assess dehydration accurately and rehydrate, preferably orally, while recognising the child who needs urgent intravenous fluids or a different diagnosis. most gastroenteritis is viral and self-limiting; treatment is rehydration, not antibiotics ors is first line for mild to moderate dehydration; iv fluids for shock or failed ors shock needs a 10 ml/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus and senior help; hypotension is a late sign continue breast feeding and early normal feeding during illness zinc supplementation reduces duration in low-income settings (who) bloody diarrhoea: think shigella, campylobacter, stec and watch for hus do not give antimotility or antiemetic drugs routinely hypernatraemia should be corrected slowly over 48 hours rotavirus vaccine (oral) is given at 2 and 3 months in the uk shock: reduced consciousness, mottled cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill bilious vomiting or abdominal distension suggesting obstruction bloody diarrhoea with falling urine output, pallor or oedema (hus) severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen or redcurrant jelly stool under 3 months of age, or fever with a toxic appearance persistent vomiting preventing oral rehydration signs of dehydration sunken eyes, tachycardia, reduced skin turgor, irritable/lethargic, dry mucosa, oliguria - the features of clinical dehydration used on the ward definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features & assessment of dehydration history: duration, stool frequency and blood, vomiting (bile?), urine output, oral intake, sick contacts, travel, antibiotics, food exposure no clinical dehydration: alert, normal urine output, moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor and capillary refill clinical dehydration: appears unwell or deteriorating, irritable or lethargic, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, tachypnoea, reduced skin turgor, normal blood pressure, reduced urine output (about 5 percent or more fluid deficit) shock (about 10 percent or more deficit): decreased level of consciousness, pale or mottled skin, cold extremities, tachycardia, weak pulses, prolonged capillary refill, hypotension (late sign) who scheme: some dehydration (restless or irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly) versus severe (lethargic or unconscious, drinks poorly or not at all, skin pinch very slow) always consider the differential: surgical abdomen, uti, dka, sepsis, meningitis, intussusception and hus in a child with bloody diarrhoea investigations most children need none; assessment is clinical stool culture if septic appearance, blood or mucus in stool, immunocompromise, or diarrhoea persisting beyond 7 days; send for virology and parasites if relevant (travel, persistent) u and e, glucose, blood gas if shock, intravenous fluids required, or clinical features suggest hypernatraemia blood culture if septic; consider hus screen (fbc, film, creatinine) if stec suspected do not routinely measure electrolytes in mild cases management zinc: who recommends zinc 20 mg daily for 10-14 days (10 mg daily in under 6 months) in developing countries to reduce duration and severity antibiotics are not routinely indicated; give for cholera, shigellosis, severe invasive disease, systemic illness, or immunocompromise antiemetics and antimotility drugs are not recommended in children hand hygiene, exclusion from school or nursery until 48 hours after last loose stool; stec and shigella need specific public health clearance complications & prognosis hypernatraemic dehydration (sodium above 150): doughy skin, irritability, jittery; correct slowly over 48 hours to avoid cerebral oedema and seizures hyponatraemia from excessive hypotonic fluids secondary lactose intolerance, post-infectious malabsorption haemolytic uraemic syndrome after stec; guillain-barre after campylobacter; reactive arthritis prevention: rotavirus vaccine, breast feeding, clean water and sanitation, handwashing; most children recover fully in under a week oral rehydration solution sodium chloride 0.9 percent bolus zinc sulphate (who)

gastro-oesophageal reflux & vomiting in infants gastroenterology & hepatology gastro-oesophageal reflux is the passage of gastric contents into the oesophagus and is extremely common and physiological in infants. gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (gord) is present when reflux causes troublesome symptoms or complications, and the main skill is separating benign regurgitation from disease and from other causes of vomiting. most infant regurgitation is physiological and resolves by 12-18 months thriving, happy infant needs reassurance and feeding advice only bilious vomiting is surgical until proven otherwise projectile vomiting at 2-8 weeks suggests pyloric stenosis trial extensively hydrolysed formula if allergy suspected ppis do not help isolated crying or irritability in infants faltering growth, haematemesis or dysphagia warrant further investigation high-risk groups: preterm, neurodisability, repaired oesophageal atresia bilious (green) vomiting projectile vomiting with weight loss (pyloric stenosis) haematemesis or blood in stool faltering growth or dehydration abdominal distension, fever or bulging fontanelle onset of vomiting after 6 months of age posseting vs vomiting thriving, happy, effortless = benign reflux (happy spitter); growth failure, distress, blood or bile = investigate definition & epidemiology differential diagnosis of vomiting in infants overfeeding and feeding technique cow milk protein allergy (often with eczema, blood or mucus in stool, irritability) pyloric stenosis (projectile non-bilious vomiting, 2-8 weeks) intestinal obstruction, malrotation (bilious vomiting) infection: uti, gastroenteritis, meningitis, otitis media, sepsis raised intracranial pressure; metabolic disease, adrenal crisis (cah) non-accidental injury and medication causes clinical features effortless regurgitation after feeds in a thriving, happy infant (so-called happy spitter) - requires reassurance only gord: back arching, crying with feeds, feed refusal, hoarse cry, chronic cough, wheeze, recurrent chest infections haematemesis or anaemia suggests oesophagitis faltering growth is a sign of significant disease sandifer syndrome: head tilt and neck arching mimicking seizures apnoea or apparent life-threatening events are rarely due to reflux investigations management complications & prognosis oesophagitis, stricture, barrett oesophagus (rare in children) faltering growth, iron deficiency anaemia aspiration pneumonia, worsening asthma prognosis: most infants resolve by 12-18 months; older children and neurologically impaired children may have persistent disease alginate (gaviscon infant) omeprazole

infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis gastroenterology & hepatology infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction in the first weeks of life. it presents with progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting and is cured by pyloromyotomy after correction of metabolic derangement. projectile non-bilious vomiting at 2-8 weeks in a hungry infant male to female ratio about 4:1;
