first-born boys hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis ultrasound confirms diagnosis; muscle thickness 3-4 mm or more correct electrolytes before surgery ramstedt pyloromyotomy is curative early erythromycin exposure is a recognised risk palpable olive found during a test feed bilious vomiting (not pyloric stenosis - exclude malrotation) severe dehydration or lethargy seizures from hypochloraemic alkalosis or hypoglycaemia apnoea after anaesthesia in uncorrected alkalosis haematemesis or abdominal distension pyloric stenosis picture projectile, non-bilious, hungry, boy, 2-8 weeks, olive - together with hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis definition & epidemiology clinical features projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds, progressively worsening, starting at 2-8 weeks infant remains hungry and feeds eagerly after vomiting weight loss or poor weight gain, dehydration constipation, reduced stool frequency and prolonged jaundice (unconjugated) in some visible gastric peristalsis (left to right waves) across the upper abdomen palpable olive-sized pyloric mass in the right upper quadrant during a test feed (best felt as the infant feeds, stomach decompressed) pathophysiology & metabolic effects investigations ultrasound is the investigation of choice: pyloric muscle thickness above 3-4 mm, canal length above 15-17 mm venous blood gas and electrolytes: low chloride, low potassium, high bicarbonate, raised ph test feed if ultrasound unavailable (palpate for the olive) barium meal is rarely needed (string sign, double track sign) check glucose, bilirubin and urea management complications & prognosis persistent vomiting after surgery in the first 24-48 hours is common and usually settles mucosal perforation, wound infection, incomplete myotomy (rare) prolonged unconjugated jaundice resolves after surgery excellent prognosis with normal growth 0.9 percent sodium chloride with 5 percent dextrose

intussusception gastroenterology & hepatology intussusception is telescoping of one segment of bowel into the next, most commonly ileocolic, causing obstruction and ischaemia. it is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in infants aged 3 months to 3 years and needs prompt reduction. peak age 5-9 months, boys more than girls ileocolic intussusception is commonest triad: colicky pain, vomiting and redcurrant jelly stool - present in only a minority ultrasound shows target sign and is diagnostic air enema reduction is first-line therapy if stable surgery for peritonitis, perforation or failed reduction consider lead points in children over 2 years think of it in any pale, lethargic infant with episodic pain shock or reduced consciousness peritonitis or abdominal rigidity bilious vomiting and distension redcurrant jelly stool abdominal mass with severe pain recurrence of symptoms after reduction intussusception signs colicky pain, currant jelly, sausage mass, pallor/lethargy definition & epidemiology clinical features sudden severe colicky abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs, episodes every 15-20 minutes with pallor between episodes the infant may be quiet, lethargic or limp vomiting, which becomes bilious as obstruction progresses redcurrant jelly stool (blood and mucus), a late sign palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant with an empty right iliac fossa (dance sign) dehydration, shock, abdominal distension in late presentation atypical presentations: lethargy, collapse, or diarrhoea mistaken for gastroenteritis investigations abdominal ultrasound is first line: target or doughnut sign on transverse view, pseudokidney sign on longitudinal view; sensitivity about 98-100 percent plain abdominal x-ray is non-specific; may show absent caecal gas, soft tissue mass, obstruction or perforation blood gas, electrolytes, fbc, group and save; blood cultures if septic contrast or air enema both diagnoses and treats management complications & prognosis bowel ischaemia, necrosis, perforation and peritonitis sepsis and shock recurrence; consider lead point investigation after a second or third episode, or in older children excellent prognosis if treated within 24-48 hours; mortality is high if untreated morphine or iv paracetamol broad-spectrum iv antibiotics

malrotation, volvulus & intestinal atresias gastroenterology & hepatology malrotation is incomplete rotation and fixation of the midgut during embryogenesis, predisposing to midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency. intestinal atresias and other causes of neonatal obstruction present with bilious vomiting, distension and failure to pass meconium, and bilious vomiting must always be treated as surgical until proven otherwise. bilious vomiting = surgical emergency until proven otherwise malrotation with volvulus can cause midgut infarction within hours upper gi contrast study is the gold standard for malrotation double bubble sign indicates duodenal atresia; associated with down syndrome meconium ileus strongly suggests cystic fibrosis ladd procedure is the operation for malrotation start ng decompression, fluids and antibiotics before surgery failure to pass meconium in 48 hours demands investigation bilious vomiting at any age abdominal distension with tenderness or discoloured abdominal wall blood per rectum or shock in a neonate no meconium passed in 24-48 hours imperforate anus or abnormal perineum antenatal polyhydramnios with vomiting vacterl vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, renal, limb anomalies - screen when one is found definition & epidemiology clinical features bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate or infant - the cardinal sign malrotation with volvulus: sudden onset, abdominal distension, tenderness, blood in stool, shock and sepsis from ischaemia duodenal atresia: bilious or non-bilious vomiting (depends on site relative to ampulla), minimal distension, antenatal polyhydramnios jejunal and ileal atresia: distension, bilious vomiting, delayed or no meconium passage anorectal malformation: absent or misplaced anus, no meconium passed; vacterl association meconium ileus: distended abdomen with doughy loops, delayed meconium, cystic fibrosis in nearly all late presentation of malrotation: intermittent vomiting, failure to thrive, chronic abdominal pain investigations abdominal x-ray: double bubble sign in duodenal atresia; multiple dilated loops in jejunoileal atresia; paucity of gas in volvulus; soap-bubble appearance in meconium ileus upper gi contrast study is the gold standard for malrotation: abnormal position of the duodenojejunal flexure (to the right of the spine and not at the level of the pylorus), corkscrew appearance in volvulus ultrasound may show reversal of the superior mesenteric vein and artery relationship (whirlpool sign) bloods: blood gas, lactate, electrolytes, fbc, clotting, cross match; cultures antenatal scan and genetic evaluation for down syndrome or cystic fibrosis (sweat test or genetic panel) management complications & prognosis midgut necrosis and short bowel syndrome, requiring parenteral nutrition sepsis, perforation, necrotising enterocolitis adhesive obstruction after surgery good outcome with early diagnosis; delayed diagnosis carries high mortality broad-spectrum iv antibiotics 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus

hirschsprung disease gastroenterology & hepatology hirschsprung disease is congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, causing functional obstruction. it typically presents with delayed passage of meconium in a term neonate and can be complicated by life-threatening enterocolitis. delayed meconium beyond 48 hours in a term infant suggests hirschsprung disease aganglionosis begins at the anus and extends proximally rectal suction biopsy is the gold standard down syndrome is the commonest chromosomal association explosive stool on rectal examination (blast sign) enterocolitis is life-threatening: fever, distension, diarrhoea treat with pull-through surgery (soave, swenson, duhamel) ret mutations; link to men2a fever with abdominal distension and diarrhoea (enterocolitis) bilious vomiting shock or sepsis no meconium for 48 hours down syndrome with constipation from birth hirschsprung features delayed meconium + distension + empty rectum with explosive release + biopsy shows no ganglion cells definition & epidemiology clinical features failure to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth in a term infant (over 90 percent of healthy babies pass meconium by 24 hours) abdominal distension and bilious vomiting in neonatal obstruction rectal examination followed by explosive release of stool and gas (blast sign) with an empty narrow rectum chronic constipation from early infancy, abdominal distension, faltering growth in later presentation enterocolitis: fever, explosive foul-smelling diarrhoea, abdominal distension, shock differs from functional constipation: onset from birth, no soiling, no faecal impaction in rectum investigations abdominal x-ray: dilated bowel loops with absent rectal gas contrast enema: transition zone between narrow aganglionic segment and dilated bowel; delayed evacuation at 24 hours rectal suction biopsy (at least 2 cm above the dentate line) is the gold standard: absent ganglion cells, hypertrophied nerve trunks and increased acetylcholinesterase staining anorectal manometry: absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex (older children) genetic testing (ret) if familial or syndromic management complications & prognosis enterocolitis (up to 30 percent), peaks before surgery but can occur afterward; major cause of mortality post-operative constipation, soiling, anastomotic stricture long-segment or total colonic aganglionosis with malabsorption most children achieve good continence but some need long-term bowel management broad-spectrum antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or cefotaxime plus metronidazole)

prolonged jaundice & biliary atresia gastroenterology & hepatology jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days if preterm) is prolonged jaundice and requires a split bilirubin to identify conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. biliary atresia is the most important cause: progressive obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts, where outcome depends on surgery (kasai) before 60 days of age. any baby jaundiced beyond 14 days (21 preterm) needs a split bilirubin conjugated bilirubin above 25 micromol/l is always pathological pale stools with dark urine strongly suggest biliary atresia kasai before 60 days gives the best outcome biliary atresia is the leading indication for paediatric liver transplant breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and a diagnosis of exclusion check thyroid function and urine culture in prolonged jaundice give vitamin k and supplement fat-soluble vitamins pale stools and dark urine conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia hepatomegaly or splenomegaly bleeding or bruising from coagulopathy jaundice with poor feeding, lethargy or fever (sepsis, metabolic) jaundice persisting after 2 weeks without split bilirubin prolonged jaundice bloods split bilirubin, fbc and film, coombs, g6pd, tfts, urine culture - the standard prolonged jaundice screen definition & epidemiology causes of prolonged jaundice unconjugated: breast milk jaundice (commonest), haemolysis (abo, rh, g6pd deficiency, spherocytosis), hypothyroidism, infection (uti, sepsis), gilbert and crigler-najjar, pyloric stenosis, prematurity conjugated: biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis (idiopathic, cmv, other torch infections), choledochal cyst, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, total parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis, alagille syndrome, pfic always check for pale stools and dark urine clinical features of biliary atresia infant is initially well and thriving with jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks pale (acholic) stools and dark urine - the key clinical clue hepatomegaly, later splenomegaly from portal hypertension progressive cholestasis with fat malabsorption, poor growth, pruritus, coagulopathy (vitamin k deficiency bleeding) check the stool colour chart in the personal child health record investigations split bilirubin (conjugated and unconjugated) in all babies jaundiced beyond 14 days (21 if preterm) liver function tests: raised ggt, alkaline phosphatase; ast and alt modestly elevated; coagulation profile full blood count, blood film, g6pd, direct coombs test, thyroid function, urine culture, blood culture if unwell alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype, galactosaemia screen, cmv, sweat test abdominal ultrasound: absent or small gallbladder, triangular cord sign, abnormal gallbladder contraction after feeding liver biopsy: bile duct proliferation, bile plugging, portal fibrosis. intraoperative cholangiogram confirms diagnosis management complications & prognosis cholangitis, portal hypertension with varices, ascites cirrhosis and liver failure hepatopulmonary syndrome, growth failure and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency without surgery death in the first 2 years is almost universal vitamin k ursodeoxycholic acid

coeliac disease gastroenterology & hepatology coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible people (hla-dq2/dq8). it causes villous atrophy and malabsorption and is treated with a lifelong strict gluten-free diet. gluten (wheat, barley, rye) triggers villous atrophy in hla-dq2/dq8 individuals first-line test: iga ttg with total iga on a gluten-containing diet biopsy-free diagnosis is possible if ttg is 10 times uln with positive ema associated with type 1 diabetes, down syndrome, turner and williams syndromes never start gluten-free diet before testing lifelong strict gluten-free diet dermatitis herpetiformis is coeliac skin disease iga deficiency gives false-negative ttg-iga faltering growth with malabsorption severe anaemia persistent diarrhoea with weight loss abdominal pain with distension and fatty stools neurological features (ataxia, neuropathy) gluten sources brow - barley, rye, oats (contamination), wheat definition & epidemiology clinical features classical (toddler): chronic diarrhoea, abdominal distension, faltering growth, muscle wasting (especially buttocks), irritability, anorexia older children: abdominal pain, constipation, short stature, delayed puberty, iron deficiency anaemia, recurrent mouth ulcers, fatigue extra-intestinal: dermatitis herpetiformis, dental enamel defects, osteopenia, raised transaminases, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, infertility many children are asymptomatic and detected by screening high-risk groups investigations serology while on a gluten-containing diet: iga anti-tissue transglutaminase (ttg-iga) with total iga; if iga deficient use igg-based tests (igg ttg or deamidated gliadin peptide) anti-endomysial antibody (ema) as confirmatory small bowel biopsy (duodenal) shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (marsh classification) biopsy-free diagnosis in symptomatic children if ttg-iga is 10 times the upper limit of normal or more, with positive ema on a second blood sample (espghan criteria), and nice and bspghan agree for selected cases hla-dq2/dq8 typing (high negative predictive value) in uncertain cases baseline: fbc, ferritin, folate, b12, vitamin d, thyroid function, lfts, bone health as indicated management complications & prognosis growth failure, delayed puberty, osteoporosis if untreated iron deficiency anaemia, vitamin deficiencies refractory coeliac disease and enteropathy-associated t-cell lymphoma in adults (very rare in children) excellent prognosis with strict adherence; poor adherence in adolescence is common iron / vitamin d / calcium

inflammatory bowel disease in children gastroenterology & hepatology inflammatory bowel disease (crohn disease, ulcerative colitis and ibd-unclassified) is chronic relapsing gut inflammation that often begins in adolescence. in children it frequently presents with growth failure and delayed puberty as well as abdominal symptoms, and needs specialist multidisciplinary care. crohn disease: transmural, skip lesions, mouth to anus, granulomas, perianal disease ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation from rectum, bloody diarrhoea, psc association faltering growth or delayed puberty can be the only presenting feature of crohn disease faecal calprotectin helps differentiate ibd from functional disease exclusive enteral nutrition induces remission in crohn disease diagnosis requires endoscopy with biopsies check tpmt before thiopurine therapy acute severe colitis is an emergency (iv steroids; rescue therapy) acute severe colitis: over 6 bloody stools daily, fever, tachycardia, anaemia abdominal distension and tenderness (toxic megacolon, perforation) perianal abscess growth arrest or weight loss signs of intestinal obstruction crohn vs uc crohn = can be anywhere, rectum spared often, obstruction, hole (fistula), narrowing, granulomas; uc = ulcers continuous, colon only, from rectum, with blood definition & epidemiology clinical features crohn disease: abdominal pain (often right lower quadrant), diarrhoea (often non-bloody), weight loss, growth failure, delayed puberty, perianal disease (fissures, fistulae, skin tags), mouth ulcers, fever, anorexia ulcerative colitis: bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus, abdominal pain, anaemia growth failure may precede gut symptoms in crohn disease; always plot height and weight and pubertal stage extra-intestinal: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, arthritis (peripheral or sacroiliitis), uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis (uc more than crohn), aphthous stomatitis, finger clubbing investigations bloods: fbc (anaemia, thrombocytosis), crp, esr, albumin (low), ferritin, vitamin d, b12 faecal calprotectin: sensitive marker of intestinal inflammation, useful for screening and monitoring; stool culture and c. difficile exclude infection upper gi endoscopy and ileocolonoscopy with biopsies are the diagnostic standard (porto criteria): crohn - skip lesions, cobblestoning, non-caseating granulomas; uc - continuous inflammation from rectum, crypt abscesses, no granulomas mr enterography or small bowel capsule to assess small bowel disease; mri pelvis for perianal disease bone age, dexa when growth impaired; tpmt status before thiopurines; screen for tb and viral serology before biologics management complications & prognosis growth failure, delayed puberty, osteopenia strictures, fistulae, abscesses, perforation (crohn); toxic megacolon and haemorrhage (uc) primary sclerosing cholangitis and colorectal cancer risk in uc with long disease duration (surveillance colonoscopy) medication side effects: steroid toxicity, thiopurine myelosuppression and lymphoma, infection with biologics chronic relapsing course; psychosocial effects and school absence exclusive enteral nutrition prednisolone mesalazine azathioprine

constipation & encopresis gastroenterology & hepatology constipation is very common in children and is functional in over 95 percent. untreated, it leads to faecal impaction and overflow soiling (encopresis), producing a vicious cycle of painful defaecation and stool withholding. treatment is disimpaction, maintenance laxatives and behavioural support. over 95 percent of paediatric constipation is functional overflow soiling is a sign of constipation, not diarrhoea macrogol (polyethylene glycol) is first-line for disimpaction and maintenance delayed meconium or onset from birth suggests hirschsprung disease do not stop laxatives early; continue for weeks to months avoid routine abdominal x-ray and rectal examination examine the back, anus and lower limbs for red flags reward charts and positive toilet routine are essential onset in first weeks of life or delayed meconium abnormal spine or neurological signs in legs faltering growth, vomiting or abdominal distension abnormal anal anatomy or perianal disease bilious vomiting or bleeding with diarrhoea constipation vicious cycle pain -> withholding -> hard stool -> rectal stretching -> overflow -> more pain definition & epidemiology clinical features infrequent stools, hard pellet or large stools, straining, painful defaecation, blood on stool surface from anal fissure abdominal pain, distension, palpable faecal mass, poor appetite overflow soiling: loose, offensive stool leakage, often unaware, with underwear staining stool withholding postures (tiptoeing, stiff-legged, hiding) urinary symptoms: frequency, uti, enuresis normal growth, normal neurological examination, normal anal position and tone red flags for organic disease delayed meconium (over 48 hours) or onset from birth: hirschsprung disease ribbon stool, abdominal distension, failure to thrive abnormal lumbosacral spine (sacral dimple, hair tuft), abnormal lower limb neurology, absent anal reflex: spinal cord pathology, tethered cord anteriorly displaced anus, anal stenosis, perianal scarring (crohn disease, abuse) systemic: hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, hypercalcaemia, cystic fibrosis, cow milk allergy, lead poisoning neurodisability and medications (opioids, anticholinergics) investigations management complications & prognosis anal fissure, rectal prolapse, haemorrhoids (rare) recurrent uti, enuresis, bladder dysfunction psychosocial effects and bullying from soiling most children recover; about one third have persistent symptoms into adolescence macrogol (polyethylene glycol 3350 with electrolytes) senna or sodium picosulfate lactulose

appendicitis & the acute abdomen gastroenterology & hepatology appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency in childhood and its diagnosis is clinical, with young children often presenting late with perforation. the acute abdomen in children has a wide differential that varies with age, and careful serial examination is key. classic migration from umbilicus to right iliac fossa young children present late with perforation ultrasound is first-line imaging; avoid ct where possible always exclude uti, pneumonia, dka and testicular torsion examine the testes in every boy with abdominal pain appendicectomy plus antibiotics is standard serial examination improves accuracy pregnancy test in all post-pubertal girls generalised peritonitis or rigid abdomen shock or sepsis persistent bilious vomiting testicular pain or swelling peritonism with rebound tenderness age under 5 years with abdominal pain and vomiting alvarado score (mantrels) migration of pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, tenderness rif, rebound, elevated temperature, leucocytosis, shift to left definition & epidemiology clinical features periumbilical colicky pain migrating to the right iliac fossa (mcburney point) with constant severe pain anorexia, nausea, vomiting (after pain onset), low-grade fever 37.5-38.5 c tenderness with guarding, rebound and percussion tenderness; pain on coughing, walking or jumping; rovsing sign retrocaecal: flank pain, psoas sign; pelvic: diarrhoea, urinary frequency, rectal tenderness young children: vomiting, irritability, lethargy, diffuse peritonitis; late presentation common perforation: high fever, generalised peritonitis, toxic appearance, sometimes brief relief of pain differential diagnosis by age infants: intussusception, malrotation/volvulus, gastroenteritis, incarcerated hernia, nec preschool: gastroenteritis, uti, constipation, mesenteric adenitis, intussusception school age: appendicitis, mesenteric adenitis, uti, pneumonia (lower lobe), hsp, dka, constipation, meckel diverticulum adolescents: appendicitis, ovarian torsion or cyst, ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, testicular torsion (always examine testes), ibd, pancreatitis investigations clinical scoring: pediatric appendicitis score (pas) combining migration of pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, rif tenderness, cough tenderness, fever, leucocytosis, neutrophilia bloods: fbc (raised wcc and neutrophils), crp; urinalysis to exclude uti; pregnancy test in post-pubertal girls ultrasound is first-line imaging: non-compressible tubular structure above 6 mm with wall thickening, periappendiceal fluid; ct or mri if equivocal and in selected cases observation with repeat examination in 4-6 hours is valuable when diagnosis uncertain management complications & prognosis perforation, peritonitis, abscess, sepsis wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess, adhesional obstruction negative appendicectomy rate should be low (below 10 percent) excellent prognosis after uncomplicated surgery; perforation increases length of stay and morbidity morphine co-amoxiclav or cefuroxime plus metronidazole ondansetron

t: Viral hepatitis & liver disease in children
h: viral hepatitis & liver disease in children gastroenterology & hepatology viral hepatitis and other liver disease in children range from asymptomatic infection to acute liver failure and chronic cirrhosis. hepatitis a is the commonest acute cause, while hepatitis b and c are important chronic infections, particularly through vertical transmission. hepatitis a is faecal-oral, self-limiting and never chronic hepatitis b vertical transmission carries the highest chance of chronicity newborns of hbsag-positive mothers get vaccine plus hbig hbsag positive for more than 6 months defines chronic infection prolonged inr unresponsive to vitamin k indicates liver failure check paracetamol level in any acute hepatitis of uncertain cause nafld is the commonest chronic liver disease in obese children wilson disease: kayser-fleischer rings, low caeruloplasmin encephalopathy, drowsiness or confusion prolonged inr or bleeding hypoglycaemia ascites and rapidly shrinking liver jaundice in a child with paracetamol exposure hepatosplenomegaly with signs of chronic liver disease faecal-oral vs blood-borne a and e = alimentary (faecal-oral, not chronic); b, c, d = blood-borne (can become chronic) definition & epidemiology types of viral hepatitis hepatitis a: rna virus, faecal-oral, outbreaks in crowded or poor sanitation; usually mild or asymptomatic in young children; self-limiting, never chronic; vaccine available hepatitis b: dna virus, blood and body fluids, vertical (perinatal), horizontal in early childhood; can become chronic; risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; vaccine in infant schedule hepatitis c: rna virus, blood-borne, vertical transmission about 5 percent; chronic in about 70 percent; direct-acting antivirals can cure; no vaccine hepatitis e: faecal-oral, genotype 1/2 water-borne and dangerous in pregnancy; usually self-limiting hepatitis d: needs hbv; superinfection worsens disease clinical features prodrome: fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, tender hepatomegaly many children are asymptomatic or anicteric extrahepatic: rash, arthralgia (hbv immune complex), glomerulonephritis acute liver failure: encephalopathy, coagulopathy (inr above 1.5), hypoglycaemia, ascites, rapidly shrinking liver chronic liver disease: spider naevi, clubbing, splenomegaly, ascites, growth failure investigations lfts: raised alt and ast (often in thousands), bilirubin; inr and albumin assess synthetic function (prolonged inr unresponsive to vitamin k = liver failure); glucose and ammonia hepatitis a: anti-hav igm; hepatitis b: hbsag (infection), anti-hbc igm (acute), hbeag and hbv dna (infectivity), anti-hbs (immunity); hepatitis c: anti-hcv and hcv rna autoimmune screen (ana, sma, lkm, igg), caeruloplasmin and urinary copper, alpha-1 antitrypsin, paracetamol level liver ultrasound; biopsy in selected cases; elastography for fibrosis management complications & prognosis acute liver failure with cerebral oedema chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension (varices, ascites) hepatocellular carcinoma in chronic hbv hepatitis a recovers fully; chronic hbv and hcv need long-term follow-up hepatitis b vaccine plus hbig n-acetylcysteine penicillamine / trientine

urinary tract infection & vesicoureteric reflux nephrology & urology urinary tract infection is one of the commonest serious bacterial infections in children, and in infants it presents non-specifically with fever. prompt diagnosis and treatment prevent renal scarring, and some children have an underlying structural problem such as vesicoureteric reflux. e. coli causes most paediatric utis infants with fever and no source: always check a urine sample dipstick positive for both leucocyte esterase and nitrite = treat as uti clean-catch or catheter samples are preferred; bag urine is unreliable for culture infants under 3 months need iv antibiotics and admission ultrasound (and later dmsa) are used for atypical or recurrent uti vur is graded i-v on mcug; most low-grade cases resolve renal scarring can lead to hypertension and ckd fever in an infant under 3 months septicaemia or shock with uti poor urine stream or palpable bladder in a boy (obstruction/posterior urethral valves) recurrent uti with failure to thrive or raised creatinine atypical features: poor response at 48 hours, non-e. coli organism, abdominal mass, raised creatinine atypical uti seriously ill, poor urine flow, abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond within 48 hours, non-e. coli organism. definition & epidemiology aetiology & risk factors escherichia coli causes about 80 percent; others include klebsiella, proteus (stones), enterococcus, pseudomonas (structural disease) and staphylococcus saprophyticus in adolescent girls female sex (short urethra), uncircumcised boys, constipation, poor hygiene, bladder-bowel dysfunction structural: vesicoureteric reflux, obstructive uropathy (posterior urethral valves, puj obstruction), duplex systems, neurogenic bladder catheters, sexual activity, immunosuppression, diabetes clinical features neonates and infants: fever, vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, prolonged jaundice, failure to thrive, septicaemia pre-school children: fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, malodorous or cloudy urine, new incontinence older children: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain (lower uti) or loin pain with fever and rigors (pyelonephritis) examination: look for abdominal or loin tenderness, palpable bladder, genital abnormalities, spinal dimples, blood pressure investigations dipstick: positive leucocyte esterase and nitrite strongly suggests infection (treat); both negative makes uti unlikely; one positive needs culture microscopy: pyuria and bacteria; urine culture with a pure growth of 10^5 colony-forming units per ml (or any growth on suprapubic aspirate) is diagnostic blood tests in ill children: fbc, crp, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, blood culture in infants ultrasound: during the acute illness in infants under 6 months with first uti that is atypical or recurrent, or in all infants in some guidelines dmsa scan (4-6 months after infection) detects renal scarring in recurrent or atypical uti; mcug (micturating cystourethrogram) demonstrates reflux and posterior urethral valves and is reserved for selected children management infants under 3 months with suspected uti: urgent hospital admission, iv antibiotics such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus amoxicillin or ampicillin (to cover enterococcus) after septic screen older children with upper tract infection or systemically unwell: iv cefotaxime/ceftriaxone or gentamicin initially, switch to oral antibiotics after clinical improvement for a total of 7-10 days lower uti in children over 3 months: oral trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin or cefalexin for 3 days (up to 7 days in some guidance); amoxicillin or co-amoxiclav only if sensitive encourage fluids, regular voiding and treatment of constipation; hygiene advice review with culture sensitivities at 48 hours; investigate recurrent or atypical infection antibiotic prophylaxis (trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin at night) is not routinely recommended but may be used in high-grade reflux or obstructive uropathy and recurrent infections vesicoureteric reflux (vur) trimethoprim cefalexin ceftriaxone trimethoprim prophylaxis

nephrotic syndrome nephrology & urology nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, with hypercholesterolaemia. in children it is most often steroid-sensitive minimal change disease and has a relapsing course, but it has important complications including infection and thrombosis. triad: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; hyperlipidaemia follows minimal change disease causes 85-90 percent of cases aged 1-10 treat empirically with prednisolone without a biopsy in a typical child steroid sensitivity defines prognosis; steroid resistance indicates biopsy relapse = urine protein 3+ or more for 3 days peritonitis (pneumococcus) and thrombosis are the dangerous complications vaccinate against pneumococcus and manage varicella exposure promptly hypertension, haematuria and low c3 suggest a nephritic alternative abdominal pain, fever and ascites (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) hypovolaemia with oedema (tachycardia, cold peripheries, high haematocrit) painful swollen leg, loin pain or macroscopic haematuria (thrombosis) exposure to chickenpox or measles while on steroids hypertension, haematuria or elevated creatinine at presentation nephrotic syndrome protein loss: proteinuria above 3 g/day (or upcr above 200 mg/mmol), albumin below 25-30 g/l, oedema, lipids raised. definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features periorbital oedema in the morning that progresses to generalised swelling, ascites, pleural effusions, scrotal or labial oedema frothy urine, weight gain, reduced urine output; often follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection blood pressure normal in mcd; hypertension, haematuria or low complement point to an alternative cause complications: peritonitis (streptococcus pneumoniae, e. coli), cellulitis, sepsis, thromboembolism (renal vein thrombosis, dvt, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis), hypovolaemia with abdominal pain, acute kidney injury, hypercholesterolaemia investigations urine dipstick (3+ or 4+ protein), spot urine protein:creatinine ratio, early morning urine for relapse monitoring blood: albumin, urea, creatinine, electrolytes (low sodium from dilution), cholesterol, complement c3 and c4, fbc, hepatitis b and c and hiv serology, varicella status renal biopsy is not routine in a typical child aged 1-10 years; indications are age under 1 year or over 12 years, persistent haematuria or hypertension, low c3, impaired renal function, steroid resistance (no remission after 4 weeks of daily prednisolone), or frequent relapses before starting second-line agents management initial episode: prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day (maximum 80 mg) as a single morning dose for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for 4 weeks, then taper (total 8-12 weeks); longer regimens reduce relapses relapse (urine protein 3+ or more for 3 consecutive days): prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day until urine is protein-free for 3 days, then 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for 4 weeks frequent relapsing (2 or more within 6 months) or steroid-dependent: steroid-sparing agents - levamisole, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, ciclosporin or tacrolimus, rituximab oedema: salt restriction, fluid restriction in severe cases, diuretics (furosemide, with or without albumin infusion in hypovolaemic or severe oedema) infection prevention: penicillin prophylaxis in some centres during oedematous phase; pneumococcal vaccination; annual influenza vaccine; chickenpox exposure needs vzig or aciclovir while on high-dose steroids thrombosis prevention: mobilise, avoid dehydration and central lines; anticoagulation if thrombosis occurs steroid-resistant disease needs biopsy, genetic testing and calcineurin inhibitors, ace inhibitors prognosis about 80 percent of steroid-sensitive children relapse at least once; about 50 percent relapse frequently most mcd resolves by adolescence; the main morbidity arises from steroid side effects (cushingoid features, growth, bone, cataracts, hypertension, behaviour) fsgs and steroid-resistant disease may progress to end-stage kidney disease and recur after transplant prednisolone furosemide penicillin v prophylaxis levamisole

nephritic syndrome & post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis nephrology & urology nephritic syndrome is glomerular inflammation producing haematuria, hypertension, oedema and reduced renal function. post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the classic paediatric cause, appearing 1-3 weeks after a throat or skin infection and usually recovering fully with supportive care. psgn follows streptococcal infection by 1-3 weeks (pharynx) or 3-6 weeks (skin) low c3 that normalises in 6-8 weeks is characteristic hypertension, haematuria, oedema, reduced urine output = nephritic picture treatment is supportive: fluid and salt restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives prognosis in children is excellent; most recover fully iga nephropathy presents 1-2 days after infection with normal c3 persistent low c3 or nephrotic features warrant biopsy alport syndrome: haematuria with deafness and eye problems severe hypertension with headache, vomiting or seizure oliguria or anuria with rising creatinine and hyperkalaemia pulmonary oedema and respiratory distress rapid fall in gfr over days (crescentic gn) low complement persisting beyond 3 months nephritic features hypertension, haematuria (red cell casts), oliguria, oedema, azotaemia (raised urea and creatinine). definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features cola-coloured or smoky urine (macroscopic haematuria), puffy face (periorbital oedema), reduced urine output hypertension (headache, visual disturbance, seizures from hypertensive encephalopathy) fatigue, loin pain, mild fever; circulatory congestion with breathlessness in severe cases history of preceding sore throat or skin infection (latent period of 1-3 weeks distinguishes it from iga nephropathy, which presents within 1-2 days of an infection) complications: acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, hypertensive encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema; rarely rapidly progressive gn with crescents investigations urinalysis: blood and protein; microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; urine protein:creatinine mild to moderate (nephrotic-range uncommon) serum c3 low in over 90 percent and returns to normal in 6-8 weeks; c4 normal; persistent low c3 beyond 3 months suggests alternative diagnosis (mpgn, lupus) evidence of streptococcal infection: aso titre (better after pharyngitis), anti-dnase b (better after skin infection), throat or skin swab urea, creatinine, electrolytes (hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia), fbc, blood pressure monitoring, chest x-ray if congestion renal biopsy is indicated for unusual features: persistent low complement over 8-12 weeks, nephrotic syndrome, rapidly rising creatinine, persistent hypertension or macroscopic haematuria beyond 4 weeks management supportive and often admitted for blood pressure and fluid balance monitoring; daily weights and strict fluid balance salt and fluid restriction; loop diuretic (furosemide) for oedema and hypertension antihypertensives: calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine), ace inhibitors cautiously, labetalol or sodium nitroprusside for hypertensive emergency penicillin v for 10 days to eradicate residual streptococci and to limit spread to contacts dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload or uraemia no role for steroids in uncomplicated psgn; immunosuppression only for crescentic disease follow-up until haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and c3 have normalised other causes of glomerulonephritis iga nephropathy (berger disease): recurrent macroscopic haematuria 1-2 days after an upper respiratory tract infection; normal c3; commonest gn worldwide henoch-schonlein purpura nephritis: palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, haematuria membranoproliferative gn: persistent low c3 lupus nephritis, anca vasculitis, anti-gbm disease (goodpasture) in rapidly progressive gn alport syndrome: x-linked, haematuria, sensorineural deafness, lens abnormalities (anterior lenticonus) thin basement membrane disease: benign familial haematuria furosemide amlodipine phenoxymethylpenicillin labetalol

haemolytic uraemic syndrome nephrology & urology haemolytic uraemic syndrome is the commonest cause of acute kidney injury in young children and is defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute renal failure. most cases follow shiga toxin-producing e. coli (stec) diarrhoea and are managed supportively. triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury commonest cause of aki in young children typical hus follows stec (e. coli o157:h7) bloody diarrhoea by 5-10 days do not give antibiotics or antimotility agents for stec diarrhoea coombs-negative haemolysis with schistocytes on film management is supportive with dialysis when needed atypical hus is complement-mediated and treated with eculizumab pneumococcal hus has a positive coombs test and needs washed blood products anuria or severe oliguria after bloody diarrhoea seizures or reduced consciousness severe hypertension hyperkalaemia with ecg changes haemoglobin below 60 g/l, or abdominal signs suggesting perforation hus triad anaemia (haemolytic, schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, and uraemia (acute kidney injury) - "a, t, u". definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features prodrome of bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and vomiting, with or without fever 5-10 days later: pallor, lethargy, irritability, reduced urine output or anuria, oedema, hypertension petechiae and bruising are less common because thrombocytopenia is rarely severe enough to bleed neurological involvement (seizures, encephalopathy, stroke) in 20-30 percent, pancreatitis, colitis with bowel perforation, cardiomyopathy, diabetes key lab findings: anaemia (haemoglobin below 100 g/l), fragmented red cells on blood film, raised ldh and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, negative coombs test, platelets below 150, raised urea and creatinine, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis investigations fbc with blood film (schistocytes, helmet cells), reticulocytes, ldh, haptoglobin, direct coombs test (negative, except in pneumococcal hus where it can be positive) urea, creatinine, electrolytes, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, glucose, amylase stool culture on sorbitol-macconkey agar and pcr for shiga toxin genes (stx1, stx2); serology for o157 complement c3 and c4, factor h and i levels, adamts13 (to exclude ttp) and genetic testing if atypical blood pressure monitoring, urine output, daily weights management supportive care is the mainstay: careful fluid management (avoid overload and dehydration; early isotonic volume expansion in the first days may reduce renal injury), strict fluid balance, nutritional support and treatment of hypertension (calcium channel blockers, ace inhibitors) treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hyponatraemia and hyperphosphataemia transfuse packed red cells slowly if haemoglobin is below 60-70 g/l (fresh, washed in pneumococcal hus); avoid platelet transfusions unless there is active bleeding or an invasive procedure is planned dialysis (peritoneal dialysis is commonly used in children) for fluid overload, refractory hyperkalaemia, uraemia and anuria; around 50-70 percent need dialysis at some point avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents (loperamide) and nsaids in stec infection; antibiotics may increase toxin release and the risk of hus atypical hus: plasma exchange or infusion, and the complement c5 inhibitor eculizumab (or ravulizumab) are first line complications & prognosis mortality in typical hus is 1-5 percent in the acute phase up to 30 percent have long-term renal sequelae: proteinuria, hypertension, reduced gfr or chronic kidney disease; around 5 percent progress to end-stage kidney disease atypical hus has a worse prognosis with frequent relapse and graft loss without complement inhibition long-term follow-up with annual blood pressure and urine protein measurement

t: Acute kidney injury & chronic kidney disease
h: acute kidney injury & chronic kidney disease nephrology & urology acute kidney injury is a sudden fall in glomerular filtration rate causing retention of urea and creatinine, disturbed fluid and electrolyte balance, and is most often prerenal or due to acute tubular necrosis in children. chronic kidney disease is a persistent reduction in gfr over at least 3 months, commonly from congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, and requires multidisciplinary care to protect growth and development. prerenal aki from dehydration is the commonest cause in children aki diagnosis uses rising creatinine or oliguria below 0.5 ml/kg/hour treat hyperkalaemia with calcium gluconate, then salbutamol, insulin and glucose avoid nephrotoxic drugs and adjust doses for gfr obstruction (posterior urethral valves) must be excluded by ultrasound in aki ckd staging uses egfr; congenital anomalies are the commonest cause ckd complications: anaemia, bone disease, acidosis, hypertension, growth failure transplantation is the preferred treatment for end-stage kidney disease potassium above 6.5 mmol/l or peaked t waves on ecg anuria or oliguria not responding to fluids pulmonary oedema, severe hypertension or encephalopathy palpable bladder in a boy with poor stream (obstruction) severe acidosis with kussmaul breathing indications for acute dialysis - aeiou acidosis, electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), intoxication, overload (fluid), uraemia. acute kidney injury - definition and causes prerenal (commonest): dehydration from gastroenteritis, haemorrhage, sepsis, burns, nephrotic syndrome with hypovolaemia, heart failure, nsaids and ace inhibitors intrinsic: acute tubular necrosis (prolonged hypoperfusion, nephrotoxins such as aminoglycosides, vancomycin, contrast, rhabdomyolysis), glomerulonephritis (psgn, hsp), hus, interstitial nephritis, tumour lysis syndrome postrenal: posterior urethral valves, bilateral ureteric obstruction, neurogenic bladder, stones neonates: perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, nephrotoxic drugs (indometacin, gentamicin), congenital anomalies aki - assessment and investigations history: fluid losses, urine output, medications, preceding infection; examination: hydration status, blood pressure, weight, palpable bladder or kidneys urea, creatinine, electrolytes (potassium, sodium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate), blood gas, fbc, glucose urinalysis (blood, protein, casts), urine sodium and osmolality; fractional excretion of sodium below 1 percent suggests prerenal azotaemia renal ultrasound (size, hydronephrosis, bladder), ecg for hyperkalaemia further tests per cause: complement, aso, anca, blood film, creatine kinase aki - management treat the cause: restore circulating volume with isotonic fluid (10-20 ml/kg boluses) in prerenal aki; relieve obstruction by bladder catheterisation or nephrostomy; stop nephrotoxic drugs once euvolaemic, restrict fluids to insensible losses (about 300-400 ml/m2/day) plus urine output and ongoing losses; weigh daily hyperkalaemia (potassium above 6.5 mmol/l or ecg changes): iv calcium gluconate 10 percent 0.5 ml/kg (cardioprotective), salbutamol nebulised or iv, insulin with glucose infusion, sodium bicarbonate if acidotic, calcium resonium, loop diuretic; dialysis if refractory treat hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, acidosis and hypertension; adjust all drug doses for renal function and give adequate nutrition indications for renal replacement therapy: refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema, severe acidosis, uraemic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis), anuria and inability to give necessary nutrition; peritoneal dialysis is the commonest in infants, haemodialysis or crrt in older or unstable children chronic kidney disease (ckd) features: growth failure, anaemia, bone disease (renal osteodystrophy), hypertension, polyuria, acidosis, delayed puberty, developmental delay; often asymptomatic early complications: anaemia (reduced erythropoietin), mineral bone disorder (low calcium, high phosphate, high pth, low active vitamin d), metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, hypertension, growth impairment, cardiovascular disease management: treat the underlying cause, dietary advice (adequate calories, controlled phosphate and potassium; protein not over-restricted), alfacalcidol and phosphate binders, bicarbonate, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents with iron, recombinant growth hormone for growth failure, blood pressure control with ace inhibitors, immunisation end-stage kidney disease (egfr below 15): dialysis (peritoneal dialysis preferred in young children) then renal transplantation, which is the treatment of choice, preferably pre-emptive, from a living donor; lifelong immunosuppression psychological support, school liaison and transition to adult services are essential calcium gluconate 10 percent salbutamol insulin and glucose calcium resonium

enuresis & bladder dysfunction nephrology & urology enuresis is involuntary urinary incontinence during sleep in a child aged 5 years or older. nocturnal enuresis is common, usually benign and often familial, and is distinguished from daytime wetting and bladder dysfunction, which require a different approach. enuresis is nocturnal wetting at 5 years or older primary = never dry for 6 months; secondary = relapse after at least 6 months dry strong family history is common always dipstick the urine to exclude uti and diabetes alarm is the most effective long-term treatment with low relapse desmopressin gives rapid short-term control; limit fluids to avoid hyponatraemia look for constipation, sleep apnoea, daytime symptoms and neurological signs daytime wetting or poor stream suggests bladder dysfunction or structural problem continuous dribbling incontinence from birth with otherwise normal voiding (ectopic ureter) weak stream, palpable bladder or kidney in a boy lower limb neurological signs, sacral dimple or hairy patch secondary enuresis with polyuria and thirst (diabetes mellitus) sudden onset after abuse or distressing event; safeguarding concerns alarm rule of thumb use the alarm for at least 6-8 weeks and continue until 14 consecutive dry nights. definition & epidemiology aetiology nocturnal polyuria from reduced overnight secretion of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) reduced functional bladder capacity or detrusor overactivity failure to arouse in response to bladder fullness (deep sleep) constipation and bladder-bowel dysfunction; obstructive sleep apnoea secondary causes: urinary tract infection, diabetes mellitus (polyuria), diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, constipation, sleep-disordered breathing, psychological stress (new sibling, bullying, abuse), spinal dysraphism, cerebral palsy assessment history: pattern (nights per week), daytime frequency, urgency, holding manoeuvres, fluid intake, bowel habit, urine stream, previous dry periods, sleep, family history, psychosocial stressors, impact on child and family examination: growth, blood pressure, abdominal palpation for faeces and bladder, genitalia (labial adhesions, meatal stenosis, phimosis), spine and lower limb neurology (sacral dimples, hairy patches, reflexes, gait), perianal sensation urinalysis for glucose, protein, blood, leucocytes and nitrite in all children; urine culture if symptomatic bladder diary and frequency-volume chart over 2-3 days; ultrasound with post-void residual if daytime symptoms or abnormal examination features requiring specialist referral: poor urinary stream, continuous dribbling incontinence (ectopic ureter), constant wetness, abnormal neurology, daytime symptoms, uti, failure of therapy management reassure the child and parents that it is common and not the child fault; avoid punishment; protect bedding general advice: adequate daytime fluids (6-8 drinks), limit evening fluids and caffeinated drinks, void before bed, treat constipation, reward charts for agreed behaviours (not for dry nights) enuresis alarm: first-line for motivated children aged 7 years or older with frequent wetting; cure rate 60-70 percent and relapse lower than medication; use for at least 6-8 weeks and continue until 14 consecutive dry nights desmopressin (synthetic vasopressin analogue): 200-400 micrograms oral tablet or 120-240 micrograms melt before bed; useful short-term (sleepovers) or in alarm failure or polyuric children; restrict fluids for 1 hour before and 8 hours after to avoid hyponatraemia and water intoxication; stop if vomiting or illness anticholinergics (oxybutynin) added for overactive bladder in non-monosymptomatic enuresis; imipramine rarely used daytime bladder dysfunction: timed voiding, double voiding, treatment of constipation, urotherapy and anticholinergics treat uti and constipation; refer if red flag features bladder dysfunction and neuropathic bladder desmopressin oxybutynin

t: Hydronephrosis, posterior urethral valves & renal anomalies
h: hydronephrosis, posterior urethral valves & renal anomalies nephrology & urology antenatal hydronephrosis is detected in 1-5 percent of pregnancies on routine ultrasound and ranges from physiological dilatation to serious obstruction. posterior urethral valves are the most important cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in boys and can cause renal failure and pulmonary hypoplasia. transient antenatal hydronephrosis is common and often resolves puj obstruction is the commonest pathological cause of antenatal hydronephrosis puv affects boys and causes bilateral hydronephrosis, keyhole sign and oligohydramnios mcug is the diagnostic test for puv; mag3 renogram for puj obstruction initial puv management is catheter drainage, then endoscopic valve ablation oligohydramnios causes pulmonary hypoplasia (potter sequence) horseshoe kidney is associated with turner syndrome cakut is the commonest cause of ckd in children boy with poor urinary stream or palpable bladder in the neonatal period bilateral hydronephrosis with oligohydramnios neonatal respiratory distress with renal anomalies (pulmonary hypoplasia) urinary infection with fever in an infant with known hydronephrosis rising creatinine after neonatal period in a child with puv potter sequence oligohydramnios -> pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened (potter) facies, limb contractures; due to renal agenesis or severe obstruction. definition & epidemiology causes transient or physiological dilatation (commonest) that resolves postnatally pelvi-ureteric junction (puj) obstruction: the commonest pathological cause; unilateral, more often boys and left side vesicoureteric junction obstruction or megaureter (primary obstructive or refluxing) vesicoureteric reflux (up to 30 percent of antenatal hydronephrosis) duplex system with ureterocele (upper pole obstruction) or ectopic ureter posterior urethral valves (puv): obstructing membrane in the posterior urethra of boys; bilateral hydronephrosis with a thick-walled distended bladder (keyhole sign) and oligohydramnios multicystic dysplastic kidney, prune belly syndrome, urethral atresia posterior urethral valves prevalence about 1 in 5000-8000 male births; the commonest cause of bladder outflow obstruction and of end-stage kidney disease from urological causes in boys antenatal: bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, dilated bladder with keyhole sign, oligohydramnios neonatal: poor urinary stream, palpable bladder, respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia (potter sequence from oligohydramnios), urinary ascites, sepsis, renal failure later presentation: uti, voiding dysfunction, daytime wetting, failure to thrive, enuresis, renal failure diagnosis: mcug shows a dilated posterior urethra with bladder trabeculation; ultrasound shows bladder wall thickening and hydronephrosis; creatinine measured after 24-48 hours management: urgent bladder drainage with a urethral catheter (or suprapubic catheter), correct electrolytes, antibiotic prophylaxis, then endoscopic valve ablation; later management of bladder dysfunction and chronic kidney disease; prognosis is related to renal dysplasia and the nadir creatinine in the first year long-term: about 30-60 percent develop ckd, bladder dysfunction (valve bladder), reflux, polyuria and need for transplantation postnatal evaluation ultrasound at 3-7 days of life (earlier if bilateral or severe, suspected puv or solitary kidney); an early scan within 48 hours may underestimate dilatation because of neonatal oliguria continuous antibiotic prophylaxis (trimethoprim or amoxicillin) for moderate or severe dilatation until investigated mcug for suspected puv, bilateral dilatation or ureteric dilatation isotope renogram (mag3) at 6-8 weeks for suspected puj obstruction to measure differential function and drainage dmsa scan for cortical scarring and function management of puj obstruction: observation for most, with pyeloplasty if function falls below 40 percent, deteriorates, pain, infection or progressive dilatation other renal anomalies renal agenesis (bilateral causes potter syndrome: oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, characteristic facies; incompatible with life) multicystic dysplastic kidney: non-functioning cystic kidney, usually involutes; contralateral anomalies in 30 percent horseshoe kidney: fused lower poles, associated with turner syndrome; usually asymptomatic autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (pkhd1): enlarged echogenic kidneys, hepatic fibrosis, oligohydramnios ectopic or duplex kidney, bladder exstrophy, prune belly syndrome (absent abdominal muscles, cryptorchidism, dilated urinary tract) trimethoprim prophylaxis

approach to haematuria, proteinuria & hypertension nephrology & urology haematuria, proteinuria and hypertension are common referral problems in paediatric nephrology. a structured approach separates benign transient causes from glomerular or structural disease that needs investigation, and ensures hypertension is diagnosed using age, sex and height-specific blood pressure centiles. confirm haematuria with microscopy and repeat testing; exclude myoglobin and food dyes dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts indicate glomerular bleeding isolated microscopic haematuria is usually benign; monitor annually orthostatic proteinuria is benign: first morning urine is protein-free spot urine pcr above 200 mg/mmol is nephrotic range hypertension needs age, sex and height centiles and correct cuff size renal parenchymal disease is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension in children always check femoral pulses and bladder in a hypertensive child macroscopic haematuria with hypertension, oedema or oliguria haematuria with abdominal mass (wilms tumour) persistent proteinuria with hypertension or raised creatinine severe hypertension with headache, seizures or visual change haematuria with hearing loss or family history of renal failure (alport) urine colour clue tea or cola coloured = glomerular; bright red with clots = lower urinary tract. haematuria glomerular features: brown or cola-coloured urine, red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, associated proteinuria, hypertension, oedema non-glomerular features: bright red or pink urine, clots, normal-shaped red cells, no or mild proteinuria glomerular causes: psgn, iga nephropathy, hsp nephritis, alport syndrome, thin basement membrane disease, lupus nephritis, mpgn, anti-gbm disease non-glomerular causes: uti, hypercalciuria, stones, trauma, tumours (wilms), cystitis, coagulopathy, sickle cell trait, loin pain-haematuria, nutcracker syndrome, urethral or meatal causes, polycystic kidney disease investigations: urine microscopy and culture, urine protein:creatinine ratio, urine calcium:creatinine ratio, u&e, creatinine, albumin, fbc, complement c3 and c4, aso, renal ultrasound; hearing test and family screening if alport suspected; biopsy for persistent haematuria with proteinuria, hypertension or falling gfr isolated microscopic haematuria with normal blood pressure, protein and creatinine rarely needs treatment and is monitored annually proteinuria transient proteinuria: fever, exercise, dehydration, seizures, stress; resolves on repeat testing orthostatic (postural) proteinuria: common in adolescents, protein excreted only when upright; first morning urine sample is normal; benign with normal renal function persistent proteinuria: glomerular (nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, reflux nephropathy, fsgs, alport) or tubular (fanconi syndrome, interstitial nephritis, dent disease; low molecular weight proteins) evaluation of persistent proteinuria: split urine collections (first morning versus daytime pcr), blood pressure, albumin, creatinine, complement, renal ultrasound; refer for biopsy if pcr above 100 mg/mmol, impaired function, haematuria or hypertension treatment: ace inhibitor or arb for persistent glomerular proteinuria and treat cause hypertension in children causes depend on age: neonates - renal artery or vein thrombosis (umbilical catheter), coarctation, renal disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia; infants and young children - renal parenchymal disease (most common), renovascular disease, coarctation; older children and adolescents - primary (essential) hypertension linked to obesity and family history, plus renal causes renal: glomerulonephritis, reflux nephropathy scarring, polycystic kidneys, renal artery stenosis (fibromuscular dysplasia; williams syndrome, neurofibromatosis), hus, ckd endocrine: phaeochromocytoma, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency), cushing syndrome, primary hyperaldosteronism, hyperthyroidism drugs: corticosteroids, stimulants, decongestants, oral contraceptive pill, ciclosporin investigation: urinalysis, u&e, creatinine, lipids, glucose, renal ultrasound with doppler, echocardiography (left ventricular hypertrophy), plasma renin and aldosterone, urinary catecholamines and metanephrines, thyroid function, renal angiography in selected cases management: treat the cause, lifestyle (weight loss, exercise, reduced salt) for primary hypertension; antihypertensives such as ace inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, diuretics; hypertensive emergency (headache, visual disturbance, seizure, encephalopathy) needs iv labetalol or nicardipine, lowering blood pressure by about 25 percent in the first 8 hours enalapril amlodipine labetalol

febrile seizures neurology a febrile seizure is a convulsion triggered by fever in a child aged 6 months to 5 years with no intracranial infection or previous afebrile seizure. it is the commonest seizure disorder of childhood, affects 2-5 percent of children, and is almost always benign, but it is terrifying for parents and must be distinguished from meningitis and epilepsy. febrile seizure: age 6 months-5 years, fever, no cns infection, no previous afebrile seizure. simple = generalised, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours; complex = any of focal, 15 minutes or longer, or recurrent in 24 hours. most are simple (70 percent) and carry an excellent prognosis. recurrence risk about one third; epilepsy risk 1-2 percent after simple febrile seizures. antipyretics do not prevent recurrence. daily anticonvulsant prophylaxis is not recommended. eeg and brain imaging are not routine after a simple febrile seizure. always exclude meningitis; lower the threshold for lp in infants under 12 months and those pre-treated with antibiotics. seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer (treat as status epilepticus) persisting drowsiness or failure to return to baseline within an hour neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, photophobia, non-blanching rash focal seizure or post-ictal weakness (todd paresis) age under 6 months or over 5 years (consider epilepsy, meningitis, metabolic cause) child with neurodevelopmental delay or history of afebrile seizures complex febrile seizure - fpr focal, prolonged (over 15 minutes), recurrent (within 24 hours) - any one makes it complex definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features sudden generalised tonic-clonic seizure, usually brief (1-3 minutes), followed by a short post-ictal drowsy period child is usually well and alert within an hour fever present or discovered shortly after the event complex features: focal onset, duration over 15 minutes, recurrence within 24 hours, incomplete recovery or todd paresis look for the source of fever: ears, throat, chest, urine, rash always exclude meningism, bulging fontanelle, petechial rash, lethargy and persisting drowsiness investigations a simple febrile seizure in a well child usually needs no investigations beyond finding the fever source blood glucose in any child still seizing or unwell; urine dipstick and culture if no source found lumbar puncture should be considered (and is strongly advised) in infants under 12 months with a first seizure and fever, anyone with meningism or signs of raised icp, an incomplete recovery, prolonged complex seizure, or those who have had antibiotics (which can mask meningitis) eeg and neuroimaging are not indicated for a simple febrile seizure; they are considered after complex seizures with persistent neurological abnormality or if features suggest epilepsy blood electrolytes only if gastroenteritis or clinical indication management seizure over 5 minutes: buccal midazolam or iv lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg if no iv access in many settings) admit infants under 12 months, complex seizures, uncertain diagnosis or anxious parents with limited access to care treat the underlying cause (e.g. antibiotics for otitis media or uti as indicated) daily prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended; rescue buccal midazolam can be supplied to families of children with prolonged seizures complications & prognosis recurrence: about 30 percent overall; higher (50 percent) if first seizure under 12 months, strong family history, low-grade fever or short fever-to-seizure interval risk of later epilepsy is 1-2 percent after simple febrile seizures (about double the general population risk), rising to 4-6 percent with complex features, pre-existing neurodevelopmental abnormality or family history of epilepsy no evidence of brain damage, cognitive decline or death after simple febrile seizures febrile status epilepticus is rare but has more risk of subsequent mesial temporal sclerosis buccal midazolam lorazepam rectal diazepam

epilepsy & epilepsy syndromes neurology epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures due to abnormal synchronous neuronal discharge. in childhood it comprises many distinct syndromes with different ages of onset, eeg patterns, treatments and outcomes, so accurate classification guides drug choice and prognosis. epilepsy: two unprovoked seizures over 24 hours apart or one with high recurrence risk. infantile spasms are a neurological emergency: prompt prednisolone or vigabatrin improves developmental outcome. absence epilepsy: 3 hz spike-and-wave, provoked by hyperventilation, ethosuximide first-line. rolandic epilepsy is benign and typically remits by puberty. valproate is teratogenic: avoid in girls and women of child-bearing age unless no alternative. avoid carbamazepine and phenytoin in generalised absence and myoclonic epilepsies; they may worsen them. normal eeg does not exclude epilepsy; abnormal eeg alone does not make the diagnosis. always consider mimics: syncope, reflex anoxic seizures and breath-holding in toddlers. infantile spasms (clusters of spasms with regression): refer urgently seizure lasting over 5 minutes or cluster without recovery (status epilepticus) developmental regression or loss of skills focal neurological signs, signs of raised icp, or onset under 2 years (needs mri) seizures with neurocutaneous markers (ash-leaf macules, cafe-au-lait spots) rash after starting carbamazepine or lamotrigine (stevens-johnson syndrome) west syndrome triad infantile spasms, hypsarrhythmia on eeg, developmental regression definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features & syndromes infantile spasms (west syndrome): onset 3-12 months, clusters of flexor/extensor spasms on waking, developmental regression, hypsarrhythmia on eeg; causes include tuberous sclerosis, hie and metabolic disease childhood absence epilepsy: age 4-10 years, many brief (5-15 s) staring spells daily, provoked by hyperventilation, 3 hz generalised spike-and-wave on eeg, good prognosis benign childhood epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes (rolandic): age 3-12 years, nocturnal facial twitching and drooling, speech arrest, remits by adolescence juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: adolescence, morning myoclonic jerks, generalised tonic-clonic seizures, sleep deprivation and photic triggers, needs lifelong treatment in most lennox-gastaut syndrome: multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absences), slow spike-wave on eeg, learning disability, refractory dravet syndrome: prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizures in infancy, then multiple types; avoid sodium channel blockers seizure mimics: breath-holding spells, reflex anoxic seizures, syncope, gastro-oesophageal reflux (sandifer), night terrors, tics, psychogenic non-epileptic events investigations detailed history including eyewitness account or video from a smartphone eeg (including sleep-deprived or ambulatory) supports classification but does not exclude epilepsy if normal mri brain for focal seizures, onset under 2 years, developmental delay, refractory epilepsy or neurological signs blood glucose, calcium, magnesium and sodium at presentation; metabolic and genetic testing in infants with encephalopathy ecg to exclude long qt in any child with episodes resembling seizures management generalised tonic-clonic: sodium valproate (avoid in girls of child-bearing potential unless other options fail, because of teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harm), lamotrigine, levetiracetam focal: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine or levetiracetam absence: ethosuximide (if absence only); valproate or lamotrigine if mixed generalised infantile spasms: urgent treatment with prednisolone or vigabatrin (vigabatrin first-line in tuberous sclerosis) refractory epilepsy: ketogenic diet, vagal nerve stimulation, epilepsy surgery assessment complications & prognosis about 60-70 percent achieve seizure freedom on medication; many childhood syndromes remit by adolescence status epilepticus; sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (sudep) is rare but real learning, behavioural and psychiatric comorbidity (adhd, anxiety, depression) drug adverse effects: valproate (weight gain, tremor, liver, pancreatitis), carbamazepine (rash, hyponatraemia, sjs in hla-b*1502 carriers), levetiracetam (irritability), vigabatrin (visual field defects) sodium valproate ethosuximide carbamazepine prednisolone (infantile spasms)

meningitis & encephalitis neurology meningitis is inflammation of the meninges and encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma, both commonly infective. bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency with high mortality and neurological sequelae, so antibiotics must not be delayed; herpes simplex encephalitis requires prompt aciclovir. do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging. neonatal meningitis: gbs, e. coli, listeria - use cefotaxime plus amoxicillin. dexamethasone is given with or before the first antibiotic dose in children over 3 months. signs of raised icp or shock are contraindications to lp. neck stiffness is frequently absent in infants; bulging fontanelle and irritability are clues. hsv encephalitis: start aciclovir empirically while awaiting pcr. sensorineural deafness is the commonest sequela; arrange audiology before discharge or within 4 weeks. notify public health and give chemoprophylaxis to close contacts of meningococcal disease. non-blanching rash with fever (meningococcal septicaemia) shock, gcs falling, or signs of raised icp seizures or focal neurology in a febrile child bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, apnoea in an infant partial antibiotic pre-treatment masking classical signs subacute course with cranial nerve palsies (tb meningitis) contraindications to lp - icp shock raised icp signs, gcs low, focal signs, shock, coagulopathy, local infection definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology neonates: group b streptococcus, e. coli and other gram-negatives, listeria monocytogenes infants and children: streptococcus pneumoniae, neisseria meningitidis; hib in unimmunised viral: enterovirus, parechovirus (infants), hsv, vzv, mumps in unvaccinated; arboviruses in endemic areas tuberculous meningitis: subacute, basal meningitis, cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus encephalitis: hsv-1, vzv, enterovirus, arboviruses (japanese b, west nile), autoimmune (anti-nmda receptor) inflammation increases blood-brain barrier permeability, cerebral oedema and raised icp, with vasculitis and impaired autoregulation clinical features older child: fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, vomiting, drowsiness, kernig and brudzinski signs, seizures infants and neonates: nonspecific - fever or hypothermia, poor feeding, irritability, high-pitched cry, hypotonia, bulging fontanelle, seizures, apnoea; neck stiffness is often absent meningococcal septicaemia: non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, shock, cold peripheries, leg pain encephalitis: altered consciousness, behavioural change, focal seizures, focal neurology; hsv often temporal lobe signs of raised icp: cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing), pupillary changes, decerebrate posturing investigations blood: fbc, crp, glucose, cultures, clotting, blood gas; meningococcal and pneumococcal pcr lumbar puncture if no contraindication: cell count, protein, glucose (paired with blood glucose), gram stain, culture, pcr (hsv, enterovirus) contraindications to lp: signs of raised icp, gcs under 9 or falling by 3 or more, focal neurology, haemodynamic instability or shock, coagulopathy, local infection, extensive purpura bacterial csf: turbid, high neutrophils, high protein, low glucose (less than 50 percent of blood) viral csf: lymphocytes, normal or mildly raised protein, normal glucose tb csf: lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose, positive afb or pcr (genexpert) ct/mri before lp only when indicated; mri and eeg in suspected encephalitis management over 3 months: ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg iv once daily (max 4 g) or cefotaxime; add vancomycin if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is suspected under 3 months: cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (covers listeria); avoid ceftriaxone in neonates with jaundice or on calcium dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 days, ideally with or before the first antibiotic dose (not in neonates) suspected encephalitis: iv aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly (20 mg/kg in neonates) for 14-21 days duration of antibiotics: 10 days for meningococcus and hib/pneumococcus (up to 14 days for pneumococcus); 21 days for gram-negatives and gbs in neonates; 14 days for listeria meningococcal contacts: ciprofloxacin or rifampicin prophylaxis, notify public health; offer vaccination as indicated restrict fluids only if siadh confirmed; otherwise maintain normal hydration to avoid hypoperfusion complications & prognosis acute: shock, dic, seizures, raised icp, siadh, subdural effusion, cerebral abscess long term: sensorineural deafness (check audiology in all), hydrocephalus, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, learning difficulties mortality 5-10 percent in resourced settings; higher in neonatal and tuberculous meningitis tb meningitis requires 12 months of therapy with adjunctive corticosteroids ceftriaxone cefotaxime dexamethasone aciclovir

hydrocephalus & neural tube defects neurology hydrocephalus is an excess of csf within the ventricular system, usually from obstruction to flow or impaired absorption, causing ventricular dilatation and raised intracranial pressure. neural tube defects (spina bifida and anencephaly) result from failed closure of the neural tube and are largely preventable with periconceptional folic acid. hydrocephalus presents with enlarging head, bulging fontanelle and sunsetting eyes in infants; headache, vomiting and papilloedema in older children. non-communicating hydrocephalus is obstructive (aqueduct stenosis, tumour); communicating is an absorption problem (post-haemorrhage, post-meningitis). shunt malfunction is a neurosurgical emergency; blockage is more common than infection. folic acid 400 microgram prevents most ntds; 5 mg daily in high-risk women. raised afp and the lemon and banana signs suggest spina bifida antenatally. myelomeningocele is associated with chiari ii malformation and hydrocephalus in most cases. children with spina bifida need a latex-free environment because of high latex allergy risk. anencephaly is incompatible with life. rapidly increasing head size or full tense fontanelle vomiting, drowsiness, new headache in a child with a shunt sunsetting eyes, apnoea or bradycardia in an infant fever and redness along shunt tract (shunt infection) open neural tube lesion with csf leak (needs urgent neurosurgery and cover) deteriorating bladder or lower limb function in spina bifida (tethered cord) antenatal spina bifida signs lemon sign (frontal bossing) and banana sign (cerebellar curvature) on ultrasound definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology non-communicating (obstructive): aqueduct stenosis, chiari ii malformation, posterior fossa tumours (medulloblastoma, ependymoma), dandy-walker malformation communicating (absorption failure): post-intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants, post-meningitic, subarachnoid haemorrhage congenital infections (cmv, toxoplasmosis) and x-linked aqueduct stenosis (l1cam) neural tube defect risk: low maternal folate, antiepileptic exposure (valproate, carbamazepine), maternal diabetes and obesity, previous affected pregnancy nearly all myelomeningocele cases have chiari ii malformation; many develop hydrocephalus clinical features infant: rapidly increasing head circumference crossing centiles, tense bulging fontanelle, split sutures, dilated scalp veins, sunsetting eyes (upgaze palsy), irritability, vomiting, poor feeding older child: morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, vi nerve palsy, drowsiness, gait disturbance, declining school performance cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) is a late sign myelomeningocele: open lesion usually lumbosacral; paraparesis, sensory loss, neuropathic bladder and bowel, hip dislocation and talipes spina bifida occulta: tuft of hair, dimple, sinus or lipoma over the spine; may be associated with tethered cord investigations cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle (infants); mri for aetiology and neural tube anomalies antenatal diagnosis: raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, detailed anomaly scan at 18-20 weeks (lemon and banana signs) serial head circumference plotted against centiles shunt malfunction: ct or mri, shunt series x-rays, ophthalmology; tap shunt if infection suspected renal ultrasound, urodynamics, spine x-ray and mri in spina bifida management shunt complications: blockage (most common), infection (usually within 6 months; coagulase-negative staphylococci), overdrainage, disconnection, abdominal complications suspect shunt malfunction in any child with headache, vomiting, drowsiness or irritability; urgent neurosurgical review lifelong multidisciplinary care: neurosurgery, urology (clean intermittent catheterisation), orthopaedics, bowel programme, physiotherapy, orthoses, education support, latex-free environment prevention: folic acid 400 microgram daily before conception and until 12 weeks;
