5 mg daily for high-risk women (previous affected child, antiepileptic therapy, diabetes, obesity) in resource-limited settings, food fortification and etv improve outcomes where shunt follow-up is unreliable complications & prognosis learning difficulties, visual problems, epilepsy; hydrocephalus can cause developmental delay if untreated myelomeningocele: neuropathic bladder with renal damage, constipation or incontinence, scoliosis, latex allergy, pressure sores, tethered cord chiari ii: brainstem dysfunction, stridor, apnoea, feeding problems prognosis depends on lesion level: thoracic lesions often wheelchair-dependent, low lumbar and sacral may walk with aids most children with a functioning shunt survive to adulthood, but need lifelong neurosurgical follow-up folic acid (prevention)

cerebral palsy neurology cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive insult to the developing fetal or infant brain. it is the commonest cause of childhood motor disability, and care centres on early identification, multidisciplinary therapy and management of associated impairments. cp is a non-progressive brain lesion causing movement and posture disorder; manifestations evolve. spastic cp is the commonest type; diplegia is linked to prematurity, dyskinetic cp to kernicterus and hypoxia. hand preference before 12 months suggests hemiplegia. gmfcs classifies gross motor function level i (mild) to v (severe). hip surveillance by x-ray is essential because of high dislocation risk. botulinum toxin, baclofen and selective dorsal rhizotomy are options for spasticity. associated epilepsy, learning disability, vision and hearing problems are common. regression or progressive signs mean the diagnosis is not cp. loss of previously acquired skills (not cp; investigate neurodegenerative or metabolic disease) persistent feeding difficulty with recurrent chest infections (aspiration) hip migration percentage rising on x-ray uncontrolled seizures or sudden change in behaviour or pain asymmetrical signs with progressive course (consider tumour or spinal cord lesion) non-accidental injury as cause in unexplained cases gmfcs level i walks without limits; ii walks with limits; iii hand-held mobility device; iv self-mobility with limitations; v transported in a wheelchair definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology antenatal (most): congenital brain malformation, intrauterine infection (cmv), vascular insult, genetic causes perinatal: hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, neonatal stroke, kernicterus, severe hypoglycaemia postnatal: meningitis, head trauma, non-accidental injury, severe dehydration prematurity: periventricular leukomalacia and ivh causing spastic diplegia risk factors: prematurity, low birth weight, multiple birth, chorioamnionitis, perinatal asphyxia, neonatal seizures, neonatal jaundice (untreated kernicterus) clinical features spastic cp (about 70-80 percent): increased tone with brisk reflexes and clonus; hemiplegia (one side, often arm more than leg), diplegia (legs more than arms, associated with prematurity), quadriplegia (all four limbs, severe) dyskinetic cp (about 10 percent): athetosis, dystonia and choreoathetosis; classically after kernicterus or severe hypoxia affecting basal ganglia ataxic cp (about 5-10 percent): hypotonia, tremor, wide-based gait; cerebellar involvement mixed forms occur early signs: persistent primitive reflexes, early hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiplegia), fisting, toe walking, scissoring on vertical suspension, delayed motor milestones, poor head control, abnormal general movements associated: epilepsy (about 30-40 percent), learning disability (about 50 percent), visual and hearing impairment, drooling, dysphagia, gastro-oesophageal reflux, constipation, scoliosis, behavioural and sleep problems investigations diagnosis is clinical; document motor type, distribution and gross motor function classification system (gmfcs) level i-v mri brain recommended in all children without a clear cause; helps prognosis and detects malformations or metabolic causes investigate progressive features or regression for alternative diagnoses (leukodystrophy, mitochondrial disease, hereditary spastic paraparesis) hip surveillance with serial pelvic x-rays (hip displacement affects up to one third) vision, hearing, swallow assessment, nutritional review and eeg if seizures management physiotherapy: stretching, strengthening, positioning, hydrotherapy; splints and orthoses spasticity: oral baclofen, diazepam or trihexyphenidyl (dystonia); botulinum toxin injections to focal muscles; intrathecal baclofen pump for severe generalised spasticity; selective dorsal rhizotomy in selected spastic diplegia orthopaedic surgery: tendon lengthening, hip reconstruction, scoliosis correction drooling: glycopyrronium, botulinum toxin to salivary glands, surgical options feeding: assess for dysphagia and aspiration; consider nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding, fundoplication if severe reflux treat epilepsy, constipation, pain, sleep problems; provide communication aids; support schooling and transition to adult services complications & prognosis contractures, hip subluxation or dislocation, scoliosis, pain aspiration pneumonia, recurrent chest infections, malnutrition osteopenia and fractures, pressure sores prognosis for walking: independent walking by age 2 (gmfcs i-ii) is likely if sitting by 2; most children with severe quadriplegia do not walk life expectancy is near normal in mild disease and reduced in severe disease with feeding and respiratory complications baclofen (oral) botulinum toxin type a glycopyrronium bromide

neuromuscular disease (dmd, sma, myasthenia) neurology neuromuscular disease includes disorders of the motor neurone, nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle. duchenne muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy and myasthenia gravis are the key childhood examples, and recognising the pattern of weakness guides diagnosis and increasingly effective disease-modifying therapy. dmd: x-linked recessive, dystrophin deficiency, very high ck, calf pseudohypertrophy, gower sign. corticosteroids prolong walking in dmd; monitor the heart and respiratory function. sma type 1 is a floppy, alert infant with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes; smn1 gene deletion is diagnostic. disease-modifying therapy in sma works best before symptoms; newborn screening helps. myasthenia presents with fatigable weakness; ptosis and diplopia are early. floppy infant with preserved alertness and face suggests a lower motor neurone problem; hypotonia with poor alertness suggests central cause. avoid suxamethonium in dmd (hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis). female carriers of dmd may have raised ck and cardiomyopathy. floppy infant with respiratory distress, weak cry or feeding failure rapidly progressive weakness or bulbar involvement myasthenic crisis (respiratory failure, bulbar weakness) cardiac symptoms, arrhythmia or heart failure in dmd hypoventilation, morning headaches and daytime somnolence (nocturnal hypoventilation) unexplained dark urine after exercise or anaesthesia (rhabdomyolysis) gower sign child uses hands to climb up own legs from the floor because of proximal pelvic girdle weakness definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology dmd: frameshift deletions (about 65 percent) in the dystrophin gene (xp21) cause absent dystrophin, leading to muscle fibre necrosis, fibrosis and fat replacement; becker is the milder in-frame form sma: loss of smn1 with progressive degeneration of anterior horn cells; smn2 copy number modifies severity myasthenia gravis: antibodies against acetylcholine receptors reduce neuromuscular transmission; associated with thymic hyperplasia transient neonatal myasthenia occurs in babies of affected mothers from placental antibody transfer other: charcot-marie-tooth (hereditary neuropathy), myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies, infant botulism clinical features dmd: boys aged 2-5 years with delayed walking, waddling gait, difficulty climbing stairs, frequent falls, calf pseudohypertrophy, positive gower sign, toe-walking; wheelchair by about age 12 dmd complications: dilated cardiomyopathy, scoliosis, respiratory failure, cognitive impairment, osteoporosis from steroids sma type 1 (werdnig-hoffmann): onset under 6 months; floppy infant, tongue fasciculations, absent reflexes, bell-shaped chest with paradoxical breathing, alert face, never sits sma types 2-3: sit (type 2) or walk (type 3) with proximal weakness, tremor and areflexia; slower course myasthenia: fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar weakness, proximal limb weakness worse in the evening and after exertion neonatal clues: hypotonia, poor suck, weak cry, respiratory distress investigations serum creatine kinase: very high (10-100 times normal) in dmd; normal or mildly raised in sma genetic testing: dystrophin deletion/duplication analysis (mlpa) then sequencing in dmd; smn1 deletion in sma; muscle biopsy now rarely needed nerve conduction studies and emg help localise (neurogenic versus myopathic) myasthenia: acetylcholine receptor and musk antibodies, edrophonium (tensilon) test, repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre emg, chest ct for thymoma baseline and surveillance echocardiogram, spirometry, sleep studies and bone density management dmd: oral glucocorticoids (prednisolone 0.75 mg/kg/day or deflazacort 0.9 mg/kg/day) prolong ambulation and delay cardiac and respiratory decline; manage steroid adverse effects (bone health, weight, growth, cataracts) dmd: exon-skipping therapies and gene therapy are available for specific mutations in some countries; avoid suxamethonium and volatile anaesthetics sma: disease-modifying therapies (nusinersen intrathecal, risdiplam oral, onasemnogene gene therapy) transform outcome when started early; newborn screening is expanding myasthenia: pyridostigmine, immunosuppression (prednisolone, azathioprine), thymectomy, ivig or plasmapheresis for crisis neonatal myasthenia: supportive, neostigmine as needed; resolves in weeks complications & prognosis dmd: death typically in the late teens to thirties from cardiac or respiratory failure; improved with steroids and ventilation sma type 1 untreated: death or ventilation by age 2; treated infants may achieve sitting or walking myasthenic crisis: respiratory failure requiring ventilation; precipitated by infection, drugs (aminoglycosides, macrolides) learning and behavioural problems in dmd; scoliosis, contractures and fractures common across disorders prednisolone (dmd) pyridostigmine (myasthenia) risdiplam / nusinersen

guillain-barre syndrome & acute ataxia neurology guillain-barre syndrome (gbs) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing ascending symmetrical weakness and areflexia, often after an infection. acute ataxia in a child is usually post-infectious cerebellitis, but intoxication, tumours and other causes must be excluded. gbs: ascending symmetrical weakness, areflexia, preceding infection (campylobacter), csf albuminocytological dissociation. monitor fvc and swallowing; respiratory failure is the major early risk. treat with ivig or plasmapheresis; steroids do not help. miller fisher: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia with anti-gq1b. most acute ataxia in toddlers is post-viral cerebellitis; always rule out intoxication and tumour. opsoclonus-myoclonus in a child requires a search for neuroblastoma. csf protein may be normal in the first week of gbs. transverse myelitis has a sensory level and bladder involvement. rapid progression of weakness, respiratory muscle or bulbar involvement falling fvc or inability to count to 20 on one breath autonomic instability: tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia acute ataxia with headache, vomiting, drowsiness or papilloedema (posterior fossa tumour) possible ingestion in a toddler with ataxia opsoclonus or myoclonus (neuroblastoma) gbs pattern ascending, symmetrical, areflexic weakness with raised csf protein and normal cells definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology gbs: molecular mimicry produces antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides, causing demyelination or axonal injury; ascending paralysis results miller fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia with anti-gq1b antibodies acute ataxia causes: post-infectious cerebellitis (commonest), drug or toxin ingestion (alcohol, benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants), posterior fossa tumour, opsoclonus-myoclonus (neuroblastoma), encephalitis, miller fisher, migraine (basilar), metabolic disease, trauma, stroke, conversion disorder chronic or progressive ataxia: friedreich ataxia, ataxia telangiectasia, cerebellar tumours, hydrocephalus, metabolic disease clinical features gbs: symmetrical ascending weakness over days to 4 weeks, areflexia, back or leg pain, paraesthesia, refusal to walk in young children cranial nerve involvement: facial weakness (vii), bulbar dysfunction, ophthalmoplegia autonomic dysfunction: arrhythmia, labile blood pressure, urinary retention, ileus respiratory failure may develop quickly; monitor forced vital capacity and ability to count in one breath acute cerebellar ataxia: sudden onset truncal and gait ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus; no drowsiness or raised icp signs; often improving within weeks features that suggest tumour: headache, vomiting, papilloedema, abnormal posture; features of intoxication: drowsiness and history of access to drugs; opsoclonus: chaotic eye movements and myoclonus investigations gbs: lumbar puncture shows albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein with normal cell count), often after the first week nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction, conduction block, prolonged f-waves or axonal loss mri spine may show nerve root enhancement; excludes cord compression and transverse myelitis (which has a sensory level, bladder involvement and brisk reflexes later) serial fvc and negative inspiratory force; ecg monitoring; anti-gm1, anti-gq1b where relevant acute ataxia: toxicology screen, glucose, mri brain urgently if any red flag; csf in suspected encephalitis; urinary catecholamines for opsoclonus management iv immunoglobulin 2 g/kg total over 2-5 days (commonly 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) or plasmapheresis corticosteroids are not beneficial in gbs monitor swallowing and consider nasogastric feeding; bladder care acute cerebellar ataxia: observation, supportive care, safe environment; most recover fully treat underlying causes: tumour (neurosurgery and oncology), drug intoxication (supportive), opsoclonus (immunotherapy and tumour resection) complications & prognosis gbs: respiratory failure (up to 20 percent need ventilation), autonomic instability, dvt, pressure sores, pain and fatigue most children recover fully over weeks to months; 5-10 percent have lasting weakness; mortality under 3 percent in children relapse or treatment-related fluctuation requires reassessment; consider cidp if progression beyond 8 weeks acute cerebellar ataxia: over 90 percent recover completely within weeks; a minority have persistent cerebellar signs or behavioural issues intravenous immunoglobulin (gbs) gabapentin

headache & raised intracranial pressure neurology headache is common in children and adolescents and is usually primary (migraine or tension-type). the challenge is to identify the small group with secondary headache from raised intracranial pressure, tumour, infection or other serious causes by recognising red flags. most childhood headaches are primary and need no imaging if examination is normal. raised icp: morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, diplopia and behavioural change. never perform lp before imaging if raised icp is suspected. early-morning vomiting and ataxia suggest a posterior fossa tumour. migraine in children is often shorter, bilateral and associated with vomiting. treat acute migraine early with adequate-dose ibuprofen or paracetamol. medication-overuse headache is common in teenagers. check blood pressure, fundi and visual acuity in every child with persistent headache. headache waking the child from sleep or present on waking with vomiting papilloedema, vi nerve palsy, ataxia or other focal neurology progressive pattern over weeks, or change in personality or school performance thunderclap onset (subarachnoid haemorrhage) or after head injury fever with neck stiffness (meningitis) age under 3 years or neurocutaneous stigmata snoop (headache red flags) systemic symptoms, neurological signs, onset sudden, older/younger age, pattern change or positional definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology primary: migraine with or without aura, tension-type, cluster (rare), cyclical vomiting and abdominal migraine in younger children secondary: viral illness, sinusitis, medication overuse, hypertension, refractive error, post-traumatic, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (iih), meningitis, tumour, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, haemorrhage migraine involves cortical spreading depression and trigeminovascular activation with release of cgrp; strong family history raised icp follows mass lesion, hydrocephalus, cerebral oedema, venous obstruction or increased csf production clinical features migraine: bilateral or unilateral (often bilateral in young children), throbbing, 1-72 hours (shorter in children), nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, relieved by sleep; aura (visual, sensory) in a minority tension-type: band-like pressure, bilateral, mild to moderate, no nausea, no worsening on activity raised icp: morning headache, worse lying down or on coughing, vomiting (often without nausea), diplopia (vi nerve palsy), papilloedema, behavioural change, declining school performance, growth failure or head tilt red flags: occipital location, waking from sleep, progressive pattern, abnormal neurology, age under 3, neurocutaneous stigmata, personality change, seizures, systemic features, trauma medication-overuse headache: analgesics on more than 15 days per month brain tumour presentation depends on location: posterior fossa tumours give ataxia and hydrocephalus; supratentorial tumours cause seizures or hemiparesis; craniopharyngioma causes visual loss and endocrine disturbance investigations careful general and neurological examination including blood pressure, fundi, visual fields, gait, head circumference and skin primary headache with a normal examination needs no imaging mri (preferred) or ct if red flags are present; ct is faster in emergencies lumbar puncture only after imaging excludes a mass; measure opening pressure in suspected iih visual acuity and refraction; sinus imaging only if clinical sinusitis; bp; headache diary management acute migraine: early simple analgesia (ibuprofen 10 mg/kg or paracetamol 15 mg/kg) in a dark quiet room; add antiemetic; nasal sumatriptan (10 mg) or triptans in adolescents if analgesia fails prophylaxis if frequent or disabling: propranolol, pizotifen, topiramate, amitriptyline; cognitive behavioural therapy and relaxation avoid opioids and limit analgesics to under 3 days per week raised icp emergencies: head up 30 degrees, treat hypoxia and hypercapnia, correct blood pressure, mannitol 0.25-0.5 g/kg or 3 percent hypertonic saline, dexamethasone for tumour oedema, urgent neurosurgical referral iih: weight loss, acetazolamide, serial lp, optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunt for vision threat complications & prognosis migraine often improves by adolescence, though some persist into adulthood chronic daily headache leads to school absence and anxiety tumour outcomes depend on histology and location; medulloblastoma survival about 70 percent with multimodal therapy visual loss from iih or papilloedema if untreated herniation (coning) from raised icp: fixed dilated pupil, cushing triad, death ibuprofen paracetamol sumatriptan nasal mannitol

neurocutaneous syndromes & the floppy infant neurology neurocutaneous syndromes are genetic disorders affecting skin and nervous system together, including neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis and sturge-weber syndrome. the floppy infant is a common presentation with a broad differential spanning central, nerve, junction and muscle causes, and a systematic approach localises the lesion. nf1: six or more cafe-au-lait macules, freckling, neurofibromas, lisch nodules, optic glioma; autosomal dominant. tsc: ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch, angiofibromas, infantile spasms, cardiac rhabdomyoma. vigabatrin is first-line for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis. sturge-weber: v1 port-wine stain, seizures, glaucoma, tram-track calcification. most floppy infants have a central cause; absent reflexes and alert face suggest sma. prader-willi: neonatal hypotonia, poor feeding, then hyperphagia and obesity; chromosome 15q11-q13 paternal deletion. check blood pressure annually in nf1. everolimus targets mtor in tsc. infantile spasms in a child with hypomelanotic macules (tuberous sclerosis) visual loss or proptosis in nf1 (optic glioma) hypertension in nf1 (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma) hypotonia with respiratory distress, absent reflexes or bulbar weakness floppy infant who is also encephalopathic, hypoglycaemic or acidotic (metabolic crisis or sepsis) rapidly enlarging neurofibroma (malignant change) nf1 rule of six six or more cafe-au-lait macules over 5 mm in prepubertal children (over 15 mm post-pubertal) is one nih criterion definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology nf1: loss of neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor regulating ras signalling; tumours and pigmentary change tsc: hamartin or tuberin loss causes over-activation of mtor; hamartomas in brain, skin, kidneys, heart, retina sturge-weber: somatic gnaq mutation causes leptomeningeal angioma and facial port-wine stain (v1 distribution) central hypotonia (about 60-80 percent): hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, malformations, chromosomal (down, prader-willi), metabolic, hypothyroidism peripheral hypotonia: sma, congenital myopathies, congenital myotonic dystrophy, neuromuscular junction (infant botulism, congenital myasthenia), peripheral neuropathy clinical features nf1 (two or more criteria): 6 or more cafe-au-lait macules (over 5 mm prepubertal), axillary or inguinal freckling, 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma, lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, distinctive bony lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, tibial pseudarthrosis), first-degree relative nf1 complications: learning disability, scoliosis, hypertension (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma), optic glioma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour nf2: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, presenting later with hearing loss tsc: ash-leaf hypomelanotic macules (wood lamp), facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), shagreen patch, ungual fibromas, infantile spasms and epilepsy, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, autism and learning disability sturge-weber: port-wine stain in v1/v2 area, seizures, contralateral hemiparesis, glaucoma, tram-track calcification on imaging floppy infant: frog-leg posture, head lag, slip-through on vertical suspension, poor suck; encephalopathic or alert, reflexes present or absent help localise investigations nf1: clinical criteria; genetic testing if uncertain; annual bp, ophthalmology for optic glioma; mri only if symptomatic or visual signs tsc: mri brain (cortical tubers, subependymal nodules), echocardiography, renal ultrasound, eeg, ophthalmology, genetic testing floppy infant: examine alertness and reflexes; ck; thyroid function; metabolic screen; genetic testing (smn1, prader-willi methylation, microarray); neuroimaging for central hypotonia; emg/nerve conduction for peripheral cause prader-willi: dna methylation analysis of chromosome 15q11-q13 sepsis and metabolic screen in an acutely hypotonic neonate management nf1: annual review with growth, bp, scoliosis, vision and school progress; mek inhibitors (selumetinib) for symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas tsc: vigabatrin first-line for infantile spasms; everolimus (mtor inhibitor) for sega and renal lesions; epilepsy surgery in selected cases; monitor cardiac rhabdomyoma (usually regresses) sturge-weber: anticonvulsants, aspirin, laser for port-wine stain, glaucoma control, hemispherectomy for refractory seizures floppy infant: treat underlying cause, feeding support (tube feeding), respiratory support, physiotherapy; sma disease-modifying therapy; hormone replacement in hypothyroidism prader-willi: early tube feeding for poor suck, growth hormone, then strict food access control in childhood complications & prognosis nf1: many have mild disease; neurological and learning problems are common; malignancy risk is raised tsc: epilepsy refractory in a third; autism and intellectual disability in a large proportion; renal failure from angiomyolipoma bleeding sturge-weber: intractable seizures, developmental delay, glaucoma floppy infant: prognosis depends on cause; central causes often have developmental disability; sma type 1 outcome transformed by early treatment vigabatrin everolimus

type 1 diabetes mellitus endocrinology & metabolism type 1 diabetes mellitus is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency, and is the commonest form of diabetes in children. lifelong insulin therapy, structured education and glucose monitoring prevent acute and long-term complications. autoimmune beta-cell destruction with absolute insulin deficiency presents with the 4 ps: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, plus fatigue about a quarter present in dka basal-bolus insulin is standard; never stop basal insulin when ill nice hba1c target 48 mmol/mol (6.5 percent) or lower screen for thyroid disease and coeliac disease at diagnosis and regularly retinopathy and nephropathy screening from 12 years treat hypoglycaemia promptly with fast-acting carbohydrate; glucagon im for severe rotate injection sites to avoid lipohypertrophy dka: vomiting, abdominal pain, deep sighing breathing, drowsiness severe hypoglycaemia with seizure or coma ketones persistently elevated during illness recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia (addison, coeliac) repeated dka - consider insulin omission and eating disorder hypoglycaemia symptoms sweating, shaking, hunger, pallor, irritability, headache - autonomic and neuroglycopenic warning symptoms definition & epidemiology clinical features classic: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, over days to weeks secondary enuresis in a previously dry child, recurrent infections, candidal infection diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) at presentation in about 25 percent in the uk, higher in young children and low-resource settings (abdominal pain, vomiting, kussmaul breathing, dehydration, drowsiness) diagnosis is often missed in infants where dka can be mistaken for gastroenteritis, bronchiolitis or pneumonia diagnosis & investigations diagnosis (who): symptoms plus random plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/l or more, or fasting 7.0 mmol/l or more; in a symptomatic child do not delay treatment for an ogtt capillary glucose and ketones at presentation; venous blood gas for acidosis islet autoantibodies; hba1c at baseline (not diagnostic alone in acute onset) baseline screening: thyroid function and antithyroid antibodies, coeliac serology (ttg), lipids, urine albumin creatinine ratio, blood pressure management hypoglycaemia & complications hypoglycaemia (below 4 mmol/l): treat with 10-20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets or juice), recheck in 10-15 minutes, then give a long-acting carbohydrate snack. severe (unconscious or seizure): im glucagon (500 mcg under 25 kg or under 8 years, 1 mg above) or iv 10 percent dextrose 2 ml/kg associated autoimmune disease: autoimmune thyroiditis, coeliac disease, addison disease microvascular complications: retinopathy (screening from 12 years), nephropathy (urine acr annually from 12 years), neuropathy; macrovascular risk later in life growth and puberty delay with poor control; mauriac syndrome in severe poor control; lipohypertrophy at injection sites psychosocial issues: diabetes distress, eating disorders (insulin omission), school support rapid-acting insulin (aspart/lispro) long-acting insulin (glargine/detemir/degludec) glucagon im 10 percent dextrose iv

diabetic ketoacidosis endocrinology & metabolism diabetic ketoacidosis is the triad of hyperglycaemia, ketosis and acidosis due to insulin deficiency, and is the leading cause of death in children with type 1 diabetes, mainly through cerebral oedema. management requires careful, slow fluid replacement, insulin infusion and meticulous monitoring. dka: glucose above 11, ph below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15, ketones 3 mmol/l or more avoid fluid boluses unless shocked; replace deficit over 48 hours add potassium early once urine is passed and potassium is below 5.5 insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour starts after fluids; no bolus cerebral oedema is the major cause of death - watch neurology closely treat suspected cerebral oedema with mannitol or hypertonic saline do not give bicarbonate routinely never stop insulin infusion until ketones clear and acidosis resolves check glucose in any child with unexplained vomiting and tachypnoea headache, bradycardia, hypertension, reduced gcs during treatment (cerebral oedema) shock or severe acidosis ph below 7.1 potassium abnormalities on ecg persistent vomiting preventing oral intake age under 2 years (higher risk) hypoglycaemia during insulin infusion dka triad diabetes (high glucose), ketones, acidosis - the three criteria cerebral oedema signs headache, bradycardia, hypertension, falling gcs (cushing response) definition & pathophysiology clinical features polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (can mimic acute abdomen) deep sighing (kussmaul) breathing, ketotic odour (pear drops) dehydration with tachycardia, dry mucosae, reduced capillary refill; usually shock is uncommon drowsiness, confusion, coma in severe cases precipitants: new diagnosis, infection, missed insulin doses, pump failure investigations capillary glucose and blood ketones; venous blood gas (ph, bicarbonate, potassium); u and e, urea, creatinine; fbc, crp ecg if potassium abnormal; cultures if sepsis suspected; infection screen calculate corrected sodium; the osmolality indicates risk of cerebral oedema monitor hourly: glucose, ketones; 2-4 hourly gas and electrolytes; strict fluid balance and neurological observations management complications & prognosis cerebral oedema (0.5-1 percent, mortality about 25 percent): headache, vomiting, bradycardia, hypertension, irritability, decreasing consciousness, pupil changes, seizures, usually 4-12 hours after treatment start. treat immediately with iv mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 10-15 minutes or 3 percent hypertonic saline 2.5-5 ml/kg over 10-15 minutes, reduce fluid rate and elevate the head, then ct only after stabilisation hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hyperchloraemic acidosis thromboembolism, aspiration, infection (mucormycosis rarely) recurrent dka signals missed insulin and psychosocial issues requiring support 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus insulin infusion (soluble) potassium chloride mannitol 3 percent hypertonic saline

thyroid disorders in children endocrinology & metabolism thyroid disorders in children include congenital hypothyroidism, detected by newborn screening and vital for neurodevelopment, acquired autoimmune hypothyroidism (hashimoto thyroiditis) and hyperthyroidism (graves disease). early diagnosis and treatment prevent intellectual disability and growth failure. newborn screening detects congenital hypothyroidism; treat within 2 weeks commonest cause worldwide is iodine deficiency; in the uk it is thyroid dysgenesis levothyroxine is lifelong in most patients prolonged jaundice, constipation and hypotonia are early clues hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest acquired hypothyroidism; associated with down syndrome and t1dm growth failure with weight gain suggests hypothyroidism graves disease: tsh receptor stimulating antibodies; treat with carbimazole warn of agranulocytosis with antithyroid drugs neonatal thyrotoxicosis results from maternal graves antibodies prolonged jaundice with hypotonia and constipation in a newborn fever or sore throat in a child on carbimazole thyroid storm: fever, tachycardia, agitation exophthalmos with visual disturbance severe growth failure in an older child hypothyroid newborn prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia, macroglossia, hernia (umbilical) - the signs of congenital hypothyroidism congenital hypothyroidism acquired hypothyroidism commonest cause is autoimmune (hashimoto) thyroiditis; associated with down syndrome, turner syndrome, t1dm and coeliac disease features: goitre, short stature with falling growth velocity, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, dry skin, bradycardia, fatigue, poor school performance, delayed puberty (or rarely precocious puberty) investigation: raised tsh, low free t4, positive anti-tpo and anti-thyroglobulin; bone age delayed treatment: levothyroxine 2-5 micrograms/kg/day titrated to tsh; excellent growth recovery hyperthyroidism (graves disease) autoimmune disease with tsh receptor stimulating antibodies; peak in adolescent girls features: weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, sweating, tachycardia, palpitations, emotional lability, deteriorating school performance, goitre, accelerated growth and bone age, exophthalmos investigation: suppressed tsh, raised free t4/t3, positive tsh-receptor antibodies treatment: carbimazole or thiamazole (methimazole) for 18-24 months with block and replace or titration regimens, beta blocker for symptoms (propranolol); monitor neutrophils (agranulocytosis: stop drug if sore throat or fever); radioiodine or total thyroidectomy for relapse or resistance thyroid storm is rare but life-threatening neonatal graves disease occurs in babies of mothers with graves disease due to transplacental tsh-receptor antibodies: irritable, tachycardic, goitre, poor weight gain; self-limiting over weeks to months but may need antithyroid drugs interpreting thyroid function tests raised tsh with low free t4: primary hypothyroidism low tsh with low free t4: central hypothyroidism (pituitary or hypothalamic) raised tsh with normal free t4: subclinical hypothyroidism - often transient in children; repeat in 6-8 weeks suppressed tsh with raised free t4: hyperthyroidism in prematurity, sick euthyroid and drug effects tsh may be misleading complications & prognosis congenital hypothyroidism untreated: severe intellectual disability, growth failure, deafness acquired hypothyroidism untreated: growth arrest, pubertal delay, myxoedema graves disease: relapse in 50 percent after medical therapy, thyroid eye disease, drug side effects prognosis for congenital hypothyroidism is normal iq if treated early levothyroxine (congenital) levothyroxine (acquired) carbimazole propranolol

short stature & growth hormone deficiency endocrinology & metabolism short stature is height below the 0.4th centile (below -2.67 sd) or markedly below the mid-parental height, and most cases are normal variants such as familial short stature or constitutional delay of growth and puberty. growth hormone deficiency and other pathological causes must be identified through careful auxology. most short children are normal variants: familial or constitutional delay always compare with mid-parental height slow height velocity is more important than a single height measurement delayed bone age suggests constitutional delay, gh deficiency or hypothyroidism karyotype all short girls to exclude turner syndrome gh deficiency diagnosed by two failed stimulation tests gh licensed for ghd, turner, prader-willi, ckd, sga, shox, noonan exclude coeliac disease, hypothyroidism and chronic illness growth failure with headaches or visual loss (craniopharyngioma) height velocity below the 25th centile neonatal hypoglycaemia with micropenis disproportionate short stature dysmorphic features suggesting a syndrome short stature with weight gain (hypothyroidism, cushing) mid-parental height boys: (dad + mum + 13) / 2; girls: (dad + mum - 13) / 2 normal growth & assessment causes of short stature normal variants: familial short stature (short parents, normal velocity, normal bone age, normal puberty timing); constitutional delay of growth and puberty (delayed bone age, family history of late puberty, catch-up eventually) endocrine: growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, cushing syndrome or prolonged steroids, rickets, precocious puberty chronic disease: coeliac disease, crohn disease, renal disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital heart disease, asthma on steroids, malnutrition syndromes: turner syndrome (45,x), noonan, prader-willi, shox deficiency, skeletal dysplasia (achondroplasia with disproportion) small for gestational age without catch-up; psychosocial deprivation investigations first-line: fbc, esr/crp, u and e, bone profile, coeliac serology, thyroid function, igf-1, igfbp-3, karyotype in all girls with unexplained short stature, urinalysis bone age x-ray of left hand and wrist (greulich-pyle or tw method): delayed in constitutional delay, gh deficiency and hypothyroidism; advanced in precocious puberty growth hormone stimulation tests (glucagon, insulin tolerance, arginine, clonidine) with peak gh below 7-10 micrograms/l indicating deficiency, typically after sex steroid priming in prepubertal short boys; two tests required pituitary mri if gh deficiency confirmed (hypopituitarism, midline defects, tumours such as craniopharyngioma) management complications & prognosis gh deficiency: hypoglycaemia in neonates, micropenis in boys with hypopituitarism, central obesity, poor growth turner syndrome: short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, cardiac (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation), renal anomalies, ovarian failure, hypothyroidism, coeliac disease psychosocial effects of short stature; good outcome with early gh treatment in deficiency recombinant growth hormone low-dose testosterone

precocious & delayed puberty endocrinology & metabolism puberty is the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. precocious puberty is onset before 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys, while delayed puberty is absence of breast development by 13 in girls or testicular enlargement by 14 in boys. the task is to separate normal variants from pathology and to treat the underlying cause. precocious puberty: before 8 years in girls, 9 in boys delayed puberty: no breasts by 13 in girls, no testicular enlargement by 14 in boys in girls precocious puberty is mostly idiopathic; in boys look for organic causes central precocious puberty has raised lh and fsh; treat with gnrh analogue peripheral precocious puberty has suppressed gonadotropins constitutional delay is the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys high fsh with delayed puberty suggests gonadal failure (turner, klinefelter) kallmann syndrome combines hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia mccune-albright triad: cafe-au-lait spots, fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty precocious puberty in a boy with neurological signs or headache rapidly progressive puberty visual field defects or papilloedema (pituitary tumour) delayed puberty with anosmia or midline defects primary amenorrhoea with short stature and webbed neck (turner) tanner stage first sign girls: breast bud first (b2); boys: testis 4 ml first (g2) normal puberty precocious puberty definition: secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys; much more common in girls and usually idiopathic in girls, whereas organic causes are commoner in boys central (gonadotrophin dependent): early activation of the hpg axis; causes: idiopathic, cns lesions (hypothalamic hamartoma, tumours, hydrocephalus, cranial irradiation, trauma, infection), mccune-albright (late), delayed treatment of cah peripheral (gonadotrophin independent): excess sex steroids from cah, adrenal or gonadal tumours (leydig cell, granulosa cell), mccune-albright syndrome (cafe-au-lait, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, endocrine hyperfunction), familial male-limited precocious puberty (testotoxicosis), hcg-secreting tumours, exogenous exposure, severe hypothyroidism premature thelarche and premature adrenarche are benign variants: isolated breast development or pubic hair without growth acceleration or advanced bone age investigations: height velocity, bone age (advanced), lh, fsh (basal or gnrh stimulation test: pubertal response indicates central), oestradiol or testosterone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, dheas, pelvic ultrasound (uterine size, ovarian cysts), thyroid tests, pituitary mri in boys, girls under 6 and in rapid progression or neurology treatment of central precocious puberty: gnrh analogues (leuprorelin, triptorelin) as depot injections every 1-3 months to halt progression and preserve final height when appropriate. treat underlying cause in peripheral disease (surgery, steroids, aromatase inhibitors, anti-androgens) delayed puberty definition: no breast development by 13 years in girls, no testicular enlargement by 14 years in boys, or more than 5 years between first and complete puberty constitutional delay of growth and puberty (commonest cause, particularly in boys): family history, delayed bone age, normal growth velocity, eventual normal puberty hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: chronic illness (coeliac disease, ibd, cf, renal failure), malnutrition or eating disorders, excessive exercise, hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinaemia, pituitary or hypothalamic tumours, kallmann syndrome (anosmia), isolated gnrh deficiency, prader-willi syndrome hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (gonadal failure): turner syndrome in girls (ovarian failure), klinefelter syndrome in boys, chemotherapy or radiotherapy, gonadal dysgenesis, autoimmune oophoritis investigations: bone age, lh, fsh, oestradiol or testosterone, tsh, prolactin, karyotype in girls and when fsh high, coeliac serology, gnrh stimulation test, pelvic ultrasound, mri pituitary if indicated management: reassurance in constitutional delay, short course of low-dose testosterone (or oestrogen/aromatase inhibitor options) for distress in boys, treat underlying disorders, long-term sex steroid replacement for hypogonadism (gradually increasing oestrogen in girls, testosterone in boys) complications & prognosis precocious puberty: early epiphyseal fusion with short final height, psychosocial difficulty, early menarche delayed puberty: reduced bone density, short stature, psychological distress; need for sex steroid replacement in hypogonadism prognosis depends on cause: idiopathic central precocious puberty has good outcome with gnrh analogue treatment; turner and klinefelter need lifelong follow-up gnrh analogue (triptorelin or leuprorelin depot) testosterone (low dose)

t: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia & disorders of sex development
h: congenital adrenal hyperplasia & disorders of sex development endocrinology & metabolism congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a group of autosomal recessive disorders of cortisol synthesis, most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency, causing cortisol deficiency with androgen excess and, in the salt-wasting form, a life-threatening adrenal crisis in the neonate. disorders of sex development (dsd) cover atypical genitalia and require sensitive multidisciplinary management. 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes over 90 percent of cah salt-wasting crisis presents at 1-3 weeks with vomiting, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia atypical genitalia in a 46,xx baby is cah until proven otherwise diagnosis: raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone emergency treatment: hydrocortisone iv, saline bolus and dextrose lifelong hydrocortisone with fludrocortisone for salt-wasters stress dose steroids during illness dsd needs multidisciplinary assessment and delay in sex assignment hypertension suggests 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency neonate with vomiting, poor feeding and collapse (adrenal crisis) atypical genitalia with no palpable gonads hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia intercurrent illness in known cah with vomiting missed hydrocortisone doses salt-wasting cah biochemistry low na, high k, low glucose, high 17-ohp definition & pathophysiology clinical features girls: atypical genitalia at birth (clitoral enlargement, labioscrotal fusion, urogenital sinus) with normal internal female organs (46,xx) - may be recognised immediately boys: normal genitalia at birth; may present with salt-wasting crisis in week 1-3: vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss, lethargy, dehydration, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia non-salt-wasting (simple virilising) later: early pubic hair, tall child with advanced bone age, then short final height, acne, hirsutism in girls non-classic (late onset): hirsutism, menstrual irregularity, acne in adolescents newborn bloodspot screening for 17-hydroxyprogesterone exists in some countries; hyperpigmentation from raised acth may be present investigations serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone markedly raised (diagnostic) with raised androstenedione and renin; low cortisol; synacthen stimulation test electrolytes (low sodium, high potassium), glucose, blood gas karyotype to establish genetic sex in atypical genitalia; pelvic and abdominal ultrasound to define internal structures; genitogram urinary steroid profile; genetic testing for cyp21a2 management disorders of sex development complications & prognosis adrenal crisis from missed steroid doses or intercurrent illness - can be fatal over-treatment: cushingoid features, growth suppression, osteoporosis; under-treatment: virilisation and tall then short stature fertility issues, polycystic ovary-like syndrome, testicular adrenal rest tumours in males normal life expectancy with good treatment and education hydrocortisone (emergency) hydrocortisone (maintenance) fludrocortisone 0.9 percent sodium chloride

inborn errors of metabolism endocrinology & metabolism inborn errors of metabolism are inherited enzyme or transporter defects, mostly autosomal recessive, that cause toxic accumulation or energy deficiency. they often present in neonates as an unexplained sepsis-like illness and must be considered in any sick infant with acidosis, hypoglycaemia or hyperammonaemia. consider a metabolic disorder in any sick neonate with sepsis-like illness and no infection ammonia, lactate, glucose and gas are essential first-line tests stop protein and give iv dextrose in an acute metabolic crisis hyperammonaemia without acidosis suggests a urea cycle defect mcad deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia; avoid fasting galactosaemia: e. coli sepsis, cataracts, jaundice; remove lactose pku is detected by newborn screening; treat with low-phenylalanine diet most are autosomal recessive; otc deficiency is x-linked involve a specialist metabolic team early neonate with lethargy, vomiting, seizures and coma without infection hypoglycaemia with absent ketones hyperammonaemia unexplained metabolic acidosis with high anion gap family history of unexplained neonatal death deterioration after protein or milk feeding metabolic screen glucose, gas, lactate, ammonia, ketones - plus plasma amino acids, urine organic acids and acylcarnitines definition & epidemiology clinical presentation neonate: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, seizures, tachypnoea, coma after a symptom-free interval of hours to days (intoxication) - resembles sepsis unusual odour (maple syrup in msud, sweaty feet in isovaleric acidaemia, mousy in pku) hepatomegaly, jaundice, cataracts and e. coli sepsis in galactosaemia fasting hypoglycaemia in fatty acid oxidation defects (mcad deficiency) triggered by illness or prolonged fasting developmental regression, coarse facies, organomegaly, dysostosis in lysosomal storage diseases (mucopolysaccharidoses, gaucher, niemann-pick, tay-sachs) consider in unexplained sudden infant death, family history of early deaths, consanguinity, recurrent unexplained vomiting, ketosis or encephalopathy investigations first-line in any suspected case: glucose, blood gas, lactate, ammonia (on ice, to lab immediately), u and e, anion gap, lfts, urinary ketones, urine reducing substances second-line: plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, acylcarnitine profile (blood spot), carnitine, very long-chain fatty acids, urine glycosaminoglycans, enzyme assays, molecular genetics interpretation: hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis and no acidosis suggests urea cycle defect; metabolic acidosis with ketosis and raised anion gap suggests organic acidaemia; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia suggests fatty acid oxidation defect or hyperinsulinism; high lactate suggests mitochondrial or pyruvate disorder newborn bloodspot screening in the uk covers phenylketonuria, mcadd, maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric acidaemia, glutaric aciduria type 1, homocystinuria, plus others (congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell, cf, scid) management key specific disorders phenylketonuria: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; detected by screening; untreated causes intellectual disability, seizures, eczema, fair hair, mousy odour; treated with low-phenylalanine diet (and sapropterin in responsive forms) mcad deficiency: fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, coma, sudden death; avoid fasting; emergency glucose galactosaemia: vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, e. coli sepsis after milk feeds; galactose-free diet urea cycle defects (otc deficiency x-linked): hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, protein intolerance msud: maple syrup odour, ketoacidosis, encephalopathy; treat with branched-chain amino acid restriction glycogen storage diseases: hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly (type i) complications & prognosis metabolic decompensation with encephalopathy, intellectual disability, and death prognosis improved by early diagnosis through screening and dietary management; many lysosomal diseases remain progressive genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis for families sodium benzoate 10 percent dextrose infusion carnitine

hypoglycaemia beyond the neonatal period endocrinology & metabolism hypoglycaemia beyond the neonatal period is a medical emergency because of the risk of seizures and brain injury. in children the commonest causes are ketotic hypoglycaemia, insulin treatment in diabetes, hyperinsulinism, hormone deficiencies, metabolic disease, drugs and sepsis, and a critical sample at the time of hypoglycaemia is the key to diagnosis. check bedside glucose in any seizure, drowsiness or unwell child treat with 10 percent dextrose 2 ml/kg iv; avoid 50 percent dextrose take the critical sample (insulin, cortisol, gh, ketones, fatty acids, lactate) at the time hypoketotic hypoglycaemia suggests hyperinsulinism or fatty acid oxidation defect ketotic hypoglycaemia is the commonest childhood cause and has a good prognosis consider adrenal insufficiency and hypopituitarism if other features glucagon im is an alternative when iv access is not available in diabetes, threshold for treatment is below 4 mmol/l do not forget drugs and poisoning (insulin, sulfonylurea) hypoglycaemic seizure or coma persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with high glucose requirement hepatomegaly with hypoglycaemia hypoglycaemia with hypotension or collapse (adrenal crisis) unexplained in a child with no diabetes - consider poisoning or abuse hypoglycaemia work-up groups hyperinsulinism, fatty acid oxidation defects, adrenal or pituitary hormone deficiency, toxins and drugs, ketotic and glycogen storage disorders definition & physiology clinical features autonomic: sweating, tremor, pallor, hunger, tachycardia, anxiety neuroglycopenic: headache, irritability, confusion, abnormal behaviour, visual disturbance, drowsiness, seizures, coma in infants: poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, irritability, apnoea, seizures always check glucose in any child with unexplained seizure, altered consciousness or unwell with vomiting causes hyperinsulinaemic (hypoketotic, high glucose requirement): congenital hyperinsulinism, insulinoma, factitious (insulin or sulfonylurea poisoning), beckwith-wiedemann syndrome hypoketotic non-hyperinsulinaemic: fatty acid oxidation defects (mcad), hypopituitarism with growth hormone and cortisol deficiency (also low ketones sometimes) ketotic: ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood (commonest, ages 1-5 years, with fasting or illness), glycogen storage diseases, adrenal insufficiency (cah, addison disease, steroid withdrawal), growth hormone deficiency, gluconeogenesis defects drugs and toxins: insulin and sulfonylureas, alcohol, salicylates, beta-blockers, quinine others: sepsis, malnutrition, liver failure, reye syndrome, malaria (and quinine) in endemic areas investigations: the critical sample management complications & prognosis seizures, permanent neurological injury, developmental delay, epilepsy ketotic hypoglycaemia usually resolves by 8-10 years prognosis depends on cause and speed of treatment; recurrent undetected hypoglycaemia in infancy leads to learning difficulty 10 percent dextrose iv bolus glucagon im hydrocortisone iv diazoxide

anaemia in children & iron deficiency haematology & oncology anaemia is a haemoglobin level below the age- and sex-specific normal range. iron deficiency is by far the commonest cause worldwide, driven by poor diet, rapid growth and blood loss, and affects development if untreated. iron deficiency is the commonest cause of anaemia in children worldwide. mcv separates microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic causes. thalassaemia trait has low mcv with normal ferritin and a raised rbc count. replace iron for 3 months after haemoglobin has normalised to restore stores. cows milk over 500 ml/day in toddlers is a major risk factor. failure to respond to iron: check compliance, ongoing loss, malabsorption and alternative diagnoses. transfuse chronic severe anaemia slowly because of risk of heart failure. ferritin may be falsely normal in infection or inflammation. pallor with bruising, bone pain or lymphadenopathy (leukaemia) jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly (haemolysis) heart failure or haemoglobin under 50-70 g/l anaemia unresponsive to iron pancytopenia (aplastic anaemia, infiltration) anaemia with fever in a child from a malaria-endemic area microcytic anaemia - tails thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, iron deficiency, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anaemia definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology microcytic (low mcv): iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anaemia normocytic: acute blood loss, haemolysis (sickle cell, spherocytosis, g6pd deficiency), chronic disease, renal failure, marrow failure or infiltration (leukaemia, aplastic anaemia, transient erythroblastopenia of childhood) macrocytic: b12 and folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease, diamond-blackfan anaemia, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide) iron deficiency: inadequate intake, increased demand (growth), malabsorption (coeliac disease, h. pylori), chronic blood loss (hookworm, cows milk protein colitis, menorrhagia, inflammatory bowel disease) hookworm and malaria are major causes of anaemia in tropical countries clinical features pallor (palmar creases, conjunctivae), fatigue, irritability, poor feeding, reduced exercise tolerance tachycardia, flow murmur, dyspnoea and heart failure when severe or rapid iron deficiency: pica, koilonychia, angular stomatitis, glossitis, poor concentration and delayed development, breath-holding spells haemolysis: jaundice, splenomegaly, dark urine, gallstones marrow failure: bruising, infection, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy suggest leukaemia chronic anaemia is often well tolerated clinically even with very low haemoglobin investigations fbc with mcv, mch, rdw, reticulocyte count and blood film iron deficiency: low mcv, low ferritin, low serum iron, high transferrin/tibc, hypochromic pencil cells and high rdw; ferritin is an acute phase protein so may be falsely normal in infection thalassaemia trait: low mcv with normal or high rbc count, normal ferritin, mentzer index (mcv/rbc) under 13, raised hba2 on electrophoresis haemolysis: reticulocytosis, raised bilirubin and ldh, low haptoglobin, dat (coombs), film showing spherocytes or sickle cells; g6pd assay chronic disease: low iron and low tibc with normal or high ferritin b12/folate, tfts, coeliac serology, stool for occult blood or ova, lead level when indicated bone marrow only for suspected leukaemia or aplasia management oral ferrous sulphate or fumarate 3-6 mg/kg/day elemental iron in 1-3 divided doses, continue for 3 months after haemoglobin normalises to replenish stores give with vitamin c and between meals; avoid with milk and tea; warn about dark stools, constipation, tooth staining with liquids dietary advice: iron-rich weaning foods, limit cows milk to under 500 ml/day, delay cows milk as the main drink until 12 months intravenous iron if intolerance or malabsorption transfusion only for severe symptomatic anaemia, heart failure or acute blood loss: transfuse slowly (3-5 ml/kg per hour, 10 ml/kg aliquots) to avoid fluid overload in chronic severe anaemia prevention: iron supplements for preterm and low birth weight infants, universal fortification, deworming and malaria prevention in endemic areas complications & prognosis iron deficiency impairs cognition, behaviour and motor development, partly irreversible if prolonged in infancy heart failure in severe chronic anaemia increased infection susceptibility prognosis is excellent when iron deficiency is corrected; underlying disease determines outcome in other anaemias ferrous sulphate / ferrous fumarate folic acid

sickle cell disease haematology & oncology sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy caused by hbs, in which deoxygenated red cells sickle, causing haemolysis and vaso-occlusion. it leads to recurrent painful crises, acute chest syndrome, stroke and lifelong infection risk, and is one of the commonest genetic diseases worldwide. hbs arises from a point mutation in the beta globin chain (glu6val); autosomal recessive. symptoms start after 4-6 months as hbf falls; dactylitis is the commonest first sign. fever in scd is an emergency: iv antibiotics early because of functional hyposplenism. acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death; treat early with oxygen, antibiotics and transfusion. penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination from infancy save lives. transcranial doppler screening and transfusion prevent stroke. hydroxycarbamide increases hbf and reduces crises. parvovirus b19 causes aplastic crisis; splenic sequestration is a cause of shock in young children. fever 38.5 c or above (sepsis risk) chest pain, hypoxia, new cough or infiltrate (acute chest syndrome) sudden pallor with massive splenomegaly and shock (sequestration) focal neurology, headache or seizure (stroke) priapism lasting over 4 hours falling hb with low reticulocytes (aplastic crisis) sickle crises - 4 types vaso-occlusive, sequestration, aplastic, haemolytic (also acute chest as a complication) definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in infants: painful swelling of hands and feet vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis: bone pain in limbs, back, abdomen, triggered by infection, dehydration, cold or stress acute chest syndrome: new pulmonary infiltrate with fever, cough, chest pain or hypoxia; leading cause of death splenic sequestration: acute splenic enlargement with falling hb and shock, usually in children under 5 aplastic crisis: parvovirus b19 causes transient red cell aplasia with low reticulocytes stroke: ischaemic stroke in 10 percent of hbss before age 20; silent cerebral infarcts common sepsis and meningitis (streptococcus pneumoniae, salmonella osteomyelitis) chronic: growth failure and delayed puberty, gallstones, priapism, leg ulcers, avascular necrosis of hips, sickle retinopathy, nephropathy, pulmonary hypertension jaundice and chronic anaemia (hb 60-90 g/l) with raised reticulocytes investigations newborn bloodspot screening with confirmation by haemoglobin electrophoresis or hplc fbc, reticulocytes, film (sickle cells, target cells, howell-jolly bodies indicating hyposplenism) acute: group and save, blood cultures, cxr, oxygen saturation, urinalysis, liver function transcranial doppler annually from age 2 to 16 for hbss: velocity over 200 cm/s indicates high stroke risk mri/mra if neurological symptoms; echo in pulmonary hypertension sickledex solubility test does not distinguish trait from disease and is unreliable in infants management fever 38.5 c or above: urgent assessment, blood cultures and iv ceftriaxone because of hyposplenism painful crisis: analgesia within 30 minutes (paracetamol, nsaids, then oral or iv morphine), hydration, warmth; avoid over-hydration; incentive spirometry to prevent chest syndrome acute chest syndrome: oxygen, antibiotics (cephalosporin plus macrolide), analgesia with caution, simple or exchange transfusion, ventilatory support splenic sequestration: resuscitation with transfusion; consider splenectomy after recurrent episodes stroke: urgent exchange transfusion; chronic transfusion programme to keep hbs under 30 percent after transcranial doppler abnormality hydroxycarbamide: raises hbf; reduces crises, chest syndrome and transfusion needs curative option: matched sibling haematopoietic stem cell transplantation; gene therapy emerging priapism: hydration, analgesia, urgent urology if over 4 hours complications & prognosis overwhelming sepsis in early childhood is the major cause of death in unscreened populations cerebrovascular disease and cognitive impairment chronic organ damage: kidney, lung, eyes, bones iron overload after repeated transfusion needs chelation life expectancy exceeds 50 years in high-resource settings with comprehensive care, much lower in sub-saharan africa penicillin v hydroxycarbamide folic acid morphine (acute pain)

thalassaemia haematology & oncology thalassaemias are inherited disorders of reduced globin chain synthesis. beta thalassaemia major presents in the first year with severe transfusion-dependent anaemia and requires lifelong transfusion with iron chelation, whereas alpha thalassaemia ranges from silent carriage to hydrops fetalis. beta thalassaemia major presents in the first year with severe anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and failure to thrive. hba2 is raised in beta thalassaemia trait; hbf dominates in major. regular transfusion plus iron chelation is the cornerstone of care. iron overload cardiomyopathy is the commonest cause of death; monitor with t2* mri. four-gene alpha deletion causes hb barts hydrops fetalis; three-gene gives hbh disease. exclude iron deficiency before labelling microcytosis as thalassaemia trait. matched sibling stem cell transplant is curative. genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis are essential for carrier couples. heart failure or arrhythmia in a transfused patient (iron overload) fever on desferrioxamine or deferiprone with neutropenia (agranulocytosis) fever in splenectomised patients (overwhelming sepsis) bone pain or fractures, spinal cord compression from extramedullary masses delayed puberty and growth failure haemolysis crisis in hbh disease with infection or oxidant drugs alpha genes lost 1 = silent carrier, 2 = trait, 3 = hbh disease, 4 = hb barts hydrops fetalis definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features beta thalassaemia major: presents at 3-18 months as hbf falls with severe anaemia, failure to thrive, pallor, jaundice, irritability, hepatosplenomegaly untreated: frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth ("chipmunk" facies), thalassaemic facies, pathological fractures, short stature thalassaemia intermedia: milder, later presentation, may need occasional transfusion beta thalassaemia trait: asymptomatic, mild microcytic anaemia hbh disease: moderate anaemia, splenomegaly, jaundice, gallstones; hydrops fetalis presents with severe antenatal oedema and stillbirth complications of iron overload: cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia (leading cause of death), endocrinopathy (diabetes, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, hypoparathyroidism), liver cirrhosis, osteoporosis investigations fbc: severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia (hb 20-60 g/l in major), raised reticulocytes; film shows target cells, nucleated red cells, basophilic stippling haemoglobin electrophoresis or hplc: raised hbf and absent hba in beta major; raised hba2 over 3.5 percent in beta trait; hbh inclusions in alpha thal ferritin (iron overload), cardiac and liver t2* mri, lfts, glucose, endocrine screening, dexa genetic testing and family screening; antenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling rule out iron deficiency before diagnosing trait management transfusion: leucodepleted, extended phenotype matched red cells (rh, kell) to prevent alloimmunisation iron chelation starting after about 10-20 transfusions or ferritin over 1000 microgram/l: desferrioxamine subcutaneous infusion 30-50 mg/kg over 8-12 hours 5 nights a week, oral deferasirox or deferiprone monitoring: ferritin 3-monthly, cardiac and liver t2* mri annually, endocrine screening from age 10, audiology and ophthalmology curative: matched sibling hsct in early childhood; gene therapy is available in some settings genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis for carrier couples; carrier screening programmes reduce births in high-prevalence regions in resource-limited settings, transfusions and chelation access are the main barriers complications & prognosis with regular transfusions and chelation, survival into the fifth decade or beyond is achievable cardiac siderosis is the commonest cause of death transfusion complications: alloimmunisation, infections (hbv, hcv, hiv), iron overload chelation toxicity: desferrioxamine (hearing and eye toxicity, growth retardation), deferiprone (agranulocytosis), deferasirox (renal and liver) untreated beta thalassaemia major is usually fatal in the first decade desferrioxamine deferasirox deferiprone folic acid

haemophilia & von willebrand disease haematology & oncology haemophilia a and b are x-linked recessive deficiencies of factor viii and ix causing bleeding into joints and muscles. von willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, affecting both sexes with mucocutaneous bleeding, and diagnosis rests on clotting tests and factor assays. haemophilia a and b are x-linked recessive; mothers are carriers, and a third of cases are new mutations. aptt prolonged with normal pt and platelets indicates a factor viii/ix/xi deficiency. haemarthroses are the hallmark of severe haemophilia; mucocutaneous bleeding suggests platelet or vwd disorders. treat a suspected bleed immediately with factor before imaging. desmopressin works for mild haemophilia a and type 1 vwd but is avoided in type 2b and type 3. emicizumab is a subcutaneous prophylaxis for haemophilia a, including with inhibitors. avoid im injections, aspirin and nsaids in bleeding disorders. vwd is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder and affects both sexes. head injury or headache in any child with haemophilia neck, throat or tongue swelling, or compartment syndrome haemarthrosis not responding to treatment, or suspicion of an inhibitor heavy bleeding after surgery or dental extraction neonatal intracranial haemorrhage or cephalhaematoma with bleeding history severe menorrhagia in a girl with iron deficiency (vwd) haemophilia sites haemarthrosis, haematoma, haematuria - the three h of bleeds in haemophilia definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features severe haemophilia: bleeding in the first year; excessive bruising on crawling, intracranial bleed (rare in the neonate), prolonged bleeding after circumcision or heel prick, haemarthroses from age 1-2 haemarthrosis: hot, swollen, painful joints (knees, elbows, ankles) after minimal trauma; repeated bleeds cause synovitis and haemophilic arthropathy muscle haematomas (iliopsoas, forearm compartment syndrome), haematuria, intracranial haemorrhage, bleeding after dental extraction mild haemophilia: bleeding only with trauma or surgery vwd: mucocutaneous bleeding - epistaxis, easy bruising, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, post-operative bleeding; joint bleeds uncommon except type 3 female carriers may have low factor levels and heavy menses always consider non-accidental injury but remember that bruising may be a presenting feature investigations haemophilia: prolonged aptt with normal pt, thrombin time and platelet count; mixing study corrects; specific factor viii/ix assays confirm vwd: platelet count normal, aptt may be prolonged (low fviii), vwf antigen, vwf activity (ristocetin cofactor), factor viii level, multimer analysis; pfa-100 abnormal inhibitor screening (bethesda assay) when treatment response is poor genetic testing and carrier detection; antenatal diagnosis when requested imaging: ultrasound/mri for joint disease; ct head urgently for any head injury or neurological symptom management haemophilia a: recombinant factor viii to target level 100 percent for life-threatening bleeds (dose in units = weight in kg x desired rise in percent x 0.5); 30-50 percent for joint bleeds haemophilia b: recombinant factor ix (dose = weight x desired rise in percent x 1 to 1.2) prophylaxis: regular factor infusions (e.g. fviii every 2-3 days) from first joint bleed, or non-factor therapy (emicizumab, a bispecific antibody mimicking fviii, given subcutaneously weekly or longer interval) mild haemophilia a and type 1 vwd: desmopressin (ddavp) 0.3 microgram/kg iv or intranasal; releases vwf and fviii; limit repeated doses (tachyphylaxis) and monitor sodium; avoid under 2 years tranexamic acid 15-25 mg/kg three times daily for mucosal bleeding and dental extractions severe vwd: vwf/fviii concentrate inhibitors (antibodies, 20-30 percent of severe haemophilia a): bypassing agents (recombinant fviia, feiba), immune tolerance induction, emicizumab rice (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and physiotherapy for joint bleeds gene therapy now approved in some countries complications & prognosis haemophilic arthropathy and chronic pain; prophylaxis largely prevents this intracranial haemorrhage is a leading cause of death inhibitor development complicates management historic transfusion-transmitted hiv, hepatitis b and c from plasma products; recombinant products have removed this risk life expectancy is near normal with prophylaxis in high-income countries; limited in regions without factor access desmopressin tranexamic acid factor viii emicizumab

itp & bleeding disorders haematology & oncology immune thrombocytopenia (itp) is the commonest cause of acute isolated thrombocytopenia in otherwise well children, presenting with sudden bruising and petechiae often after a viral illness. most children recover spontaneously, but clinicians must exclude leukaemia, aplastic anaemia and other causes of bleeding before labelling it itp. itp: isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child with sudden bruising or petechiae after a viral illness. most childhood itp resolves spontaneously within weeks to months. bone marrow should be done if any atypical feature or before steroid treatment. treat for bleeding, not the platelet number alone. ivig works fastest; steroids carry risk of masking leukaemia. intracranial haemorrhage occurs in under 0.5 percent. avoid aspirin, nsaids and intramuscular injections. consider hus, dic and malignancy when there are additional findings. headache, vomiting, drowsiness or neurological signs (intracranial bleed) pallor, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy (leukaemia) fever with non-blanching rash and unwell appearance (sepsis/meningococcal) pancytopenia or abnormal film uncontrolled mucosal bleeding or melaena platelet count under 10 x10^9/l with active bleeding itp typical picture well child, petechiae, platelets low, no organomegaly, post-viral definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features sudden onset of petechiae, purpura and bruising in a well child, often generalised mucosal bleeding: epistaxis, gum bleeding, haematuria, melaena and menorrhagia no hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain or pallor (if present suggests alternative) intracranial haemorrhage in under 0.5 percent, usually with platelets under 10 x10^9/l bleeding severity does not always correlate with platelet count; bleeding scores guide management henoch-schonlein purpura gives palpable purpura on buttocks and legs with normal platelets; meningococcal septicaemia gives a non-blanching rash with a very sick child investigations fbc and film: isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets and normal red and white cells bone marrow aspiration is required if atypical features: abnormal white count or haemoglobin, hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, or before starting steroids coagulation screen (pt, aptt normal), blood group and dat, hiv, hepatitis c, ana, immunoglobulins in older children or chronic disease h. pylori testing in chronic itp in some settings pregnancy test in adolescent girls neonatal: maternal platelet count and antibodies; cranial ultrasound if neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia suspected management observation with clear safety-netting is appropriate for mild symptoms (skin bruising only) even with platelets under 20 x10^9/l treatment options: iv immunoglobulin 0.8-1 g/kg single dose (raises count within 24-48 hours); oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day for up to 14 days (after marrow to exclude leukaemia); iv anti-d (0.05 mg/kg) in rh-positive non-splenectomised children life-threatening bleeding (intracranial haemorrhage): platelet transfusion, ivig plus high-dose iv methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg, tranexamic acid; urgent senior review chronic itp: thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy as last resort (vaccinate and give penicillin prophylaxis) avoid intramuscular injections and use compression for bleeding treat other causes: hus with supportive dialysis, dic with treating the underlying cause and blood products complications & prognosis about 70-80 percent recover within 6 months; 20 percent develop chronic itp intracranial haemorrhage is rare but the most feared complication risks of treatment: ivig headache and aseptic meningitis, haemolysis with anti-d, steroid adverse effects older children and those with insidious onset are more likely to develop chronic itp and secondary causes such as sle or hiv iv immunoglobulin prednisolone anti-d immunoglobulin tranexamic acid

acute leukaemia haematology & oncology acute leukaemia is the commonest childhood cancer, with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (all) accounting for about 80 percent of cases and aml most of the rest. marrow replacement produces anaemia, bleeding, infection and bone pain, and modern risk-adapted chemotherapy cures over 85-90 percent of children with all in high-resource settings. all is the commonest childhood cancer, peak at 2-5 years; b-cell precursor all predominates. suspect leukaemia in a child with fever, bruising, pallor, bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly. diagnosis is by bone marrow showing at least 20-25 percent blasts. favourable all: age 1-10, white count below 50, hyperdiploidy, etv6-runx1; unfavourable: age under 1 or over 10, philadelphia chromosome, high count, mrd positive. cns prophylaxis with intrathecal methotrexate is essential because the cns is a sanctuary. febrile neutropenia needs iv antibiotics within 1 hour. tumour lysis syndrome requires hydration, rasburicase and monitoring. apl (aml m3) causes dic and is treated with atra. fever with neutropenia (neutrophils under 1.0 x10^9/l) respiratory distress or svc obstruction (mediastinal mass; avoid sedation or lying flat) hyperleucocytosis (white count over 100 x10^9/l) with leucostasis dic or severe bleeding in aml/apl raised uric acid, potassium, phosphate with oliguria (tumour lysis) back pain with neurological deficit (spinal cord compression) leukaemia presentation - brief bone pain, reticuloendothelial enlargement (nodes, liver, spleen), infection, easy bruising, fatigue/pallor definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology clinical features marrow failure: pallor and fatigue (anaemia), fever and infection (neutropenia), bruising, petechiae, bleeding (thrombocytopenia) bone and joint pain, limp or refusal to walk (can mimic jia) hepatosplenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy t-cell all: mediastinal mass causing respiratory distress, svc syndrome, very high white count cns involvement: headache, vomiting, cranial nerve palsy; testicular enlargement aml: gum hypertrophy, chloromas, dic (especially m3 acute promyelocytic leukaemia), hyperleucocytosis symptoms usually over days to weeks; constitutional features: fever, weight loss, night sweats investigations fbc and film: anaemia, thrombocytopenia, variable white count with blasts (may be normal or leucopenic) bone marrow aspirate: over 25 percent blasts (who requires 20 percent); immunophenotyping, cytogenetics, fish and molecular testing lumbar puncture with csf cytospin once safe and coagulopathy corrected (cns staging) chest x-ray (mediastinal mass), uric acid, ldh, u&e, calcium, phosphate, clotting (dic), liver function, viral serology blood group and crossmatch; irradiated, cmv-negative, leucodepleted products echocardiogram before anthracyclines; fertility counselling and sperm storage in pubertal boys management risk stratification by age (1-10 years favourable), initial white count (below 50 x10^9/l), cytogenetics, cns status and early response (minimal residual disease at end of induction) ph-positive all: add tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib); high-risk disease and relapse: hsct; refractory b-all: car-t cell therapy or blinatumomab aml: intensive chemotherapy (cytarabine, anthracycline) with high supportive needs; atra plus arsenic trioxide for acute promyelocytic leukaemia; hsct in high-risk cases supportive care: central venous line, blood products, antibiotic prophylaxis, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for pneumocystis, antifungals, vaccination review, allopurinol or rasburicase for tumour lysis febrile neutropenia (temperature over 38 c with neutrophils under 1.0 x10^9/l) is an emergency: iv broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour psychosocial support, school liaison, palliative input when needed; long-term survivor follow-up complications & prognosis tumour lysis syndrome (hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, acute kidney injury) infections: neutropenic sepsis, fungal infection, pneumocystis jirovecii treatment toxicity: asparaginase pancreatitis and thrombosis, vincristine neuropathy and constipation, methotrexate mucositis, steroid avascular necrosis and hyperglycaemia relapse (marrow, cns, testes); 5-year survival about 90 percent for childhood all in resourced settings, 60-70 percent for aml, much lower in under-resourced regions late effects: cardiomyopathy (anthracyclines), growth and endocrine problems, infertility, neurocognitive deficits, second cancers vincristine methotrexate (intrathecal) mercaptopurine rasburicase
