solid tumours (wilms, neuroblastoma, brain tumours) haematology & oncology solid tumours make up about 40 percent of childhood cancers and include brain tumours (the commonest solid tumours), neuroblastoma, wilms tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma and bone sarcomas. many present with an abdominal mass or non-specific features, and early recognition and referral to a specialist centre improves survival. brain tumours are the commonest solid tumours in children; most are infratentorial in under-10s. wilms tumour: asymptomatic abdominal mass not crossing the midline; associated with wagr and beckwith-wiedemann. neuroblastoma: arises from adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain; raised urinary catecholamines; mycn amplification is poor prognosis. stage 4s neuroblastoma in infants can regress spontaneously. leukocoria means retinoblastoma until proved otherwise. do not biopsy wilms tumour before surgery in siop protocol (risk of tumour spillage). hereditary retinoblastoma (rb1) carries a risk of second malignancy such as osteosarcoma. late effects surveillance is a major component of care. abdominal mass in a child (urgent ultrasound and referral) leukocoria or absent red reflex persistent headache with early-morning vomiting or ataxia back pain with leg weakness or sphincter changes (spinal cord compression) unexplained bone pain with a soft tissue mass or fever hypertension with abdominal mass (wilms or neuroblastoma) wagr wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, retardation (11p13 deletion) neuroblastoma features - hva and vma raised urinary homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology wilms (nephroblastoma): embryonal renal tumour; wt1 mutation associated with wagr (wilms, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, retardation), denys-drash and beckwith-wiedemann (hemihypertrophy, macroglossia) neuroblastoma: tumour of sympathetic nervous system precursors in adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain; mycn amplification is poor prognosis medulloblastoma, ependymoma, pilocytic astrocytoma and craniopharyngioma are the common brain tumours; most are infratentorial in children under 10 retinoblastoma: rb1 mutation, hereditary (bilateral, increased risk of osteosarcoma) or sporadic li-fraumeni (tp53) predisposes to sarcomas, brain tumours and leukaemia; nf1 predisposes to optic glioma clinical features wilms tumour: well child with asymptomatic abdominal mass that does not cross the midline, haematuria, hypertension, occasionally pain or fever; associated syndromes (aniridia, hemihypertrophy) neuroblastoma: abdominal mass crossing the midline, fatigue, weight loss, bone pain, periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), proptosis, horner syndrome, opsoclonus-myoclonus, spinal cord compression, hypertension, secretory diarrhoea (vip); skin nodules in infants (stage 4s) brain tumours: raised icp (morning headache, vomiting), cerebellar signs and head tilt (posterior fossa), seizures or hemiparesis (supratentorial), endocrine and visual disturbance (suprasellar), failure to thrive or diencephalic syndrome retinoblastoma: leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), squint, red eye; test with red reflex osteosarcoma: pain and swelling of distal femur or proximal tibia in adolescents; ewing sarcoma: pain, swelling, fever with diaphysis involvement rhabdomyosarcoma: painless mass in head and neck, orbit, bladder, vagina or limbs investigations abdominal mass: ultrasound first, then mri/ct, chest ct for metastases; urine catecholamines (vma, hva) and mibg scan for neuroblastoma; biopsy for neuroblastoma or atypical wilms (usually no biopsy before nephrectomy in wilms to avoid tumour spill) blood: fbc, u&e, lfts, ldh, ferritin, alpha-fetoprotein (hepatoblastoma and germ cell), beta-hcg (germ cell tumours) brain: mri brain and whole spine with contrast; csf cytology for medulloblastoma after surgery; eeg not routinely bone marrow aspirate and trephine in neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, ewing sarcoma genetics: mycn amplification, 1p and 11q status, wt1 and tp53 testing echo and audiology before cisplatin/anthracycline management wilms tumour: nephrectomy plus chemotherapy (vincristine, dactinomycin +/- doxorubicin); preoperative chemotherapy in europe (siop) or upfront surgery (cog); radiotherapy for advanced or unfavourable histology; over 90 percent survival in localised disease neuroblastoma: risk-stratified from observation (infants with low-risk and stage 4s often regress spontaneously) to intensive chemotherapy, surgery, myeloablative therapy with stem cell rescue, radiotherapy, isotretinoin and anti-gd2 immunotherapy (dinutuximab) for high risk medulloblastoma: maximal surgical resection, craniospinal radiotherapy (avoid under 3 years), chemotherapy; treat hydrocephalus with ventriculostomy or shunt low-grade gliomas: surgery or observation; targeted braf/mek inhibitors in selected tumours retinoblastoma: intra-arterial or systemic chemotherapy, laser, enucleation for advanced disease; genetic counselling osteosarcoma and ewing sarcoma: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, limb-salvage surgery, radiotherapy (ewing) supportive and palliative care, fertility preservation, psychological support, school reintegration complications & prognosis survival: localised wilms over 90 percent; high-risk neuroblastoma about 50-60 percent with modern therapy; medulloblastoma about 70-80 percent in standard risk; dipg very poor late effects: cardiomyopathy (anthracyclines), hearing loss and nephrotoxicity (cisplatin), infertility, neurocognitive deficits and endocrine problems (cranial radiation), second malignancies, growth impairment surgical complications: posterior fossa syndrome, hydrocephalus, vascular injury lifelong survivorship surveillance is mandatory vincristine dactinomycin dinutuximab

lymphoma & oncological emergencies haematology & oncology lymphomas (hodgkin and non-hodgkin) are the third commonest childhood cancer group and present with painless lymphadenopathy or rapidly growing masses. oncological emergencies such as tumour lysis syndrome, superior vena cava obstruction, spinal cord compression and febrile neutropenia are time-critical and often occur at diagnosis. hodgkin lymphoma: painless rubbery nodes, b symptoms, reed-sternberg cells; excellent cure rates. burkitt lymphoma: myc t(8;14), fastest-growing tumour, high tumour lysis risk; jaw tumours in endemic form. biopsy the most abnormal node; fna alone is inadequate. tumour lysis syndrome needs hydration and rasburicase before chemotherapy. febrile neutropenia is an emergency: iv antibiotics within the hour. mediastinal mass: avoid sedation, ga and lying flat until airway safety is planned. spinal cord compression: urgent mri and dexamethasone. ann arbor staging with b symptoms defines hodgkin stage. orthopnoea, stridor, facial plethora (svc syndrome / mediastinal mass) back pain with weakness or sphincter disturbance (cord compression) oliguria with high k, urate or phosphate (tumour lysis) fever with neutropenia rapidly enlarging node or hard supraclavicular node over 2 cm abdominal pain and distension with a mass (burkitt, intussusception) b symptoms fever over 38 c, drenching night sweats, weight loss over 10 percent in 6 months tumour lysis electrolytes high potassium, high phosphate, high urate, low calcium definition & epidemiology aetiology & pathophysiology burkitt: t(8;14) translocation placing myc under immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter; fastest growing human tumour; doubling time 24-48 hours, with high risk of spontaneous tumour lysis hodgkin: clonal b-cell lymphoma with reed-sternberg cells; ebv association; subtypes include nodular sclerosing (commonest) and mixed cellularity t-lymphoblastic lymphoma: mediastinal mass; overlaps with t-all (differentiated by marrow blasts under 25 percent) anaplastic large cell lymphoma: alk-positive, cd30+; skin, nodes and extranodal disease predisposition: immunodeficiency (ataxia telangiectasia, wiskott-aldrich), hiv, post-transplant, ebv clinical features hodgkin: painless firm rubbery cervical or supraclavicular nodes, mediastinal mass causing cough or dyspnoea; b symptoms (fever over 38 c, drenching night sweats, weight loss over 10 percent), pruritus, alcohol-induced node pain nhl: rapidly enlarging mass, abdominal pain and distension, intussusception (burkitt), jaw swelling, mediastinal mass with svc syndrome, pleural effusion, cns involvement constitutional features: fever, fatigue, weight loss, anaemia and splenomegaly persistent lymphadenopathy over 4-6 weeks, node over 2 cm, supraclavicular location, hard fixed nodes, or associated systemic symptoms warrant investigation differential: reactive nodes, infectious mononucleosis, tb lymphadenitis, atypical mycobacteria, cat scratch disease, leukaemia, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma investigations excision biopsy of the most abnormal node (not needle aspiration alone); fresh tissue for histology, immunophenotype and cytogenetics chest x-ray (mediastinal width) and ct/pet-ct for staging; abdominal ultrasound or ct; marrow aspirate and trephine; csf cytospin blood: fbc, esr (hl), ldh, uric acid, u&e, calcium, phosphate, lfts, hiv and hepatitis serology ann arbor stage i-iv with a (no b symptoms) or b suffix; murphy (st jude) staging for nhl safety before biopsy: do not give general anaesthesia or sedation to a child with a large mediastinal mass without senior anaesthetic planning; consider less invasive diagnostic route (pleural fluid, peripheral node, bone marrow) management oncological emergencies tumour lysis syndrome: hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia, hypocalcaemia and renal failure; prevent with hyperhydration (2-3 l/m2/day), allopurinol or rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg, strict fluid balance, frequent electrolytes, treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin-glucose, salbutamol), dialysis if refractory; avoid potassium and phosphate in fluids febrile neutropenia: temperature over 38 c and neutrophils under 1.0 x10^9/l; treat as sepsis with iv broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour after cultures, fluid resuscitation, escalate for resistant organisms or fungal infection svc syndrome and mediastinal mass: facial swelling, plethora, orthopnoea, stridor; keep upright, avoid sedation and supine position, urgent specialist airway planning; steroids or chemotherapy often treat urgently spinal cord compression: back pain, weakness, sphincter dysfunction; urgent mri spine and high-dose dexamethasone with oncology and neurosurgery input hyperleucocytosis with leucostasis: hydration, leukapheresis rarely; avoid transfusion without need raised icp from brain tumour: dexamethasone, head elevation, neurosurgery haemorrhage and dic: platelets, ffp, cryoprecipitate; treat underlying cause typhlitis (neutropenic enterocolitis): right iliac fossa pain and fever in neutropenia; broad-spectrum antibiotics, bowel rest, surgery rarely complications & prognosis overall survival over 90 percent for hl and for most nhl in high-income settings late effects: cardiomyopathy (anthracycline), secondary cancers (radiotherapy, alkylators), infertility, hypothyroidism after neck radiation in resource-limited settings burkitt lymphoma is curable with low-cost cyclophosphamide-based regimens rasburicase allopurinol calcium gluconate 10 percent dexamethasone

t: Childhood exanthems (measles, rubella, roseola, scarlet fever)
h: childhood exanthems (measles, rubella, roseola, scarlet fever) infectious diseases childhood exanthems are fever-associated rashes caused mainly by viral infections (measles, rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum) and by toxin-mediated bacterial disease (scarlet fever). recognising the pattern of prodrome, rash distribution and associated signs allows correct diagnosis, infection control and timely treatment of complications, especially for measles in malnourished or vitamin a deficient children. measles: 3 cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) plus koplik spots, then a rash from the face downwards pneumonia is the commonest cause of measles death; blindness from keratitis is a leading cause of childhood blindness all children with measles in resource-limited settings get vitamin a on 2 consecutive days measles is airborne - isolate with airborne precautions roseola: rash appears as the fever resolves; a common cause of febrile seizure rubella is mild in children but teratogenic in the first trimester parvovirus b19 causes aplastic crisis in children with chronic haemolysis scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and perioral pallor; treat with penicillin for 10 days sspe is a late fatal complication of measles, years after infection fever with a non-blanching rash and ill appearance (meningococcal sepsis) measles with fast breathing, chest indrawing or hypoxia measles with corneal clouding or ulceration severe malnutrition or hiv with measles - high mortality rash with mucosal involvement, skin sloughing or hypotension (sjs/ten, scalded skin, toxic shock) pregnant contact of rubella or parvovirus - needs urgent serology and obstetric advice measles 3 cs and k cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, then koplik spots before the rash measles complications think of the ears, lungs, gut, eyes and brain: otitis, pneumonia, diarrhoea, keratitis, encephalitis definition & epidemiology measles complications: otitis media, pneumonia (commonest cause of measles death), diarrhoea, croup, keratitis and corneal ulceration leading to blindness, malnutrition, oral ulceration neurological: post-infectious encephalomyelitis (about 1 in 1000), subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (sspe) years later, and measles inclusion body encephalitis in the immunocompromised measles causes immune amnesia and increases susceptibility to other infections for months to years diagnosis is clinical in endemic areas; confirm by measles-specific igm or salivary/pcr testing in elsewhere and notify the public health authority management is supportive: fluids, antipyretics, nutrition, treat bacterial complications, isolate (airborne precautions) who: vitamin a 200,000 iu orally daily for 2 days (100,000 iu if 6-11 months, 50,000 iu if under 6 months), with a third dose 2-4 weeks later if there are eye signs post-exposure prophylaxis: mmr within 72 hours or normal human immunoglobulin within 6 days for susceptible contacts, infants and immunocompromised rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum and scarlet fever rubella (german measles): mild fever, pink maculopapular rash starting on the face and spreading in 24 hours, tender postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy, arthralgia in adolescents. self-limiting; the danger is congenital rubella syndrome (cataracts, sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus/pulmonary stenosis, microcephaly) when infection occurs in early pregnancy roseola infantum (hhv-6, hhv-7): infants 6 months to 2 years; 3-5 days of high fever in a well-looking child, then the fever abruptly settles as a pink macular rash appears on the trunk. a common cause of febrile convulsions erythema infectiosum (parvovirus b19): "slapped cheek" bright red facial erythema followed by a lacy reticular rash on the limbs. child is no longer infectious when rash appears. risks: aplastic crisis in haemolytic anaemias (sickle cell, spherocytosis), hydrops fetalis in pregnancy, arthropathy in adults scarlet fever (group a streptococcus, pyrogenic exotoxin): sore throat, fever, fine erythematous sandpaper-like rash sparing the area around the mouth (circumoral pallor), strawberry tongue, accentuated rash in skin folds (pastia lines), desquamation of fingertips in the second week scarlet fever is treated with 10 days of penicillin v; this prevents rheumatic fever and reduces spread. complications include peritonsillar abscess, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic fever kawasaki disease and drug eruptions are important mimics; always consider them in persistent fever with rash differential diagnosis & approach to the febrile rash ask about immunisation status, contacts, travel, drugs taken, duration of fever before rash and rash evolution non-blanching rash with fever suggests meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise - treat as an emergency other causes: enteroviral infection (hand, foot and mouth disease), adenovirus, infectious mononucleosis (rash with amoxicillin), kawasaki disease, stevens-johnson syndrome, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, toxic shock syndrome exclusion from school: measles 4 days from rash onset, rubella 5 days, scarlet fever until 24 hours of antibiotics, erythema infectiosum none once the rash has appeared prevention & public health vitamin a (measles) phenoxymethylpenicillin (scarlet fever) paracetamol

chickenpox, mumps & other viral infections infectious diseases varicella (chickenpox), mumps and other common viral infections are highly infectious childhood illnesses that are usually self-limiting but can cause serious complications in neonates, the immunocompromised and the unvaccinated. vaccination has dramatically reduced their burden, and recognising complications such as bacterial superinfection, encephalitis and orchitis is essential. varicella lesions appear in crops with all stages present simultaneously avoid nsaids and aspirin in chickenpox neonates born to mothers with rash from 7 days before to 7 days after delivery need vzig mumps commonest cns complication is aseptic meningitis; orchitis affects post-pubertal boys mumps is a leading cause of acquired unilateral sensorineural deafness before widespread vaccination hand, foot and mouth disease is usually coxsackie a16; ev71 causes severe neurological disease shingles represents reactivation of vzv in a dorsal root ganglion secondary group a streptococcus infection is the major cause of serious morbidity from chickenpox in healthy children chickenpox with spreading erythema, pain out of proportion, or toxic appearance (necrotising fasciitis) haemorrhagic or bleeding lesions, especially in immunosuppressed children respiratory distress, ataxia, or reduced consciousness in varicella neonate with lesions or with maternal rash within 7 days either side of birth mumps with severe headache, neck stiffness or testicular swelling with severe pain hand, foot and mouth with drowsiness, myoclonus or breathing difficulty (ev71) mumps complications parotitis, orchitis, meningitis, pancreatitis, deafness - the prompt approach chickenpox (varicella) treatment is supportive: paracetamol, trimmed nails, calamine or emollients, hydration. avoid nsaids (increased risk of necrotising fasciitis and invasive group a streptococcal disease) and aspirin (reye syndrome) oral aciclovir within 24 hours of rash onset can be considered for adolescents, secondary household cases and those on steroids; iv aciclovir for immunocompromised, neonates and complicated disease complications: secondary bacterial skin infection (staph aureus, group a strep), pneumonia (more in adults), cerebellar ataxia, encephalitis, thrombocytopenia and purpura fulminans, haemorrhagic varicella in the immunosuppressed reactivation of latent vzv in dorsal root ganglia causes herpes zoster (shingles), a dermatomal vesicular rash high-risk varicella and pregnancy varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (vzig) is given to susceptible high-risk contacts: immunosuppressed children, neonates whose mother developed chickenpox from 7 days before to 7 days after delivery, preterm infants with no maternal immunity, and susceptible pregnant women neonatal varicella from maternal rash around delivery has up to 30 percent mortality without treatment; give vzig and iv aciclovir if the infant develops lesions fetal varicella syndrome (first 20 weeks): limb hypoplasia, cutaneous scarring, eye defects (chorioretinitis, cataracts) and microcephaly susceptible exposed contacts can receive vaccine within 3-5 days of exposure if immunocompetent admit any child with varicella plus immunosuppression, haemorrhagic lesions, respiratory or neurological signs mumps complications: aseptic meningitis (most common cns involvement), encephalitis, sensorineural deafness (usually unilateral, may be permanent), orchitis in post-pubertal boys (rarely causes infertility), oophoritis, pancreatitis diagnosis: clinical; confirm with salivary swab pcr or serum igm, and notify. raised serum amylase is common management is supportive with analgesia; there is no antiviral therapy two doses of mmr vaccine give good protection; a third dose may be used in outbreaks other common viral infections hand, foot and mouth disease (coxsackie a16, enterovirus 71): fever, painful oral ulcers and vesicles on palms, soles and sometimes buttocks. self-limiting; ev71 can cause brainstem encephalitis and pulmonary oedema herpangina (coxsackie a): vesicles and ulcers on the soft palate and tonsillar pillars, fever, odynophagia herpes simplex gingivostomatitis: painful gum ulceration, fever, drooling; treat with aciclovir if severe or immunocompromised, and maintain hydration molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus): pearly umbilicated papules, self-resolving over months adenovirus: pharyngoconjunctival fever, sore throat and prolonged fever slapped cheek, roseola and measles are covered separately under exanthems prevention aciclovir (oral, varicella) aciclovir (iv, immunocompromised or neonate) varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (vzig)

t: Fever in a young child & fever without focus
h: fever in a young child & fever without focus infectious diseases fever is the commonest reason for a child to present to healthcare and in most cases is due to self-limiting viral infection, but a small proportion hide serious bacterial infection such as sepsis, meningitis or urinary tract infection. young infants, in particular, need careful risk stratification because clinical signs are subtle and the risk of invasive bacterial infection is highest. any fever of 38 c or more in an infant under 3 months needs urgent assessment urine culture is essential in a febrile child with no source use the traffic light system: colour, activity, respiratory, hydration, other antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions and do not exclude serious illness pneumococcal and hib vaccines have reduced occult bacteraemia to under 1 percent add listeria cover (amoxicillin or ampicillin) for infants under 1 month kawasaki disease should be considered in any child with fever lasting 5 days in endemic areas always test for malaria in febrile children fever with pale, mottled, ashen or blue colour, or no response to social cues grunting, tachypnoea over 60/min, moderate to severe chest indrawing non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, status epilepticus or focal neurological signs bile-stained vomiting, reduced skin turgor, signs of dehydration age under 3 months with temperature 38 c or above weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; hypotonia traffic light domains colour, activity, respiratory, hydration, other (carho) - assess each for green, amber or red kawasaki crash and burn conjunctivitis, rash, adenopathy, strawberry tongue/mucosa, hands and feet changes, and burn (fever for 5 days) definition & epidemiology assessment measure temperature: electronic axillary thermometer under 4 weeks, ear or axillary (or rectal) for older children; avoid mercury glass and forehead strips history: duration, behaviour, feeding, wet nappies, rash, vomiting, contacts, travel, immunisations, prematurity, previous illness, medication examination: full set of vital signs, capillary refill, hydration, ent, chest, abdomen, skin including non-blanching rash, joints, fontanelle, neck stiffness, hips, genitalia apply the nice traffic light system (green, amber, red) using colour, activity, respiratory, hydration and other signs neonates and infants under 3 months: any fever is regarded as serious until proved otherwise as they can have bacteraemia or meningitis with minimal signs in infants 3-6 months with temperature 39 c or above, treat as higher risk (amber) investigation and management by risk septic screen: full blood count, crp, blood culture, urine culture (catheter or suprapubic sample in infants), csf (unless contraindicated) and chest x-ray if respiratory signs infants under 1 month: lumbar puncture, empirical iv benzylpenicillin/ampicillin plus cefotaxime (or gentamicin), plus aciclovir if herpes simplex is possible (maternal hsv, skin vesicles, seizures, raised transaminases) infants 1-3 months who are unwell or have abnormal inflammatory markers: iv ceftriaxone (avoid in the first weeks if jaundiced or on calcium) and add ampicillin or amoxicillin for listeria cover consider enteroviral and parechoviral infection in young infants with fever and irritability or hypotonia in malaria-endemic areas, test for malaria in every febrile child regardless of other findings (see malaria topic) do not use antipyretics with the sole aim of reducing temperature; use paracetamol or ibuprofen if the child is distressed, but they do not prevent febrile convulsions and alternating them is discouraged causes of serious bacterial infection urinary tract infection - commonest, often no localising symptoms in infants bacteraemia/sepsis with strep pneumoniae, n. meningitidis, s. aureus, group b strep (young infants), e. coli bacterial meningitis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, bacterial gastroenteritis in under-immunised children the risk of hib, pneumococcus and meningococcus rises typhoid, rickettsia, brucellosis, tb, hiv and malaria in tropical settings prolonged fever and kawasaki disease paracetamol ibuprofen ceftriaxone iv immunoglobulin (kawasaki)

sepsis & meningococcal disease infectious diseases sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, and it remains a leading cause of child death worldwide. meningococcal disease, caused by neisseria meningitidis, can progress from first symptom to death within hours, so early recognition, immediate antibiotics and aggressive resuscitation are the key interventions. give antibiotics within the first hour; never delay for lumbar puncture hypotension is a late sign in children non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal sepsis until proved otherwise meningococcal disease can kill within hours of first symptoms early signs of leg pain, cold hands and feet, and abnormal skin colour precede the rash dexamethasone is given with or before first antibiotic dose in suspected pneumococcal or hib meningitis close contacts of meningococcal disease need chemoprophylaxis neonatal sepsis requires cover for group b strep, e. coli and listeria persistent shock after 40-60 ml/kg needs inotropes and ventilatory support altered consciousness, floppiness or unresponsiveness capillary refill over 3 seconds, mottled skin, cold peripheries tachycardia out of keeping with fever, tachypnoea or grunting non-blanching rash spreading rapidly persistent hypotension, oliguria or rising lactate seizures, bulging fontanelle or purpuric rash with meningism sepsis six three in: oxygen, iv/io fluids, iv antibiotics. three out: blood cultures (with glucose), lactate, and urine output monitoring glass test press a glass against the rash: if it does not fade the rash is non-blanching and may be meningococcal definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features early, non-specific: fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, limb pain, cold hands and feet, abnormal skin colour later: tachycardia, tachypnoea, prolonged capillary refill over 2 seconds, mottled skin, altered consciousness, hypotension and oliguria rash: begins as blanching macular or petechial, becomes non-blanching purpura (use the glass test); may be absent early in up to 1 in 5 cases meningism: neck stiffness, photophobia, headache in older children; bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, opisthotonos and seizures in infants neonatal sepsis may present only with temperature instability, apnoea, feeding intolerance, jaundice or hypoglycaemia management fluids: 10 ml/kg (who 10-20 ml/kg) isotonic crystalloid bolus, reassess, repeat up to 40-60 ml/kg; be cautious in severe malnutrition and severe anaemia where fluid boluses are restricted per who inotropes (adrenaline for cold shock, noradrenaline for warm shock) early if shock persists after 40-60 ml/kg; consider intubation and ventilation empirical antibiotics: ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg (or cefotaxime) for children over 1 month; add ampicillin or amoxicillin under 3 months; vancomycin if resistant pneumococcus is suspected; consider additional cover for mrsa or toxic shock correct hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and acidosis; transfuse blood and clotting factors for dic when bleeding dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg given before or with the first antibiotic dose in bacterial meningitis (not neonates, not in septic shock without meningitis) if pneumococcus or hib is suspected meningococcal disease: ceftriaxone for 7 days (5 days if cleared); notify urgently; give chemoprophylaxis (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) to close contacts, plus vaccination where appropriate complications, prognosis & prevention mortality of meningococcal septicaemia is 10-20 percent despite treatment; meningitis alone about 5 percent sequelae: skin and limb necrosis requiring amputation, hearing loss, hydrocephalus, seizures, learning difficulty waterhouse-friderichsen syndrome: bilateral adrenal haemorrhage with refractory shock late immune complex disease (arthritis, pericarditis) occurs 4-10 days into treatment vaccination: menacwy, menb, hib, pneumococcal conjugate and meningococcal a conjugate in the meningitis belt are effective test for complement deficiency after second episode or unusual serotypes ceftriaxone cefotaxime dexamethasone (meningitis) rifampicin (contact prophylaxis) normal saline bolus

malaria infectious diseases malaria is a mosquito-borne protozoal disease and a leading killer of children under five in sub-saharan africa. plasmodium falciparum causes severe disease in children, including cerebral malaria and severe anaemia, and prompt diagnosis and artemisinin-based treatment saves lives. any febrile child from or travelling to an endemic area must be tested. test every febrile child in or from an endemic area for malaria three negative films 12-24 hours apart are needed to exclude malaria iv artesunate is first-line for severe falciparum malaria severe anaemia, cerebral malaria and respiratory distress are the commonest severe forms in african children hypoglycaemia is common - check glucose in every sick child p. vivax and p. ovale need primaquine after g6pd testing to prevent relapse co-infection with bacterial sepsis is common in severe malaria travellers who did not take prophylaxis are at highest risk of imported malaria impaired consciousness, seizures or prostration respiratory distress with acidotic (deep) breathing severe anaemia with pallor or haemoglobin below 5 g/dl hypoglycaemia (glucose under 3 mmol/l, or under 2.6) parasitaemia over 2 percent in non-immune children (hyperparasitaemia) dark urine, jaundice, bleeding or oliguria severe malaria signs think crash: coma, respiratory distress, anaemia, shock, hypoglycaemia (also convulsions and jaundice) definition & epidemiology life cycle & pathophysiology clinical features uncomplicated malaria: fever (often irregular in children), chills, headache, vomiting, diarrhoea, cough, malaise, myalgia, splenomegaly and anaemia classic tertian or quartan periodicity is rarely seen in children with falciparum malaria incubation: 7-14 days for p. falciparum; symptoms rarely appear after 3 months in falciparum, but vivax and ovale may relapse months to years later severe malaria (any one): impaired consciousness or coma, prostration, multiple convulsions, respiratory distress (acidotic breathing), pulmonary oedema, shock, jaundice, haemoglobinuria (blackwater fever), spontaneous bleeding, severe anaemia (hb under 5 g/dl), hypoglycaemia, acute kidney injury, hyperparasitaemia cerebral malaria: unrousable coma (blantyre score 2 or lower) with p. falciparum parasitaemia and no other cause; retinal changes (whitening, haemorrhages) support the diagnosis complications: hypoglycaemia (also quinine-induced), neurological sequelae in 10-20 percent of survivors, post-malaria neurological syndrome, and splenic rupture investigations thick and thin blood films stained with giemsa (gold standard): thick film for detection, thin film for species and parasite density; repeat 12-24 hours apart up to three times before excluding malaria rapid diagnostic tests (hrp2/pldh antigens): useful at point of care, but may remain positive after treatment full blood count (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), glucose, u&e, lactate, blood culture (co-infection with bacterial sepsis is common), urinalysis in severe disease: blood gas, liver function, group and save, lumbar puncture if meningitis cannot be excluded management supportive care: treat hypoglycaemia with 5 ml/kg of 10% glucose, correct anaemia with blood transfusion if hb below 5 g/dl (or below 4), control convulsions with benzodiazepines, avoid excess fluids (risk of pulmonary oedema and cerebral oedema in non-shocked children) treat suspected co-existing bacterial infection with iv antibiotics until excluded p. vivax or p. ovale: chloroquine (or act) plus primaquine for 14 days to eradicate hypnozoites after g6pd testing; tafenoquine is an option in older patients antipyretics for comfort; avoid steroids, mannitol and heparin in cerebral malaria monitor parasitaemia, glucose, consciousness and urine output; mortality of cerebral malaria is 15-20 percent prevention insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor residual spraying seasonal malaria chemoprevention (sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine) for children 3-59 months in sahel regions intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy and infancy malaria vaccines rts,s/as01 and r21/matrix-m are recommended by who for children in endemic areas travellers: awareness, bite avoidance, chemoprophylaxis (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline over 12 years, mefloquine) and prompt testing for fever up to 3 months after return artemether-lumefantrine iv artesunate primaquine (vivax/ovale) glucose 10%

typhoid & tropical enteric infections infectious diseases typhoid (enteric) fever is a systemic illness caused by salmonella enterica serovar typhi (and paratyphi a, b, c), spread by faecal-oral contamination of food and water. it is a major cause of prolonged fever in children in south asia and sub-saharan africa, and rising antibiotic resistance, including extensively drug-resistant strains, makes diagnosis and rational treatment increasingly important. suspect enteric fever in prolonged fever with abdominal symptoms in travellers from south asia and africa blood culture before antibiotics is the key investigation widal test is unreliable and shouldn't be used in isolation relative bradycardia, leucopenia and rose spots are classic but not universal intestinal perforation and haemorrhage occur typically in the third week treat based on local resistance: azithromycin for uncomplicated, ceftriaxone for severe, meropenem for xdr fluoroquinolone resistance is widespread in south asian strains chronic carriage is linked to gallstones severe abdominal pain, rigidity or sudden fall in temperature with tachycardia (perforation) melaena or rectal bleeding altered consciousness, delirium or seizures persistent fever beyond 7 days despite appropriate antibiotics (resistance or complications) shock, hypotension or hypothermia sickle cell child with bone pain after typhoid (salmonella osteomyelitis) typhoid by week fever steps up in week 1, rose spots and splenomegaly in week 2, complications (perforation, bleeding) in week 3, recovery in week 4 definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features incubation 7-14 days (range 3-30) week 1: stepwise rising fever, headache, malaise, dry cough, abdominal discomfort, constipation (or diarrhoea in young children), relative bradycardia week 2: sustained fever (39-40 c), toxic appearance, "typhoid state" (delirium), splenomegaly, abdominal distension, rose spots (small blanching erythematous macules on the trunk), pea-soup diarrhoea week 3: complications appear: intestinal haemorrhage and perforation, encephalopathy, myocarditis, hepatitis, cholecystitis week 4: slow recovery if untreated; relapse in 5-10 percent after treatment young children often have atypical, milder illness with diarrhoea, vomiting or simply prolonged fever, and infants can develop severe disease and sepsis neurological: confusion, meningism, guillain-barre, cranial nerve palsies; others include osteomyelitis (especially in sickle cell disease), pneumonia and abscesses investigations blood culture (positive in 40-80 percent in the first week, best before antibiotics); bone marrow culture is the most sensitive and stays positive after antibiotics stool and urine culture are more useful in the later weeks and for carriers full blood count: leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis, anaemia and thrombocytopenia; raised liver enzymes widal test is unreliable (poor sensitivity and specificity; requires paired titres) and should not be used alone; rapid serological tests (typhidot, tubex) have moderate accuracy abdominal x-ray or ultrasound for suspected perforation (free air, free fluid) always test for malaria in endemic areas, as both can coexist management uncomplicated: oral azithromycin 10-20 mg/kg once daily (max 1 g) for 7 days; or cefixime; fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin only if the strain is susceptible severe: iv ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg once daily for 7-14 days; carbapenem (meropenem) for xdr typhoid, with azithromycin as an oral step-down dexamethasone 3 mg/kg iv loading, then 1 mg/kg every 6 hours for 8 doses, for severe typhoid with shock or altered mental state (as per classic trials) supportive: oral or iv fluids, nutrition, antipyretics; treat anaemia surgery for perforation: laparotomy with peritoneal toilet and broad-spectrum cover including metronidazole fever clearance takes 4-5 days on treatment; persistence beyond this does not alone indicate failure prevention & carriers safe water, sanitation, hand washing and food hygiene vi polysaccharide vaccine (2 years and older) and vi-conjugate vaccines (from 6 months, for example typbar-tcv) are recommended in endemic regions; oral ty21a from 6 years chronic carriers need prolonged antibiotics (for example 4-6 weeks of ciprofloxacin) and sometimes cholecystectomy; food handlers should be excluded until stool cultures are negative notifiable in most countries; public health follow-up of contacts azithromycin ceftriaxone meropenem ciprofloxacin

hiv in children & pmtct infectious diseases hiv infection in children is mostly acquired by mother-to-child transmission, which can be almost eliminated by antiretroviral therapy in pregnancy, safe delivery and infant prophylaxis (pmtct). without treatment, about half of infected infants die by two years. early infant diagnosis, prompt antiretroviral therapy (art), cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections transform outcomes. mtct can occur in utero, intrapartum and postnatally via breastfeeding maternal art with suppressed viral load reduces transmission to under 1-2 percent use pcr (dna/rna) for infants under 18 months - antibodies reflect maternal igg start cotrimoxazole prophylaxis at 4-6 weeks for all exposed infants who: treat all children with hiv immediately regardless of cd4 count dolutegravir-based regimens are now first-line for most children tb and pjp are the major opportunistic infections; pjp peaks at 3-6 months of age iris may occur in the first weeks of art infant with tachypnoea, hypoxia and dry cough at 2-6 months (pjp) severe acute malnutrition or failure to thrive in exposed infants headache, fever and neck stiffness (cryptococcal meningitis, tb meningitis) neurological regression or encephalopathy clinical deterioration within weeks of starting art (iris) adolescent defaulting on art or presenting with virological failure pmtct in four prongs prevent hiv in women, prevent unintended pregnancy in hiv-positive women, prevent transmission from mother to child (art, safe delivery, infant prophylaxis), and provide care and support epidemiology & transmission prevention of mother-to-child transmission (pmtct) test all pregnant women and offer lifelong art to all hiv-positive women regardless of cd4 count (option b+), ideally started before conception or as early as possible aim for undetectable viral load by delivery; vaginal delivery is safe if viral load is below 50 copies/ml, otherwise consider elective caesarean at 38 weeks infant prophylaxis: zidovudine (or nevirapine) for 4-6 weeks if low risk; dual or triple prophylaxis (zidovudine, lamivudine, nevirapine or raltegravir) for high-risk infants in high-income settings advise formula feeding; in resource-limited settings who recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while mother continues art, with continued breastfeeding to 12 months or beyond cotrimoxazole prophylaxis from 4-6 weeks of age in all hiv-exposed infants until infection excluded avoid invasive procedures at delivery, prolonged rupture of membranes and mixed feeding diagnosis infants under 18 months: antibody tests are unreliable due to maternal igg; use hiv dna or rna pcr (nucleic acid test) test at birth in high-risk infants, at 4-6 weeks, and again 6 weeks after cessation of breastfeeding; a final antibody test at 18 months confirms positive result: repeat on a second sample before starting art, but do not delay treatment children over 18 months: hiv antibody (rapid) test, confirmed by another assay baseline: cd4 count and percentage, viral load, full blood count, liver and renal function, tb screen, hepatitis b/c, resistance testing where available clinical features & staging stage 4 conditions include severe wasting, pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (pjp), oesophageal candidiasis, extrapulmonary tb, cryptococcal meningitis, cmv retinitis, toxoplasmosis and hiv encephalopathy pjp: typically 3-6 months of age with hypoxia, tachypnoea, dry cough and a bilateral interstitial pattern; treat with high-dose cotrimoxazole plus prednisolone tb is the commonest opportunistic infection and cause of death in hiv-infected children in endemic regions immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (iris): paradoxical worsening of infection or unmasking of subclinical infection (tb, cryptococcus) within weeks of starting art treatment typical first-line: abacavir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (children over 4 weeks and 3 kg); for neonates, nevirapine or lopinavir/ritonavir based check hla-b*5701 before abacavir where available; monitor for hypersensitivity adherence support and disclosure counselling are essential, particularly in adolescents monitor viral load at 6 months then yearly; virological failure is two consecutive viral loads above 1000 copies/ml after adherence counselling immunisation: give all routine vaccines including bcg if asymptomatic and live vaccines (measles, mmr) unless severely immunosuppressed; pneumococcal and annual influenza are especially important isoniazid preventive therapy for exposed or asymptomatic children older than 12 months after active tb excluded; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis continues until immune recovery nutritional support, treatment of coinfections and psychosocial care including orphan and vulnerable child support zidovudine (infant prophylaxis) nevirapine (prophylaxis) cotrimoxazole (prophylaxis) dolutegravir

infectious mononucleosis, cmv & parvovirus infectious diseases epstein-barr virus (ebv), cytomegalovirus (cmv) and parvovirus b19 are common viruses that usually cause mild or asymptomatic illness in children but can cause important disease in adolescents, pregnant women, neonates and the immunocompromised. infectious mononucleosis, congenital cmv and parvovirus aplastic crisis are the key clinical scenarios. infectious mononucleosis: fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy with atypical lymphocytes amoxicillin causes a rash in mononucleosis - not true allergy avoid contact sports for 4-8 weeks after ebv because of splenic rupture risk ebv is linked to burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and hodgkin lymphoma congenital cmv is the commonest congenital infection and a leading cause of non-genetic sensorineural hearing loss diagnose congenital cmv with pcr within 3 weeks of birth valganciclovir for 6 months for symptomatic congenital cmv with cns disease parvovirus b19 causes aplastic crisis in haemolytic anaemias and hydrops fetalis in pregnancy airway compromise from massive tonsillar swelling left upper quadrant pain after trauma in mononucleosis (splenic rupture) pancytopenia, high fever and hyperferritinaemia (hlh) neonate with jaundice, petechiae and microcephaly (congenital cmv) pallor and lethargy with low reticulocytes in a child with chronic haemolysis (aplastic crisis) pregnant contact of parvovirus or cmv needing urgent assessment congenital infections torch: toxoplasma, other (syphilis, vzv, parvovirus), rubella, cmv, hsv infectious mononucleosis (ebv) features: fever, exudative tonsillitis, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly (50 percent), hepatomegaly, palatal petechiae, periorbital oedema, fatigue lasting weeks to months a maculopapular rash occurs in most patients given ampicillin or amoxicillin; this is not true penicillin allergy complications: splenic rupture (rare; avoid contact sports for 4-8 weeks), airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hepatitis, guillain-barre, encephalitis, bell palsy ebv-associated malignancy: burkitt lymphoma (endemic in malaria belt), nasopharyngeal carcinoma, hodgkin lymphoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder x-linked lymphoproliferative disease causes fulminant ebv in boys; hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (hlh) can complicate infection diagnosis & management of ebv full blood count with film: lymphocytosis with more than 10 percent atypical lymphocytes; mild thrombocytopenia; abnormal liver enzymes monospot / paul-bunnell heterophile antibody test: positive in most older children and adults but often negative in under 4-year-olds and early illness ebv serology: vca igm (acute), vca igg and ebna (past infection; ebna appears late) management is supportive: rest, fluids, analgesia, advice to avoid contact sports and heavy exertion for 4-8 weeks corticosteroids for airway obstruction, severe haemolysis or thrombocytopenia; aciclovir has no proven benefit penicillin treatment of coexistent group a strep tonsillitis should use a non-amoxicillin agent where mononucleosis is suspected cytomegalovirus congenital cmv: about 10 percent are symptomatic at birth - petechiae and blueberry-muffin rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, chorioretinitis, intrauterine growth restriction, thrombocytopenia even asymptomatic infants may develop late sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental problems; screen hearing at intervals for several years diagnosis: urine, saliva or blood pcr for cmv within the first 3 weeks of life (later positives may be postnatal); guthrie blood-spot pcr is less sensitive treatment of symptomatic congenital cmv with cns involvement: valganciclovir 16 mg/kg orally twice daily for 6 months, with monitoring of neutrophils; iv ganciclovir for severe disease preterm infants may acquire cmv from breast milk; this seldom matters in term infants prevention in pregnancy: hygiene advice (hand washing after contact with young child saliva, urine); no licensed vaccine parvovirus b19 erythema infectiosum (fifth disease): fever and mild illness, then bright red cheeks and lacy rash; infectious before rash appears arthropathy in adolescents and adults, mainly girls and women transient aplastic crisis in children with chronic haemolysis (sickle cell, thalassaemia, spherocytosis) - low reticulocytes and haemoglobin chronic anaemia (pure red cell aplasia) in immunocompromised patients - treat with iv immunoglobulin fetal infection (first half of pregnancy): hydrops fetalis, fetal anaemia and miscarriage; manage with antenatal ultrasound surveillance and intrauterine transfusion diagnosis: b19 igm, pcr; no specific therapy for healthy children; supportive care; transfusion for aplastic crisis valganciclovir (congenital cmv) ganciclovir (severe cmv) prednisolone (severe mononucleosis)

helminths & parasitic infections infectious diseases helminth and protozoal infections affect over a billion children worldwide, causing anaemia, malnutrition, impaired growth and cognitive delay. soil-transmitted helminths, schistosomiasis and giardiasis are the commonest, and mass deworming with safe single-dose antihelminthics, together with sanitation, is a key public health intervention. heavy helminth infection causes anaemia, malnutrition, stunting and impaired cognition hookworm causes iron-deficiency anaemia through chronic blood loss threadworm causes nocturnal perianal itch; treat the whole household albendazole single dose is the standard for ascaris, hookworm and mass deworming praziquantel is used for schistosomiasis and tapeworms eosinophilia suggests tissue-invasive parasites neurocysticercosis is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic areas mass drug administration plus wash reduces transmission intestinal obstruction or biliary colic from an ascaris bolus severe anaemia with hookworm in malnourished children hyperinfection syndrome with strongyloides in a child about to start steroids new seizures with a history of pork or taeniasis exposure (neurocysticercosis) haematuria after freshwater exposure in endemic areas (s. haematobium) fever, hepatomegaly and weight loss in a child with exposure to leishmaniasis nematode drugs abc: albendazole or mebendazole for roundworm, whipworm and hookworm; ivermectin for strongyloides; praziquantel for flukes and tapeworms definition & epidemiology intestinal nematodes ascaris: faecal-oral transmission of eggs; larvae migrate through the lungs (loeffler syndrome with cough, wheeze and eosinophilia) and adults live in the small bowel. heavy infection causes malnutrition, intestinal obstruction (bolus), biliary or pancreatic duct obstruction, appendicitis and volvulus. treat with albendazole 400 mg single dose or mebendazole trichuris (whipworm): egg ingestion; heavy infection causes bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus and rectal prolapse, anaemia and growth failure. treat with albendazole or mebendazole for 3 days hookworm: larvae penetrate bare feet; adults attach to the small intestinal mucosa and suck blood, leading to iron-deficiency anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia. ground itch at the entry site. treat with albendazole, iron supplementation and nutrition threadworm (pinworm, enterobius): perianal itching, particularly at night, vulvovaginitis in girls; diagnosed by sticky tape test or seeing worms. treat child and household with mebendazole 100 mg (over 6 months) single dose, repeated after 2 weeks, with hygiene measures strongyloides stercoralis: autoinfection and can cause fatal hyperinfection in those on steroids or immunosuppression; treat with ivermectin toxocariasis: ingested eggs from dog or cat faeces cause visceral larva migrans (fever, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia, wheeze) or ocular larva migrans cestodes and trematodes taenia saginata (beef) and t. solium (pork) tapeworms: adult worm in intestine causes mild symptoms and segments in stool; t. solium eggs cause cysticercosis (neurocysticercosis is a leading cause of epilepsy in endemic areas). treat intestinal worm with praziquantel; neurocysticercosis with albendazole plus steroids and anticonvulsants hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm): common in children; praziquantel echinococcus granulosus (hydatid disease): dog contact; liver and lung cysts; treated with albendazole and surgery or pair schistosoma haematobium (urinary): haematuria, dysuria, later bladder fibrosis, hydronephrosis and squamous cell bladder cancer; s. mansoni and s. japonicum cause hepatosplenic disease, portal hypertension, and bloody stool. infection follows freshwater exposure to snail-borne cercariae; swimmer itch, then katayama fever; diagnosis by egg detection in urine or stool and serology; treat with praziquantel 40 mg/kg single dose protozoa giardia lamblia: waterborne; causes chronic watery or greasy diarrhoea, bloating, malabsorption and weight loss. diagnosed by stool antigen or pcr; treat with metronidazole (or tinidazole single dose) entamoeba histolytica: amoebic dysentery (bloody mucoid stools) and liver abscess; treat with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent cryptosporidium: self-limiting watery diarrhoea in healthy children but severe, prolonged in hiv and malnutrition; nitazoxanide may be used visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), trypanosomiasis and toxoplasmosis are other important protozoal infections in specific regions investigation, treatment & control treat anaemia with iron and nutrition; transfuse only for severe symptomatic anaemia peripheral eosinophilia suggests tissue-invasive helminths (strongyloides, toxocara, schistosomiasis, filariasis) ascaris-induced obstruction: nil by mouth, fluids and piperazine or albendazole after decompression; surgery if volvulus or perforation pregnancy and children under 12 months: albendazole is used cautiously after 12 months of age (who supports from 12 months) albendazole mebendazole praziquantel ivermectin metronidazole (giardia)

anaphylaxis & food allergy allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology food allergy affects about 5-8 percent of young children and is the commonest trigger of anaphylaxis in childhood. anaphylaxis is a rapid-onset, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction that requires immediate intramuscular adrenaline; prompt recognition, appropriate emergency treatment and a plan for long-term allergen avoidance and self-management save lives. adrenaline im into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis antihistamines and steroids do not treat anaphylaxis and must not delay adrenaline asthma and adolescence are risk factors for fatal food anaphylaxis a positive skin prick or ige shows sensitisation, not necessarily clinical allergy peanut, tree nut, fish and shellfish allergy usually persist; milk and egg usually resolve early introduction of peanut and egg reduces the risk of allergy in high-risk infants prescribe two auto-injectors and train the family and school biphasic reactions need observation after recovery check mast cell tryptase after a suspected anaphylactic reaction stridor, hoarse voice, tongue swelling or inability to speak wheeze or respiratory distress in a child with known food allergy floppiness, pallor, collapse or hypotension after exposure poorly controlled asthma plus food allergy repeated or persistent vomiting with pallor and lethargy 1-4 hours after a food (fpies) any need for more than one adrenaline dose abcde of anaphylaxis airway swelling, breathing wheeze, circulation shock, disability (consciousness), exposure (skin: rash, urticaria) anaphylaxis adrenaline doses under 6 years 150 micrograms (0.15 ml of 1:1000), 6-12 years 300 micrograms (0.3 ml), over 12 years 500 micrograms (0.5 ml) definition & epidemiology anaphylaxis: recognition airway: throat tightness, hoarse voice, stridor, tongue or lip swelling breathing: wheeze, dyspnoea, cyanosis, persistent cough circulation: pallor, tachycardia, hypotension, collapse, floppiness in infants skin and mucosa: urticaria, flushing, angioedema (present in 80-90 percent, but absent in some cases) gastrointestinal: abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea neurological: agitation, sense of doom, confusion, reduced consciousness biphasic reactions occur in up to 5 percent, 1-72 hours after the initial episode, so observation is needed emergency management call for help, remove the trigger, lie the child flat (or sit up if breathing difficulty), do not stand or walk them adrenaline (epinephrine) 1:1000 intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh: 150 micrograms (0.15 ml) for under 6 years, 300 micrograms for 6-12 years, 500 micrograms for over 12 years; repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement high-flow oxygen, iv access, fluid bolus 10 ml/kg crystalloid for hypotension, repeated as needed adjuncts only after adrenaline: antihistamine (chlorphenamine or cetirizine), hydrocortisone and inhaled salbutamol; they do not treat airway or circulatory compromise refractory shock: iv adrenaline infusion by an experienced team and icu referral observe for at least 6 hours (12 hours if severe or needed more than one dose of adrenaline); take mast cell tryptase within 1-2 hours of onset diagnosis of food allergy history is key: food, quantity, timing, reproducibility, symptoms, and co-factors (exercise, illness, nsaids) skin prick test: wheal 3 mm or more above negative control indicates sensitisation (not proof of allergy); positive predictive value is limited specific ige blood tests (including component testing such as ara h 2 for peanut) improve specificity; sensitisation alone is not allergy oral food challenge (supervised, usually double-blind placebo-controlled in research, open in practice) is the gold standard avoid unvalidated tests such as igg panels, hair analysis and kinesiology non-ige allergy: trial of elimination for 2-6 weeks then supervised reintroduction long-term management & prevention strict avoidance of the allergen with careful label reading, and school and nursery allergy plans written personalised emergency action plan and prescription of two adrenaline auto-injectors, with training for the family and carers; carry them at all times medical alert identification; dietitian input to ensure adequate nutrition for milk or multiple food allergy cows milk protein allergy in infants: extensively hydrolysed formula (or amino acid formula if severe); breastfed infants continue breastfeeding with maternal avoidance early introduction of allergenic foods (peanut and well-cooked egg from around 6 months, not before 4 months) reduces risk, particularly in infants with eczema (leap and eat trials); high-risk infants with severe eczema or egg allergy may need prior assessment oral immunotherapy for peanut is available in specialist centres reassess annually for tolerance to milk, egg and wheat adrenaline 1:1000 im chlorphenamine hydrocortisone salbutamol (nebulised or inhaled)

atopic eczema allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology atopic eczema is a chronic, relapsing, intensely itchy inflammatory skin disease that affects up to 15-20 percent of children and usually begins in infancy. treatment centres on regular emollients, topical anti-inflammatory therapy in a stepped approach, trigger avoidance, and recognition and treatment of complications such as bacterial infection and eczema herpeticum. itch is mandatory for the diagnosis of atopic eczema emollients are the cornerstone and should be used generously and regularly use the weakest effective steroid for the shortest time; hydrocortisone 1 percent for face and flexures eczema herpeticum needs urgent iv aciclovir infants: face and extensors; older children: flexures early severe eczema is a risk factor for food allergy, especially peanut and egg proactive twice-weekly topical therapy reduces relapse nappy area is typically spared in infantile atopic eczema punched-out vesicles, fever and malaise on eczematous skin (eczema herpeticum) widespread weeping and crusting with systemic illness (bacterial infection) erythroderma poor growth, failure to thrive, recurrent infections or severe early eczema with thrombocytopenia (consider immunodeficiency such as wiskott-aldrich or hyper-ige) unresponsive eczema despite good adherence severe sleep deprivation or psychological distress steroid fingertip unit one fingertip unit (0.5 g) covers an area equal to two adult palms; use to guide how much to apply definition & epidemiology pathophysiology clinical features pruritus is essential for the diagnosis; sleep disturbance and irritability are common infants: face (cheeks), scalp, extensor surfaces, trunk; the nappy area is usually spared children: flexural distribution (antecubital and popliteal fossae, wrists, ankles, neck) acute: erythema, vesicles, weeping and crusting; chronic: lichenification, excoriation, dry scaly plaques, post-inflammatory hypo- or hyperpigmentation associated features: dry skin (xerosis), dennie-morgan infraorbital folds, hyperlinear palms, keratosis pilaris, pityriasis alba diagnostic criteria (uk working party): itchy skin plus 3 or more of flexural involvement, personal history of asthma/hay fever, history of dry skin, visible flexural eczema, onset before age 2 severity: mild (dry skin, infrequent itching), moderate (redness, frequent itching, sleep disturbance), severe (widespread, persistent itch, bleeding, major impact on quality of life) management emollients: ointments for very dry skin, creams or lotions for mild; use as soap substitute and leave-in topical corticosteroids: mild (hydrocortisone 1%) for face and flexures, moderate (clobetasone) for body, potent (betamethasone valerate) briefly for severe flares on trunk and limbs; apply once or twice daily to affected areas until 48 hours after clearance; use the fingertip unit to guide quantity proactive therapy: twice weekly application to previously affected areas prevents relapse topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) as steroid-sparing agents for face and flexures in moderate to severe disease wet wrap therapy for severe flares; bandages for lichenified plaques; antiseptic bath additives where infected sedating antihistamines at night for short periods only in sleep disturbance; non-sedating antihistamines are not helpful for itch itself phototherapy, systemic ciclosporin, methotrexate, azathioprine; dupilumab (anti-il-4/13), tralokinumab and jak inhibitors for severe refractory disease in specialist hands dietary elimination only with a clear history or positive tests and dietitian input, since unnecessary exclusion increases risk complications bacterial infection (s. aureus, group a strep): weeping, crusting, golden crusts, pustules; treat with topical or oral flucloxacillin (or erythromycin if penicillin allergic) and swab if recurrent eczema herpeticum: hsv superinfection with punched-out monomorphic vesicles and erosions, fever, malaise; a dermatological emergency requiring iv aciclovir molluscum contagiosum and viral warts are more frequent psychosocial effects: sleep loss, poor school performance, bullying; growth impairment in severe disease or excessive steroid use topical steroid side effects: skin thinning, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis, rarely hpa suppression with long-term potent use over large areas hydrocortisone 1% cream/ointment emollient flucloxacillin (infected eczema) aciclovir (eczema herpeticum)

skin infections & infestations (impetigo, scabies, tinea) allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology skin infections and infestations are among the commonest reasons for children to attend primary care. impetigo, cellulitis, scabies, head lice and tinea are usually easy to diagnose and treat, but spread in families and schools, and rarer complications such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, necrotising fasciitis and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis require recognition. impetigo: honey-coloured crusts; topical therapy for localised, oral flucloxacillin for widespread impetigo can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever ssss: toxin-mediated peeling with positive nikolsky sign and no mucosal involvement scabies: nocturnal itch, burrows; treat all contacts at once and repeat permethrin at 7 days scabies in infants involves palms, soles, face and scalp tinea capitis needs oral antifungals (griseofulvin or terbinafine) head lice: wet combing and dimeticone; no routine exclusion from school pubic lice in children warrant safeguarding consideration pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema or crepitus (necrotising fasciitis) periorbital swelling with proptosis, pain on eye movement or reduced vision (orbital cellulitis) widespread skin peeling in a feverish infant (ssss) cellulitis with fever and systemic upset or in a neonate dark urine, oedema and hypertension after skin infection crusted scabies in an immunosuppressed child scabies sites finger webs, wrists, axillae, waist, genitalia - and in infants also palms, soles, face and scalp bacterial skin infections localised non-bullous impetigo: topical fusidic acid or hydrogen peroxide 1 percent cream (topical antibiotics are not used for long courses to avoid resistance) widespread, bullous or systemically unwell: oral flucloxacillin for 5-7 days (clarithromycin or erythromycin if penicillin allergic) cellulitis: spreading warm erythema, pain and fever; usually strep pyogenes or s. aureus; oral flucloxacillin (or iv benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin if systemic); periorbital cellulitis needs urgent assessment to distinguish pre-septal from orbital cellulitis staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (ssss): exfoliative toxin a/b causes fever, tender erythema, perioral crusting and sheets of epidermal peeling with positive nikolsky sign in infants and young children; no mucosal involvement; treat with iv flucloxacillin (plus clindamycin) and fluids, analgesia folliculitis, boils and abscesses: incision and drainage with antibiotics for associated cellulitis or systemic features; consider mrsa and pvl toxin-producing strains if recurrent necrotising fasciitis: severe pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, crepitus, shock; emergency surgical debridement and broad-spectrum iv antibiotics complications of impetigo: post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (not rheumatic fever), cellulitis, lymphangitis, ssss scabies and head lice signs: burrows (linear grey tracks), papules, vesicles, excoriation, nodules in the axillae and groin, and secondary impetiginisation; crusted (norwegian) scabies in the immunosuppressed diagnosis is clinical; confirm with dermoscopy or skin scraping when needed treatment: permethrin 5 percent cream applied to the whole body (including scalp, face and neck in infants) left for 8-12 hours then washed off, repeated after 7 days; alternatives include malathion 0.5 percent and oral ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg (over 15 kg) treat all household members and close contacts simultaneously, wash bedding and clothes at 50 c or above, and reassure that itch can persist for weeks after successful treatment; use emollients and consider mild steroids or antihistamines for itch head lice (pediculus humanus capitis): scalp itch, with live lice or nits (empty egg cases) seen on detection combing; do not treat prophylactically; options include dimeticone lotion (applied and left for 8 hours, repeated at 7 days), wet combing every 3-4 days for 2 weeks, and isopropyl myristate; school exclusion is not necessary pubic lice in children may indicate sexual abuse and should prompt safeguarding assessment fungal infections (tinea) and other infestations tinea corporis (ringworm): annular, scaly plaque with active edge and central clearing; topical clotrimazole or terbinafine for 2-4 weeks tinea capitis: scaling, hair loss and broken hairs, sometimes boggy kerion with pustules and lymphadenopathy; requires oral therapy - terbinafine (for trichophyton) or griseofulvin (preferred for microsporum; 10-20 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks) - with antifungal shampoo to reduce spread; topical treatment alone is ineffective tinea pedis (athletes foot) and tinea cruris: topical antifungals; the nails (onychomycosis) require prolonged oral therapy tinea incognito: altered appearance after topical steroid use pityriasis versicolor: malassezia, hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly macules on trunk; selenium sulfide shampoo or topical ketoconazole candidal nappy rash: beefy red rash with satellite lesions in skin folds; topical clotrimazole or nystatin, with barrier cream molluscum contagiosum and warts are viral; usually self-resolving cutaneous larva migrans (hookworm larvae from beaches): serpiginous track, treat with ivermectin or albendazole prevention & school advice impetigo: exclude from school until lesions are crusted and healed or 48 hours after starting antibiotics scabies: exclude until after first treatment ringworm and head lice: no exclusion needed once treatment started handwashing, avoid sharing towels and bedding, treat underlying eczema and scabies promptly check urine for blood and bp in a child with recent skin infection who develops dark urine or oedema (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis) flucloxacillin permethrin 5% cream griseofulvin ivermectin

juvenile idiopathic arthritis allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology juvenile idiopathic arthritis (jia) is the commonest chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, defined as arthritis of unknown cause lasting at least 6 weeks with onset before 16 years. it comprises several subtypes with different patterns and complications, especially uveitis, and modern biologic therapy has greatly improved outcomes when started early. jia is arthritis of 6 weeks or more in a child under 16 years after excluding other causes oligoarticular jia is commonest and is associated with ana positivity and chronic anterior uveitis uveitis is often asymptomatic - screen by slit lamp regularly systemic jia: quotidian fever, salmon-pink rash, arthritis and raised inflammatory markers intra-articular steroid is first-line for oligoarthritis; methotrexate for persistent and polyarticular disease enthesitis-related arthritis is hla-b27 associated and causes painful acute anterior uveitis mas is a life-threatening complication of systemic jia always consider septic arthritis and leukaemia in an acute monoarthritis hot, swollen, painful joint with fever (septic arthritis) - needs urgent aspiration and iv antibiotics persistent fever, falling platelets and esr, hyperferritinaemia (mas) painful red eye with photophobia (acute anterior uveitis) night pain, bone pain, cytopenias, weight loss (leukaemia) neck stiffness with cervical spine involvement and neurological symptoms missed eye screening in ana-positive child systemic jia features fever (quotidian), rash (salmon-pink), arthritis, serositis, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy - and screen for mas with ferritin definition & classification clinical features by subtype oligoarticular (commonest, about 50 percent): girls aged 1-5 years, asymmetric large joints (knee, ankle), often limp or reluctance to walk in the morning, minimal pain; ana positive in about 70 percent and high risk of chronic anterior uveitis polyarticular rf negative: symmetrical small and large joints, any age; rf positive resembles adult rheumatoid arthritis with erosive disease in adolescent girls systemic (still disease): quotidian (daily spiking) fever for 2 weeks or more, evanescent salmon-pink macular rash with fever, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis; high crp, esr, ferritin and platelets enthesitis-related arthritis: older boys, lower limb arthritis, enthesitis (heel pain), sacroiliitis, hla-b27 positive, acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye) psoriatic arthritis: arthritis plus psoriasis or dactylitis, nail pitting or family history typical findings: morning stiffness and gelling, joint swelling with warmth and restricted range, limp, growth disturbance (leg length discrepancy, micrognathia from temporomandibular arthritis), muscle wasting often painless in young children; stiffness and behavioural change (not wanting to walk) may be the only clues investigations jia is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion; tests rule out other causes (infection, malignancy, reactive arthritis, lyme, kawasaki, sle) fbc, crp, esr (often normal in oligoarticular), ana, rf and anti-ccp, hla-b27, ferritin in systemic disease; blood cultures if septic arthritis possible joint ultrasound and mri show synovitis, effusion and erosion; plain x-ray is of limited use early (soft tissue swelling, periarticular osteopenia, later erosions and growth abnormalities) aspiration if septic arthritis or other diagnosis is considered; synovial fluid is inflammatory (raised white cells, sterile) regular slit-lamp examination for uveitis, including in asymptomatic children, with frequency determined by ana status, age at onset and subtype (every 3 months in high-risk ana-positive oligoarticular disease) consider leukaemia in a child with bone pain, night pain, cytopenias and raised ldh management nsaids (naproxen, ibuprofen) for symptom relief; they do not alter disease course intra-articular corticosteroid injection (triamcinolone hexacetonide) is highly effective for oligoarticular disease and avoids systemic steroids methotrexate (weekly, with folic acid) is first-line disease-modifying drug for persistent oligoarticular, polyarticular and extended disease biologics: tnf inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab) for refractory polyarticular, enthesitis-related and uveitis (adalimumab); tocilizumab (il-6 inhibitor), abatacept; for systemic jia, anakinra and canakinumab (il-1 inhibitors) and tocilizumab oral corticosteroids are used sparingly for systemic jia flares or while awaiting dmard effect uveitis: topical steroids, mydriatics, methotrexate and adalimumab for chronic disease screen for tb and hepatitis before biologics, update immunisations (inactivated vaccines; avoid live vaccines on immunosuppression) complications & prognosis chronic anterior uveitis (often asymptomatic) can cause synechiae, cataract, glaucoma and blindness macrophage activation syndrome (mas) in systemic jia: persistent fever, falling esr and platelets, cytopenias, very high ferritin, raised triglycerides and transaminases, coagulopathy; a life-threatening emergency treated with high-dose steroids, ciclosporin and anakinra growth failure, leg length discrepancy, joint contractures, osteoporosis, and psychological impact prognosis: oligoarticular disease usually remits; polyarticular rf positive and systemic jia with persistent arthritis have more risk of joint damage; with modern therapy many children achieve remission naproxen methotrexate triamcinolone hexacetonide (intra-articular) adalimumab

henoch-schonlein purpura & vasculitis allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology henoch-schonlein purpura (iga vasculitis) is the commonest systemic vasculitis of childhood, presenting with palpable purpura on the lower limbs, arthritis, abdominal pain and nephritis. it is usually self-limiting, but renal involvement determines long-term outcome and requires follow-up of urinalysis and blood pressure. other paediatric vasculitides include kawasaki disease and anca-associated vasculitis. palpable purpura on buttocks and legs with normal platelets is hsp until proved otherwise triad: purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain; renal disease determines outcome monitor urine and bp for at least 6 months, as nephritis may be delayed abdominal pain can precede the rash intussusception is a recognised complication; scrotal swelling may mimic torsion steroids ease abdominal and joint pain but do not prevent nephritis kawasaki disease causes coronary aneurysms; treat with ivig within 10 days anca-associated vasculitis is rare but causes pulmonary-renal syndrome severe abdominal pain, bilious vomiting or bloody stools (intussusception, bowel ischaemia) hypertension, heavy proteinuria or oedema acute scrotal pain (torsion versus hsp orchitis) rash plus fever with ill appearance (meningococcal sepsis) neurological symptoms, seizures or severe headache reduced urine output or rising creatinine hsp tetrad palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement (paar) definition & epidemiology clinical features palpable purpura (essential) on the buttocks, extensor surfaces of the legs and feet, sometimes the arms and face; may begin as urticarial or erythematous macules and papules; infants may have scrotal and facial swelling arthritis or arthralgia (60-80 percent): knees and ankles, painful swelling, no deformity, transient abdominal pain (50-75 percent): colicky, vomiting, melaena or haematochezia from bowel wall oedema and haemorrhage; may precede the rash by days, leading to diagnostic difficulty renal involvement (20-50 percent): microscopic or macroscopic haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, nephritic or nephrotic syndrome; typically in the first 4-6 weeks scrotal swelling and pain in boys (up to 20 percent): hsp orchitis can mimic testicular torsion rare: cns (seizures, headache), pulmonary haemorrhage, orchitis, mesenteric ischaemia course: self-limited over 4-6 weeks, with relapses in about a third diagnostic criteria (eular/printo/pres): palpable purpura (mandatory) with predominant lower limb distribution, plus at least one of: diffuse abdominal pain, arthritis or arthralgia, renal involvement (haematuria or proteinuria), or biopsy showing iga deposits investigations diagnosis is clinical; platelets are normal or raised (distinguishes it from itp and leukaemia), coagulation normal urinalysis and urine protein:creatinine ratio at presentation and repeated; blood pressure measurement fbc, crp, urea and creatinine, albumin; consider blood cultures if unwell and meningococcal sepsis cannot be excluded stool occult blood if gut involvement; abdominal ultrasound for intussusception or severe abdominal pain (ileo-ileal intussusception is common in hsp, unlike idiopathic ileocolic) renal biopsy for heavy proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome or declining renal function: mesangial iga deposition with proliferation and crescents in severe disease scrotal ultrasound with doppler if testicular pain, with urgent surgical review when torsion cannot be excluded management mainly supportive: rest, hydration, paracetamol; nsaids for joint pain are acceptable if renal function and bp are normal and no gi bleeding short course of oral prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks, then taper) for severe abdominal pain, gi bleeding, testicular involvement or severe oedema; it does not prevent renal disease admit for severe abdominal pain, gi bleeding, significant renal involvement, inability to take oral fluids or doubt about the diagnosis nephritis: ace inhibitors for persistent proteinuria; severe nephritis (nephrotic range, crescents) is treated with steroids, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate or azathioprine under paediatric nephrology surgical treatment for intussusception, bowel infarction or perforation follow-up with bp and urinalysis weekly initially, then monthly to at least 6 months (and 12 months in some guidelines) because nephritis may appear late other paediatric vasculitides kawasaki disease (medium vessel): fever for 5 days or more, conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes, cervical nodes; coronary artery aneurysms in 25 percent if untreated; ivig 2 g/kg and aspirin anca-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis): pulmonary-renal syndrome, sinusitis, positive canca or panca; treat with steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab polyarteritis nodosa: medium vessel; fever, hypertension, skin nodules and necrosis, mononeuritis, abdominal pain takayasu arteritis: large vessel; hypertension, absent pulses, bruits behcet disease: recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis paracetamol prednisolone enalapril (persistent proteinuria) iv immunoglobulin (for kawasaki)
