paediatric lupus, mis-c & autoinflammatory disease allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology paediatric systemic lupus erythematosus (sle) is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease that is more severe in children than in adults, with frequent renal and neuropsychiatric involvement. multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (mis-c) is a post-infectious hyperinflammatory condition following sars-cov-2 infection, and autoinflammatory diseases are caused by dysregulated innate immunity producing periodic fever and inflammation. childhood sle is more severe than adult disease, with more renal and neuropsychiatric involvement ana is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsdna and anti-sm are more specific low c3/c4 and high anti-dsdna suggest active lupus nephritis hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all patients with sle neonatal lupus: anti-ro/la antibodies cause congenital heart block mis-c appears 2-6 weeks after sars-cov-2 infection with fever, gi symptoms, shock and cardiac involvement mis-c treatment is ivig and/or steroids with cardiac monitoring pfapa is a benign periodic fever that responds to a single dose of steroid; fmf is treated with colchicine lupus with hypertension, oedema, haematuria or rising creatinine (nephritis) lupus with seizures, psychosis or focal neurology persistent fever with shock, abdominal pain and rash after covid-19 exposure (mis-c) raised troponin or coronary dilatation massive fall in blood counts with fever in sle (mas) recurrent serositis with renal protein loss (fmf with amyloidosis) pfapa periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis sle features (soap brain md) serositis, oral ulcers, arthritis, photosensitivity, blood disorders, renal disease, ana, immunologic, neurologic, malar rash, discoid rash paediatric systemic lupus erythematosus constitutional: fever, fatigue, weight loss, lymphadenopathy mucocutaneous: malar (butterfly) rash sparing nasolabial folds, discoid lesions, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, alopecia, raynaud phenomenon musculoskeletal: non-erosive arthritis and arthralgia, myositis renal (50-80 percent): proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension, nephrotic syndrome; biopsy classifies lupus nephritis class i-vi haematological: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, leucopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia; antiphospholipid antibodies with thrombosis risk neuropsychiatric: seizures, psychosis, mood disorder, headache, chorea, cognitive dysfunction cardiopulmonary: pericarditis, pleuritis, pulmonary haemorrhage, libman-sacks endocarditis investigations: fbc, esr (raised) with normal crp, urinalysis, upcr, creatinine, ana (nearly all, but non-specific), anti-dsdna and anti-sm (specific), low c3 and c4, direct coombs, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-ro/la; renal biopsy if nephritis suspected classification: acr/eular 2019 criteria require ana positivity as an entry criterion plus weighted clinical and immunological domains sle management & neonatal lupus sun protection, hydroxychloroquine for all (reduces flares; annual eye screening), nsaids for arthritis corticosteroids for flares (high-dose oral or iv pulse methylprednisolone for severe disease), steroid-sparing agents: azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate lupus nephritis class iii-iv: induction with mycophenolate or iv cyclophosphamide plus steroids; biologics such as belimumab and rituximab for refractory disease manage cardiovascular risk, bone health, vaccinations (inactivated vaccines), contraception and avoid oestrogen-containing contraceptives in active disease or antiphospholipid antibodies transition planning and psychological support, as adolescent adherence is a major challenge neonatal lupus: transplacental anti-ro (ssa) and anti-la (ssb) antibodies cause annular rash, transient cytopenias, hepatitis and congenital heart block (permanent, 2 percent risk in anti-ro positive mothers); maternal hydroxychloroquine reduces risk; infants with complete heart block may need pacing mis-c (pims-ts) features: fever 3 days or more, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea (often mimicking appendicitis), rash, conjunctivitis, oral changes, headache and meningism, hypotension and shock requiring inotropes in many cardiac: myocardial dysfunction, raised troponin and bnp, coronary artery dilatation or aneurysm, arrhythmias laboratory: very high crp, ferritin, d-dimer, il-6, neutrophilia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminaemia, hyponatraemia, positive sars-cov-2 serology or pcr management: abcde and picu if shocked; echocardiography; exclude sepsis (give empirical antibiotics); iv immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and/or methylprednisolone (10-30 mg/kg, max 1 g daily for 1-3 days or prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg); anakinra or infliximab if refractory; aspirin and anticoagulation where indicated follow-up cardiac imaging at 2 weeks and 6 weeks; most children recover fully autoinflammatory diseases autoinflammatory diseases result from dysregulated innate immunity (inflammasome, il-1 pathways) with recurrent fever and inflammation without infection or autoantibodies pfapa (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis): regular fever every 3-6 weeks lasting 3-6 days in a well child, resolves with a single dose of prednisolone 1 mg/kg; tonsillectomy can be curative familial mediterranean fever (mefv gene, autosomal recessive): recurrent 1-3 day fevers with serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis), arthritis and erysipeloid rash in eastern mediterranean ancestry; risk of aa amyloidosis; treat with daily colchicine cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (caps), traps and hyper-igd syndrome (mevalonate kinase deficiency): treated with il-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) systemic jia is also considered an autoinflammatory disease and responds to il-1 and il-6 blockade rule out infection, malignancy, immunodeficiency and cyclic neutropenia, which also cause periodic fever hydroxychloroquine methylprednisolone (iv pulse) colchicine (fmf) iv immunoglobulin (mis-c)

primary immunodeficiency allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology primary immunodeficiencies (inborn errors of immunity) are over 450 inherited disorders of immune function that present with recurrent, severe, unusual or opportunistic infections, autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation or malignancy. early recognition prevents irreversible organ damage and death; severe combined immunodeficiency is a paediatric emergency that is curable by early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. lymphopenia in an infant with infections suggests scid until proven otherwise x-linked agammaglobulinaemia presents after 6 months, when maternal igg wanes, with absent b cells avoid live vaccines (bcg, rotavirus) in suspected t-cell deficiency until immunology review use irradiated, cmv-negative blood products in t-cell deficiency cgd causes catalase-positive organism infections: staph aureus, aspergillus, serratia delayed umbilical cord separation with high neutrophil count suggests leucocyte adhesion deficiency selective iga deficiency is the commonest primary immunodeficiency, usually asymptomatic hsct within the first 3.5 months gives best outcomes in scid infant with persistent thrush, chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive and lymphopenia pjp or other opportunistic infection in a child without hiv disseminated bcg disease after vaccination recurrent meningococcal disease (complement deficiency) deep organ abscesses (liver, lung) with staph aureus or aspergillus (cgd) hypocalcaemic seizures in a neonate with a cardiac defect (22q11 deletion) infection pattern by defect b cells = bacteria (encapsulated, sinopulmonary); t cells = viruses, fungi, pjp; phagocytes = skin abscesses (staph, aspergillus); complement = neisseria warning signs (spur) severe, persistent, unusual, recurrent infections recognising immunodeficiency ten warning signs (adapted): 4 or more ear infections in a year, 2 or more serious sinus infections, 2 or more pneumonias in a year, failure to gain weight or grow normally, recurrent deep skin or organ abscesses, persistent oral or skin thrush after 1 year, need for iv antibiotics to clear infection, 2 or more deep-seated infections including sepsis, family history of primary immunodeficiency other clues: chronic diarrhoea, eczema with infections, autoimmune cytopenias, lymphopenia, absent thymic shadow, delayed umbilical cord separation (leucocyte adhesion deficiency) pattern of infection indicates the defect: antibody deficiency causes sinopulmonary and encapsulated bacterial infection; t cell deficiency causes viral, fungal and opportunistic infection; neutrophil defects cause staphylococcal, gram-negative and fungal skin and organ abscesses; complement deficiency causes neisseria infection and lupus-like disease classification and key conditions antibody deficiencies (commonest): x-linked agammaglobulinaemia (bruton, btk gene; boys; infections after 6 months when maternal igg wanes; absent b cells and very low immunoglobulins), common variable immunodeficiency (cvid; later onset with recurrent infections, autoimmunity and granulomatous disease), selective iga deficiency (commonest; often asymptomatic, risk of anaphylaxis with blood products in anti-iga antibody patients), transient hypogammaglobulinaemia of infancy combined t and b cell deficiencies: severe combined immunodeficiency (scid; x-linked il2rg or ada deficiency; presentation in first months with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea, persistent thrush, pjp, severe viral infection; lymphopenia is the clue; absent thymus on cxr); digeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion; hypocalcaemia, cardiac defects, thymic hypoplasia); wiskott-aldrich (eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, infections); ataxia telangiectasia (cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia, sinopulmonary infection, malignancy) phagocytic defects: chronic granulomatous disease (cgd; nadph oxidase defect; recurrent staph aureus, aspergillus, serratia and burkholderia infections with granulomas; nitroblue tetrazolium/dhr test), leucocyte adhesion deficiency (delayed cord separation, very high neutrophil count without pus), severe congenital neutropenia complement deficiency: c5-c9 and properdin deficiency cause recurrent meningococcal infection; early component deficiency (c1q, c2, c4) causes sle-like disease; c1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema innate and cytokine defects: il-12/interferon gamma pathway defects (mycobacterial infection), mendelian susceptibility to herpes encephalitis (tlr3) investigations first-line: fbc and differential (lymphopenia in scid is under 2.5 x 10^9/l in infants; neutropenia), blood film, immunoglobulins (igg, iga, igm, ige) with age-specific reference ranges, specific vaccine antibody titres (tetanus, pneumococcal) second-line: lymphocyte subsets by flow cytometry (cd3, cd4, cd8, cd19, cd16/56), neutrophil oxidative burst (dhr) and complement ch50/ap50, hiv test, chest x-ray (thymic shadow), hiv antibody and pcr before diagnosis genetic testing (targeted panels or whole exome sequencing) for definitive diagnosis and family counselling newborn screening for scid by t-cell receptor excision circles (trecs) on the dried blood spot is available in many countries exclude secondary causes: hiv, malnutrition, malignancy, protein-losing states, immunosuppressive drugs management scid is a paediatric emergency: protective isolation, avoid live vaccines (including bcg and rotavirus), irradiated, cmv-negative blood products, pjp prophylaxis, antifungal prophylaxis, immunoglobulin replacement; definitive treatment with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (best before 3.5 months of age), enzyme replacement or gene therapy (ada-scid, x-scid) antibody deficiency: lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy (iv 400-600 mg/kg every 3-4 weeks or subcutaneous weekly) to keep trough igg above 6-8 g/l; prophylactic antibiotics; physiotherapy for bronchiectasis cgd: lifelong antibacterial (cotrimoxazole) and antifungal (itraconazole) prophylaxis, interferon gamma; stem cell transplantation in selected cases complement deficiency: vaccination (meningococcal acwy, b, pneumococcal) and antibiotic prophylaxis general: treat infections early and aggressively, avoid live vaccines in t-cell deficiency, genetic counselling, psychosocial support maintain high suspicion in a child with unexplained recurrent infections, and refer to paediatric immunology immunoglobulin replacement (iv/sc) cotrimoxazole (pjp prophylaxis) itraconazole (cgd prophylaxis) interferon gamma (cgd)

birthmarks & other paediatric skin conditions allergy, immunology, rheumatology & dermatology birthmarks and other common paediatric skin conditions such as infantile haemangioma, port-wine stain, congenital melanocytic naevi and mongolian blue spots are frequent reasons for parental concern. most are benign and need only reassurance, but some are associated with systemic or neurological disease, or require early treatment, so knowing the red flags is essential. infantile haemangiomas proliferate in the first months and involute over years; they are glut1-positive propranolol is first-line for problematic haemangiomas (periocular, airway, ulcerated, disfiguring) segmental facial haemangioma raises concern for phace syndrome five or more haemangiomas: ultrasound the liver and check tfts a port-wine stain in the v1 distribution suggests sturge-weber syndrome six or more cafe-au-lait macules over 5 mm suggest neurofibromatosis type 1 mongolian blue spots are benign; document them to avoid misdiagnosis as bruising giant congenital melanocytic naevi have melanoma and neurocutaneous melanosis risk three or more ash-leaf macules suggest tuberous sclerosis periocular haemangioma threatening vision (amblyopia) beard-distribution haemangioma with stridor (airway) ulcerating haemangioma in nappy area or lip port-wine stain on the forehead or upper eyelid with seizures or glaucoma multiple haemangiomas with hepatomegaly or heart failure multiple cafe-au-lait macules with freckling or neurological signs phace posterior fossa anomalies, haemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects, eye anomalies nf1 diagnosis (cafe-nf) cafe-au-lait spots (6+), axillary freckling, fibromas (neurofibromas), eye lisch nodules, plus neuro-optic glioma, family history, bone lesions vascular birthmarks superficial (strawberry), deep (blue bulge) and mixed haemangiomas; segmental lesions are more likely to be associated with complications complications: ulceration (commonest, painful, in lip, nappy area and flexures), visual obstruction and amblyopia (periocular), airway haemangioma (segmental beard distribution with stridor), high-output cardiac failure from hepatic lesions phace syndrome: segmental facial haemangioma with posterior fossa malformations, haemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects, eye anomalies; evaluate with mri/mra and echocardiography multiple (5 or more) cutaneous haemangiomas: ultrasound of the liver for hepatic haemangiomas; check thyroid function (consumptive hypothyroidism) treatment: observation for small, low-risk lesions; oral propranolol 2-3 mg/kg/day divided in 2-3 doses, started under monitoring (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose), for problematic lesions (periocular, airway, ulcerated, disfiguring facial or segmental) - ideally started in the first few weeks to months; topical timolol for superficial small lesions; laser or surgery for residual deformity port-wine stain (capillary malformation): flat pink-red stain present at birth that persists lifelong and darkens and thickens with age; treated with pulsed dye laser; a v1 (ophthalmic) distribution lesion suggests sturge-weber syndrome (leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, learning difficulty, glaucoma) and requires mri and ophthalmology review salmon patch (stork bite, naevus simplex): pale pink flat patches on nape, glabella and eyelids, fading within 1-3 years (nape persists); no treatment klippel-trenaunay syndrome: capillary malformation with venous malformation and limb overgrowth; kasabach-merritt phenomenon complicates kaposiform haemangioendothelioma with severe thrombocytopenia pigmented birthmarks mongolian blue spots (dermal melanocytosis): blue-grey patches over sacrum and buttocks, common in asian, african and hispanic infants; fade by school age; document to avoid being mistaken for bruising (and safeguarding concerns) cafe-au-lait macules: uniform light-brown macules; 6 or more over 5 mm (prepubertal) suggest neurofibromatosis type 1 (also axillary freckling, lisch nodules, neurofibromas, optic glioma, bony lesions); mccune-albright syndrome has large irregular ("coast of maine") macules with precocious puberty and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia congenital melanocytic naevi: giant (projected adult size over 20 cm) carry increased melanoma risk and neurocutaneous melanosis with multiple satellite lesions; refer for mri and dermatology follow-up naevus of ota and ito, nevus depigmentosus and hypomelanotic macules: 3 or more ash-leaf macules suggest tuberous sclerosis (wood lamp) acquired melanocytic naevi appear in childhood; apply abcde criteria; change should prompt referral epidermal naevi: warty, linear plaques following blaschko lines, may be associated with neurological or skeletal anomalies incontinentia pigmenti: x-linked dominant, blistering then warty then swirled hyperpigmentation in a female infant, with eye and cns involvement other common paediatric skin conditions neonatal rashes: erythema toxicum (white pustules on erythematous base, benign, eosinophils), milia, miliaria, sebaceous hyperplasia, transient pustular melanosis, neonatal acne seborrhoeic dermatitis (cradle cap): greasy yellow scale on scalp, behind ears; emollients and mild keratolytic or ketoconazole shampoo; nappy dermatitis (irritant or candida) managed with barrier cream, frequent changes, antifungal if candidal psoriasis: well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques on extensor surfaces, scalp, napkin area, guttate psoriasis after strep infection; topical emollients, vitamin d analogues, mild steroids; systemic therapies for severe disease molluscum contagiosum: pearly umbilicated papules, usually self-limiting over 6-18 months; reassure; treat if symptomatic viral warts: self-resolving in most; salicylic acid or cryotherapy acne vulgaris and acne in infancy; urticaria (acute, often viral) and papular urticaria (insect bites); alopecia areata: patchy non-scarring hair loss hypopigmented conditions: pityriasis alba, vitiligo (autoimmune, associated with thyroid disease) epidermolysis bullosa and ichthyosis are genetic skin disorders needing specialist input and wound care propranolol (haemangioma) timolol 0.5% gel emollient and barrier cream

patterns of inheritance genetics & dysmorphology genetic disease follows chromosomal, single-gene (mendelian), mitochondrial and multifactorial patterns. understanding the modes of inheritance allows accurate pedigree interpretation, recurrence risk estimation and counselling of families, and recognition of non-classical mechanisms such as imprinting, anticipation and mosaicism. autosomal dominant: vertical transmission, male-to-male transmission possible, 50 percent risk autosomal recessive: horizontal pattern, 25 percent risk, consanguinity common x-linked recessive: males affected, no male-to-male transmission, carrier mother has 50 percent risk to sons mitochondrial inheritance is maternal; all children of an affected woman inherit the mutation imprinting explains prader-willi (paternal deficiency) versus angelman (maternal deficiency) trinucleotide repeat disorders show anticipation germline mosaicism can cause recurrence in unaffected parents multifactorial conditions carry a recurrence risk of about 2-5 percent for a sibling family history of unexplained early deaths or neonatal deaths suggesting a metabolic disorder consanguinity with multiple affected children unexplained developmental delay with dysmorphism possible x-linked disease in a boy with a family history of affected maternal relatives asymptomatic parent of a child with a new dominant condition (consider mosaicism or non-penetrance) dominant versus recessive enzyme/structure dominant disorders tend to affect structural proteins and receptors; recessive disorders tend to affect enzymes prader-willi versus angelman prader-willi = paternal gene lost (pa = p); angelman = maternal gene lost (ma = a) autosomal dominant inheritance examples: neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis, marfan syndrome, noonan syndrome, achondroplasia, familial hypercholesterolaemia, huntington disease, hereditary spherocytosis, osteogenesis imperfecta, polycystic kidney disease (adult type) autosomal recessive inheritance examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, phenylketonuria, spinal muscular atrophy, galactosaemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, tay-sachs disease, most inborn errors of metabolism carrier screening and newborn bloodspot testing detect many conditions x-linked and mitochondrial inheritance non-classical mechanisms imprinting: gene expression depends on parental origin. deletion of paternal 15q11-q13 causes prader-willi syndrome; deletion of the maternal copy causes angelman syndrome. uniparental disomy (both copies from one parent) causes the same syndromes trinucleotide repeat expansion: unstable repeats expand across generations causing anticipation (earlier, more severe disease). fragile x (cgg), huntington disease (cag, paternal expansion), myotonic dystrophy (ctg, maternal expansion causing congenital form), friedreich ataxia (gaa) mosaicism: two or more cell lines from one zygote; somatic mosaicism causes patchy disease (mccune-albright), germline mosaicism explains recurrence of dominant disease in unaffected parents multifactorial inheritance: interaction of genes and environment (neural tube defects, congenital heart disease, cleft lip and palate, pyloric stenosis, type 1 diabetes); recurrence risk is about 2-5 percent after one affected child and higher with more affected relatives or more severe disease chromosomal: numerical (aneuploidy, polyploidy) and structural (translocation, deletion, duplication, inversion); balanced robertsonian translocation carriers have normal phenotype but a risk of affected offspring pedigrees and counselling

down syndrome genetics & dysmorphology down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, affecting about 1 in 700 births. it has recognisable facial features and a predictable pattern of associated medical problems including congenital heart disease, hypotonia, hearing and visual issues, thyroid disease and leukaemia. proactive surveillance and multidisciplinary care substantially improve outcomes. trisomy 21 accounts for 95 percent; robertsonian translocation 4 percent; mosaicism 1-2 percent most common cardiac lesion is atrioventricular septal defect (avsd) duodenal atresia (double bubble) is associated; hirschsprung disease also occurs screen thyroid function yearly and test hearing and vision regularly increased risk of acute leukaemia and transient abnormal myelopoiesis atlantoaxial instability: neck pain, gait change or new weakness needs urgent assessment karyotype is needed to determine recurrence risk (translocation versus trisomy) early-onset alzheimer disease occurs due to the extra app gene on chromosome 21 cyanosis, poor feeding and sweating suggesting heart failure in early infancy bilious vomiting (duodenal atresia, malrotation) or delayed meconium passage (hirschsprung) new neck pain, gait disturbance or incontinence (atlantoaxial subluxation) pallor, bruising or fever with abnormal blood count (leukaemia) regression in skills (hypothyroidism, depression, dementia, coeliac, sleep apnoea, epilepsy) infantile spasms in a baby with developmental plateau features of down syndrome flat face, upslanting eyes, brushfield spots, single palmar crease, sandal gap, floppy tone genetics and epidemiology clinical features face and head: brachycephaly, flat occiput, flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, brushfield spots on the iris, small ears, protruding tongue, small mouth neck and limbs: excess nuchal skin, short neck, short broad hands with single palmar crease (simian crease), clinodactyly of the fifth finger, wide sandal gap between first and second toes, hypotonia with joint laxity neonatal: hypotonia (floppy infant), poor moro reflex, poor feeding, duodenal atresia, hypotonia, jaundice and polycythaemia development: moderate intellectual disability on average (iq 35-70), delayed motor milestones (walking at about 2 years), language delay worse than comprehension, usually pleasant, sociable; autism spectrum and adhd more common associated problems and surveillance cardiac (about 40-50 percent): atrioventricular septal defect (commonest), vsd, asd, patent ductus, tetralogy of fallot; echocardiogram in the first weeks of life for all babies; early surgery prevents pulmonary vascular disease gastrointestinal: duodenal atresia (double bubble sign), hirschsprung disease, anal atresia, coeliac disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux, constipation hearing and vision: conductive and sensorineural hearing loss (glue ear), cataracts, strabismus, refractive errors, keratoconus, nystagmus; regular audiology and ophthalmology endocrine: congenital and acquired hypothyroidism (annual tfts), obesity, type 1 diabetes haematological: transient abnormal myelopoiesis in neonates, polycythaemia, increased risk of acute leukaemia (all and aml-m7, 10-20 fold) musculoskeletal and neurological: atlantoaxial instability (symptoms of cord compression: neck pain, gait change), epilepsy including infantile spasms, early-onset alzheimer disease in adulthood respiratory and sleep: recurrent chest infections, obstructive sleep apnoea, pulmonary hypertension immune: increased susceptibility to infection; routine immunisations plus annual flu and pneumococcal vaccine antenatal screening and diagnosis management and giving the diagnosis

turner & klinefelter syndromes genetics & dysmorphology turner syndrome (45,x) and klinefelter syndrome (47,xxy) are the two most common sex chromosome disorders. turner syndrome causes short stature and gonadal dysgenesis in girls with cardiac and renal anomalies, while klinefelter syndrome causes hypogonadism, tall stature and learning difficulty in boys. both need lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up and hormone replacement. turner syndrome is 45,x (or mosaic): short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, primary ovarian failure neonatal lymphoedema of the hands and feet is a classic turner sign coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve are the main cardiac lesions; check blood pressure in all four limbs treat turner syndrome with growth hormone and later oestrogen replacement look for y chromosome material in turner mosaics (gonadoblastoma risk) klinefelter syndrome is 47,xxy: tall, small firm testes, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, infertility klinefelter syndrome is treated with testosterone from puberty both syndromes are diagnosed by karyotype absent femoral pulses or hypertension in a girl with turner features (coarctation) chest or back pain with aortic root dilatation (dissection risk) primary amenorrhoea with short stature or no breast development by 13 years girl with turner syndrome and virilisation (y chromosome material) boy with delayed puberty, tall stature and learning difficulty new breast lump in a male with klinefelter syndrome turner features short, shield chest, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, coarctation, streak ovaries turner syndrome: genetics turner syndrome: clinical features turner syndrome: associations and management cardiac (about 30-50 percent): bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, aortic root dilatation with risk of dissection; echocardiogram and cardiac mri and regular follow-up renal: horseshoe kidney, duplex systems; renal ultrasound at diagnosis endocrine and autoimmune: hypothyroidism (hashimoto), coeliac disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity, osteoporosis ent: recurrent otitis media and sensorineural hearing loss; ophthalmology for strabismus growth: recombinant growth hormone (higher doses than in gh deficiency) from around age 4-6 years improves final height by about 5-8 cm; oxandrolone sometimes added puberty: low-dose oestrogen from 11-12 years, increased gradually, then cyclical oestrogen with progestogen; supports uterine growth and bone health; fertility is usually absent, though assisted reproduction (donor oocytes) may be possible with cardiac risk assessment diagnosis: karyotype (at least 30 cells); look for y material (risk of gonadoblastoma, prophylactic gonadectomy); also in any girl with unexplained short stature or delayed puberty klinefelter syndrome klinefelter syndrome: investigations and management growth hormone (somatropin) in turner syndrome testosterone in klinefelter syndrome

t: Fragile X, Prader-Willi, Angelman & other syndromes
h: fragile x, prader-willi, angelman & other syndromes genetics & dysmorphology fragile x syndrome, prader-willi syndrome and angelman syndrome are classic genetic disorders causing intellectual disability with recognisable behavioural and physical phenotypes. they illustrate trinucleotide repeat expansion and genomic imprinting. cri du chat, wolf-hirschhorn, rett and 22q11 or smith-magenis syndromes are other important examples. fragile x: fmr1 cgg repeat expansion (over 200), commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability, macro-orchidism full mutation arises only through maternal transmission; anticipation occurs in female transmission prader-willi: loss of paternal 15q11-q13; hypotonia then hyperphagia and obesity angelman: loss of maternal ube3a; happy puppet affect, ataxia, seizures, absent speech both pws and angelman can be due to deletion, uniparental disomy or an imprinting defect; diagnose by methylation analysis rett syndrome: girls with regression, hand wringing and mecp2 mutation cri du chat: 5p deletion with high-pitched cry beckwith-wiedemann syndrome requires tumour surveillance floppy infant with feeding difficulty and hypogonadism (consider pws) hyperphagia with rapid weight gain in a child with learning difficulty developmental regression in a girl at 6-18 months (rett) refractory seizures in a child with severe delay and ataxia (angelman) hypoglycaemia in a baby with macroglossia and omphalocele (beckwith-wiedemann) respiratory or sleep problems with obesity in pws (acute illness can be missed because of pain insensitivity and temperature instability) imprinting prader-willi: paternal gene missing. angelman: maternal gene missing (ube3a) fragile x features big ears, long face, big testes, flat feet, hyperextensible joints, autistic traits fragile x syndrome prader-willi syndrome neonatal and infant: severe hypotonia, poor suck and feeding difficulty requiring tube feeding, failure to thrive, weak cry, hypogonadism (cryptorchidism, small genitalia) childhood: hyperphagia and food seeking from 2-4 years with progressive obesity if uncontrolled, short stature, small hands and feet, almond-shaped eyes, narrow bifrontal diameter, fair skin and hair, learning disability (mild to moderate), temper tantrums, skin picking, obsessive compulsive behaviours endocrine: growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadism and delayed or incomplete puberty, central adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, type 2 diabetes with obesity other: sleep apnoea, scoliosis, osteoporosis, temperature instability management: multidisciplinary; strict dietary supervision and environmental food control (locked kitchen), exercise, recombinant growth hormone (improves body composition and growth), sex steroid replacement, behaviour and psychiatric support, monitoring of sleep and endocrine function angelman syndrome other syndromes cri du chat (5p deletion): high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy, microcephaly, round face, hypertelorism, intellectual disability, hypotonia; cry usually disappears by 2 years wolf-hirschhorn syndrome (4p deletion): greek warrior helmet facial appearance, growth restriction, seizures, cardiac and midline defects rett syndrome (mecp2, x-linked dominant): girls with normal early development then regression at 6-18 months, loss of purposeful hand use, hand wringing, acquired microcephaly, seizures, breathing irregularities, autism features smith-magenis syndrome (17p11.2 deletion): sleep disturbance with inverted melatonin rhythm, self-injurious behaviour, intellectual disability beckwith-wiedemann syndrome (11p15 imprinting): macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, neonatal hypoglycaemia, risk of wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma needing ultrasound surveillance

marfan, noonan, williams & digeorge syndromes genetics & dysmorphology marfan, noonan, williams and digeorge syndromes are important genetic syndromes that every paediatrician should recognise because of life-threatening cardiovascular and immunological consequences. marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder, noonan syndrome a rasopathy, williams syndrome a contiguous gene deletion and digeorge syndrome the commonest microdeletion syndrome. marfan: fbn1 mutation, aortic root dilatation, ectopia lentis (upward), arachnodactyly; give beta-blocker or losartan and monitor with echocardiography noonan: normal karyotype, webbed neck, pulmonary stenosis, ptpn11 mutation, bleeding tendency williams: 7q11.23 deletion (eln), supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcaemia, friendly personality digeorge: 22q11.2 deletion, catch-22 - cardiac, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcaemia check calcium and lymphocyte subsets in any baby with a conotruncal heart defect use irradiated cmv-negative blood in suspected digeorge syndrome until t cell function known ectopia lentis in homocystinuria is downward; in marfan it is upward noonan syndrome affects boys and girls and has normal chromosomes, unlike turner syndrome chest or back pain in a patient with marfan syndrome (aortic dissection) hypocalcaemic seizures in a neonate with a heart murmur (digeorge) cyanosis with cleft palate and dysmorphism (tetralogy of fallot with 22q11 deletion) unusual bleeding in a child with noonan syndrome syncope or exertional chest pain in williams syndrome (supravalvular aortic stenosis, coronary compromise) recurrent severe infections or candidiasis in a child with a conotruncal defect catch-22 cardiac, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcaemia - on chromosome 22 marfan syndrome skeletal: tall with long limbs (arm span greater than height, reduced upper to lower segment ratio), arachnodactyly (thumb and wrist signs), pectus excavatum or carinatum, scoliosis, joint laxity, flat feet, high-arched palate, long narrow face ocular: ectopia lentis (upward and temporal lens dislocation), myopia, retinal detachment cardiovascular: aortic root dilatation and dissection (main cause of death), mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, dilated pulmonary artery other: striae, dural ectasia, spontaneous pneumothorax, hernias management: annual echocardiography (more often if dilated), beta-blockers or angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan) to slow aortic growth, elective aortic root replacement when the root reaches about 45-50 mm (lower thresholds in children and with family history), avoiding contact sports and isometric exercise, ophthalmology review, pregnancy counselling with cardiology noonan syndrome williams syndrome digeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome cardiac defects (conotruncal): tetralogy of fallot, interrupted aortic arch, truncus arteriosus, vsd abnormal facies: hooded eyelids, bulbous nasal tip, small ears, micrognathia thymic hypoplasia: t cell deficiency and recurrent infections; complete digeorge (athymia) needs urgent immunology care, irradiated cmv-negative blood products, and thymic transplantation or stem cell transplant; live vaccines contraindicated if t cells are low cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism (neonatal tetany or seizures) additional: learning difficulties, speech delay, psychiatric illness (schizophrenia risk about 25 percent), autoimmune disease, renal anomalies investigations: fish or microarray for 22q11.2, calcium, pth, lymphocyte subsets, chest x-ray (absent thymic shadow), echocardiogram losartan calcium gluconate 10 percent

dysmorphology, genetic testing & counselling genetics & dysmorphology dysmorphology is the study of abnormal physical development, and genetic testing allows a specific diagnosis in a growing proportion of children with congenital anomalies, developmental delay or familial disease. paediatricians should know how to describe dysmorphic features, choose appropriate tests and counsel families with sensitivity about uncertainty, recurrence and ethical issues. chromosomal microarray is first-line for unexplained intellectual disability, autism and multiple congenital anomalies karyotype remains useful for known aneuploidy syndromes, balanced translocations and recurrent miscarriage methylation testing is required for imprinting disorders (prader-willi, angelman, beckwith-wiedemann) a malformation is intrinsic; a deformation is due to mechanical forces; a disruption is breakdown of normal tissue association (vacterl) is non-random but without a known single cause genetic counselling is non-directive and includes recurrence risk and reproductive options predictive testing for adult-onset disease is generally deferred in minors trio whole-exome sequencing has the highest yield in severe developmental disorders multiple major anomalies in a newborn ambiguous genitalia (urgent assessment for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and salt loss) dysmorphism with developmental regression or metabolic decompensation suspected teratogen exposure in pregnancy (anticonvulsants, alcohol, isotretinoin) consanguinity with multiple affected family members vacterl association vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, renal anomalies, limb anomalies charge coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth/development, genital anomalies, ear anomalies (chd7 mutation) terminology and approach to the dysmorphic child genetic testing karyotype (g-banded): detects aneuploidy and large structural rearrangements (above 5-10 mb); used for down, turner and klinefelter syndromes and for translocations and recurrent miscarriage fluorescence in situ hybridisation (fish): targeted probes for known microdeletions (22q11.2, 7q11.23), rapid aneuploidy detection chromosomal microarray (array cgh or snp array): detects copy number variants at 50-100 kb resolution; first-line for unexplained developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism and multiple congenital anomalies; yields a diagnosis in about 15-20 percent; cannot detect balanced rearrangements, point mutations or repeat expansions; variants of uncertain significance may be found targeted molecular tests: pcr and southern blot for repeat expansions (fragile x, huntington), methylation analysis (prader-willi, angelman, beckwith-wiedemann), single gene sequencing next generation sequencing: gene panels, whole exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing (trio analysis improves diagnosis; yield about 25-40 percent in severe developmental disorders); the 100,000 genomes project and national genomic medicine services in the uk; incidental findings and consent issues biochemical and enzymatic tests for metabolic disease; mitochondrial dna analysis prenatal diagnosis and screening genetic counselling and ethics

paediatric assessment: pat, abcde & triage emergencies & critical care structured assessment of the sick child begins with a 30-second visual paediatric assessment triangle (appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin), followed by the abcde approach in which life threats are treated as they are found. triage systems (manchester, etat in resource-limited settings) then prioritise who is seen first. this is the foundation of every paediatric emergency. the pat (appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin) gives a sick/not-sick impression in under 30 seconds. treat life threats as you find them; reassess after every intervention. most paediatric arrests follow hypoxia and shock, not primary cardiac disease. hypotension is a late sign of shock; tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill come first. always check blood glucose in any child with altered consciousness, seizure or shock. minimum systolic bp is about 70 + (2 x age) mmhg for ages 1-10 years. capillary refill over 2 seconds (over 3 seconds in who etat) with weak fast pulse suggests shock. tiring child with slowing respiratory rate and falling consciousness is pre-arrest. silent chest, exhaustion, or bradypnoea in a child with respiratory distress heart rate falling to bradycardia in a sick child (pre-arrest sign) responds only to pain or unresponsive (p or u on avpu) non-blanching purpuric rash with shock or fever hypotension or mottled, cold peripheries with prolonged capillary refill central cyanosis or oxygen saturation under 92% despite oxygen avpu alert, responds to voice, responds to pain, unresponsive. p or u roughly equals gcs 8 or below. ticls tone, interactiveness, consolability, look/gaze, speech/cry - the appearance elements of the pat. tpr-mots (who priority signs) tiny infant, temperature, trauma, pallor, poisoning, pain, respiratory distress, restless, referral, malnutrition, oedema, burns. principles and the first look abcde assessment airway: look, listen and feel. stridor, snoring, gurgling or silent chest signal obstruction. open with head tilt and chin lift (neutral position in infants), jaw thrust if trauma is suspected, suction under vision only, consider an oropharyngeal airway in the unconscious child. breathing: respiratory rate, effort (recession, grunting, nasal flaring, accessory muscle use), air entry, added sounds, oxygen saturation, skin colour. give high-flow oxygen through a reservoir mask to any seriously ill child. slow or irregular breathing in a tired child is pre-terminal. circulation: heart rate, pulse volume, capillary refill time (normal 2 seconds or less, pressed centrally for 5 seconds), skin temperature, blood pressure (a late sign - children maintain pressure until about 25-30% of blood volume is lost), urine output. gain iv or intraosseous access and take bloods including glucose and gas. disability: avpu (alert, responds to voice, responds to pain, unresponsive) or the paediatric gcs, pupils, posture, blood glucose. hypoglycaemia is below 3 mmol/l in the acutely ill child (many units treat below 3.5-4). exposure: undress fully, look for rash (non-blanching), injuries, burns, signs of abuse, and check temperature, while keeping the child warm. normal values by age (apls) weight estimation and drug calculation use a length-based tape (broselow or paediatric emergency tape) where available, or a formula: infants 0-12 months weight = (0.5 x age in months) + 4 kg; children 1-5 years weight = (2 x age) + 8 kg; children 6-12 years weight = (3 x age) + 7 kg. the older apls formula (age + 4) x 2 for ages 1-10 years remains widely quoted. fluid bolus 10 ml/kg crystalloid, glucose 2 ml/kg of 10% dextrose, adrenaline in arrest 10 micrograms/kg (0.1 ml/kg of 1 in 10,000), defibrillation 4 j/kg. cuffed tracheal tube internal diameter = (age/4) + 3.5. check calculations with a second person where possible; many errors arise from tenfold dosing mistakes. triage and resource-limited settings communication and teamwork allocate roles early (team leader, airway, circulation, drugs, scribe) and use closed-loop communication. involve parents, explain what is happening and allow them to stay if they wish. call for senior or anaesthetic help early; do not wait for deterioration. use track-and-trigger tools (pews) on wards. oxygen glucose 10% crystalloid bolus

paediatric basic & advanced life support emergencies & critical care cardiac arrest in children is usually secondary to hypoxia and shock, so paediatric basic life support starts with five rescue breaths and uses a 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio. advanced life support follows the shockable and non-shockable algorithms, with weight-based defibrillation (4 j/kg) and adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg every 3-5 minutes while reversible causes are sought and treated. paediatric arrests are mainly asphyxial; always start with 5 rescue breaths. compression:ventilation ratio is 15:2 for healthcare providers, 30:2 for lay rescuers. compress to one third of chest depth at 100-120/min. shockable rhythm dose: 4 j/kg biphasic. adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg (0.1 ml/kg of 1 in 10,000) every 3-5 minutes. amiodarone 5 mg/kg after the 3rd and 5th shocks. in bradycardia with poor perfusion, ventilate first; hypoxia is the commonest cause. intraosseous access should be used promptly if iv access is not obtained quickly. child not breathing normally - start rescue breaths immediately heart rate below 60/min with poor perfusion - start compressions shockable rhythm on monitor - defibrillate without delay prolonged pauses in compressions (over 10 seconds) cold-water drowning or hypothermia - continue resuscitation until rewarmed 4hs and 4ts hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyper/hypokalaemia (and metabolic), hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thromboembolism. infant choking 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts; child over 1 year: 5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts. epidemiology and why children arrest differently basic life support (infants and children) ensure safety, check responsiveness (shout and stimulate gently), shout for help. open the airway: head tilt and chin lift (neutral position in infants, slight extension in children). look, listen and feel for breathing for no more than 10 seconds. if not breathing normally, give 5 initial rescue breaths, each over about 1 second (infant: cover mouth and nose; child: pinch nose, seal mouth). check for signs of life or a pulse for up to 10 seconds (brachial in infants, carotid or femoral in children). if no signs of life or definite pulse, or heart rate below 60/min with poor perfusion, start chest compressions. compressions: lower half of sternum, depth at least one third of chest diameter (about 4 cm infant, 5 cm child), rate 100-120/min, allow full recoil. infants: two-thumb encircling technique (two rescuers) or two fingers (single rescuer). children: heel of one hand, or two hands for larger children. ratio 15 compressions to 2 breaths for trained healthcare providers with two or more rescuers (lay rescuers 30:2). if alone, perform 1 minute of cpr before leaving to call help, unless the collapse was witnessed and sudden (then call first and get an aed). use an aed as soon as available; paediatric pads or attenuated shock for ages 1-8 years, adult pads if none are available. infants under 1 year may also be defibrillated with an aed if a manual defibrillator is not available. choking and airway obstruction advanced life support non-shockable (asystole/pea): give adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg iv/io (0.1 ml/kg of 1 in 10,000) as soon as access is available, then every 3-5 minutes (alternate loops). continue 2-minute cpr cycles. shockable (vf/pulseless vt): give one shock of 4 j/kg (biphasic), resume cpr immediately for 2 minutes without a pulse check. after the 3rd shock give adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg and amiodarone 5 mg/kg; repeat adrenaline every 3-5 minutes, amiodarone again after the 5th shock. treat reversible causes throughout: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyper/hypokalaemia and metabolic disorders, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade (cardiac), toxins, thromboembolism. give a 10 ml/kg crystalloid bolus if hypovolaemia is suspected, and 2 ml/kg 10% glucose if hypoglycaemic. calcium is not given routinely. peri-arrest rhythms bradycardia with poor perfusion: ventilate with 100% oxygen first (hypoxia is the commonest cause). if heart rate stays below 60/min with poor perfusion, start compressions. give adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg; atropine 20 micrograms/kg (min 100 micrograms) for increased vagal tone or av block. supraventricular tachycardia with shock: synchronised cardioversion 1 j/kg (then 2 j/kg). without shock: vagal manoeuvres then adenosine 100 micrograms/kg rapid iv bolus (then 200, then 300 micrograms/kg). broad complex tachycardia without a pulse is treated as vf/pvt. post-resuscitation care and stopping return of spontaneous circulation: aim for spo2 94-98%, normocapnia, avoid hypotension, check glucose, treat seizures, avoid hyperthermia (targeted temperature management, 36-37.5 degrees celsius). find and treat the cause; arrange transfer to paediatric intensive care. debrief the team and support the family. duration: no firm rule; consider stopping after 20 minutes or more without rosc if no reversible cause, with a senior decision (except hypothermia, drowning in cold water, poisoning where prolonged efforts are justified). parental presence during cpr is supported. adrenaline (1 in 10,000) amiodarone atropine adenosine glucose 10%

shock & fluid resuscitation emergencies & critical care shock is acute circulatory failure in which oxygen delivery fails to meet tissue demand. in children it presents with tachycardia and poor perfusion long before hypotension, and the commonest causes worldwide are hypovolaemia (diarrhoea), sepsis, and anaphylaxis. early recognition, rapid access, careful fluid resuscitation and treatment of the cause save lives. compensated shock: tachycardia, poor perfusion, normal bp. hypotension is a late, pre-arrest sign. give boluses of 10 ml/kg and reassess after each; stop if overload develops. in suspected sepsis give antibiotics within 1 hour after cultures where possible. anaphylaxis: im adrenaline 1 in 1000 first, into the lateral thigh. avoid large fluid boluses in cardiogenic shock and febrile african children without hypotension (feast). cold shock needs adrenaline; warm shock needs noradrenaline. check glucose in every shocked child and treat hypoglycaemia with 2 ml/kg 10% glucose. intraosseous access is acceptable if iv access is not quickly achieved. heart rate rising then falling with worsening perfusion capillary refill over 3 seconds with altered consciousness hypotension in a child (pre-arrest) non-blanching rash with shock neonate with collapse in first weeks (consider duct-dependent cardiac lesion or sepsis) persistent shock after 40-60 ml/kg crystalloid sepsis six (paediatric adaptation) oxygen, iv/io access with cultures and bloods, antibiotics, fluids, lactate/glucose measurement, early senior involvement/vasoactives - within one hour. anaphylaxis adrenaline doses under 6 months 100-150 mcg, 6 months to 6 years 150 mcg, 6-12 years 300 mcg, over 12 years 500 mcg im, using the 1 mg/ml (1 in 1000) solution. definition and classification hypovolaemic: diarrhoea and vomiting, haemorrhage, burns, dka, third-space losses. distributive: sepsis (warm early, cold late), anaphylaxis, neurogenic (spinal injury). cardiogenic: congenital heart disease (duct-dependent lesions in neonates), myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia. obstructive: tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolus. clinical features tachycardia, tachypnoea, weak thready peripheral pulses with bounding pulses in warm shock. capillary refill over 2 seconds; cold, mottled, pale peripheries (warm vasodilated in early sepsis with flash capillary refill). reduced urine output (under 1 ml/kg/h), altered consciousness, irritability or lethargy. hypotension is a late finding. metabolic acidosis (deep sighing acidotic breathing) and raised lactate. features suggesting the cause: fever and non-blanching rash (meningococcal sepsis), urticaria and wheeze (anaphylaxis), hepatomegaly, murmur and gallop (cardiogenic), trauma, history of diarrhoea. initial management fluids: give 10 ml/kg boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride or balanced crystalloid over 5-10 minutes, reassessing after each bolus (hr, crt, bp, liver size, work of breathing). current uk sepsis guidance recommends 10 ml/kg boluses; larger 20 ml/kg boluses are used in some settings. stop fluids if signs of overload develop (hepatomegaly, crepitations, rising respiratory effort) or if cardiogenic shock is suspected. haemorrhage: control the bleeding source, give blood early (10-20 ml/kg), activate massive transfusion protocol, and avoid excessive crystalloid. refractory fluid shock after 40-60 ml/kg: involve paediatric intensive care, intubate if needed, start vasoactive infusions (adrenaline for cold shock, noradrenaline for warm shock) through a peripheral or io line initially, consider hydrocortisone in catecholamine-resistant shock. cardiogenic or duct-dependent shock: avoid large fluid boluses (5-10 ml/kg only), start prostaglandin e1 in neonates with suspected duct-dependent lesions, inotropes, urgent cardiology advice. anaphylaxis resource-limited settings and who approach monitoring and prognosis continuous ecg, spo2, frequent bp, urine output by catheter, serial lactate and glucose. complications: multi-organ failure, dic, ards, myocardial dysfunction, acute kidney injury. outcome depends on speed of recognition and treatment; mortality in septic shock rises with each hour of delay. crystalloid bolus adrenaline im (anaphylaxis) ceftriaxone adrenaline infusion

status epilepticus emergencies & critical care status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness between them. it is a medical emergency with risk of hypoxia, brain injury and death, so treatment follows a time-based protocol of abcde care, glucose check and escalating anticonvulsants while the cause is sought. treat any seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer; do not wait for 30 minutes. always check blood glucose and treat hypoglycaemia with 2 ml/kg 10% glucose. first line is lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg iv, or buccal midazolam / rectal diazepam if no access. give no more than two benzodiazepine doses before second-line therapy. second-line options: levetiracetam 40 mg/kg, phenytoin 20 mg/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg. neonatal seizures: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg is first-line. refractory status needs rsi with thiopental and picu care. consider meningitis/encephalitis and give antimicrobials early if febrile and unwell. seizure lasting over 5 minutes or not regaining consciousness between seizures hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia or other metabolic cause signs of cns infection (fever, neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, rash) head trauma or suspected non-accidental injury respiratory depression after benzodiazepines focal seizures or persisting focal deficit 5-20-40 rule treat at 5 minutes (benzodiazepine), 20 minutes (second-line anticonvulsant), 40 minutes (rsi and picu). reversible causes glucose, sodium, calcium, infection, trauma, drugs - check them in every child in status. definition and epidemiology aetiology febrile status (commonest in under 5 years), including complex febrile seizures. acute cns infection: meningitis, encephalitis (hsv), cerebral malaria in endemic areas, neurocysticercosis. metabolic: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, inborn errors of metabolism, pyridoxine dependency in infants. structural/trauma: intracranial haemorrhage, abusive head trauma, tumour, stroke. known epilepsy with missed or sub-therapeutic anticonvulsants, drug withdrawal, or intoxication (tricyclics, theophylline, isoniazid). genetic epilepsy syndromes (dravet syndrome) and autoimmune encephalitis. initial assessment airway with oxygen at 10-15 l/min, protect the airway, position safely, suction if needed; support breathing (benzodiazepines cause respiratory depression). check blood glucose immediately; if below 3 mmol/l, give 2 ml/kg 10% glucose iv. gain iv or io access, take bloods (glucose, u&e, calcium, magnesium, blood gas, fbc, culture, anticonvulsant levels, toxicology) and give antibiotics and aciclovir if cns infection is suspected. monitor ecg, spo2, blood pressure and temperature; note time of seizure onset and each drug given. stepwise anticonvulsant management first line (5 minutes): lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg iv/io (max 4 mg) over 30-60 seconds, or if no access buccal midazolam (6 months-1 year 2.5 mg, 1-4 years 5 mg, 5-9 years 7.5 mg, 10 years and over 10 mg), or rectal diazepam 0.5 mg/kg (max 10 mg). repeat the benzodiazepine once after 5-10 minutes if the seizure persists; do not give more than two doses (risk of respiratory depression). second line (about 20 minutes): levetiracetam 40 mg/kg iv over 5-10 minutes (max 3 g), or phenytoin 20 mg/kg iv over 20 minutes with ecg monitoring (max 2 g), or sodium valproate 40 mg/kg iv (avoid in suspected mitochondrial disease, liver disease or under 2 years if metabolic disorder is possible). the esett trial found levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate equally effective. third line (about 40 minutes, refractory status): senior and paediatric intensive care involvement, rapid sequence induction with thiopental 4 mg/kg iv (or propofol/midazolam infusions), intubation, ventilation and eeg monitoring. neonates: phenobarbital 20 mg/kg iv is first line; consider pyridoxine and exclude hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, infection and hie. investigations and further care bloods as above; lumbar puncture only when the child is stable and no raised icp contraindication. ct head if trauma, focal signs, persisting abnormal consciousness or suspected raised icp; mri and eeg afterwards for unexplained or recurrent status. further tests for infants: ammonia, lactate, urine organic acids and metabolic screen as indicated. observe for post-ictal todd paralysis (resolves within 24-48 hours) and nonconvulsive status if consciousness fails to recover. complications and prognosis hypoxia, aspiration, hypoglycaemia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, raised icp and cerebral oedema, cardiovascular instability. neurological sequelae and later epilepsy depend more on the underlying cause than the duration. parents of children with prolonged febrile or epileptic seizures need a rescue medication plan (buccal midazolam) and training. lorazepam midazolam buccal diazepam rectal levetiracetam phenytoin phenobarbital

head injury & raised intracranial pressure emergencies & critical care head injury is a leading cause of death and disability in children, mostly from falls and road traffic collisions, with abusive head trauma in infants. management aims to prevent secondary brain injury through abcde care, correct triage for ct scanning, and treatment of raised intracranial pressure when present. prevent secondary brain injury: avoid hypoxia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyperthermia. use the paediatric gcs; gcs 8 or below needs a secured airway. cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration) is a late sign of raised icp. ct head is indicated within 1 hour for high-risk features such as gcs under 14, focal deficit or suspected skull fracture. suspect non-accidental injury in any infant with head injury and an inconsistent history. initial hyperosmolar therapy: 3% saline 2-5 ml/kg or mannitol 0.25-0.5 g/kg. position head up 30 degrees, midline, avoid venous obstruction. target paco2 4.5-5 kpa; avoid prolonged hyperventilation. gcs falling by 2 or more points or 8 or below unequal or fixed dilated pupil bradycardia with hypertension and irregular respiration seizures after head injury, vomiting that persists, tense fontanelle csf leak, depressed skull fracture, penetrating injury infant with head injury and inconsistent history cushing triad hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration - late sign of raised icp. raised icp symptoms in older children morning headache, vomiting, drowsiness, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy; infants: bulging fontanelle, sunsetting eyes. definition and epidemiology pathophysiology of raised icp assessment primary survey with cervical spine immobilisation if there is a significant mechanism or neck pain/tenderness, altered consciousness or focal deficit. glasgow coma scale adapted for age: eye opening, best verbal (child: orientated, confused, inappropriate words, incomprehensible sounds, none; infant version for pre-verbal children), best motor. gcs 13-15 is mild, 9-12 moderate, 8 or below severe (needs a definitive airway). pupils, focal deficit, scalp haematoma (infant boggy swelling), fontanelle tension, signs of basal skull fracture (panda eyes, battle sign, csf rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea, haemotympanum). cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) is a late sign of impending herniation; in infants may present with apnoea and bradycardia. always search for other injuries, check glucose and consider non-accidental injury. imaging criteria (nice-based) management airway and breathing: high-flow oxygen; intubate if gcs 8 or below, falling gcs of 2 or more, loss of protective reflexes, seizures not controlled, or inability to maintain oxygenation. use rapid sequence induction with in-line cervical stabilisation. target paco2 4.5-5.0 kpa and spo2 above 94%; brief hyperventilation only as a rescue for herniation. circulation: treat hypotension aggressively with isotonic fluids and blood if needed; hypotension doubles mortality. raised icp measures: head up 30 degrees with neck in midline, avoid tight cervical collars or tapes, adequate analgesia and sedation, treat fever and seizures, maintain normoglycaemia and normothermia, keep serum sodium 140-150 mmol/l. hyperosmolar therapy: 3% hypertonic saline 2-5 ml/kg over 10-20 minutes (preferred in children) or mannitol 0.25-0.5 g/kg iv over 20 minutes (watch for hypotension and diuresis). dexamethasone is not used for traumatic brain injury. neurosurgical referral for expanding haematomas, depressed fractures and refractory raised icp (evd, decompressive craniectomy). seizure prophylaxis is considered in severe injury. mild injury: observe, give written head injury advice, avoid return to sport until symptom-free, and consider concussion rest and graded return. abusive head trauma and complications suspect when there is a history inconsistent with the injury or no history, subdural haematomas, retinal haemorrhages, rib or metaphyseal fractures, apnoea or seizures in an infant. perform skeletal survey, ophthalmology review and refer to child protection. complications: post-traumatic seizures, post-concussive syndrome, hydrocephalus, csf leak and meningitis, cognitive and behavioural sequelae, growing skull fracture. 3% hypertonic saline mannitol 20% levetiracetam

poisoning & overdose emergencies & critical care accidental poisoning is common in toddlers, while deliberate self-poisoning predominates in adolescents. assessment is by abcde, history of agent, dose and time, and use of poisons information services (toxbase, national poisons information service). few agents have specific antidotes, so supportive care is the mainstay, with decontamination and antidotes used selectively. do not induce vomiting; activated charcoal 1 g/kg is only for adsorbable toxins within 1 hour with a protected airway. paracetamol: level at 4 hours; nac 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. iron is poorly adsorbed by charcoal; use desferrioxamine for symptomatic poisoning. opioid toxidrome: pinpoint pupils, bradypnoea, coma; give naloxone. tricyclic poisoning: qrs widening -> sodium bicarbonate; avoid flumazenil. carbon monoxide: spo2 is unreliable; treat with high-flow oxygen. oesophageal button battery is an emergency requiring endoscopic removal within hours. always consider intentional self-harm and non-accidental poisoning. reduced consciousness, seizures or airway compromise cardiac arrhythmia or qrs widening on ecg delayed presentation of paracetamol or iron toxicity (hepatic failure) button battery or magnets ingestion unknown ingestion in an adolescent with possible self-harm poisoning in an infant (non-accidental) one tablet can kill (toddlers) calcium channel blockers, sulfonylureas, tricyclics, opioids, clonidine, quinine, camphor, chloroquine, iron-containing tablets. toxidromes opioid: pinpoint pupils; anticholinergic: hot, dry, dilated pupils; cholinergic (sludge): salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation, gi upset, emesis; sympathomimetic: tachycardia, hyperthermia, dilated pupils. epidemiology and approach general management abcde: secure the airway, give oxygen and treat shock; check glucose and ecg; monitor temperature. seizures: benzodiazepines (not phenytoin for toxic seizures). hypoglycaemia: 2 ml/kg 10% glucose. gastric decontamination: do not induce vomiting (salt water, ipecac are dangerous) and gastric lavage is rarely indicated. activated charcoal 1 g/kg (max 50 g) is given within 1 hour of ingestion of a significant dose of a toxin that adsorbs (paracetamol, salicylates, tricyclics, carbamazepine, theophylline) provided the airway is protected. it does not adsorb iron, lithium, alcohols, acids, alkalis or hydrocarbons. enhanced elimination: urinary alkalinisation for salicylates, haemodialysis for severe lithium, salicylate, methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning. do not give flumazenil routinely (risk of seizures in mixed overdoses). specific poisons paracetamol: hepatotoxicity from napqi depletion of glutathione. concern with a single ingestion over 150 mg/kg (or 75 mg/kg in at-risk groups). take a serum level at 4 hours or later and plot on the nomogram (uk single treatment line: 100 mg/l at 4 hours); give n-acetylcysteine (nac) 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. nac is started immediately for staggered or unknown-time ingestions or if the 4-hour level is unavailable. check lfts, inr and creatinine; refer early to a liver unit if inr rises or encephalopathy appears. iron: toxic above 20 mg/kg elemental iron with vomiting, haematemesis, shock, hepatic failure and later gastric scarring. abdominal x-ray shows tablets; serum iron at 4-6 hours. treat with iv desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/hour if symptomatic or high levels. salicylates: tinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis, hyperthermia. treat with fluids, urinary alkalinisation with iv sodium bicarbonate, glucose, and haemodialysis if severe. opioids (including methadone, codeine, tramadol): pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, coma. naloxone 10 micrograms/kg iv, increasing up to 100 micrograms/kg, repeated or given by infusion as its half-life is shorter than most opioids. tricyclic antidepressants: anticholinergic features, seizures, qrs widening, arrhythmia. treat with iv sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg for qrs over 100 ms, and benzodiazepines for seizures. organophosphates: cholinergic crisis (miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, salivation, fasciculations). give atropine 20-50 micrograms/kg iv repeatedly and consider pralidoxime. carbon monoxide: headache, vomiting, coma; spo2 may be falsely normal. give 100% oxygen via reservoir mask and consider hyperbaric oxygen in severe cases. button batteries: if lodged in the oesophagus, they cause burns within 2 hours and are a surgical emergency (remove endoscopically). for children over 12 months who are alert and have ingested a battery within 12 hours, give 10 ml honey every 10 minutes (up to 6 doses) while awaiting removal. corrosives and hydrocarbons: avoid emesis and charcoal; give small sips of water, observe airway, and monitor for aspiration pneumonitis. others: calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, sulfonylureas (delayed hypoglycaemia), clonidine, and single-tablet toxins in toddlers - always check toxbase. disposition and prevention observe for the expected time course (for example 6-8 hours for most, longer for modified-release preparations). psychiatric assessment for deliberate self-harm; safeguarding review for toddlers and unusual patterns. prevention: child-resistant containers, locked storage, blister packs, education. activated charcoal n-acetylcysteine (paracetamol) naloxone desferrioxamine sodium bicarbonate

burns, drowning & environmental emergencies emergencies & critical care burns, drowning and temperature-related illness are major causes of injury and death in children, and are often preventable. management centres on airway and breathing (inhalation injury and hypoxia), fluid resuscitation in larger burns, rewarming or cooling as appropriate, and recognising non-accidental injury. cool burns with running water for 20 minutes within 3 hours of injury. a child's palm including fingers is about 1% of tbsa. fluid resuscitate burns over 10% tbsa; parkland 4 ml x kg x %tbsa with half in the first 8 hours. airway at risk with facial burns, soot, hoarseness - intubate early. drowning is a hypoxic arrest: start with 5 rescue breaths. observe symptomatic drowning survivors for at least 6-8 hours. heatstroke: core temperature over 40 degrees celsius with cns dysfunction; cool rapidly. consider nai in every burn in an infant. burns of face, neck, airway or enclosed space smoke exposure circumferential limb or chest burns burn over 10% tbsa or shock burns inconsistent with history or in non-mobile infants submersion with persistent hypoxia or reduced consciousness core temperature below 32 degrees celsius or above 40 degrees celsius lund and browder / palm rule palm plus fingers of the patient = about 1% tbsa; use for small or scattered burns. burn first aid '20-20-3' cool for 20 minutes with running water within 3 hours. burns - epidemiology and assessment first aid and initial management stop the burning process and remove clothing and jewellery (not adherent material). cool with running tap water at 8-25 degrees celsius for 20 minutes, within 3 hours of injury; do not use ice, and avoid hypothermia in young children. cover with cling film (not circumferentially) or a non-adherent dressing; give adequate analgesia early (intranasal fentanyl, oral paracetamol/ibuprofen, opioid iv for major burns). abcde: airway at risk if facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in mouth or sputum, hoarse voice, stridor or enclosed space fire - early intubation is safer than waiting for oedema. give high-flow oxygen for suspected carbon monoxide or cyanide exposure (smoke inhalation). circulation: gain iv access (through unburned skin if possible). fluid resuscitation is needed for burns over 10% tbsa in children (over 15% in adults). parkland formula: 4 ml x weight (kg) x %tbsa of hartmann solution over 24 hours from time of injury, giving half in the first 8 hours, plus maintenance fluid for children. titrate to urine output of 1 ml/kg/hour (0.5 ml/kg/hour in adults) and clinical state; include hypoglycaemia monitoring in small children. tetanus status, analgesia, nasogastric feeding, temperature control. circumferential full-thickness burns of limb or chest need escharotomy. referral criteria burns over 2% tbsa in a child, or any burn involving face, hands, feet, perineum, genitalia, major joints; full-thickness burns of any size. circumferential burns, chemical or electrical burns, inhalation injury, suspected nai or other injuries. infants, very young children or those with comorbidity. drowning environmental emergencies hypothermia (core temperature below 35 degrees celsius): shivering, confusion, bradycardia, osborn j waves, vf. handle gently, remove wet clothes, passive then active external rewarming, warm iv fluids, extracorporeal rewarming in arrest. 'not dead until warm and dead'. heat exhaustion versus heatstroke: heatstroke is core temperature over 40 degrees celsius with cns dysfunction. cool rapidly with evaporative cooling and cold water immersion, fluids, treat complications (rhabdomyolysis, dic, renal failure). never leave a child in a parked car. antipyretics are ineffective. electrical injury: low-voltage household shocks may cause arrhythmia; ecg and observation if loss of consciousness or abnormal ecg; high voltage causes deep tissue injury and rhabdomyolysis. snake bite and envenomation: immobilise limb, keep calm, use antivenom according to local protocol; avoid tourniquets and cutting. anaphylaxis from stings and bites: see shock. prevention burns: lower water heater temperature to 48 degrees celsius or below, hot drink safety, smoke alarms, guards on fires. drowning: constant adult supervision of infants in baths, pool fencing, lifejackets, swimming lessons. safeguarding review for every burn in a pre-mobile child. hartmann solution (parkland) intranasal fentanyl paracetamol

fluid, electrolyte & acid-base disorders emergencies & critical care understanding maintenance fluid requirements, dehydration assessment and common electrolyte and acid-base disorders is essential for safe paediatric prescribing. most dehydration is managed with oral rehydration; intravenous fluids must be isotonic and monitored carefully to avoid hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema. holliday-segar: 100/50/20 ml/kg/day (4-2-1 ml/kg/hour). use isotonic maintenance fluids in unwell children to avoid hyponatraemia. who plan b: ors 75 ml/kg over 4 hours; plan c: 100 ml/kg ringer lactate. correct hypernatraemia no faster than 10-12 mmol/l per 24 hours. symptomatic hyponatraemia: 3% saline 2 ml/kg over 10-15 minutes. hyperkalaemia with ecg changes: iv calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 ml/kg. anion gap = na - (cl + hco3); high gap implies dka, lactate, toxins or uraemia. pyloric stenosis gives hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. seizures or reduced consciousness with abnormal sodium hyperkalaemia with ecg changes severe dehydration with shock sodium falling or rising too fast during treatment persistent metabolic acidosis with unclear cause hypovolaemic hyponatraemia with hyperpigmentation or ambiguous genitalia (salt-losing cah) 4-2-1 rule maintenance per hour: 4 ml/kg for first 10 kg, 2 ml/kg for next 10 kg, 1 ml/kg for each kg after 20 kg. mudpiles high anion gap acidosis causes: methanol, uraemia, dka, paraldehyde/propylene glycol, isoniazid/iron, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates. maintenance fluids dehydration mild (3-5%): thirsty, dry mouth, normal vital signs. moderate (5-10%): sunken eyes and fontanelle, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, dry mucosae, reduced urine. severe (over 10%): lethargy, cool mottled peripheries, prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension, deep acidotic breathing. who plan a (no dehydration): increase fluids, continue feeding, zinc 10-20 mg daily for 10-14 days, return if worse. who plan b (some dehydration): ors 75 ml/kg over 4 hours, reassess; give extra ors for ongoing stool losses. who plan c (severe dehydration): iv ringer lactate 100 ml/kg - infants under 12 months: 30 ml/kg in 1 hour then 70 ml/kg over 5 hours; older children 30 ml/kg in 30 minutes then 70 ml/kg over 2.5 hours; reassess hourly, switch to ors when able to drink. in high-income settings: ors first-line (low osmolarity); ng ors if refusing; iv 10 ml/kg boluses of isotonic fluid for shock, followed by deficit replacement over 24 hours with maintenance. avoid antidiarrhoeals. hypernatraemic dehydration is slower to correct (over 48 hours) because of cerebral oedema risk. sodium disorders hyponatraemia (below 135 mmol/l): classify by volume status. hypovolaemic (gi loss, salt-wasting, adrenal insufficiency), euvolaemic (siadh, hypotonic fluid), hypervolaemic (nephrotic syndrome, heart failure). symptomatic (seizures, coma): give 3% saline 2 ml/kg over 10-15 minutes (can repeat once or twice) to raise sodium to 125-130 mmol/l, but no faster than 10 mmol/l per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination. asymptomatic hyponatraemia: treat cause, fluid restrict in siadh, replace deficits. hypernatraemia (above 145 mmol/l): usually dehydration (high-sodium feeds, breast-milk insufficiency in neonates), diabetes insipidus, or sodium load. rehydrate with isotonic fluid and reduce sodium by no more than 10-12 mmol/l per 24 hours (0.5 mmol/l per hour). seizures from cerebral oedema occur if correction is too fast. potassium disorders hyperkalaemia (over 6.0 mmol/l): causes include renal failure, haemolysed samples, dka, adrenal crises, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis. ecg: peaked t waves, wide qrs, loss of p waves, sine wave. treatment: calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 ml/kg iv over 5-10 minutes (max 20 ml) for cardioprotection, salbutamol nebuliser 2.5-5 mg, insulin with glucose infusion, sodium bicarbonate if acidotic, resonium or dialysis for refractory cases. hypokalaemia (below 3.5 mmol/l): vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, dka treatment, renal tubular disorders, pyloric stenosis. ecg: flat t waves, u waves. replace orally if possible; iv potassium at no more than 0.2 mmol/kg/hour with monitoring (central line for higher concentrations). acid-base disorders prescribing safely check u&e and glucose before and at least daily on iv fluids; recalculate weight-based volumes and subtract oral or enteral intake. fluid restrict to two-thirds maintenance in siadh and raised icp in some contexts, and use boluses of 10 ml/kg for shock. in dka avoid large boluses and rapid correction due to cerebral oedema risk. use paediatric protocols and a fluid balance chart; reassess regularly. 3% sodium chloride calcium gluconate 10% salbutamol nebulised oral rehydration solution zinc

pain, sedation & palliative care emergencies & critical care children experience pain as intensely as adults but it is frequently under-recognised and under-treated. good practice combines age-appropriate pain assessment, multimodal analgesia, procedural sedation with safe monitoring, and a holistic palliative care approach for children with life-limiting conditions. assess pain with an age-appropriate tool and reassess after every intervention. use multimodal analgesia: paracetamol, nsaid, opioid, local anaesthesia and non-drug methods. codeine and tramadol should be avoided in under 12 years; use morphine for moderate-to-severe pain. safe maximum plain lidocaine dose is 3 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with adrenaline). procedural sedation requires trained staff, continuous monitoring and rescue skills. palliative care starts at diagnosis of a life-limiting illness and is not just end-of-life care. naloxone must be available whenever opioids are given. always involve the child and family in decisions. oversedation with respiratory depression after opioids or sedatives local anaesthetic toxicity (perioral numbness, seizures, arrhythmia) unrecognised pain in non-verbal or cognitively impaired children nsaid use in dehydration or renal impairment ketamine or sedation without airway-skilled staff flacc face, legs, activity, cry, consolability - each scored 0-2, total 0-10. who analgesic principles by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, by the child. pain assessment analgesic principles use the who analgesic ladder: step 1 non-opioid (paracetamol, ibuprofen), step 2 weak opioid (the use of codeine is not recommended in under 12 years because of ultra-rapid cyp2d6 metabolism), step 3 strong opioid (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone). give by mouth where possible, by the clock, and by the child (individualise). multimodal: combine paracetamol, nsaids, opioids, regional blocks and non-drug methods (distraction, play, sucrose in neonates, kangaroo care, breast-feeding, play specialists). paracetamol 15 mg/kg po every 4-6 hours (max 4 doses/24 hours; neonates lower). ibuprofen 5-10 mg/kg po every 6-8 hours (over 3 months old; avoid in dehydration, renal impairment, uncontrolled asthma, varicella). never give aspirin under 16 years except kawasaki disease. opioids: morphine oral 200-300 micrograms/kg every 4 hours;
