iv 100 micrograms/kg bolus titrated; infusions or pca in older children. intranasal diamorphine 0.1 mg/kg or fentanyl 1.5 micrograms/kg for rapid analgesia in fractures and burns. monitor sedation, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation; have naloxone (10 micrograms/kg) available; prescribe laxatives; antiemetics and antipruritics as needed. neuropathic pain: gabapentin, amitriptyline; refer to a specialist pain team. local and regional anaesthesia topical agents (lidocaine/prilocaine cream, amethocaine gel, lat gel) for cannulation and venepuncture; ethyl chloride spray as an alternative. maximum safe doses: plain lidocaine 3 mg/kg; with adrenaline 7 mg/kg (1% = 10 mg/ml); bupivacaine 2 mg/kg (plain), 0.25% = 2.5 mg/ml. reduce doses in neonates and give slowly with aspiration. lipid emulsion (intralipid 20%) 1.5 ml/kg bolus is the treatment for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. regional blocks (caudal, femoral, ilioinguinal) reduce opioid requirements after surgery. procedural sedation agents: nitrous oxide 50% (entonox) for older, cooperative children; intranasal midazolam 0.2-0.3 mg/kg or dexmedetomidine 2-3 micrograms/kg; oral midazolam 0.5 mg/kg; ketamine 1-2 mg/kg iv (dissociative sedation for painful procedures, avoid in raised icp, psychosis, under 3 months); propofol and fentanyl by anaesthetists or trained emergency physicians. chloral hydrate 50 mg/kg oral is used for imaging in infants in some centres. document pre-sedation assessment, consent, drug doses, monitoring and recovery criteria. discharge only when fully awake with a responsible adult. palliative care symptom control: pain (morphine), dyspnoea (opioids, fan, oxygen if hypoxic), seizures (midazolam buccal/subcutaneous), secretions (hyoscine butylbromide or glycopyrronium), nausea, constipation, agitation. subcutaneous syringe drivers can deliver drugs when oral route fails. advance care planning with the family and young person: place of care, resuscitation status (respect or dnacpr decisions), emergency health care plans, organ donation discussion. hospice and community team involvement, respite, siblings and bereavement support; honest, compassionate communication; best interests and the child's own voice. paracetamol ibuprofen morphine oral morphine iv intranasal fentanyl ketamine (sedation)

h: autism spectrum disorder child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics autism spectrum disorder (asd) is a neurodevelopmental condition defined by persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction, together with restricted, repetitive behaviours, interests or sensory responses, present from early childhood. prevalence is about 1 in 100 children with a male predominance of roughly 3-4:1. early recognition and tailored support improve communication, learning and quality of life. core features: social communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviours loss of previously acquired language is a red flag requiring urgent assessment no evidence links the mmr vaccine to autism ados-2 and adi-r are standard diagnostic tools; m-chat screens toddlers always test hearing in a child with speech delay or suspected autism genetic conditions linked to asd include fragile x, tuberous sclerosis and rett syndrome early behavioural and communication interventions improve outcomes comorbidities (adhd, epilepsy, anxiety, sleep problems) are common and treatable girls are under-recognised because they may mask difficulties regression of language or social skills no babble by 12 months, no words by 16 months, no two-word phrases by 24 months no response to name, no pointing or gestures seizures or dysmorphic features suggesting an underlying syndrome self-injury, aggression or severe distress needing urgent support autism core domains social communication deficits plus restricted and repetitive behaviours - the diagnostic dyad definition and epidemiology aetiology clinical features by age infancy and toddler: reduced eye contact, no response to name by 12 months, absent social smile, lack of pointing or showing, absent joint attention, delayed or absent babble and speech, no gestures such as waving. preschool: language delay or regression (loss of previously acquired words is a red flag), echolalia, reduced pretend play, lining up toys, insistence on sameness, distress with change, preference for solitary play. school age: difficulty making friends, literal understanding, poor reading of social cues, special interests, restricted routines, sensory sensitivities (noise, textures), emotional dysregulation, meltdowns. motor stereotypies (hand flapping, toe walking, rocking), unusual food selectivity and sleep disturbance are common. assessment and diagnosis developmental and behavioural history from parents, school and nursery reports; observe the child in play and interaction. multidisciplinary assessment (paediatrician, speech and language therapist, psychologist, occupational therapist) using standardised tools such as ados-2 (observation), adi-r or 3di (interview) and cognitive assessment. screening tools include m-chat-r/f at 16-30 months. hearing test (audiology) is essential to exclude hearing loss; vision check. medical work-up guided by findings: examine for dysmorphism, neurocutaneous stigmata (wood lamp for tuberous sclerosis), head circumference. genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, fragile x testing) when there is intellectual disability, dysmorphism or relevant history; eeg if seizures or regression; thyroid, lead and metabolic tests only if indicated. differential diagnosis: hearing impairment, global developmental delay, specific language impairment, adhd, social (pragmatic) communication disorder, selective mutism, attachment disorders, rett syndrome and landau-kleffner syndrome in regression. management there is no cure; aim to maximise function and wellbeing. early intervention (naturalistic developmental behavioural interventions, parent-mediated social communication therapy such as pact) improves social communication. educational support: specialist teaching, ehcp (uk) or individual education plan, visual timetables, structured environment, social skills groups. speech and language therapy, occupational therapy for sensory issues, behavioural strategies for challenging behaviour, sleep hygiene and melatonin for persistent insomnia. treat co-occurring conditions: adhd, anxiety, epilepsy, constipation, sleep disorders, intellectual disability. medication (risperidone or aripiprazole) is reserved for severe irritability/aggression under specialist care; no drug treats core symptoms. support families: parent training, peer support and respite; screen for mental health problems in the child and parents. avoid unproven treatments (gluten-free casein-free diet, chelation, hyperbaric oxygen, secretin). prognosis melatonin risperidone

u: Child Mental Health, Behaviour & Social Paediatrics
h: adhd & conduct problems child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics adhd is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that are inappropriate for developmental level and impair function in more than one setting. it affects about 5 percent of children and often persists into adulthood. conduct problems (oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder) frequently co-occur and are managed with parent training. adhd requires symptoms in two or more settings with onset before age 12 three core domains: inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity parent training is first-line for preschool children and for conduct problems methylphenidate is first-line drug for school-aged children with moderate to severe adhd monitor height, weight, pulse and blood pressure on stimulants atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options comorbidity (odd, anxiety, autism, learning difficulties) is the rule rather than the exception untreated adhd increases risk of accidents, school failure and substance misuse symptoms only in one setting - consider other causes new onset after a change in circumstances suggesting abuse or trauma syncope, palpitations or family history of sudden cardiac death before starting stimulants suicidal ideation, psychosis or marked mood change on treatment severe aggression, fire-setting or cruelty to animals adhd triad inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity - needing two or more settings and onset under 12 definition and epidemiology aetiology clinical features inattention: careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention, appears not to listen, fails to finish tasks, disorganised, loses things, easily distracted, forgetful. hyperactivity: fidgeting, leaving seat, running or climbing excessively, difficulty playing quietly, always on the go, talks excessively. impulsivity: blurts out answers, difficulty waiting turn, interrupts others, risk-taking and accidents. consequences: academic underachievement, peer rejection, low self-esteem, family conflict, injuries and later substance misuse. assessment full developmental, medical, psychosocial and family history; school reports; structured questionnaires (conners, sdq, vanderbilt) completed by parents and teachers. observation and mental state examination; look for comorbidity: oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, tic disorders, autism, specific learning difficulties, language disorder, sleep disorders and epilepsy. exclude alternative causes: hearing or vision problems, sleep apnoea, hyperthyroidism, lead exposure, child abuse or adverse environment, absence seizures, medication effects (e.g. salbutamol, anticonvulsants). baseline cardiovascular examination (heart rate, blood pressure), height, weight and family history of cardiac disease or sudden death before starting stimulants. management parent training and education programmes for all families; classroom adjustments and school liaison. under 5 years: first-line parent training, no medication. school-aged children and young people with moderate to severe impairment: pharmacological treatment alongside psychological support. first line is methylphenidate (short or long acting); second line lisdexamfetamine; atomoxetine or guanfacine (non-stimulants) if stimulants are ineffective, not tolerated or contraindicated. monitor height, weight, heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, appetite, mood and tics; plan drug holidays only if needed; review regularly. side effects of stimulants: appetite suppression, weight loss and growth slowing, insomnia, abdominal pain, headache, irritability, tics and rare psychosis; use with caution in cardiac disease. dietary restriction is not recommended; omega-3 supplements are not recommended routinely. conduct problems methylphenidate atomoxetine

h: child abuse, neglect & safeguarding child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics child abuse and neglect cover physical, sexual and emotional abuse, neglect and fabricated or induced illness. every clinician has a duty to recognise, document and report concerns, working within multi-agency safeguarding systems. the child's welfare is paramount, and a clinician does not need certainty to refer. neglect is the commonest form of child maltreatment registered in the uk bruising in a non-mobile baby is abuse until proven otherwise posterior rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions are highly specific for abuse skeletal survey is indicated in suspected abuse under 2 years of age abusive head trauma presents with subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy never promise confidentiality to a child disclosing abuse delay in presentation and inconsistent history are red flags a clinician does not need proof to refer - concern alone is enough look for risk factors: domestic violence, parental mental illness and substance misuse any injury in a non-mobile infant bruising to ears, neck, buttocks, genitals or in a patterned shape infant with unexplained apnoea, seizures, vomiting or encephalopathy a history that does not fit the injury or the child's developmental stage disclosure of abuse by the child delay in seeking care for injuries ten-4-facesp bruising clinical decision rule: bruising to the torso, ear or neck in a child under 4 years, or any bruise in an infant under 4 months (ten-4), or bruising of the frenulum, angle of jaw, cheek, eyelid, subconjunctivae or patterned bruising at any age (facesp) definitions and epidemiology physical abuse - suspicious features bruising: bruising in a non-mobile infant ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise'), bruises on the ears, neck, face, torso, buttocks, genitalia or upper arms; multiple bruises, patterned bruises (hand, belt, ligature, bite), clusters, petechiae in non-accidental distribution. fractures: rib fractures (especially posterior), classic metaphyseal lesions (corner or bucket handle), multiple fractures of different ages, skull fractures (complex, bilateral), spiral fractures of long bones in non-walking children, scapula, sternum and spinous process fractures. burns and scalds: immersion (stocking and glove pattern, sparing flexure creases), cigarette burns (round 8 mm), contact burns of defined shape. head injury: abusive head trauma (shaken baby) with subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy, often with rib fractures; lethargy, vomiting, irritability, seizures in infants. other: torn frenulum, intra-oral injuries, abdominal trauma (duodenal haematoma, bowel perforation), unexplained poisoning. features of concern in the history: delay in seeking help, changing or inconsistent explanation, history not compatible with injury or developmental stage, injury attributed to a sibling, repeated attendance, parental indifference. investigations skeletal survey for all suspected physical abuse under 2 years (repeat at 11-14 days), selected older children; bone scan or ct if needed. neuroimaging (ct head or mri) for any infant with suspected abusive head trauma, with ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages. bloods: fbc, clotting, von willebrand screen, bone profile, vitamin d, calcium, phosphate and alp to exclude bleeding or bone disorders; consider osteogenesis imperfecta. photographs and body maps, careful contemporaneous documentation using the child's own words, and forensic samples where indicated. sexual abuse, neglect and emotional abuse sexual abuse: disclosure, sexualised behaviour inappropriate for age, genital or anal injury, recurrent uti, stis, enuresis or encopresis, self-harm, eating disorders, sleep disturbance, school problems; examination is performed by trained paediatricians with forensic support. absence of physical findings does not exclude abuse. neglect: failure to thrive, poor hygiene, untreated medical conditions, missed appointments and immunisations, inadequate supervision, repeated accidents, developmental delay and poor school attendance. emotional abuse: persistent emotional ill-treatment affecting development, withdrawn or aggressive behaviour, low self-esteem, attachment difficulties. fabricated or induced illness: unusual or inconsistent illness without objective findings, multiple opinions, carer seeking excessive investigation; refer to child protection early. safeguarding response child's safety first: treat injuries, admit if needed for safety, and do not confront parents in a way that endangers the child. responding to disclosure: listen, stay calm, do not ask leading questions, do not promise confidentiality, record verbatim, and refer to children's social care and police. share information with senior paediatrician, named doctor for safeguarding and children's social care; strategy discussion, child protection medical, child protection conference and plan, care proceedings if required. legal frameworks (uk): children act 1989 (significant harm, section 47 enquiries, emergency protection orders, police protection), children act 2004; each country has analogues. document thoroughly; consider siblings and other children in the household who may also be at risk.

h: adolescent mental health, eating disorders & self-harm child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics half of all adult mental illness begins before age 14 and three-quarters by 24. depression, anxiety, self-harm and eating disorders are common in adolescence and carry significant morbidity and mortality. paediatricians should recognise these conditions, assess risk and refer early to child and adolescent mental health services (camhs). use headss to structure the adolescent psychosocial history fluoxetine is the ssri of choice for adolescent depression, with therapy all self-poisoning must be taken seriously; paracetamol overdose needs nac treatment family-based therapy is first-line for adolescent anorexia nervosa refeeding syndrome causes hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia bradycardia and hypokalaemia are key medical risks in eating disorders suicide is a leading cause of death in adolescents confidentiality has limits when there is risk of serious harm suicidal ideation with plan, intent or means heart rate under 40-50 bpm, hypotension, syncope or ecg changes in anorexia electrolyte abnormalities especially hypokalaemia or hypophosphataemia self-harm with escalating severity or overdose disclosure of abuse, exploitation or severe bullying headss home, education/employment, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide/depression - the adolescent psychosocial assessment assessment of the adolescent depression and anxiety depression: low or irritable mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite change, fatigue, poor concentration, worthlessness, suicidal thoughts for at least 2 weeks; often presents with somatic complaints or school refusal. mild depression: watchful waiting, supportive therapy; moderate to severe: cbt or interpersonal therapy; fluoxetine (ssri) with psychological therapy for moderate to severe depression in 12-18 year-olds, under specialist supervision with monitoring for suicidality. anxiety disorders (generalised anxiety, social anxiety, separation anxiety, panic, phobias, ocd): cbt is first-line; ssris for severe or non-responding cases. school refusal: look for anxiety, depression, bullying and learning problems; early return to school with support. self-harm and suicide self-harm includes cutting, burning, overdose and self-poisoning; most is non-suicidal self-injury used to cope with distress, but it increases later suicide risk. paracetamol overdose requires medical treatment with n-acetylcysteine regardless of stated intent; always take overdose seriously. psychosocial assessment before discharge covering intent, planning, precautions against discovery, mental state, protective factors, family support and access to means; safeguarding review for under-16s. risk factors: previous self-harm, depression, substance misuse, abuse, bullying, lgbt+ identity, family conflict, access to means, family history of suicide. suicide is a leading cause of death in adolescents. management: safety planning, restrict means, therapy (dbt-a, cbt), follow-up and camhs referral. eating disorders eating disorders - complications and management examination: bmi or % median bmi, pulse (bradycardia under 50 by day), postural hypotension, cold peripheries, lanugo hair, dental erosion and russell sign in bulimia, parotid swelling and hypokalaemia. complications: bradycardia, prolonged qt, hypokalaemia (especially bulimia), hypophosphataemia and refeeding syndrome, amenorrhoea, osteopenia, growth failure and delayed puberty, hypoglycaemia, anaemia and fatty liver. investigations: electrolytes, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, urea and creatinine, lfts, fbc, ecg, dexa if prolonged; exclude coeliac, ibd, thyroid, diabetes, malignancy. management: family-based therapy (fbt/maudsley) is first line for anorexia in adolescents; cbt-ed for bulimia; nutritional rehabilitation with careful refeeding, monitoring of phosphate, potassium and glucose. admission criteria: very low bmi (under 70-75 percent median), heart rate under 40-50, bp under 80/50, postural drop, electrolyte disturbance, syncope, prolonged qtc, acute food refusal, failure of outpatient care, high suicidal risk. mortality of anorexia is among the highest of psychiatric disorders (from medical complications and suicide). consent and confidentiality fluoxetine n-acetylcysteine

u: Child Mental Health, Behaviour & Social Paediatrics
h: sleep problems, tantrums & toilet training child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics sleep difficulties, tantrums and toilet training are among the commonest concerns raised by parents of young children. most are normal developmental variations that respond to consistent routines and reassurance, but they can reveal underlying medical, developmental or psychosocial problems. a structured history and practical behavioural advice are the cornerstones of management. most sleep problems in young children are behavioural and respond to consistent routines night terrors occur in the first third of the night and the child does not remember them nightmares come from rem sleep later in the night and the child recalls them snoring with pauses suggests obstructive sleep apnoea - consider adenotonsillectomy tantrums peak at 18 months to 3 years and are normal toilet training is best started when the child shows readiness, usually 2-3 years enuresis alarm is first-line for motivated children over 7 with bedwetting; desmopressin for short-term control faecal soiling in children is usually overflow from constipation snoring with apnoeic pauses, failure to thrive or daytime sleepiness stereotyped nocturnal episodes suggesting seizures day-time wetting with continuous dribbling or neurological signs in legs secondary enuresis with polyuria and polydipsia - test glucose sudden regression of toilet training or behaviour - consider abuse or physical illness night terror vs nightmare terrors = early night (slow wave), no recall; nightmares = late night (rem), recalled normal sleep common sleep problems settling difficulty and night waking: usually due to inconsistent routines, learned sleep associations (feeding or rocking to sleep), separation anxiety, or parental difficulty with limit setting. management: regular bedtime routine, consistent bed and wake time, put the child to bed drowsy but awake, graded extinction or checking, limit setting and positive reinforcement, avoid screens before bed, daytime activity and light. night terrors: arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night, aged 3-8 years; the child screams, appears terrified and unresponsive, has no memory next day. reassure parents, do not wake the child, ensure safety; scheduled awakenings occasionally used for frequent episodes. nightmares: arise from rem sleep in the later night; the child wakes fully, recalls the dream and can be comforted. sleepwalking: slow wave sleep partial arousal; ensure safe environment, consistent sleep schedule and treat triggers (sleep deprivation, fever). obstructive sleep apnoea: snoring, pauses in breathing, restless sleep, mouth breathing, daytime sleepiness or hyperactivity, enuresis; adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the commonest cause; investigate with overnight oximetry or polysomnography; treat with adenotonsillectomy. other causes of poor sleep: eczema, asthma, reflux, restless legs and iron deficiency, medications (stimulants, steroids), adhd and autism (melatonin may be used by specialists), anxiety and depression. temper tantrums and behaviour toilet training readiness signs: dry for 2 hours, awareness of wet/dirty nappy, can walk to the toilet, follow instructions, desire for independence; usually 2-3 years of age. approach: child-led, consistent, positive reinforcement, regular potty sitting after meals, avoid punishment; daytime control is usually achieved by 3-4 years, night-time later. faecal control precedes urinary; nocturnal control is last. boys tend to achieve control later than girls. nocturnal enuresis: persistent bedwetting after age 5. primary (never dry) versus secondary (after 6 months dryness, often stress, uti, diabetes, constipation, sleep apnoea). management: reassurance, fluid advice, reward systems, then enuresis alarm (first line for motivated children over 7) or desmopressin 200-400 mcg at night for short-term control. exclude uti, diabetes mellitus, constipation and neurological disease. encopresis: faecal soiling is usually overflow from chronic constipation; treat with disimpaction (macrogol/movicol), maintenance laxatives and toilet routine. when to refer sleep: suspected osa, parasomnias with atypical features (to exclude seizures), severe insomnia in neurodevelopmental conditions, narcolepsy (cataplexy, excessive sleepiness). behaviour: persistent severe aggression, developmental regression, signs of abuse, parental mental health concerns. continence: day wetting with constant dribbling, ectopic ureter, spina bifida occulta, neuropathic bladder, failure of first-line treatment, constipation not responding. desmopressin macrogol (movicol paediatric)

t: Chronic illness, consent & ethics in paediatrics
u: Child Mental Health, Behaviour & Social Paediatrics
h: chronic illness, consent & ethics in paediatrics child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics children with chronic illness face challenges that go beyond their disease: school, family, adolescence and transition to adult services. paediatric practice also raises distinctive ethical issues, including consent, confidentiality, best interests and end-of-life decisions. a sound grasp of the frameworks (gillick competence, best interests, four principles) is essential. gillick competence is decision-specific and not tied to a fixed age fraser guidelines relate to contraception for under 16s the child's best interests are paramount in decision-making 16 and 17-year-olds are presumed competent to consent but refusal may be overridden in some cases four principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice transition planning should begin in early adolescence courts decide when clinicians and parents disagree about life-sustaining treatment non-adherence is common in adolescents with chronic illness child refusing life-saving treatment poor adherence leading to deterioration (e.g. dka, rejection) signs of depression, eating disorder or self-harm in a child with chronic illness safeguarding concern or disclosure during a confidential consultation loss to follow-up around transition to adult services four principles autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice (abnj) living with chronic illness transition to adult services transition is a planned, gradual process starting in early adolescence (from age 11-14), distinct from the transfer event. components: building self-management skills, joint clinics, a named key worker, written transition plan, introduction to adult team, and attention to education, work, sexual health, substance use and contraception (teratogenic medicines). poor transition leads to loss to follow-up, deteriorating control and avoidable complications. consent and capacity parental responsibility allows parents to consent for children under 16, but a competent child may consent independently. gillick competence: a child under 16 who has sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully understand the proposed treatment can consent. competence is decision-specific and can fluctuate. fraser guidelines apply to contraceptive advice: the young person understands the advice, cannot be persuaded to inform parents, is likely to have sex with or without treatment, health would suffer without treatment, and treatment is in their best interests. 16-17-year-olds are presumed competent to consent (family law reform act 1969) but refusal of life-saving treatment can be overridden by parents or the court in england and wales. in scotland, the age of legal capacity act gives competent children under 16 the right to consent; refusal rules vary across jurisdictions. under 16s refusing treatment: assess competence and involve parents; the court may be asked to authorise treatment in the child's best interests. capacity assessment under the mental capacity act 2005 applies from age 16. ethical principles disagreement and end-of-life decisions parents usually make decisions; clinicians can challenge them if the decision is not in the child's best interests (for example refusal of life-saving transfusion by jehovah's witness parents) and seek a court order (specific issue or inherent jurisdiction). withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment may be appropriate when treatment is futile, burdensome or does not offer a reasonable chance of benefit (rcpch framework: no chance, burdens outweigh benefits, unbearable condition). involve palliative care, ethics committee, second opinions and parents in open communication. cases such as charlie gard and alfie evans illustrate court involvement in best interests disputes. do not resuscitate (dnr) decisions need multidisciplinary discussion, documentation and parental agreement. medical research with children requires ethical approval, consent and assent; non-therapeutic procedures must involve minimal risk.

u: Child Mental Health, Behaviour & Social Paediatrics
h: sids, child death & bereavement child mental health, behaviour & social paediatrics sudden infant death syndrome (sids) is the sudden unexpected death of an infant under 1 year that remains unexplained after a thorough investigation. risk-reduction campaigns have dramatically reduced its incidence. caring for a family after any child death requires structured investigation, compassionate communication and long-term support. sids is a diagnosis of exclusion after full investigation back to sleep reduced sids incidence by more than 70 percent peak incidence is 2-4 months of age smoking, bed sharing and overheating are key modifiable risks dummies and breastfeeding are protective joint agency response and cdop review follow all unexpected child deaths siblings need honest, age-appropriate explanations and support spikes helps structure breaking bad news unexpected infant death with injuries or inconsistent history - safeguarding concern siblings with similar symptoms or family history of unexplained deaths - consider metabolic or cardiac disease parents with severe grief, suicidal thoughts or substance use after a bereavement persistent complicated grief in a child with functional decline apparent life-threatening events (alte/brue) in infants need investigation spikes setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, empathy, strategy/summary - a protocol for breaking bad news back to sleep back, feet-to-foot, own cot, smoke-free, no overheating - safe sleep advice definition and epidemiology risk factors and prevention modifiable: prone or side sleeping, maternal smoking in pregnancy and in the home, bed-sharing particularly on sofas or after alcohol or drug use, overheating or head covering, soft bedding, lack of breastfeeding, dummy use is protective. non-modifiable: prematurity, low birth weight, male sex, young maternal age, multiple births, socioeconomic deprivation, previous sids in a sibling. triple-risk model: vulnerable infant, critical developmental period and exogenous stressor. advice: place baby on the back to sleep on a firm flat mattress in own cot in parents' room for the first 6 months; feet to foot of cot; no pillows, duvets or soft toys; no smoking; avoid overheating; avoid sharing a bed in high-risk circumstances; breastfeeding; offer a dummy at sleep times once breastfeeding is established. response to sudden unexpected infant death joint agency response (uk): paediatrician and police attend, take history, examine the infant, and visit the scene; samples (blood, urine, csf, nasopharyngeal aspirate, swabs, skin biopsy, genetics), imaging, postmortem examination by a paediatric pathologist. child death overview panel (cdop) reviews all child deaths to identify modifiable factors. differential diagnosis: infection (sepsis, meningitis, myocarditis), inborn errors of metabolism (mcadd), congenital heart disease, arrhythmia (long qt syndrome), airway obstruction, accidental suffocation, and non-accidental injury or smothering. consider siblings: medical assessment and safeguarding review; future pregnancies may benefit from support such as the coni scheme. grief in children and parents children's understanding of death depends on age: under 5 years do not appreciate permanence; 5-10 understand irreversibility but may magical think; adolescents grasp death like adults but may show risk-taking, withdrawal or anger. typical grief reactions: shock, denial, anger, guilt, sadness, yearning, somatic symptoms, regression, sleep and behavioural problems; may be delayed. complicated grief persists beyond 6-12 months with impaired function. support siblings: honest, age-appropriate explanation using clear words (dead, died), involve them in rituals if they wish, maintain routines, school liaison and bereavement counselling. parental grief is intense; parents may feel guilt and blame; relationships may be strained; ensure follow-up meeting with the paediatrician after the postmortem results, memory-making (hand and footprints, photographs), signposting to organisations such as the lullaby trust and child bereavement uk. communication and breaking bad news prepare: private setting, uninterrupted time, introductions, sit down, check what parents know. spikes protocol: setting, perception, invitation, knowledge (warning shot and clear language), empathy, strategy/summary. use plain words and avoid euphemisms; allow silence and emotion; avoid false reassurance; do not blame; offer to arrange follow-up and written information. support staff as well as families: debriefing after a child death.

t: Inguinal hernia, undescended testis & the acute scrotum
h: inguinal hernia, undescended testis & the acute scrotum paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes inguinal hernia, undescended testis and the acute scrotum are common paediatric surgical problems. hernias in infants need timely repair to avoid incarceration, undescended testes should be operated on by about 12 to 18 months, and acute scrotal pain in a boy is torsion until proven otherwise. paediatric inguinal hernias are indirect and result from a patent processus vaginalis repair inguinal hernias promptly in infants because incarceration risk is highest early transillumination differentiates hydrocele from hernia orchidopexy for undescended testis should be done by 12 to 18 months impalpable bilateral testes with hypospadias in a newborn is a dsd emergency (check 17-ohp) testicular torsion is a surgical emergency: salvage within 6 hours peak ages for torsion are neonatal and adolescence; for appendix testis 7 to 12 years operate on the contralateral side to fix both testes in torsion irreducible tender groin lump with vomiting or distension sudden severe scrotal pain with nausea and vomiting high-riding horizontal testis with absent cremasteric reflex bilateral impalpable testes with hypospadias red, swollen scrotum with sepsis features torsion triad sudden pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex inguinal hernia and hydrocele management of hernia reducible hernia: surgical repair (herniotomy) as soon as feasible after diagnosis, within days to weeks in neonates and young infants because the risk of incarceration is highest in the first year premature infants are repaired before discharge from nicu or shortly after because of a high incarceration risk incarcerated hernia: a tender, irreducible, firm groin mass with vomiting, irritability and abdominal distension; attempt manual reduction after sedation/analgesia, then repair within 24 to 48 hours; urgent surgery if reduction fails or there are signs of strangulation complications: incarceration, bowel obstruction, strangulation, testicular infarction (compression of spermatic vessels), ovarian torsion in girls hydrocele: most resolve by 12 to 24 months; refer if persistent beyond 2 years or if communicating (variable size) undescended testis (cryptorchidism) refer at 3 months if not descended; orchidopexy ideally between 6 and 18 months (before 12 months in many guidelines) palpable testis: open inguinal orchidopexy; impalpable: laparoscopy to locate the testis or confirm absence bilateral impalpable testes with hypospadias: urgent endocrine evaluation for disorder of sex development (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) complications of untreated cryptorchidism: infertility, testicular cancer (seminoma, risk increased 2 to 8 fold), torsion, hernia, psychological retractile testes do not need surgery but need annual review as some become ascending testes the acute scrotum torsion of the testis: peaks in neonates and at puberty (12 to 18 years); sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding testis with horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex, loss of normal anatomy torsion of the appendix testis: 7 to 12 years; localised tenderness at the upper pole, blue dot sign; managed conservatively with analgesia epididymo-orchitis: gradual onset, fever, urinary symptoms; positive prehn sign; treat with antibiotics, consider underlying anomaly others: incarcerated hernia, idiopathic scrotal oedema, henoch-schonlein purpura, trauma, mumps orchitis, tumour investigations and management of torsion diagnosis is clinical; do not delay surgery for imaging if suspicion is high doppler ultrasound shows reduced or absent flow but a normal study does not exclude intermittent torsion urgent scrotal exploration, detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy (the contralateral testis has the same anatomical risk, bell-clapper deformity) orchidectomy if necrotic; counsel on fertility and testicular prosthesis neonatal perinatal torsion is often extravaginal and testis non-viable, but contralateral fixation is still considered

developmental dysplasia of the hip paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes developmental dysplasia of the hip (ddh) is a spectrum from mild acetabular dysplasia to dislocation of the femoral head. early detection by newborn examination and ultrasound allows simple treatment with a pavlik harness, whereas late diagnosis may need surgery and risks early osteoarthritis. ddh is more common in girls, firstborns, breech and positive family history barlow dislocates; ortolani reduces ultrasound before 4 to 6 months; x-ray afterwards pavlik harness is first-line for infants under 6 months late presentation: limp, trendelenburg gait, limited abduction risk of avascular necrosis with forced abduction or prolonged immobilisation swaddling in extension and adduction increases risk bilateral ddh produces waddling gait and lordosis hip clunk or instability on examination limited abduction or asymmetrical skin folds limping child with leg length discrepancy positive family history with breech presentation failure to attend or complete screening barlow vs ortolani barlow provokes dislocation (pushes head out posteriorly); ortolani reduces a dislocated hip (clunk back in) definition & epidemiology risk factors female sex, positive family history breech presentation (especially frank breech, whatever the mode of delivery) oligohydramnios, large baby, first pregnancy postnatal swaddling with hips extended and adducted associated: torticollis, talipes calcaneovalgus, metatarsus adductus, neuromuscular disease clinical examination newborn and 6 to 8 week examination: barlow test (adduct and posteriorly push the flexed hip to dislocate) and ortolani test (abduct and lift to reduce a dislocated hip with a clunk) asymmetry of skin creases, leg length discrepancy (galeazzi sign), limited hip abduction (under 60 degrees) in older infants older child: trendelenburg gait, waddling gait if bilateral, toe walking, hyperlordosis clicks without instability are common and benign; a clunk is abnormal examination must be done on a relaxed, calm baby on a firm surface investigations ultrasound is the investigation of choice up to 4 to 6 months (before femoral head ossification): graf classification assesses acetabular angles and head coverage pelvic x-ray after 4 to 6 months: shenton line broken, acetabular index increased, delayed ossification of the femoral head, hilgenreiner and perkin lines screening programmes: uk selective ultrasound at 6 weeks for high-risk infants (breech, family history) and for clinical instability; some countries do universal screening management newborn instability: observe with repeat examination and ultrasound; many stabilise spontaneously by 3 to 6 weeks under 6 months with dislocation or persistent dysplasia: pavlik harness (hips flexed about 100 degrees and abducted) worn full time for 6 to 12 weeks; success over 90 percent in early use failure of pavlik harness or presentation at 6 to 18 months: closed reduction under anaesthesia with arthrogram and hip spica cast over 18 months: open reduction, with femoral and/or pelvic osteotomy avoid hips in extension and adduction when carrying or swaddling; encourage hip-healthy swaddling complications & prognosis avascular necrosis of the femoral head (risk with forced abduction or harness misuse) femoral nerve palsy with pavlik harness residual dysplasia, leg length discrepancy, early osteoarthritis, gait problems, limp late diagnosis needs major surgery and carries a worse outcome

t: The limping child (Perthes, SCFE, transient synovitis)
h: the limping child (perthes, scfe, transient synovitis) paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes a limp in a child has many causes ranging from trivial injury to septic arthritis, malignancy and slipped upper femoral epiphysis. a systematic, age-based approach identifies the dangerous conditions that need urgent treatment. hip pathology often presents as knee pain transient synovitis: commonest cause of hip pain in 3 to 8 year olds, diagnosis of exclusion kocher criteria stratify risk of septic arthritis perthes: 4 to 8 years, boys, avascular necrosis, painless limp scfe: obese adolescent, limited internal rotation, needs urgent pinning night pain, systemic upset or a cytopenia should prompt consideration of leukaemia x-ray needs ap and frog-leg views of the hip unstable scfe and septic arthritis are emergencies fever with refusal to weight-bear night pain, weight loss or pallor obese adolescent with hip or knee pain limp with raised inflammatory markers and kocher score of 2 or more unexplained injury in a non-mobile infant (consider abuse) kocher non-weight-bearing, esr above 40, fever above 38.5 c, wbc above 12 - one point each approach to the limping child differential by age 1 to 3 years: toddler fracture, septic arthritis, transient synovitis, ddh, discitis, non-accidental injury 3 to 10 years: transient synovitis (commonest), perthes disease, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, leukaemia, trauma 10 to 16 years: slipped upper femoral epiphysis (scfe), sports injuries, osteochondritis (osgood-schlatter), bone tumours (osteosarcoma, ewing), jia, sle any age: trauma, infection, inflammatory arthritis, malignancy, haematological (haemophilia, sickle cell), neuromuscular transient synovitis kocher criteria (predict septic arthritis): non-weight-bearing, esr over 40 mm/h, fever over 38.5 c, wbc over 12,000; 0 criteria less than 0.2 percent, 1 criterion 3 percent, 2 criteria 40 percent, 3 criteria 93 percent, 4 criteria 99 percent probability (caird adds crp over 20 mg/l) ultrasound may show effusion; aspirate if septic arthritis suspected management: rest, nsaids (ibuprofen), review in 24 to 48 hours; resolution within 1 to 2 weeks perthes disease x-ray (ap and frog-leg lateral): sclerosis, flattening, fragmentation of epiphysis; early films may be normal; mri is more sensitive management is containment: observation and activity modification for young children; physiotherapy; surgery (femoral or pelvic osteotomy) for older children with severe involvement prognosis better with onset under 6 years; poor outcome with age over 8, lateral pillar c involvement bilateral perthes: consider hypothyroidism, skeletal dysplasia, sickle cell disease slipped upper femoral epiphysis (scfe) x-ray: ap and frog-leg lateral views show klein line failing to intersect the femoral head; "ice cream slipping off the cone" stable scfe (able to weight-bear) vs unstable (unable to bear weight, high risk of avascular necrosis): unstable is an emergency management: non-weight-bearing, urgent in situ pinning with a single cannulated screw; prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip is often considered atypical scfe (age under 10 or over 16, thin child, bilateral): check endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, renal osteodystrophy) complications: avascular necrosis, chondrolysis, femoroacetabular impingement, premature osteoarthritis investigations bloods: fbc, crp, esr, blood culture if febrile x-ray ap pelvis and frog-leg lateral for children with persistent hip pain or inability to bear weight ultrasound hip for effusion; aspiration if septic arthritis suspected mri for suspected osteomyelitis, perthes, tumour, or occult fracture consider blood film or bone marrow if night pain, systemic upset or abnormal blood counts (leukaemia) ibuprofen

septic arthritis & osteomyelitis paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes septic arthritis and osteomyelitis are bacterial infections of joints and bone that cause fever, pain and loss of function in children. they are orthopaedic emergencies: delayed treatment risks permanent joint destruction and growth disturbance. staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause at all ages kingella kingae is a leading cause in under 4 year olds septic arthritis of the hip is an emergency needing urgent washout crp is the best marker to monitor response x-ray is normal in the first week of osteomyelitis; mri is the best imaging take blood cultures before antibiotics total antibiotic course is 3 weeks for septic arthritis and 4 to 6 weeks for osteomyelitis sickle cell disease predisposes to salmonella osteomyelitis fever with a hot swollen joint and pseudoparalysis infant with irritability, poor feeding and a limb not moved sepsis or shock raised crp with failure to improve in 48 hours sickle cell disease with bone pain and fever septic joint vs transient synovitis fever, refuses to bear weight, high crp/esr, high wbc -> think septic; use kocher/caird score definition & epidemiology organisms staphylococcus aureus (commonest at all ages, including mrsa and panton-valentine leukocidin strains) streptococcus pyogenes and s. pneumoniae kingella kingae (increasingly recognised in children under 4, subtle presentation) haemophilus influenzae type b (unvaccinated) neonates: group b streptococcus, gram-negative bacilli, s. aureus sickle cell disease: salmonella and s. aureus puncture wounds of foot: pseudomonas aeruginosa tuberculosis and brucellosis in endemic regions clinical features fever, malaise, localised bone tenderness (osteomyelitis) or joint swelling with severely restricted painful movement (septic arthritis) refusal to use the limb (pseudoparalysis), refusal to weight-bear, limp hip septic arthritis: held flexed, abducted and externally rotated; pain with any movement neonates and infants: may be afebrile with irritability, poor feeding, pseudoparalysis, and multiple foci sub-acute osteomyelitis: insidious pain, minimal fever; brodie abscess investigations bloods: fbc, crp, esr (crp rises faster and falls with treatment), blood culture (positive in 30 to 50 percent), take before antibiotics joint aspiration (under ultrasound or in theatre) for gram stain, culture, cell count and pcr; synovial wbc over 50,000 supports septic arthritis x-ray: normal early in osteomyelitis (changes take 7 to 14 days: periosteal reaction, lucency); useful to exclude other pathology ultrasound detects effusion and subperiosteal collection mri is the most sensitive and specific imaging for osteomyelitis; bone scan if mri unavailable kocher criteria (fever, non-weight-bearing, esr, wbc) predict septic hip management empirical iv antibiotics: flucloxacillin (cover for s. aureus) with or without cefuroxime or ceftriaxone; clindamycin or vancomycin if mrsa risk or penicillin allergy; add cover for salmonella in sickle cell disease and gram-negatives in neonates switch to oral antibiotics once clinically improved with falling crp (often 2 to 4 days iv): total 3 weeks for septic arthritis and 4 to 6 weeks for osteomyelitis (shorter oral courses acceptable in uncomplicated disease) rest, analgesia, splinting, then physiotherapy resource-limited settings: cloxacillin plus gentamicin or ceftriaxone; surgical drainage remains key complications chronic osteomyelitis with sequestrum and involucrum, requiring debridement growth plate damage, limb length discrepancy, deformity avascular necrosis and joint destruction (hip), dislocation septicaemia, toxic shock, metastatic foci pathological fracture flucloxacillin iv ceftriaxone iv clindamycin

t: Otitis media, glue ear & hearing loss
h: otitis media, glue ear & hearing loss paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes otitis media is inflammation of the middle ear, presenting as acute otitis media (aom) with ear pain and fever, or as otitis media with effusion (glue ear) causing conductive hearing loss. most aom resolves without antibiotics, while persistent glue ear can affect speech and school performance and sometimes needs grommets. aom peaks at 6 to 24 months; pneumococcus, haemophilus and moraxella are common causes analgesia is the cornerstone; most aom does not need antibiotics glue ear causes conductive hearing loss of about 20 to 40 db type b tympanogram is typical for glue ear grommets for persistent bilateral ome over 3 months with hearing loss mastoiditis shows post-auricular swelling with a protruding pinna newborn hearing screening uses oae followed by aabr down syndrome and cleft palate predispose to glue ear post-auricular swelling and erythema or protruding ear facial weakness or neck stiffness with ear infection persistent offensive otorrhoea (cholesteatoma) speech or language delay with hearing concern toxic child or high fever with aom aom otoscopy red, bulging, opaque drum with loss of light reflex and landmarks acute otitis media symptoms: ear pain (tugging at the ear in infants), fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, otorrhoea if the drum perforates (pain then often relieved) otoscopy: red, bulging, opaque tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks; air-fluid level; perforation with discharge management: analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen) is first-line; most cases settle within 3 days antibiotics: immediate if systemically unwell, under 2 years with bilateral disease, otorrhoea, or high risk (immunocompromise, cleft palate); otherwise a watchful-waiting or delayed prescription for 48 to 72 hours; amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days (clarithromycin or erythromycin if penicillin allergic) otitis media with effusion (glue ear) features: hearing difficulty, inattention, speech delay or poor school performance, balance problems; may be asymptomatic otoscopy: dull, retracted, amber or grey drum with air bubbles; tympanometry shows type b (flat) trace; audiometry shows conductive loss management: watchful waiting for 3 months with repeat audiometry and tympanometry; hearing tactics (face the child, reduce background noise); hearing aids for those not suitable for surgery surgical: grommets (ventilation tubes) if bilateral persistent ome with hearing loss over 25 to 30 db for 3 or more months; adenoidectomy if adenoid hypertrophy or recurrent disease in older children; special consideration in down syndrome and cleft palate complications of grommets: otorrhoea, tympanosclerosis, persistent perforation; avoid water entry with antiseptic ear drops for otorrhoea chronic suppurative otitis media and complications csom: persistent or recurrent otorrhoea through a perforated drum for over 6 weeks; treat with topical quinolone drops (ciprofloxacin), aural toilet and keep ear dry; refer to ent; common in low-resource settings and in children with lower socioeconomic status cholesteatoma: keratinising squamous epithelium in middle ear causing foul discharge, conductive loss, erosion of ossicles; needs surgery acute mastoiditis: post-auricular swelling, protruding ear, tenderness; needs iv antibiotics and sometimes mastoidectomy intracranial: meningitis, brain abscess, lateral sinus thrombosis, extradural abscess facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, hearing loss, tympanic membrane perforation hearing loss in children newborn hearing screening programme: otoacoustic emissions followed by automated auditory brainstem response if fails; aim to identify permanent hearing loss by 6 weeks and intervene by 6 months congenital sensorineural loss causes: genetic (connexin 26), congenital cmv, rubella, pendred syndrome, waardenburg, usher acquired: meningitis, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, furosemide), noise, trauma, kernicterus, hypoxia assessment by age: distraction testing (6 to 18 months), visual reinforcement audiometry, play audiometry (2.5 to 5 years), pure tone audiometry; refer for genetics, imaging, cochlear implant assessment when needed managing: hearing aids, speech therapy, early intervention, education support, cochlear implant for profound sensorineural hearing loss amoxicillin paracetamol ibuprofen ciprofloxacin ear drops

t: Tonsillitis, sleep apnoea & upper airway problems
h: tonsillitis, sleep apnoea & upper airway problems paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes sore throat, tonsillitis and obstructive sleep apnoea are common upper airway problems in children. most tonsillitis is viral and self-limiting, while adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the leading cause of paediatric sleep-disordered breathing, which can affect growth, behaviour and cardiovascular health. most sore throats are viral and do not need antibiotics phenoxymethylpenicillin is first-line for streptococcal tonsillitis avoid amoxicillin in suspected glandular fever quinsy presents with trismus, uvula deviation and muffled voice retropharyngeal abscess needs urgent imaging and surgical drainage adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the commonest cause of paediatric osa polysomnography is the gold standard; adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment tonsillectomy criteria: 7, 5 or 3 episodes per year for 1, 2 and 3 years drooling, stridor or inability to swallow saliva trismus and uvula deviation neck stiffness, torticollis or neck swelling with fever severe or witnessed apnoeas and cyanosis during sleep post-tonsillectomy bleeding unilateral tonsillar enlargement (consider lymphoma) centor score tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever, no cough - 1 point each; mcisaac adds age adjustment acute tonsillitis and pharyngitis centor/mcisaac features: tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever over 38 c, absence of cough; feverpain adds symptoms onset within 3 days and severe tonsil inflammation strep throat: sudden sore throat, fever, headache, abdominal pain, scarlatiniform rash (scarlet fever), strawberry tongue ebv (glandular fever): exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical and generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes; amoxicillin can cause a maculopapular rash; avoid contact sport for 4 weeks if splenomegaly diagnosis: throat swab or rapid antigen test where indicated treatment: analgesia and fluids; phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin v) for 5 to 10 days if strep confirmed or high score; azithromycin or clarithromycin if penicillin allergic complications of tonsillitis peritonsillar abscess (quinsy): unilateral severe sore throat, trismus, uvula deviation, muffled "hot potato" voice; needs aspiration or incision and drainage and iv antibiotics retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal abscess: young children with fever, neck stiffness, torticollis, drooling, stridor; urgent ct and ent rheumatic fever (2 to 4 weeks after untreated strep) and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (1 to 3 weeks after throat infection) scarlet fever, otitis media, sinusitis airway obstruction in severe ebv tonsillitis: steroids and sometimes airway support obstructive sleep apnoea (osa) night: loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, gasping, restless sleep, mouth breathing, sweating, nocturnal enuresis, unusual sleep positions day: hyperactivity and inattention, irritability, poor school performance, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness (less common than in adults), poor growth examination: large tonsils, adenoid facies, nasal obstruction, hyponasal speech, obesity, hypertension investigations: overnight pulse oximetry, polysomnography (gold standard), nasendoscopy complications: poor growth, neurocognitive and behavioural impairment, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale, systemic hypertension management adenotonsillectomy is first-line for osa caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy; peri-operative risk higher in under 3s, severe osa and comorbidity, who require overnight monitoring intranasal corticosteroids and montelukast for mild disease; weight loss for obese children cpap or non-invasive ventilation when surgery fails or is unsuitable, and in craniofacial disorders tonsillectomy for recurrent tonsillitis: 7 or more well-documented episodes in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years (sign/paradise criteria), with disabling symptoms; also peritonsillar abscess history, suspected malignancy adenoidectomy for persistent nasal obstruction, recurrent otitis media with effusion, chronic rhinosinusitis post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage (primary within 24 hours or secondary at 5 to 10 days) is the main risk; advise parents on diet, hydration and return if bleeding phenoxymethylpenicillin azithromycin paracetamol

squint, amblyopia & visual screening paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes squint (strabismus) is misalignment of the eyes and is a major cause of amblyopia, the loss of vision from abnormal visual development. early detection through red reflex checks and vision screening allows treatment before the critical period for visual development closes at about 7 to 8 years. persistent squint after 3 to 4 months of age needs ophthalmology referral pseudo-strabismus has symmetrical corneal light reflexes and a normal cover test amblyopia is treated by correcting refractive error and patching or atropine of the good eye critical period for amblyopia treatment is up to about 7 to 8 years leukocoria requires urgent assessment to exclude retinoblastoma acute paralytic squint suggests raised icp or brain tumour newborn and 6-8 week red reflex checks are standard screening congenital cataracts need surgery within weeks to prevent deprivation amblyopia white pupil or absent red reflex acute squint with diplopia, headache or vomiting constant squint after 3 to 4 months of age proptosis, painful red eye with reduced vision family history of retinoblastoma or congenital cataract cover test cover the fixing eye and watch the other eye: if it moves to take up fixation, a tropia is present squint (strabismus) concomitant (non-paralytic): angle of deviation constant in all gaze directions; due to refractive error (hypermetropia causes accommodative esotropia), amblyopia or idiopathic paralytic: deviation varies with direction of gaze due to cranial nerve palsy (iii, iv, vi) or restrictive disease; causes include raised intracranial pressure, tumour, trauma, congenital acute-onset paralytic squint with diplopia, headache or neurological signs requires urgent neuroimaging risk factors: family history, prematurity, low birth weight, cerebral palsy, down syndrome, congenital eye disease examination red reflex (brueckner test) at birth and 6 to 8 weeks: bilateral equal red/orange reflex expected; absent, white (leukocoria) or asymmetric reflex is abnormal corneal light reflex (hirschberg test): symmetrical reflection in both pupils; displaced reflection indicates tropia cover test: tropia (manifest squint, eye moves to take up fixation when the straight eye is covered) and cover-uncover test: phoria (latent) eye movements in all directions to assess palsies; visual acuity appropriate for age (preferential looking, cardiff cards, kay pictures, snellen after age 5) check for ptosis, pupil responses and fundus examination; cycloplegic refraction by the ophthalmologist amblyopia management: treat the cause (cataract surgery, spectacles) then force use of the weaker eye with patching of the good eye for several hours per day or atropine penalisation early treatment is crucial: results are better before the age of 5 to 7 years spectacles correct refractive error and can alone improve many squints and amblyopia strabismus surgery (recession and resection of extraocular muscles) aligns the eyes; botulinum toxin is an alternative in selected cases binocular function and stereopsis may be lost if treatment is delayed visual screening and urgent referral newborn: red reflex examination within 72 hours and at 6 to 8 weeks preschool and school entry vision screening (about 4 to 5 years) to detect amblyopia and refractive errors leukocoria: absent red reflex or white pupil. differential: retinoblastoma (commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood), congenital cataract, retinopathy of prematurity, persistent fetal vasculature, coats disease, toxocara; urgent same-day or within 24 hours referral retinoblastoma: rb1 gene mutation (chromosome 13q14), hereditary forms are bilateral, presents with leukocoria or squint; treatment with chemotherapy, laser, enucleation; later risk of osteosarcoma congenital cataract: urgent surgery within first 6 to 8 weeks to prevent deprivation amblyopia retinopathy of prematurity screening in babies born before 32 weeks or under 1500 g congenital glaucoma: large hazy corneas, epiphora, photophobia

t: Congenital surgical anomalies (abdominal wall, oesophageal atresia, CDH)
h: congenital surgical anomalies (abdominal wall, oesophageal atresia, cdh) paediatric surgery, orthopaedics, ent & eyes congenital surgical anomalies include abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, exomphalos), oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula, and congenital diaphragmatic hernia. many are detected on antenatal ultrasound, and good outcomes depend on delivery at a specialist centre and early surgical management. gastroschisis has no sac; exomphalos has a membrane and associated anomalies exomphalos needs karyotype and echocardiogram: trisomies and beckwith-wiedemann oesophageal atresia: frothy saliva, choking at first feed, ng tube fails to pass commonest oa type is a blind upper pouch with a distal fistula (type c) vacterl association should be screened for in oa cdh: avoid bag-mask ventilation, intubate and decompress the stomach pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension drive cdh mortality bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation until proven otherwise bilious vomiting in a newborn respiratory distress with scaphoid abdomen frothy secretions and cyanosis with first feed exposed bowel that is dusky or ischaemic failure to pass meconium within 24 to 48 hours vacterl vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal, limb anomalies abdominal wall defects exomphalos is associated with other anomalies in 50 to 70 percent: trisomies 13, 18, 21, beckwith-wiedemann syndrome (macroglossia, hypoglycaemia, gigantism), cardiac, pentalogy of cantrell; echocardiography and karyotype are needed gastroschisis: raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, bowel thick and inflamed from amniotic fluid exposure, high risk of hypothermia, fluid loss, infection and ischaemia management: immediate wrapping of the bowel in warm saline-soaked gauze or place the lower body in a bowel bag, nasogastric tube decompression, iv fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, keep warm and in lateral position to avoid kinking the mesentery surgery: primary closure or staged closure with a silo; parenteral nutrition is often required until bowel function returns giant exomphalos: delayed closure with topical agents (conservative approach) when closure is impossible oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula presentation: excessive frothy saliva, choking and cyanosis on first feed, inability to pass a nasogastric tube (it coils in the upper pouch on x-ray), respiratory distress, abdominal distension (gas through the distal fistula) diagnosis: x-ray with the ng tube in the pouch; gas in the stomach implies a distal fistula, a gasless abdomen implies pure atresia without fistula initial management: keep nil by mouth, replogle tube to continuous low suction of the upper pouch, positioning head up, iv fluids, avoid positive pressure ventilation screen for vacterl: echocardiography, renal ultrasound, spine x-ray, anal inspection surgery: thoracotomy or thoracoscopic ligation of fistula and primary end-to-end anastomosis; long gap atresia requires delayed repair or oesophageal replacement complications: anastomotic leak, stricture, gord, tracheomalacia with a barking cough, recurrent chest infections congenital diaphragmatic hernia (cdh) antenatal diagnosis on ultrasound is common; prognosis assessed with lung-to-head ratio and liver position; fetal endoluminal tracheal occlusion (feto) in severe cases at specialist centres presentation: respiratory distress at birth, scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest, displaced heart sounds, cyanosis diagnosis: chest x-ray with bowel loops in the hemithorax and mediastinal shift management: intubate immediately (avoid bag-mask ventilation), ng tube on suction, gentle ventilation with permissive hypercapnia, treat pulmonary hypertension with inhaled nitric oxide or sildenafil, ecmo in selected cases surgery is delayed until the infant is physiologically stable; repair by primary closure or patch prognosis: survival about 70 to 90 percent; lung hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension are the main determinants general principles in neonatal surgery keep warm, nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, iv access and fluids, glucose monitoring and vitamin k transfer to a regional neonatal surgical unit with a specialist transport team bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise (malrotation with volvulus) other anomalies: duodenal atresia (double bubble, down syndrome), anorectal malformation, hirschsprung disease, pyloric stenosis (presents at 2 to 8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis) resource-limited settings: simple measures of warmth, decompression, fluids and early referral improve survival; delayed presentation is common
